pages.searchText: Home Resources Emergency Substitute Lessons Bridge Design Analysis Emergency Substitute Lesson • POE Bridge Design Analysis Compare bridge concepts and recommend a design using load paths and tradeoffs. 45–60 minutes Individual work No prior knowledge required No specialized equipment Print lesson Back to lesson library Name: Period: Date: Design Scenario A park needs a 24-meter pedestrian bridge across a drainage canal. The bridge must support people and small maintenance carts, remain open during heavy rain, and stay within budget. Design Estimated cost Material Key characteristics A: Beam bridge $180,000 Steel beams and concrete deck Simple; few parts; requires a center pier B: Truss bridge $230,000 Steel members No center pier; many connected members; easy to inspect C: Arch bridge $285,000 Concrete and steel No center pier; strong abutments required; visually distinctive 1. Understand Load Paths A load path is the route force follows from the bridge deck to the supports and then into the ground. Describe the likely load path for each design. Which design places many members in tension and compression? Which design may experience large outward forces at its supports? 2. Decision Matrix Score each design from 1 to 5. Multiply by the importance weight. Criterion Weight Beam Truss Arch Cost 3 No obstruction in canal 5 Ease of inspection 3 Appearance 1 Construction simplicity 2 Weighted total 3. Concept Sketch Sketch your recommended bridge. Label the deck, supports, likely tension areas, likely compression areas, and the load path. 4. Engineering Recommendation Recommend one design. Use at least three pieces of evidence and acknowledge one drawback. Submission Checklist All analysis questions are answered. Required calculations, tables, sketches, or diagrams are complete. The final recommendation uses evidence from the lesson. Your name, class period, and date are included. pages.searchText: Home Resources Emergency Substitute Lessons Energy System Comparison Emergency Substitute Lesson • POE Energy System Comparison Select an energy system for a remote research station using data and tradeoffs. 45–60 minutes Individual work No prior knowledge required No specialized equipment Print lesson Back to lesson library Name: Period: Date: Mission Scenario A remote coastal research station needs an average of 48 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electrical energy each day. It must operate year-round with limited fuel deliveries. Option Expected daily energy Reliability Estimated installed cost Notes Solar array 36 kWh average Low at night and during storms $42,000 Quiet; low maintenance Wind turbine 30 kWh average Variable; strongest in winter $51,000 Needs open exposure Diesel generator Up to 100 kWh High if fuel is available $18,000 plus fuel Noise, emissions, deliveries Battery bank Stores up to 60 kWh Depends on charging source $38,000 Storage, not generation 1. Analyze the Need How much energy is needed in seven days? Can solar alone meet the average daily requirement? Show the shortfall. Can wind alone meet the requirement? Show the shortfall. How much average energy would solar and wind produce together? 2. Compare System Designs System Meets average demand? Main strength Main risk Solar + battery Wind + battery Solar + wind + battery Solar + diesel backup 3. Reliability Event A three-day storm reduces solar production to 8 kWh per day. Wind produces 38 kWh per day during the same period. How much energy is produced each storm day? What is the daily deficit or surplus? Could a 60 kWh battery cover the full three-day deficit? 4. Recommendation Recommend a primary system and backup strategy. Use numerical evidence, reliability, cost, and environmental impact. Submission Checklist All analysis questions are answered. Process Best suited for Main limitation 3D printing Complex prototypes and low quantities Slow per part; layered finish CNC machining Accurate metal or plastic parts Material waste; machine time Injection molding Large quantities of plastic parts High mold cost Casting Complex metal shapes Tooling and finishing may be needed Sheet-metal forming Brackets, covers, and enclosures Limited by bends and tooling Laser cutting Flat sheet profiles Primarily two-dimensional cuts 1. pages.searchText: Home Resources Emergency Substitute Lessons Assembly-Line Optimization Emergency Substitute Lesson • ADM Assembly-Line Optimization Find a production bottleneck and redesign work assignments to improve output. 45–60 minutes Individual work No prior knowledge required No specialized equipment Print lesson Back to lesson library Name: Period: Date: Production Scenario A four-station line assembles small emergency flashlights. One worker is assigned to each station. The line can only move as fast as its slowest station. Station Tasks Time per unit 1 Install battery contacts and wiring 42 seconds 2 Install switch and LED module 68 seconds 3 Close housing and install four screws 55 seconds 4 Function test, label, and package 35 seconds 1. Analyze the Current Line Which station is the bottleneck? What is the line cycle time? Approximately how many units can the line produce in one hour? Use 3,600 seconds per hour. Which station has the most idle time each cycle? 2. Task Details Task Time Install battery contacts 22 s Connect wiring 20 s Install switch 28 s Install LED module 40 s Close housing 15 s Install screws 40 s Function test 20 s Label and package 15 s 3. Rebalance the Line Reassign tasks among four stations. Each task must remain intact and every unit must complete all tasks. New station Assigned tasks Total time 1 2 3 4 4. Evaluate the Improvement What is the new bottleneck time? What is the new estimated hourly output? How many additional units could be produced in an eight-hour shift? What practical problem might make your plan difficult to implement? 5. Recommendation Write a short recommendation describing the bottleneck, your change, and the expected production improvement. pages.searchText: Home Resources Emergency Substitute Lessons Quality Control Investigation Emergency Substitute Lesson • ADM Quality Control Investigation Use dimensional data to identify rejected parts and diagnose a process problem. 45–60 minutes Individual work No prior knowledge required No specialized equipment Print lesson Back to lesson library Name: Period: Date: Inspection Scenario A CNC process produces aluminum mounting blocks. The specified width is 25.00 mm ± 0.20 mm . Acceptable parts must measure from 24.80 mm through 25.20 mm. Part Measured width (mm) Accept or reject? Deviation from 25.00 mm 1 24.96 2 25.04 3 25.17 4 25.23 5 25.21 6 25.28 7 25.31 8 25.26 9 25.19 10 25.14 11 25.09 12 25.05 1. Inspect the Batch Complete the acceptance and deviation columns. How many parts are accepted? What percentage of the batch is rejected? 2. Identify the Pattern Are the rejected values randomly high and low, or do they show a direction? At what part number does the process appear to move out of tolerance? Does the process later move back toward the target? 3. Diagnose Possible Causes Rank the following possible causes from most to least likely and explain your top choice: Tool wear Incorrect initial program dimension Loose fixture Temperature change Measurement error 4. Corrective Action Plan Describe what the operator should do immediately, what should be inspected, and how the process should be verified before production resumes. 5. Quality Report Write a four-sentence report summarizing the specification, findings, likely cause, and recommended action. Submission Checklist All analysis questions are answered. pages.searchText: Home Resources Emergency Substitute Lessons Engineering Failure Analysis Emergency Substitute Lesson • IED Engineering Failure Analysis Investigate why a folding phone stand failed and recommend a redesign. 45–60 minutes Individual work No prior knowledge required No specialized equipment Print lesson Back to lesson library Name: Period: Date: Failure Scenario A school purchased 200 folding phone stands for student workstations. After two weeks, 37 stands had cracked near the hinge, 22 tipped backward when phones were placed upright, and 11 could no longer hold their viewing angle. Evidence Observation Material Thin molded plastic; visible whitening near cracked hinges Base 70 mm long and 55 mm wide Phone position Phone center is approximately 40 mm behind the front edge Hinge Small pin with thin plastic surrounding it User behavior Some students adjust the angle while the phone is still on the stand 1. Describe the Failure Separate the visible symptoms from possible root causes. Symptoms: what happened? Possible causes: why might it have happened? 2. Build a Cause-and-Effect Chain Complete at least two chains. Cause → Immediate effect → Product failure → User impact 3. Evaluate Design Factors How could the material contribute to cracking? How could the base dimensions contribute to tipping? How could the hinge geometry contribute to failure? How might user behavior make the problem worse? 4. Redesign Sketch an improved stand. Label at least four changes. Consider base size, material thickness, hinge support, angle adjustment, and phone placement. 5. Recommendation Write a short engineering recommendation identifying the most likely root cause, two design changes, and one test that should be completed before producing more stands. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Principles of Engineering POE Principles of Engineering Explore systems, mechanisms, energy, forces, materials, circuits, data, and engineering analysis through applied design challenges. Start Unit 0 All Courses Course Focus POE connects engineering analysis to planetary rover design work: energy transfer, lightweight structures, automated controls, sensor feedback, test data, and mission-ready documentation. Mission readiness, safety, and systems thinking VEX mechanisms and aerospace machines Materials, structures, and physical testing Rovers, controls, and mission-performance data Course landing page Start with the course pathway Use this page to open the current unit, review the course structure, and find course-specific tools and resources. Your Responsibility Document your evidence Each unit connects classroom work to engineering evidence: notes, sketches, CAD/CAM files, code, photos, testing data, revisions, and final reflections. Course overview How POE is organized POE connects engineering analysis to systems, mechanisms, structures, energy, controls, data, and design challenges. Analyze Use engineering principles Apply forces, energy, materials, mechanisms, circuits, and data to explain system behavior. Build Develop working systems Create prototypes that combine structure, motion, control, testing, and revision. Evaluate Use performance evidence Measure outcomes, compare design decisions, and support claims with data. Scope & Sequence Course pathway Each unit keeps the core POE concepts while connecting the work to aerospace systems, testing, fabrication, controls, and data-based decisions. Unit 0 Engineering Readiness & CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Begin with aerospace systems, documentation, and FabLab safety, then design and manufacture a 4-inch open-frame CubeSat structure. Teams optimize a 3D-printed frame and laser-cut acrylic plates for the lowest qualified mass. Unit 1 Mechanisms for Space Missions: Energy, Power & Aerospace Machines You will investigate how aerospace machines redirect force, speed, distance, and motion through mechanisms and energy transfer. Using VEX systems and physical testing, they design and evaluate a mechanism that performs a launch-support, deployment, lifting, or positioning task. Unit 2 Bridge Structures & Materials You will learn how structures carry load while staying lightweight and stiff, then design, manufacture, load-test, and defend a lightweight bridge using statics, truss analysis, material evidence, and physical test data. Unit 3 Autonomous Rover Systems: Controls, Sensors & Fluid Power You will explore how automated aerospace systems use logic, sensors, feedback, actuators, and fluid power to complete missions safely and reliably. VEX rover platforms and VEX ground-support systems become the platform for programming, testing, and refining open-loop and closed-loop rover behavior. Unit 4 Mission Performance: Statistics, Kinematics & Test Data You will use repeated trials, graphs, statistics, and kinematics to explain how aerospace systems move and perform. Mission, launch, projectile, glider, or rover data become the basis for predicting motion, measuring variation, and making data-supported design decisions. Unit 5 Aerospace Rover Systems Capstone: Design, Test & Defend You will bring the course together by designing, building, testing, and defending an integrated aerospace system. The capstone requires students to connect mechanisms, structures, controls, materials, fabrication, data, and documentation into one clear engineering solution. Aerospace Design Challenges Major project direction Projects will use VEX rover platforms, laser cutting, 3D printing, physical testing, and engineering documentation. CNC is intentionally left out of POE for now. Unit 0 CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Design, CAD, manufacture, assemble, and qualify an open-frame CubeSat structure. The lightest structure that passes every requirement wins. Unit 1 VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge Design and test a VEX mechanism that redirects force, speed, distance, or motion for an aerospace support task. Unit 2 Bridge Structures & Materials — Engineering Mechanics and Bridge Challenge Develop mechanics and materials knowledge, then design, manufacture and test a lightweight open-web bridge. Unit 3 Rover Mission + VEX Ground Support System Program an autonomous rover mission and build a VEX or fluid-power support system connected to the mission environment. Unit 4 Mission Data Investigation Collect and analyze repeated motion or rover trials using statistics, graphs, and kinematic calculations. Unit 5 Integrated Aerospace Rover Systems Capstone Combine mechanisms, structures, controls, fabrication, testing, and data into one final aerospace engineering design review. Student Outcomes What you will be able to do By the end of this course, you will connect engineering science to the design and testing of aerospace systems. Analyze systems Use diagrams, measurements, calculations, and test data to explain how engineering systems transfer energy, carry loads, move, and respond. Build and test prototypes Create physical models, test them under controlled conditions, collect evidence, and revise designs based on performance. Communicate engineering decisions Use sketches, calculations, graphs, CAD models, presentations, and engineering documentation to justify design choices. pages.description: Home Courses ADM Python Programming Crash Course ADM Supplemental Unit Python Programming Crash Course Rebuild the Python skills you need for the VEX CTE Workcell by reading, traci
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Python Programming Crash Course ADM Supplemental Unit Python Programming Crash Course Rebuild the Python skills you need for the VEX CTE Workcell by reading, tracing, debugging, modifying, and writing realistic Workcell-style Python code. No robotic arm is required for this crash course. Start Lesson P.1 Back to ADM Course Goal Python through industrial automation Every lesson uses Workcell movement, routing, palletizing, repetition, and reusable robot actions as the programming context. Students can edit and run code directly in the browser while the site simulates Workcell commands as text output. How each lesson works Learn → Check → Predict → Fix → Modify → Program Learn It: read a short explanation tied to the VEX Workcell. Check It: answer built-in questions and reveal the answers only after attempting them. Predict It: trace Workcell code and predict what it would do. Fix It: debug syntax, indentation, variable, or logic errors. Modify It: change working code to meet a new requirement. Program It: write a short Workcell solution independently. Mastery Gate: confirm you can explain and apply the skill before moving on. Interactive Code-Only Practice Run Python in the browser This crash course is entirely code-based. Each lesson includes an editable Python Practice Lab with Run, Reset, output, and error feedback. VEX-style arm commands are simulated as text, so no Workcell hardware is required. Edit Change starter code Experiment with variables, conditions, loops, functions, and Workcell-style commands directly on the lesson page. Run Run Python directly on the lesson page See printed output, simulated arm actions, and Python error messages without installing software or connecting hardware. Recover Reset and try again Reset the starter code at any time. Long-running code is automatically stopped so an accidental infinite loop does not lock the lesson. Lesson pathway Crash Course Lessons Work through these lessons in order. Each page is self-guided with built-in answer reveals, debugging checks, application tasks, and a mastery gate before the next lesson. Lesson Title Focus Open P.1 Reading Workcell Python Program order, comments, method calls, and predicting robot behavior Open Lesson P.2 Variables as Workcell Settings Variables for coordinates, speeds, counters, and destinations Open Lesson P.3 Workcell Math & Coordinate Offsets Arithmetic operators and calculated robot positions Open Lesson P.4 Comparisons & Boolean Decisions Comparison operators and True/False conditions in automation Open Lesson P.5 Routing with if / elif / else Decision logic for pickup zones and pallet destinations Open Lesson P.6 Repeating Workcell Actions with for Loops Using loops to repeat predictable manufacturing actions Open Lesson P.7 Production Loops with while Repeating until a production target or condition is met Open Lesson P.8 Combining Loops + Decisions Using decision logic inside repeated automation cycles Open Lesson P.9 Functions for Reusable Workcell Actions Turning repeated robot sequences into reusable functions Open Lesson P.10 Workcell Python Skills Challenge Integrating variables, decisions, loops, and functions in one automation program Open Lesson Practice Assignments Apply the Python Skills Complete these short assignments as you move through the crash course. Each assignment includes an interactive browser Python lab and requires no physical Workcell. Practice 1 • 10 pts Coordinate Setup & Variable Control Use after P.1–P.3. Practice variables, coordinate math, and configurable movement code. Open Practice 1 Practice 2 • 10 pts Part Inspection & Routing Logic Use after P.4–P.5. Practice comparisons, Boolean logic, and if/elif/else routing. Open Practice 2 Practice 3 • 10 pts Production Loops & Batch Processing Use after P.6–P.8. Practice loops, counters, and repeated production decisions. Open Practice 3 Practice 4 • 10 pts Reusable Pick-and-Place Functions Use after P.9. Turn repeated movement sequences into reusable functions. Open Practice 4 Practice 5 • 10 pts Workcell Programming Mini-Challenge Use after P.10. Integrate variables, loops, decisions, functions, validation, and production tracking. Open Practice 5 Core VEX Methods Workcell movement code arm.move_to(x, y, z) and arm.move_inc(x, y, z) appear as realistic code examples for students to read, correct, and write. End Effector Magnet control Practice uses arm.set_end_effector_magnet(True/False) as a code context for part handling; students do not operate the physical end effector. Reference VEX CTE Python API Use the official API when you need to check command names, arguments, or behaviors. Open VEX API

pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 2 POE Unit 2 Bridge Structures & Materials Driving question: How can engineers design a lightweight bridge that safely carries load while minimizing mass and deformation? Start Lesson 2.1 Challenge Requirements Lesson Map POE Hub 18-Lesson Design Sequence Learn structural engineering concepts by using them to engineer a real bridge. Every lesson produces evidence for the final team bridge design and testing presentation to the class. Unit Challenge Lightweight Bridge Structural Design Challenge Design and manufacture a lightweight bridge that spans a fixed 400 mm gap between two supports. The focus is load paths, truss and beam behavior, stiffness, mass, materials, joints, fabrication quality, and test evidence. 400 mm Required clear span between supports. 65 mm maximum Maximum overall bridge width. 100 N Required centered design load. ≤ 10 mm Maximum midspan deflection at design load. ≤ 150 g Maximum finished structural mass. Standard Supports Common teacher-provided support locations. Fabrication + Testing Rules Review the complete approved-material, laser-cutting, M3 fastening, and printed-connector limits below before fabrication. A one-piece laser-cut open-web plywood side truss is allowed; acrylic and fully printed bridges are not. Instructional Sequence Learn the Engineering, Then Build the Bridge Lesson 2.1 Challenge Launch Introduce the bridge goal and manufacturing constraints. Lessons 2.2–2.10 Engineering Mechanics Centroids, deflection, free-body diagrams, vectors, moments and truss analysis using examples beyond bridges. Lessons 2.11–2.14 Materials & Testing Materials properties, structural failure, experimental testing and efficiency. Lessons 2.15–2.20 Bridge Engineering Capstone Research, analyze, design, fabricate, test and present the engineering results to the class. Lesson Map Unit 2 Lessons & Deliverables Lessons 2.2–2.14 teach foundational mechanics and materials using diverse examples. Lessons 2.15–2.20 apply that knowledge to the bridge capstone. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 POE Unit 0 Engineering Readiness & CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Unit mission: Use engineering documentation, safety, CAD, additive manufacturing, laser cutting, and assembly skills to build the lightest 4-inch CubeSat structure that can pass every qualification requirement. Lesson Map Challenge Rules Back to POE Hub Unit Competition Passing is required. Mass determines the winner. Design Build Qualify All teams use the same material rules and basic architecture. The engineering challenge is to remove unnecessary mass without creating a structural failure. Unit Structure Foundation → CubeSat Project Lessons 0.1–0.3 establish the POE systems, documentation, and safety foundation. Lessons 0.4–0.10 apply those skills to one continuous CubeSat engineering challenge. 0.1–0.3 Mission Readiness Connect POE concepts to aerospace systems, establish engineering documentation expectations, and complete the required PPE/FabLab safety work. 0.4–0.6 Define → Select → CAD Create the design brief, generate and evaluate structural concepts, then turn the selected idea into a complete manufacturable CAD assembly. 0.7–0.10 Manufacture → Assemble → Compete Optimize the printed frame and acrylic plates, complete the relevant certifications, assemble with M3 hardware, and qualify the final structure. Project Brief CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Design freedom exists inside a deliberately narrow solution space so teams can begin engineering immediately. Requirement Specification Competition objective Lightest fully assembled structure that passes every qualification requirement wins. Maximum external size 4 in × 4 in × 4 in, including all hardware. Top + bottom Laser cut from the team’s single 4 in × 12 in × 1/8 in acrylic sheet. Sides Open; side panels are not permitted. Primary frame 3D printed using the same teacher-selected filament material for every team. Assembly M3 screws for primary structural connections; no structural adhesive. Serviceability Structure can be disassembled and reassembled with normal hand tools. Print documentation Layer height, wall/perimeter count, infill %, infill pattern, print orientation, estimated print time, and estimated filament use. Qualification load Support a standardized 10 lb vertical load for 30 seconds using the teacher-provided load plate without fracture, separation, or visible permanent deformation. Official mass Includes acrylic, printed frame, M3 hardware, inserts/nuts/washers, and all permanent components; measured to 0.1 g. Lesson Map Unit 0 Lessons The project begins in Lesson 0.4 and advances one required milestone each day through the final competition. Lesson Title Success Target Evidence Open 0.1 Engineering for the Mission Classify aerospace systems and connect POE concepts to mission needs. Engineering for the Mission worksheet: system analysis, mission connections, and decision defense Open Lesson PPTX 0.2 Engineering Notebook & Documentation Refresher Create records that another engineer can follow and reproduce. Complete engineering notebook setup entry Open Lesson PPTX 0.3 PPE and FabLab Safety Control hazards before project work begins. PPE and FabLab safety certification evidence Open Lesson PPTX 0.4 CubeSat Challenge: Define & Design The design brief captures the fixed rules and each sketch clearly shows how the acrylic plates, printed frame, and M3 connections work together. CubeSat Design Brief + 3 annotated concept sketches Open Lesson PPTX 0.5 Evaluate & Develop The selected concept is supported by evidence-based scoring and includes enough dimensions and connection detail to begin CAD. Decision Matrix + selected concept + detailed annotated sketch Open Lesson 0.6 CAD & Assembly Design The CAD model fits inside 4 in × 4 in × 4 in, preserves open sides, uses 1/8 in acrylic top/base plates, and shows all M3 assembly interfaces. Complete CAD assembly + CubeSat design check Open Lesson 0.7 Additive Manufacturing The frame is printable, uses the class-standard filament, and all required slicing settings are documented before production. 3D Printer Certification verification + print settings record + print-ready frame files Open Lesson PPTX 0.8 Laser Manufacturing Both required plates fit on the single 4 in × 12 in × 1/8 in acrylic sheet, include M3 interfaces, and are approved before cutting. Laser Cutter Certification + 4 in × 12 in cutting layout + laser-ready files Open Lesson 0.9 Fabrication & Assembly The CubeSat is fully assembled with M3 screws, remains within the 4-inch envelope, has open sides, and is ready for qualification. Hand Tools Certification + completed CubeSat structure Open Lesson 0.10 CubeSat Lightweight Structure Competition The structure passes every required check before weigh-in, and the team can connect its final mass and performance to specific design decisions. Final CubeSat + qualification record + official mass + short engineering design review Open Lesson Competition Logic Strong Enough, Then Lightest 1 Meet the architecture 4-inch maximum cube, open sides, laser-cut acrylic top/base, printed frame, and M3 structural assembly. 2 Pass qualification Dimension, construction, load, and assembly-integrity checks are pass/fail. 3 Weigh the survivors Only structures that qualify receive an official mass. Lowest qualified mass wins.

pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit Inspect a simulated engineering workspace, identify hazards,
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit Inspect a simulated engineering workspace, identify hazards, and produce a corrected setup plan. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace prototyping team is preparing for a rapid repair task. Before work begins, the team needs an independent safety review of tools, PPE, cords, materials, and traffic flow. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common FabLab and shop hazards Match PPE to the task Communicate corrective actions clearly Apply stop-work authority responsibly Materials What You Need Teacher-provided workstation or safety photo Safety checklist Engineering notebook PPE examples Procedure Instructions Review the assigned workstation without touching anything. Record at least eight observations: safe practices, hazards, or missing controls. Classify each hazard by severity: low, medium, or high. For every hazard, write one corrective action and who should complete it. Create a revised workstation sketch showing safe tool placement, material flow, and walking space. Perform a second inspection after corrections are made. Write a brief go/no-go recommendation for starting work. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least five legitimate hazards or risk controls Include PPE, housekeeping, electrical, cutting/tool, and movement considerations Every hazard must have a specific corrective action Final recommendation must be supported by evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not operate tools during the audit Do not stage unsafe conditions for a photograph Follow your teacher’s directions for handling PPE and equipment Deliverables What You Submit Completed safety audit Annotated workstation sketch Corrective-action table Final go/no-go recommendation Notebook reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which hazard had the highest potential consequence? Which correction was easiest to implement? How can a safe workspace also improve efficiency? When should a student stop work and ask for help? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Separate the probability of an incident from the severity of its outcome when ranking risk. Common Mistake Listing “be careful” is not a corrective action. State what must physically or procedurally change. Stretch Goal Create a 60-second safety briefing that a team leader could deliver before the task begins. Career Connection Aerospace technicians, test engineers, and manufacturing engineers complete pre-task hazard reviews before high-risk work. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Lesson 0.7 POE Unit 0 • Lesson 0.7 Additive Manufacturing Focus question: How can print settings and frame geometry reduce mass without sacrificing the strength needed to qualify? Today’s Deliverable Challenge Rules Unit 0 Overview CubeSat Project Design for qualification first. Optimize mass everywhere you can justify it. Define Design Prove The final winner is the lightest CubeSat structure that passes every required qualification gate. Challenge Rules CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Every team works inside the same architecture and material limits. Your engineering advantage comes from how efficiently you use them. Competition Objective Pass first. Then weigh in. Structural qualification is pass/fail. Among the structures that pass every requirement, the lowest total assembled mass wins. Fixed Architecture Maximum assembled envelope: 4 in × 4 in × 4 in, including hardware. Top and bottom: laser cut from the team’s single 4 in × 12 in × 1/8 in acrylic sheet. Sides: remain open; no side panels. Primary frame: 3D printed using the same teacher-selected filament material for every team. Assembly: M3 screws for all primary structural connections; structural glue is not permitted. Manufacturing Limits Serviceability: the structure must be able to be disassembled and reassembled with normal hand tools. Competition: the lightest structure that passes every qualification requirement wins. Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can prepare the 3D-printed CubeSat frame for manufacturing and justify print settings as engineering variables. Evidence 3D Printer Certification verification + print settings record + print-ready frame files Success Looks Like The frame is printable, uses the class-standard filament, and all required slicing settings are documented before production. Activity Flow How Today Advances the CubeSat 1. Identify the load path Decide where the printed frame actually needs material. 2. Choose slicing variables Set walls, infill, pattern, orientation, and layer height intentionally. 3. Verify and release the print Complete certification verification and document settings before starting the final frame. Optimization Variables The Filament Is Standardized; Your Print Strategy Is Not Walls vs. Infill Additional walls may strengthen thin structural members more efficiently than simply increasing infill. Your team must justify the balance it chooses. Print Orientation Layer direction changes how the frame responds to tension, bending, and connection loads. Geometry Ribs, gussets, hollow sections, and cross-sectional shape can create stiffness without filling the entire member with material. Project Milestone Today’s Required Deliverable Additive Manufacturing Release Submit or record: 3D Printer Certification evidence or instructor verification if already certified. Layer height. Wall/perimeter count. Infill percentage. Infill pattern. Print orientation. Estimated print time. Estimated filament use. Print-ready frame file(s). Short justification explaining how the settings balance mass, strength, and reliability. Engineering Decision Document the Reasoning Decision What did your team decide today? Evidence What measurements, requirements, comparisons, calculations, or manufacturing information support that decision? Reasoning Why does that evidence make the decision appropriate for a lightweight structure that still has to qualify? pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Mission Team Communication Protocol POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol Design and test a concise communication protocol for
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Mission Team Communication Protocol POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol Design and test a concise communication protocol for a multi-station engineering task. Intermediate 1 class period Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover test team must coordinate a driver, sensor observer, data recorder, and safety lead. Miscommunication could damage hardware or invalidate test data. Objectives What You Will Practice Define clear team roles Create standardized callouts Use closed-loop communication Evaluate communication performance Materials What You Need Role cards Simple timed team task Communication log Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Assign four team roles and define each role’s authority. Write standard callouts for ready, start, stop, fault, data confirmed, and reset. Create a rule requiring the receiver to repeat critical commands. Run a baseline task using normal conversation and record errors or delays. Run the task again using the protocol. Compare completion time, errors, and missed information. Revise two parts of the protocol. Requirements Engineering Requirements Every critical command must receive confirmation One person must have stop-work authority Protocol must distinguish normal completion from emergency stop Testing must include before/after evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a low-risk teacher-approved task No running or unsafe movement The safety lead may stop the task at any time Deliverables What You Submit Role chart Communication protocol Baseline and final performance table Revision notes Team reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which callout prevented the most confusion? Did the protocol slow the team down or make it faster overall? What information should never be assumed? How could the protocol work in a noisy environment? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use short, unique phrases that cannot be confused with casual conversation. Common Mistake Adding too many callouts can make the system harder to use. Standardize only critical information. Stretch Goal Add a hand-signal or visual backup for two critical commands. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Black-Box System Investigation POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Black-Box System Investigation Analyze an unknown input-output system and develop a functional
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Black-Box System Investigation POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Black-Box System Investigation Analyze an unknown input-output system and develop a functional model without opening it. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Mission engineers frequently work with subsystems supplied by another team. They may know the inputs and outputs but not every internal detail. Your team must characterize an unknown classroom system. Objectives What You Will Practice Define system boundaries Identify inputs, processes, outputs, and feedback Plan controlled tests Create and revise a functional model Materials What You Need Teacher-provided black-box device or simulation Approved test inputs Stopwatch or measurement tools Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Observe the system without operating it and define the system boundary. List possible inputs, outputs, energy transfers, and internal processes. Plan at least four controlled tests that change one input at a time. Run the tests and record quantitative and qualitative outputs. Create an initial block diagram. Use evidence to revise the model and predict a new result. Run one confirmation test and evaluate the prediction. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least four controlled tests At least one quantitative output Functional model must show input, process, output, and feedback if present Final prediction must be tested Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not open, alter, overload, or bypass safety limits on the system Use only approved inputs Stop testing if behavior becomes unsafe or inconsistent Deliverables What You Submit Test plan Data table Initial and revised system diagrams Prediction and confirmation result Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which test provided the most useful information? What part of the internal process remains uncertain? How did your model change after testing? What additional sensor would improve the investigation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Choose tests that isolate one variable rather than changing several conditions at once. Common Mistake Assuming the first explanation is correct can lead to confirmation bias. Actively look for evidence that could disprove it. Stretch Goal Create a fault scenario and explain how the outputs would change. Career Connection Systems engineers use functional models to integrate propulsion, avionics, structures, and controls developed by different teams. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Lesson 0.9 POE Unit 0 • Lesson 0.9 Fabrication & Assembly Focus question: How do accurate fabrication and M3 assembly choices affect the final mass and structural integrity of the CubeSat? Today’s Deliverable Challenge Rules Unit 0 Overview CubeSat Project Design for qualification first. Optimize mass everywhere you can justify it. Define Design Prove The final winner is the lightest CubeSat structure that passes every required qualification gate. Challenge Rules CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Every team works inside the same architecture and material limits. Your engineering advantage comes from how efficiently you use them. Competition Objective Pass first. Then weigh in. Structural qualification is pass/fail. Among the structures that pass every requirement, the lowest total assembled mass wins. Fixed Architecture Maximum assembled envelope: 4 in × 4 in × 4 in, including hardware. Top and bottom: laser cut from the team’s single 4 in × 12 in × 1/8 in acrylic sheet. Sides: remain open; no side panels. Primary frame: 3D printed using the same teacher-selected filament material for every team. Assembly: M3 screws for all primary structural connections; structural glue is not permitted. Manufacturing Limits Serviceability: the structure must be able to be disassembled and reassembled with normal hand tools. Competition: the lightest structure that passes every qualification requirement wins. Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can manufacture and assemble the CubeSat safely, check fit and alignment, and produce a complete competition-ready structure. Evidence Hand Tools Certification + completed CubeSat structure Success Looks Like The CubeSat is fully assembled with M3 screws, remains within the 4-inch envelope, has open sides, and is ready for qualification. Activity Flow How Today Advances the CubeSat 1. Inspect manufactured parts Check dimensions, holes, print quality, and acrylic edges before assembly. 2. Assemble with M3 hardware Use the planned fastener sequence and correct hand tools. 3. Complete pre-competition inspection Verify size, open sides, secure joints, and total assembly readiness. Assembly Quality Mass Is Not the Only Thing That Can Disqualify a Design Fit Do not force mismatched holes or printed parts. Diagnose tolerance problems before tightening hardware. Fasteners M3 joints should be secure without crushing acrylic or stripping printed connection features. Alignment Top and bottom plates should remain aligned and the structure should sit squarely without obvious twist. Project Milestone Today’s Required Deliverable Completed CubeSat Prototype Hand Tools Certification completed. Laser-cut acrylic top and bottom installed. 3D-printed structural frame installed. Primary structural connections use M3 screws. No structural adhesive used. All four sides remain open. Assembly can be disassembled and reassembled. Team performs a final 4-inch envelope check before competition day. Engineering Decision Document the Reasoning Decision What did your team decide today? Evidence What measurements, requirements, comparisons, calculations, or manufacturing information support that decision? Reasoning Why does that evidence make the decision appropriate for a lightweight structure that still has to qualify? pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Preflight Readiness Review POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Preflight Readiness Review Create and conduct the most reliable preflight inspection for a classroom rover or mechanism. Advanced 1-2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Two student teams are preparing identical systems for a mission demonstration. The winning team is not simply the fastest; it is the team whose checklist catches the most faults while remaining efficient. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate failure risks into inspection steps Sequence checks efficiently Use objective pass/fail criteria Validate a checklist through fault insertion Materials What You Need Classroom rover or mechanism Fault cards or teacher-inserted issues Checklist template Timer Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions List at least ten possible mission-preventing faults. Rank each fault by likelihood and consequence. Write a checklist with observable pass/fail criteria. Arrange checks from safe/no-power inspection through powered functional checks. Exchange systems with another team; your teacher inserts approved faults. Conduct the inspection while being timed. Record detected faults, missed faults, and unnecessary checks. Revise the checklist and repeat one validation round. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 12 checklist items Checklist must include identity, physical condition, power, movement, sensor/control, and final configuration No item may use vague wording such as “looks good” Score balances detection rate and completion time Constraints Constraints & Safety Only teacher-approved faults may be inserted Do not defeat guards or create electrical hazards Power must remain off during physical inspection unless instructed Deliverables What You Submit Risk-ranked fault list Preflight checklist Validation results Revised checklist Competition score summary Reflection Reflection Questions Which fault was easiest to miss? Which checklist item had the clearest pass/fail standard? What check could be automated? How did time pressure affect performance? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write checklist items as actions with a condition: “Verify battery connector is fully seated and locked.” Common Mistake A long checklist is not automatically better. Repeated or low-value checks can hide critical items. Stretch Goal Convert the final checklist into a QR-linked digital form. Career Connection Aerospace operations teams use configuration-controlled checklists for aircraft, launch vehicles, and ground support equipment. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Replacement rover components arrived without complete inspection records. Your team must verify critical dimensions before the parts are released for assembly. Objectives What You Will Practice Use rulers and calipers correctly Evaluate repeatability and measurement variation Record measurements with appropriate precision Make an evidence-based accept/recheck decision Materials What You Need Three to five teacher-selected parts Metric ruler Digital or dial caliper Measurement data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Identify the dimensions that are most important to fit or assembly. Measure each critical dimension three times without looking at previous results. Have a partner independently measure the same dimensions. Calculate the range for each set of measurements. Compare your readings with the partner readings and any reference dimension provided. Mark each dimension Accept, Recheck, or Reject and explain why. Write one improvement to the measurement procedure. Requirements Engineering Requirements Record units and instrument used for every dimension Use three repeated measurements per dimension Measurements must be readable and traceable to a labeled feature Decisions must cite numerical evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not force caliper jaws onto a part Use only approved parts Do not treat instrument display resolution as guaranteed accuracy Deliverables What You Submit Labeled part sketch Measurement table Range calculations Accept/recheck/reject decisions Procedure improvement note Reflection Reflection Questions What caused the largest measurement variation? Which instrument was most appropriate for each feature? How would temperature or surface damage affect results? What measurement would you verify first before assembly? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the same contact points and instrument orientation each time you repeat a measurement. Common Mistake Changing where you measure a feature can create apparent variation that is actually a setup difference. Stretch Goal Design a simple go/no-go gauge concept for one critical dimension. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 0 Lesson 0.10 POE Unit 0 • Lesson 0.10 CubeSat Lightweight Structure Competition Focus question: Which engineering choices produced the lightest CubeSat structure that can still pass every qualification requirement? Today’s Deliverable Challenge Rules Unit 0 Overview CubeSat Project Design for qualification first. Optimize mass everywhere you can justify it. Define Design Prove The final winner is the lightest CubeSat structure that passes every required qualification gate. Challenge Rules CubeSat Lightweight Structure Challenge Every team works inside the same architecture and material limits. Your engineering advantage comes from how efficiently you use them. Competition Objective Pass first. Then weigh in. Structural qualification is pass/fail. Among the structures that pass every requirement, the lowest total assembled mass wins. Fixed Architecture Maximum assembled envelope: 4 in × 4 in × 4 in, including hardware. Top and bottom: laser cut from the team’s single 4 in × 12 in × 1/8 in acrylic sheet. Sides: remain open; no side panels. Primary frame: 3D printed using the same teacher-selected filament material for every team. Assembly: M3 screws for all primary structural connections; structural glue is not permitted. Manufacturing Limits Serviceability: the structure must be able to be disassembled and reassembled with normal hand tools. Competition: the lightest structure that passes every qualification requirement wins. Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can complete a final qualification check, interpret competition data, and defend the engineering decisions that shaped my team’s structure. Evidence Final CubeSat + qualification record + official mass + short engineering design review Success Looks Like The structure passes every required check before weigh-in, and the team can connect its final mass and performance to specific design decisions. Activity Flow How Today Advances the CubeSat 1. Qualify the structure Complete dimensional, construction, and standardized structural checks. 2. Official weigh-in Only qualifying structures receive an official competition mass. 3. Defend the design Connect final performance to geometry, material removal, print settings, and assembly decisions. Qualification Sequence Pass Every Gate Before the Scale Qualification determines whether a structure is eligible. Mass ranks only the structures that qualify. Gate Requirement Result 1. Envelope Entire assembled structure fits within 4 in × 4 in × 4 in. PASS / FAIL 2. Construction Laser-cut 1/8 in acrylic top/base, open sides, 3D-printed frame, M3 structural assembly, no structural adhesive. PASS / FAIL 3. Structural Load Support a standardized 10 lb vertical load for 30 seconds using the teacher-provided load plate without fracture, joint separation, or visible permanent deformation. PASS / FAIL 4. Assembly Integrity M3 joints remain secure and the structure remains serviceable after the load test. PASS / FAIL 5. Weigh-In Qualifying structure is measured to the nearest 0.1 g. Official Mass Winner Lowest Qualified Mass The lightest CubeSat structure that passes all four qualification gates wins. Tie Breaker Structural Efficiency If official masses are within 1.0 g, lower measured deflection during the same load test wins. If still tied, greater usable interior volume wins. Project Milestone Today’s Required Deliverable Final Competition Record & Design Review Final assembled mass, including acrylic, printed frame, M3 hardware, inserts/nuts/washers, and all permanent components. Pass/fail results for every qualification requirement. Final print settings and estimated filament use. One design decision that reduced mass. One design decision that supported structural strength. One change the team would make if a second version were allowed. Engineering Decision Document the Reasoning Decision What did your team decide today? Evidence What measurements, requirements, comparisons, calculations, or manufacturing information support that decision? Reasoning Why does that evidence make the decision appropriate for a lightweight structure that still has to qualify? Trace the load path Count only rope segments that directly support the moving load. 2. Predict mechanical advantage Estimate ideal input force and required pull distance. 3. Evaluate a lifting task Select a configuration that meets the force limit without ignoring distance or complexity. Lesson Interactive Configure a Payload Lift A 120 N payload must be lifted 0.50 m. Configure an ideal pulley system requiring no more than 35 N of input force. Pulley Configuration Supporting rope segments: Only rope segments directly supporting the moving load contribute to ideal mechanical advantage. Ideal Prediction Input force Rope pulled Check Configuration Increase supporting segments until the force requirement is met, then note the distance tradeoff. pages.title: Unit 1 Final Project: VEX Cargo Lift Engineering Challenge
pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.9 POE Unit 1 • Final Project • Lesson 1.9 Unit 1 Final Project: VEX Cargo Lift Engineering Challenge Challenge: Design and build a VEX cargo lift t
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.9 POE Unit 1 • Final Project • Lesson 1.9 Unit 1 Final Project: VEX Cargo Lift Engineering Challenge Challenge: Design and build a VEX cargo lift that raises a 500 g payload at least 400 mm vertically and completes three consecutive successful trials . Start Here Design Brief Unit 1 Overview First Open-Ended Build Turn the winch you built in 1.8 into a complete guided lifting system. Your team chooses the structure, guide system, gearing, winch arrangement, and bracing. Start Here What You Need to Do Use this as your checklist throughout the challenge. Work On Detailed concept sketches or a CAD model with a labeled mechanism plan Freestanding VEX cargo lift Guided payload platform Motor-powered lifting system Three official test trials At least one engineering revision Work and power calculations Submit Initial detailed concept sketches or CAD model Mechanical-system / gear-ratio explanation Three-trial test data Average lift time Work calculation Power calculation Problem observed + design revision Final reflection Done When Your lift raises the 500 g payload at least 400 mm , remains freestanding, keeps the payload guided, and completes three successful trials in a row . Requirements Your Lift Must Include Structural Frame A freestanding VEX structure that supports the lift and remains upright without being held. Payload Platform The payload must sit on a platform, tray, or carrier. It may not simply hang from the string. Guided Vertical Motion Use rails, channels, rollers, wheels, sliding guides, or another approved method so the platform moves primarily up and down. Motor-Powered Lift A VEX motor must provide the lifting power. No manual assistance is allowed during an official trial. Power Transfer Use a winch/drum, gears, chain and sprockets, pulleys, or an appropriate combination. Stable Base The lift must support itself throughout operation. Students may not stabilize it by hand. Performance Standard What Counts as Success? Requirement Standard Payload mass 500 g Vertical lift distance 400 mm minimum Successful trials 3 consecutive trials Power source VEX motor Student assistance None during official trial Payload retention Payload remains on platform Structure Freestanding and functional Design Freedom What Your Team Gets to Decide Structure Overall geometry Frame width and height Structural bracing Base design Lift System Platform design Guide system Winch/drum design Cable/string routing Power & Motion Motor location Gear ratio Gears, chain, sprockets, or pulleys Speed-versus-torque strategy Rules What You May Not Do Hold or stabilize the lift during an official trial. Touch the payload or platform while it is moving. Manually assist the motor, axle, drum, or lifting string. Change the standardized payload mass. Begin with the payload partially raised. Allow the payload to hang freely instead of using a guided platform. Use non-VEX structural components unless specifically approved. If the lift jams, tips, drops the payload, or requires assistance, the trial is unsuccessful. Before You Build Document Your Design Before building, document your proposed lift using detailed concept sketches or a CAD model . A CAD model may be substituted for the detailed concept sketches as long as it clearly communicates the complete design. Your sketches or CAD model must clearly show and label: overall lift structure payload platform vertical guide system motor location power-transfer system winch/drum or lifting mechanism planned gear ratio major structural bracing Before building, your team should be able to explain how power travels from the motor to the payload. Engineering Concepts What You Should Be Thinking About Gear Ratio How will your ratio change output speed and torque? Mechanical Advantage Does your mechanism increase the force available to raise the payload? Work W = Fd Use the payload force and vertical lift distance. Power P = W/t Use the work performed and lift time. Friction & Alignment Look for rubbing, binding, uneven winding, or platform tilt. Structure & Load Path Follow how the payload force travels through the cable, frame, bracing, and base. Official Testing Three Consecutive Trials Start each trial with the platform at the LOW position and the complete 500 g payload resting on it. Remove your hands before the test begins. Timing starts when the motor begins moving and stops when the payload reaches the required height. Trial Payload Lift Height Lift Time Success? 1 500 g _____ mm _____ s Yes / No 2 500 g _____ mm _____ s Yes / No 3 500 g _____ mm _____ s Yes / No Iteration Required Design Revision Your first working design is not automatically your final design. Identify at least one problem, make a meaningful engineering revision, and document the change. Possible issues include platform tilt, motor stalling, slow lifting, frame flex, gear skipping, uneven string winding, binding, base instability, excessive friction, or unnecessary mass. Submission What You Will Submit Initial detailed concept sketches or CAD model Completed VEX cargo lift Gear ratio and/or mechanical-system explanation Three-trial testing data Average lift time Work calculation Power calculation One problem observed during testing One documented design revision Final reflection: Explain the most important tradeoff your team made between speed, torque, stability, and reliability. ← Previous Lesson Continue to Unit 2 →

pages.title: Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox
pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox Design and justify a gear train that provides an approximately 4:1 spee
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Design a 4:1 Rover Gearbox Design and justify a gear train that provides an approximately 4:1 speed reduction for a rover drive system. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover motor spins too quickly and produces insufficient wheel torque. Your mechanical team must create a compact reduction system using available gears. Objectives What You Will Practice Calculate gear ratio Relate speed and torque Compare multiple gear-train layouts Document a mechanical recommendation Materials What You Need Available classroom gears or VEX gear inventory Axles and supports or CAD layout tools Calculator Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Inventory available gear tooth counts. Create three possible gear-train combinations near a 4:1 reduction. Calculate theoretical ratio and output speed for each. Sketch or model each layout and identify required shafts and supports. Compare size, number of parts, direction of rotation, and likely friction. Select one design and build or mock up the gear train. Measure input and output rotations to verify the actual ratio. Recommend the best design for the rover. Requirements Engineering Requirements Target reduction between 3.8:1 and 4.2:1 Output shaft must rotate continuously without gear interference All calculations must show driver and driven gears Recommendation must compare at least three concepts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only available gears and approved structural parts Do not apply motor power until alignment is checked by hand Keep hair and fingers clear of moving gears Deliverables What You Submit Three concept layouts Gear-ratio calculations Built or CAD-modeled final design Measured ratio data Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Questions Why might actual performance differ from the theoretical ratio? Which layout used the fewest parts? How did the reduction affect output torque and speed? What support would prevent gear skipping? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip For compound gear trains, multiply the ratio of each stage rather than adding ratios. Common Mistake Using pitch diameter or tooth count inconsistently will produce an incorrect ratio. Stretch Goal Redesign the gearbox to provide two selectable ratios. Career Connection Mechanical and drivetrain engineers size gear reductions for robotic explorers, aircraft actuators, and test equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget
pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget Build and test a rubber-band-powered vehicle, then account fo
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Rubber-Band Rover Energy Budget Build and test a rubber-band-powered vehicle, then account for where stored energy goes. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A lightweight inspection rover needs a simple stored-energy demonstration for a training program. The vehicle must travel predictably rather than merely as far as possible. Objectives What You Will Practice Describe energy transformations Measure distance and time Control experimental variables Use data to select an operating condition Materials What You Need Small wheeled chassis materials Rubber bands Meter tape Stopwatch Masses Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Build a vehicle with a repeatable rubber-band winding method. Choose three winding levels such as 10, 20, and 30 turns. Run three trials at each level. Record distance, travel time, and any wheel slip or path deviation. Calculate average distance and average speed. Create a graph of winding level versus distance. Select the best operating condition for predictable travel and justify it. Requirements Engineering Requirements Same vehicle configuration for all baseline trials Three trials per winding level Release method must be consistent Vehicle must remain within a defined lane Recommendation must use data, not the single longest run Constraints Constraints & Safety Wear eye protection if required Inspect rubber bands for cracks Keep faces and hands away from stretched bands Use a clear test lane Deliverables What You Submit Vehicle sketch Trial data table Graph Energy-flow diagram Operating recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions What evidence suggested energy was lost to friction or wheel slip? Why did the highest winding level not necessarily give the best result? How did mass affect acceleration or consistency? What variable would you test next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark the axle so every trial begins with the same winding reference. Common Mistake Changing the release angle or starting position between trials makes the data difficult to compare. Stretch Goal Add payload and determine the best winding level for transporting it. Career Connection Test engineers characterize stored-energy devices, springs, deployment systems, and small mobility platforms before mission use. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Gears and Drive Ratios
pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.4 Gears and Drive Ratios Focus question: How do gear ratios and gear trains change rotational speed, torque, and direction
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.4 Gears and Drive Ratios Focus question: How do gear ratios and gear trains change rotational speed, torque, and direction to meet a design need? Start Gear Lab Download Worksheet Unit 1 Overview Simulation Investigation Predict first. Change the gear system. Observe the motion. Use the data to explain the tradeoff. Predict Simulate Defend Your evidence is the completed Gear Ratio & Gear Train Simulation Worksheet. Start Here What You Need to Do Use this section as your checklist before moving through the lesson resources below. Work On Build and test the assigned gear combinations. Record driver/driven gear information and calculate each ratio. Describe how each ratio changes speed, torque, and direction. Submit Completed gear-ratio investigation table Done When Your table contains the ratio, observed motion, and correct speed/torque tradeoff for each setup. Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do The simulation is the main learning tool for this lesson. 1 Analyze a gear pair Identify driver and driven gears, calculate gear ratio, and predict output speed and torque. 2 Track direction Use the number of external gear meshes to predict clockwise or counterclockwise output. 3 Explain idler gears Show why an idler can change direction or spacing without changing the overall simple-train ratio. Launch Prediction Before You Touch the Controls Make a prediction first. Then use the simulation to find evidence. 12T driver → 36T driven Will the output be faster or slower? What happens to ideal torque? Will direction match the driver? 40T driver → 20T driven Will the output be faster or slower? What happens to ideal torque? Will direction match the driver? 24T driver → 24T driven What stays the same in a 1:1 pair? What still changes because the gears are externally meshed? Interactive Lab Gear Ratio & Gear Train Simulation Work through the worksheet while you use the simulation. Record actual values rather than guessing from the animation alone. POE 1.4 Gear Lab Gear pairs • gear trains • idlers • mission challenge Open Full Screen If the embedded simulation feels cramped on a smaller screen, use Open Full Screen . Your worksheet remains the required lesson evidence. Worksheet Roadmap Complete the Investigation in Four Parts The page and worksheet use the same sequence so you can move between them without hunting for the next step. Part A Predict Predict speed, torque, and direction for three gear pairs, then check each prediction in the simulation. Part B Explore Gear Pairs Run four trials: a reduction, a speed-up, a 1:1 pair, and one system of your choice. Part C Build a Gear Train Change the idler size in a 20T → idler → 40T train and determine what does and does not change. Part D Make a Mission Decision Compare three lunar sample-storage door options and defend the strongest choice with numerical evidence. Core Math Use the Simulation to Check the Equations Gear Ratio GR = driven teeth / driver teeth Output Speed rpm_out = rpm_in × (driver / driven) Ideal Torque T_out = T_in × (driven / driver) Direction Rule Every external gear mesh reverses rotation direction. One mesh reverses once. Two meshes reverse twice. Track direction separately from the ratio. Mission Challenge Lunar Sample-Storage Door Use the third simulation mode and the worksheet table to make an engineering recommendation. Design Need The motor operates efficiently near 1200 rpm . The storage door should rotate slowly and gain ideal torque so it is less likely to stall in lunar dust. Option A: 12T driver → 24T driven Option B: 12T driver → 48T driven Option C: 24T driver → 36T driven Your recommendation must use at least two numerical pieces of evidence. Exit Check Close the Loop 1 What happens to output speed and ideal torque when a small driver turns a much larger driven gear? 2 What is the purpose of an idler gear in a simple external gear train? 3 How does each external gear mesh affect rotation direction? Resources Lesson Resources Required Simulation Worksheet Record predictions, four gear-pair trials, the idler investigation, and your lunar storage-door recommendation. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.3 Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage Focus question: How can force and distance measurements prove whether a m
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.3 Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage Focus question: How can force and distance measurements prove whether a mechanism provides mechanical advantage? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Mechanical advantage is evidence. It compares input and output force or distance so a design claim can be tested. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Start Here What You Need to Do Use this section as your checklist before moving through the lesson resources below. Work On Complete the work and mechanical-advantage calculations. Show substitutions and units. Use the measured or provided force and distance values. Submit Completed work and mechanical-advantage calculation set Done When Calculations include correct formulas, units, and a reasonable interpretation of the result. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can calculate work and mechanical advantage using measured force and distance data from a mechanism. Evidence Work and mechanical advantage calculation set Success Looks Like Calculations use correct units and connect force-distance tradeoffs to mechanical advantage and efficiency. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. PowerPoint POE 1.3 Lesson Presentation Download the Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage presentation used with this lesson. Download Presentation 1. Measure force and distance Record input and output force and travel over the same mechanism cycle. 2. Calculate performance Determine work, actual mechanical advantage, and efficiency. 3. Interpret the tradeoff Explain why increased output force requires increased input distance or another cost. Lesson Interactive Analyze Force, Distance, Work, and Mechanical Advantage A mechanism uses 25 N of input force over 0.80 m to move an 80 N load through 0.20 m. Calculate the performance values. Measured Data 25 N Input force 0.80 m Input distance 80 N Output force 0.20 m Output distance Use W = Fd, AMA = output force ÷ input force, and efficiency = output work ÷ input work × 100. Your Analysis Input work (J) Output work (J) Actual mechanical advantage Efficiency (%) Best conclusion Choose The mechanism increases force by requiring more input distance and losing some energy. The mechanism creates additional energy. The output moves farther than the input. Check Activity Complete all four calculations and choose the conclusion supported by the data. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Work and Mechanical Advantage Calculation Set Complete one evidence table for a tested or provided mechanism. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A drone recovery station has a small motor but must lift equipment safely. Your team must balance drum radius, speed, torque, and structural support. Objectives What You Will Practice Relate torque, radius, force, speed, and power Use calculations to guide design Test a mechanism under load Evaluate design tradeoffs Materials What You Need Low-voltage motor or hand-crank simulation Spools of different radii String Masses Timer Structural materials Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Record the available motor speed or hand-input condition. Create at least three drum-radius concepts. Predict which radius will lift fastest and which will lift the greatest load. Build a supported winch with one selected drum. Test a standard load and record lift time. Increase load in approved increments until the design reaches the limit. Calculate output work and average power for one successful lift. Revise the drum or support and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Lift through a fixed height No uncontrolled dropping or slipping Include a stable axle support and secure string attachment Use at least one calculation before selecting the final drum Final design must complete three repeatable lifts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use teacher-approved voltage and masses Keep hands clear of winding string Do not stall a motor for extended time Use a catch zone below the load Deliverables What You Submit Concept comparison Torque/radius calculations Test data Final winch photo or CAD Design tradeoff explanation Reflection Reflection Questions How did drum radius affect speed and lifting force? What limited the design first: motor, structure, traction, or string? Where was power lost? What safety factor would be appropriate for real cargo? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A smaller drum increases available line force but requires more rotations to lift the same distance. Common Mistake Calculating torque without using consistent units is a common source of error. Stretch Goal Add a ratchet or brake that prevents rollback during a power loss. Career Connection Actuation engineers design winches, reels, and deployment systems for aircraft recovery equipment and spacecraft mechanisms. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.16 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.16 Prototype Build Day 2: Power, Load, and Troubleshooting Focus question: How can troubleshooting connect a failure point to a targeted design revision? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Troubleshooting is evidence-driven: observe the failure, identify the cause, revise one thing, and retest. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can troubleshoot a mechanism by identifying causes of failure and making targeted revisions. Evidence Troubleshooting log and revised prototype evidence Success Looks Like Troubleshooting follows symptom → evidence → likely cause → targeted revision → retest, with only one major variable changed at a time. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Reproduce the symptom Use the same load and test setup so the failure can be observed reliably. 2. Isolate the cause Check power, transmission, alignment, friction, fastening, and structural deflection. 3. Revise and retest Change the most likely cause, then compare new evidence with the original test. Lesson Interactive Diagnose a Power-Transmission Failure The motor shaft spins, but the large output gear and lift arm remain stationary. Choose the most likely cause, targeted revision, and verification evidence. Observed Symptom Motor sound is normal. Motor shaft rotates. Gear on the same shaft does not rotate consistently. No major frame rubbing is visible. Troubleshooting Path Most likely cause Choose Dead battery Loose gear hub or shaft connection Bent frame rail Targeted revision Choose Replace the motor Secure the hub/collar connection Add lubricant everywhere Verification evidence Choose Mark the shaft and gear, then observe whether they rotate together Listen for a different sound Repaint the output arm Check Activity Choose the path that directly addresses the observed break in motion transfer. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Troubleshooting Log and Revised Prototype Evidence Complete one full troubleshooting cycle on the powered mechanism. Record the symptom, evidence, likely cause, revision, and retest result. Include a before-and-after photo, sketch, measurement, or data point.
