pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift Build a compact lifting mechanism that raises a simulated p
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift Build a compact lifting mechanism that raises a simulated payload with limited input force. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A lunar crew must raise a damaged equipment package onto a rover platform. The crew has limited force available and needs a lightweight mechanical aid. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply mechanical advantage Measure input and output force Compare ideal and actual performance Identify friction losses Materials What You Need String Pulleys or lever materials Spring scale Mass set Meter stick Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select either a pulley or lever concept. Calculate the ideal mechanical advantage before building. Build the mechanism with secure supports. Measure the input force required to raise the assigned payload at constant speed. Calculate actual mechanical advantage and efficiency. Identify two locations where energy is lost. Modify one feature to improve performance. Repeat the force measurement and compare results. Requirements Engineering Requirements Lift the assigned payload at least 20 cm Input force must be below the teacher-set limit Payload must remain controlled and not swing freely Include ideal MA, actual MA, and efficiency calculations Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved masses Never place hands below a suspended load Inspect supports before every test Do not lift the payload above the approved height Deliverables What You Submit Concept sketch Calculations Force data table Before/after efficiency comparison Final recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Where did friction reduce performance? Did increasing mechanical advantage change the distance pulled? What design feature improved control? How would lunar gravity affect the force requirement? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Move the load slowly and steadily; acceleration will distort force readings. Common Mistake Ignoring the input distance can make a high mechanical advantage system seem “free.” Work must still be transferred. Stretch Goal Add a self-locking or braking feature that holds the load without continuous input. Career Connection Mechanical systems engineers design hoists, deployment mechanisms, and cargo-handling equipment for spacecraft and ground operations. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.17 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.17 Mechanism Testing and Data Analysis Focus question: How can repeatable data show whether a mechanism met the design cri
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.17 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.17 Mechanism Testing and Data Analysis Focus question: How can repeatable data show whether a mechanism met the design criteria? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Test data must be repeatable enough to support a claim about performance, reliability, power, or efficiency. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can collect repeatable test data and use calculations to evaluate mechanism performance. Evidence Final test data table and analysis Success Looks Like The test controls variables, uses repeated trials, identifies anomalies, calculates meaningful metrics, and compares results with the criteria. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Standardize the procedure Define load, starting condition, distance, timing method, and success criteria. 2. Collect repeated trials Record enough trials to identify consistency and possible anomalies. 3. Analyze and conclude Calculate averages or performance metrics and state whether each criterion was met. Lesson Interactive Analyze Repeatability and an Anomalous Trial A mechanism completed four lift trials in 42 s, 41 s, 43 s, and 58 s. Interpret the data before making a performance claim. Trial Data 42 s Trial 1 41 s Trial 2 43 s Trial 3 58 s Trial 4 Do not delete a trial only because it is inconvenient. Identify a plausible procedural or mechanical reason and retest. Data Decision Likely anomalous value Choose 41 s 42 s 43 s 58 s Mean of the three consistent trials (s) Best next step Choose Ignore Trial 4 and make the final claim immediately. Investigate the cause, repeat the trial, and document how the anomaly is handled. Average all values without discussing consistency. Check Activity Identify the data cluster, calculate its mean, and choose a transparent next step. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Final Test Data Table and Analysis Run a repeatable test and use the data to judge mechanism performance. Include units, trial conditions, repeated measurements, and any excluded anomaly with justification. Write a criterion-by-criterion conclusion supported by calculated results. Exit Ticket Mission Debrief 1 One way today’s lesson connects to an aerospace mechanism or VEX rover system. 2 One type of evidence you could use to support a design decision. 3 One question you still have about mechanisms, energy, power, or the Unit 1 challenge. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown Compete to transfer a fixed payload through a required path using
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown Compete to transfer a fixed payload through a required path using the least input energy or force. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A ground-support team needs a mechanism to move a delicate payload between two stations. Multiple teams will propose machines and compare efficiency, reliability, and complexity. Objectives What You Will Practice Combine simple machines Measure input force and distance Calculate work and efficiency Defend a design using performance evidence Materials What You Need Approved pulleys, gears, levers, wheels, axles, or linkages Spring scale Meter tape Fixed payload Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the payload path and boundaries. Sketch two mechanism concepts that use at least two simple-machine elements. Estimate mechanical advantage and input travel. Build one design and complete a low-load functional test. Measure average input force and input distance for three official trials. Calculate input work and compare it with useful output work. Record success rate and completion time. Prepare a one-minute defense of the design. Requirements Engineering Requirements Move the payload from start to finish without direct hand contact Use at least two mechanical elements Complete three official trials Provide work and efficiency calculations Scoring includes efficiency, reliability, and simplicity Constraints Constraints & Safety No launching or free-falling payloads Use only approved stored energy Inspect supports and connections before testing Stop immediately if parts bind or fail Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Calculations Official trial table Efficiency result Design defense Reflection Reflection Questions What feature improved efficiency most? Did the most efficient design also finish fastest? How did part count affect reliability? What would you change for a more fragile payload? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Measure force while the system moves at steady speed; peak starting force may not represent the full trial. Common Mistake Comparing only completion time ignores input effort and reliability. Stretch Goal Redesign to complete the same task with 25% fewer parts. Career Connection Mechanical design and operations engineers evaluate cargo-handling systems using efficiency, reliability, maintainability, and safety. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.7 Guided VEX Gear & Sprocket Drive Systems Focus question: How do we correctly build gear and sprocket drive systems so tha
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.7 Guided VEX Gear & Sprocket Drive Systems Focus question: How do we correctly build gear and sprocket drive systems so that calculated mechanical relationships work in a physical VEX mechanism? Start Lesson Open Build Guide Unit 1 Overview Guided Build Lab Copy the build first. Test it. Explain it. Then make one small change. Build Test Modify This lesson is intentionally step-by-step so every team gains confidence with VEX shafts, collars, bearings, gears, sprockets, and chain. Start Here What You Need to Do Use this section as your checklist before moving through the lesson resources below. Work On Complete the guided VEX mechanism build. Check spacing, fastening, axle support, alignment, and structural rigidity. Correct any build-quality problems before submitting. Submit Completed VEX build VEX mechanism build-quality checklist Done When The mechanism moves freely, stays aligned, and does not rely on loose or unsupported components. Lesson Snapshot What You Will Be Able to Do This is a training-wheels-on lesson before later open-ended mechanism challenges. 1 Build a gear reduction Construct a 12T driver gear meshed with a 36T driven gear and test smooth rotation. 2 Add an idler gear Use an idler to change direction or transfer motion across more distance while tracking the overall ratio. 3 Build a chain drive Connect a 12T driver sprocket to a 24T driven sprocket using chain, proper alignment, and good tension. Today’s Flow How the Lesson Moves Parts check Guided gear build Stop and check Idler gear build Guided chain build Mini modification Exit ticket Learning Target Main Objective and Evidence Learning Target I can build functional VEX gear and sprocket drive systems using correct shaft support, spacing, alignment, collars, spacers, and chain tension. Deliverable Guided VEX Gear & Sprocket Drive Systems Build Guide with calculations, stop-and-check boxes, troubleshooting notes, and photos. Success Looks Like Your mechanisms spin freely by hand, the gears do not skip, the chain stays on, and your team can explain speed, torque, and direction changes. Build Sequence Copy - Build - Test - Understand - Modify Follow the build guide exactly until both drive systems work. Open-ended design comes later. Part System Required Evidence A Identify drive-system parts Parts checklist and vocabulary table B-C 12T gear driver to 36T gear driven Gear ratio calculation and motion observations D Idler gear system Direction tracking and explanation of what the idler changes E-F 12T sprocket driver to 24T sprocket driven Sprocket ratio calculation and chain-quality check G Mini modification challenge One small change to make output rotate faster than input Build Checks Stop Before You Continue Do not keep building on top of a problem. If a shaft binds, a gear skips, or the chain climbs off the sprocket, stop and fix alignment, spacing, collars, or chain tension before moving to the next step. Gear drive should... Spin freely by hand Mesh without jamming Show slower output with more ideal torque Reverse direction with one external mesh Idler gear should... Mesh smoothly with both gears Change the direction pattern Transfer motion across more distance Keep the overall simple-train ratio based on first and last gears Chain drive should... Have aligned sprockets Use chain that is not too tight or too loose Keep the chain on the teeth Rotate input and output in the same direction Resources Lesson Resources Use the guided build packet during class. It is designed to print cleanly in black and white. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.6 Sprockets, Chain Drives, and Direction of Motion Focus question: How do sprockets and chain drives transfer motion and ch
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 POE Unit 1 • Lesson 1.6 Sprockets, Chain Drives, and Direction of Motion Focus question: How do sprockets and chain drives transfer motion and change speed or torque? Interactive Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Sprockets and chains transfer rotation while keeping direction, alignment, and ratio under control. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Start Here What You Need to Do Use this section as your checklist before moving through the lesson resources below. Work On Build and compare the assigned VEX sprocket/chain configurations. Calculate drive ratios. Record direction of rotation and observed speed/torque changes. Submit Completed sprocket-drive comparison chart Done When Your comparison correctly connects sprocket size and drive ratio to output behavior. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Opening prompt Concept vote Aerospace link Compare options Evidence challenge Quick check Exit ticket Lesson Targets What You Will Be Able to Do Learning Target I can explain how sprockets and chains transfer motion and calculate a simple drive ratio. Evidence Sprocket drive comparison chart Success Looks Like The chain-drive analysis predicts ratio, speed, torque trend, and shaft direction without treating it like a meshed gear pair. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves This page highlights the lesson elements you need for practice, evidence, and submission. 1. Identify drive components Mark the driver sprocket, driven sprocket, chain path, and shaft axes. 2. Calculate drive ratio Use sprocket tooth counts to predict speed and torque change. 3. Check system behavior Verify whether the two shafts rotate in the same or opposite direction. Lesson Interactive Analyze a Chain Drive Adjust the driver and driven sprockets, then predict speed, torque trend, and rotation direction for an open chain. Drive Inputs Driver teeth Driven teeth Input speed (rpm) Output Prediction Ratio Output speed Ideal torque factor Rotation direction Same direction Opposite direction Performance trend Slower, more ideal torque Faster, less ideal torque Same speed Check Activity Unlike meshed external gears, an open chain drive does not reverse the second shaft. Today’s Work Main Deliverable Sprocket Drive Comparison Chart Compare two sprocket combinations for the rover mechanism. Calculate ratio and predicted output speed for each combination. pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 3 Line-Following Recovery Logic POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Line-Following Recovery Logic Program a rover to follow a path and recover when the line is tem
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 3 Line-Following Recovery Logic POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Line-Following Recovery Logic Program a rover to follow a path and recover when the line is temporarily lost. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A warehouse-style rover transports equipment through a marked route. Dust or damaged floor markings may interrupt the path, so the rover needs recovery behavior. Objectives What You Will Practice Use feedback control Create state-based logic Test fault recovery Measure path performance Materials What You Need Rover with optical or line sensors Marked course with one intentional gap Programming environment Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Create baseline line-following logic and test it on a continuous path. Define the conditions that indicate the line has been lost. Design a recovery sequence such as stop, search left, search right, and timeout. Add a safe stop if the line cannot be found. Run five trials through a path containing a gap. Record recovery success, completion time, and any departures from the lane. Tune the logic and repeat five official trials. Requirements Engineering Requirements Follow the normal path without manual control Recover from the designated gap Stop safely after the search timeout Complete at least four of five official trials Code must include meaningful comments Constraints Constraints & Safety Use low operating speed during development Maintain a clear test area Provide immediate stop control Do not allow uncontrolled searching outside the boundary Deliverables What You Submit State diagram Commented code Baseline and final results Recovery success rate Tuning explanation Reflection Reflection Questions What event caused the rover to enter recovery mode? Which search pattern worked best? How did timeout length affect safety? What additional sensor could improve recovery? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Draw the control states before writing code: Follow, Lost, Search Left, Search Right, Stop. Common Mistake Adding more nested conditionals without a state plan can make recovery behavior unpredictable. Stretch Goal Add a second fault such as an obstacle that interrupts the path. Career Connection Autonomy engineers design fault-handling states so robotic vehicles remain safe when sensors or navigation references are lost. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Landing-Zone Probability Model POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Landing-Zone Probability Model Use repeated test data to estimate the probability that a paylo
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Landing-Zone Probability Model POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Landing-Zone Probability Model Use repeated test data to estimate the probability that a payload lands inside a target zone. Advanced 2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A relief drone drops small emergency packages. The team must determine whether the current deployment method is reliable enough for a defined landing zone. Objectives What You Will Practice Use descriptive statistics Model target success probability Visualize two-dimensional test data Communicate risk and limitations Materials What You Need Approved drop or launch simulation Target grid At least 20 trial coordinates Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define the target-zone boundaries and coordinate origin. Collect or analyze at least 20 landing coordinates. Plot every point on a scaled scatter plot. Calculate mean x and y position and spread in each direction. Count successful landings and calculate observed success rate. Identify directional bias and possible environmental causes. Recommend an aim-point adjustment or process change. Predict the expected number of successes in 50 future drops. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 20 trials Target success defined before data collection All points shown, including misses Include observed probability and directional bias Recommendation must acknowledge sample-size limits Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a safe simulation or approved low-energy system Maintain a clear test zone Do not alter data after seeing target results Deliverables What You Submit Coordinate data Scatter plot Success-rate calculation Bias analysis Aim-point recommendation Future-performance prediction Reflection Reflection Questions Did the mean landing point fall inside the target? Can a high average accuracy still produce poor reliability? How would wind change the distribution? What sample size would increase confidence? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep both coordinate directions; reducing the result to distance alone can hide a directional bias. Common Mistake Assuming the observed percentage is an exact future probability ignores limited sample size. Stretch Goal Create an elliptical landing zone that contains approximately 80% of the observed points. Career Connection Guidance, navigation, and test engineers quantify dispersion and probability for payload delivery, landing, and release systems. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson →

pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Rover Acceleration Characterization POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Rover Acceleration Characterization Measure rover motion and determine whether accelerati
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Rover Acceleration Characterization POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Rover Acceleration Characterization Measure rover motion and determine whether acceleration is approximately constant during startup. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A mission-planning team needs a simple model of rover startup motion to estimate stopping and maneuvering distance. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect position-time data Calculate velocity and acceleration Interpret motion graphs Judge whether a model is appropriate Materials What You Need Rover Straight measured track Video camera or motion sensor Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Mark a straight test track and choose a consistent rover command. Collect position versus time using video frames or a motion sensor. Create a position-time graph. Calculate interval velocities and create a velocity-time graph. Estimate acceleration from the graph. Repeat the trial two more times. Compare acceleration values and decide whether a constant-acceleration model is reasonable. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least three trials Consistent battery and command settings Show calculation method for velocity and acceleration Use graphs with labeled axes and units Model conclusion must include evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a clear track Maintain immediate stop control Do not stand in front of the rover Secure loose cables and equipment Deliverables What You Submit Test method Position data Position-time and velocity-time graphs Acceleration estimate Model evaluation Reflection Reflection Questions Where was acceleration most constant? How did sampling interval affect the graph? What caused differences among trials? How would payload mass change startup motion? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use consistent time intervals and identify the center time for interval velocity values. Common Mistake Calculating one acceleration value from the entire run can hide changes during startup and steady motion. Stretch Goal Repeat with an added payload and compare acceleration statistically. Career Connection Vehicle dynamics and controls engineers characterize acceleration, braking, and traction for autonomous vehicles. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Projectile Test-Range Analysis POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.1 Projectile Test-Range Analysis Collect launch data, model projectile motion, and evaluate how well predictions match the test. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small payload-deployment system must place a sensor inside a target zone. Your team will analyze a safe classroom launcher or simulation. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure launch conditions Apply horizontal and vertical kinematics Create graphs and uncertainty statements Compare model predictions with test results Materials What You Need Approved launcher or simulation Meter tape Angle tool if applicable Stopwatch or video timing Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define launch height, angle, and target coordinate system. Record at least five trials at one controlled setting. Calculate predicted flight time and horizontal range using the assigned model. Measure actual landing positions. Calculate average range, range spread, and percent difference from prediction. Graph the landing positions or range results. Identify at least three causes of model-test disagreement. Recommend a setting adjustment for the target zone. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least five valid trials Consistent launch setting All equations and units shown Include average and variation, not only one trial Recommendation must cite prediction and data Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the approved range and launcher No aiming toward people or breakable objects Retrieve projectiles only after the range is clear Follow all eye-protection requirements Deliverables What You Submit Test setup diagram Calculations Trial data Graph Prediction comparison Targeting recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which assumption in the model was least realistic? Was the error systematic or random? How would launch-height uncertainty affect the result? What additional measurement would improve the prediction? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use a coordinate system and clearly define where horizontal distance begins. Common Mistake Comparing a prediction to the single closest trial hides the actual variation in performance. Stretch Goal Use your data to create a 90% target interval for expected landing position. Career Connection Flight-test engineers compare analytical trajectories with instrumented tests for release systems, drones, and launch vehicles. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Mission Data Dashboard POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.5 Mission Data Dashboard Create the clearest and most useful dashboard for a rover test data set. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A mission manager needs to make a quick go/no-go decision using data from speed, temperature, battery voltage, sensor faults, and task completion. Objectives What You Will Practice Select meaningful data displays Avoid misleading graphs Create performance thresholds Communicate an engineering decision Materials What You Need Teacher-provided rover test data Spreadsheet or visualization software Mission requirements Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the data dictionary and mission success criteria. Identify the five most decision-relevant measures. Choose an appropriate chart, table, or status indicator for each. Create threshold colors or flags based on stated requirements. Build a one-page dashboard. Write a go/no-go recommendation using evidence from the dashboard. Exchange dashboards and have another team answer three mission questions. Revise any display that caused confusion. Requirements Engineering Requirements One-page dashboard At least three different visualization types Every visual must include labels and units Thresholds must come from mission criteria No decorative chart may obscure data Recommendation must be traceable to the dashboard Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not alter source data Clearly identify missing data Avoid color-only communication when possible Deliverables What You Submit Dashboard Data-selection rationale Go/no-go recommendation Peer usability results Revised final version Reflection Reflection Questions Which visual supported the fastest decision? What information was unnecessary? How did you display uncertainty or missing data? What graph choice could mislead a viewer? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Design the dashboard around decisions the user must make, not around every variable available. Common Mistake Using a visually impressive but inappropriate graph can hide patterns or exaggerate differences. Stretch Goal Create a live version that automatically updates when new rows are added. Career Connection Flight-test, systems, and mission-operations teams use dashboards to monitor vehicle health and test readiness. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson →

pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Sensor Data Quality Investigation POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation Determine whether a sensor data set is accurate, precise,
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 4 Sensor Data Quality Investigation POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation Determine whether a sensor data set is accurate, precise, biased, or affected by noise. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover environmental sensor is producing inconsistent readings. Before replacing hardware, the test team must characterize the data and identify likely error sources. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish accuracy and precision Calculate mean, range, and standard deviation Detect bias and outliers Recommend a calibration or filtering method Materials What You Need Sensor or Teacher-provided data set Reference standard Spreadsheet Graphing tools Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Collect or receive at least 20 readings under a constant condition. Record a trusted reference value. Calculate mean, range, standard deviation, and error of the mean from the reference. Create a time-series graph and a histogram or dot plot. Identify any outliers using an teacher-approved rule. Repeat measurements after one controlled change such as repositioning, shielding, or recalibration. Compare the two data sets. Recommend keep, calibrate, filter, reposition, or replace. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 20 readings per primary condition Reference value clearly identified Include numerical measures of center and spread Do not remove outliers without documenting the rule Recommendation must be supported by evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not expose sensors to unsafe conditions Do not fabricate readings Keep environmental variables controlled unless intentionally tested Deliverables What You Submit Raw data Calculations Two graphs Outlier decision Before/after comparison Sensor recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Was the main problem bias or variation? What evidence supported removing or retaining an outlier? Which controlled change improved data quality most? What filter could reduce noise without hiding real changes? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Plot data in time order before summarizing it; drift may disappear in a simple average. Common Mistake Removing all unusual values because they look inconvenient can hide a real fault. Stretch Goal Implement and compare a moving-average filter with two different window sizes. Career Connection Instrumentation and test engineers validate sensors used for navigation, structures, propulsion, and environmental monitoring. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson →

pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 5 Rover Mission Requirements Audit POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.1 Rover Mission Requirements Audit Turn a broad rover mission statement into clear, testable engineering requirements. Intermediate 1 class period Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A client has requested “a reliable rover that can transport a payload across rough terrain.” The statement is not specific enough to design or verify. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish needs from requirements Write measurable shall-statements Identify verification methods Detect conflicting or missing requirements Materials What You Need Mission statement Requirements template Engineering notebook Optional sample rover data Procedure Instructions Underline every user need or desired function in the mission statement. Convert each need into one or more measurable requirements. Add units, limits, conditions, and success criteria. Assign a verification method: inspection, analysis, demonstration, or test. Identify at least two missing requirements and one possible conflict. Prioritize requirements as Must, Should, or Could. Conduct a peer audit and revise unclear statements. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least ten measurable requirements Every requirement uses a defined condition and limit Each requirement has a verification method Avoid solution-specific wording unless required by the client Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not invent unrealistic performance limits Maintain traceability to the original mission need Clearly mark assumptions Deliverables What You Submit Need-to-requirement table Prioritized requirement list Verification matrix Conflict/missing-information note Revised final set Reflection Reflection Questions Which user need was hardest to make measurable? What requirement could unintentionally restrict design creativity? Which requirement has the highest mission risk? What question should be returned to the client? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A strong requirement states what the system must accomplish, not how the designer must accomplish it. Common Mistake Words such as reliable, fast, lightweight, and easy are not testable without a number or condition. Stretch Goal Add interface requirements for charging, payload attachment, or data transfer. Career Connection Systems engineers manage requirements and verification across complex aerospace projects. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Rover Anomaly Review Board
pages.description: Home Courses POE Unit 5 Rover Anomaly Review Board POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board Investigate a failed mission trial, identify the most likely cause, and
pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 5 Rover Anomaly Review Board POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board Investigate a failed mission trial, identify the most likely cause, and approve a corrective action. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context During a rover mission rehearsal, the vehicle stopped early, missed the sample, or returned with incomplete data. Your team will act as an anomaly review board. Objectives What You Will Practice Separate facts from assumptions Build a fault tree or cause map Use evidence to rank causes Define corrective and preventive actions Materials What You Need Teacher-provided anomaly scenario and evidence packet Fault-tree template Test logs or code excerpts Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Create a timeline of confirmed events. List facts, unknowns, and assumptions in separate columns. Define the top failure event. Build a fault tree or cause-and-effect diagram with at least three branches. Use available evidence to eliminate or rank causes. Identify the most likely root cause and one contributing factor. Write a corrective action and a verification test. Present a return-to-test recommendation: approve, approve with limits, or hold. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use only evidence in the packet unless assumptions are labeled At least three plausible cause branches Corrective action must address the identified cause Verification test must have measurable pass/fail criteria Final recommendation includes residual risk Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not blame individuals; focus on system, process, design, and evidence Protect any provided student/team identifiers Do not modify original logs Deliverables What You Submit Event timeline Facts/unknowns/assumptions table Fault tree Root-cause statement Corrective-action plan Return-to-test decision Reflection Reflection Questions What evidence most strongly changed your conclusion? What cause remained possible but unproven? How could the process prevent recurrence? What additional data should future tests record? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Preserve multiple plausible causes until evidence supports eliminating them. Common Mistake Choosing the first obvious cause can lead to corrective action that does not prevent recurrence. Stretch Goal Create a revised checklist or code monitor that detects the anomaly earlier. Career Connection Aerospace anomaly review boards investigate test and mission failures before hardware returns to operation. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson →

Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context The project team has several promising rover concepts but limited time and budget. Objectives What You Will Practice Select decision criteria Assign defensible weights Score concepts consistently Perform sensitivity analysis Materials What You Need Three concept descriptions or team sketches Decision matrix template Mission requirements Calculator or spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the mission requirements and identify six to eight decision criteria. Assign weights totaling 100%. Define a 1-5 scoring scale for every criterion before scoring concepts. Score all three concepts and document evidence. Calculate weighted totals. Change the two largest weights by plus/minus 10 percentage points and recalculate. Identify whether the winner changes. Recommend a concept and state the largest unresolved risk. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least three concepts and six criteria Weights total 100% Scoring definitions written before final scoring All scores supported by evidence or assumptions Include one sensitivity analysis Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change criteria solely to make a preferred concept win Label uncertain assumptions Use the same scoring standard for all concepts Deliverables What You Submit Criteria and weights Scoring definitions Completed trade matrix Sensitivity comparison Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion drove the decision most strongly? Did sensitivity analysis change confidence in the winner? What missing test data would reduce uncertainty? Where might personal bias have affected scoring? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write scoring anchors such as “5 = meets requirement with at least 20% margin.” Common Mistake Assigning numbers without defined scoring rules creates a false appearance of precision. Stretch Goal Add cost and schedule uncertainty using best-case and worst-case scores. Career Connection Systems engineering teams use formal trade studies to select architectures, sensors, propulsion, and mission concepts. Start Fabrication Safety Gate Laser Workflow Assembly Build Log Pre-Test Inspection Bridge Capstone · Build & Inspection Produce, verify, document. Work from your teacher-approved 2.17 manufacturing files , track every part and approved revision, and finish with measured inspection evidence. Next lesson: 2.19 Bridge Load Testing. This lesson does not include the official 100 N load test. Learning outcomes Five stages from CAD to finished bridge Complete these stages in order, with teacher-approved access to the school's OMTech laser systems and Bambu printers where those tools are needed. 1 FILE APPROVAL CAD, cut/print files 2 MAKE PARTS Laser / 3D / wood 3 DRY FIT Measure & align 4 ASSEMBLE Clamp & cure 5 INSPECT Mass, span, width Evidence and version-controlled changes are recorded at every step Step 01 Approval & setup Confirm instructor-signed design revision, machine certifications, permitted stock and accurate DXF/slicer files. Step 02 Manufacture components Cut wood/plywood and print approved joint fittings under the FabLab's machine procedures; identify every part. Step 03 Dry fit & inspect Count usable parts, verify thickness and hole fit, remove rejected parts, and match the approved assembly drawing. Step 04 Assemble & cure Build two square side frames, connect cross-bracing and center load transfer, use only approved adhesive/hardware. Step 05 Measure & document Check actual span, total outside width, complete mass, gusset and fitting limits, defects, and teacher review. Suggested pacing: 3–5 45–50 minute periods, depending on machine queue, adhesive cure and team complexity. Students should alternate between file review, part organization, assembly preparation, documentation and inspection while machine access is scheduled. Teacher-selected curing requirements take precedence over class timing. 01 / Fabrication rules What students may and may not build ≥400 mm Clear span measured between real support contact positions ≤65 mm Overall outside width including bolt heads and fittings ≤150 g Actual finished bridge mass including glue and hardware 100 N load Official test in 2.19, not during fabrication ≤10 mm deflection At the 100 N test load; not proven by visual inspection Approved wood Primary structural members only Approved construction Balsa, basswood, craft sticks or plywood for primary members. One-piece laser-cut open-web plywood side trusses are permitted if manufacturing rules are met. Connections may use PVA glue, CA glue, interlocking wood joints, local plywood gussets, approved PLA/PETG connectors or M3 nuts with bolts and permitted washers. Prohibited during construction No acrylic, solid plywood side plates, printed chords/diagonals/decks, hot glue, epoxy, staples, nails, screws, wire or non-M3 bolt sizes. No unauthorized strengthening after the design package is approved. All corrections before the official test must be documented and, if the design changes, resubmitted for teacher approval. Official rule: No repairs are allowed after official testing begins. Before the test, controlled revisions are allowed only with documented changes and teacher approval. Read the complete Unit 2 rules ↗ . 02 / Before using any machine FabLab safety and job release checklist Machine and operator readiness Teacher-approved revision of CAD, cut profiles and print files is available. Eye protection and other PPE are used according to classroom and machine SOP. Work area is clear, ventilation and machine safety devices are functioning. Teacher verifies the machine setup and decides who may run the operation. Know the stop procedure and alert the teacher immediately for a defect, flare-up, unusual smell or machine issue. Specific hazards to recognize Laser: fire and smoke, improper material, ventilation failure and cuts/burns after operation. Never operate with defeated interlocks or leave a running laser unattended. Only the trained supervisor handles an abnormal or emergency event. 3D printer: hot bed/nozzle, moving parts, unsuitable slicing settings, detached prints and sharp post-processing tools. Wait until the part and plate are cool enough to handle according to the machine SOP. Wood/adhesives: dust, sharp cutters, wood splinters, CA bonding skin/eyes and poor ventilation. Keep fingers away from cutting paths, use teacher-approved clamping and follow each adhesive label and cure requirements. Authoritative safety references: Georgetown laser pre/during/post-cut checklist ↗ and Illinois laser cutter safe-use guidance ↗ . Classroom equipment SOPs and direct instructor directions govern the actual procedure. 03 / Video learning resources Watch, identify the process controls, then build Workshop Companion Why Glue Alone Won't Make Strong Joints Watch for: Surface contact, wood grain, force direction, fit and clamp pressure. Do not copy unapproved adhesives or joining methods. pages.title: Structural Efficiency
pages.description: POE Unit 2 2.14 Principles of Engineering · Unit 2 · Lesson 2.14 Structural Efficiency Engineering question: How can we make a structure lighter while still meeting every strength,
pages.searchText: POE Unit 2 2.14 Principles of Engineering · Unit 2 · Lesson 2.14 Structural Efficiency Engineering question: How can we make a structure lighter while still meeting every strength, stiffness and manufacturing requirement? Start Learning Watch Videos Use 2.13 Lab Data Compare Designs Mass Budget What to Submit Analyze · Compare · Optimize Mass matters—but so do the requirements. Calculate load-per-mass and stiffness-per-mass ratios, then apply qualification limits to proposed bridge designs. Materials: your six-specimen 2.13 testing report, calculator, engineering notebook and mass estimates or actual measurements. Learning targets Use evidence to make a lightweight design decision 1 · Measure efficiency Calculate a performance-to-mass ratio with the correct units and understand what each ratio proves. 2 · Apply experimental results Use actual stiffness and mass data from the six different 2.13 specimens without claiming the experiment measured breaking strength. 3 · Budget and qualify Plan complete bridge mass and reject numerically noncompliant concepts before comparing them. Suggested pacing: 10 minutes for key concepts, 10 minutes for videos, 15 minutes for material analysis and 15 minutes for bridge comparison and mass budgeting. Finish independent practice as assigned. 01 / Understand structural efficiency Don't remove material without understanding its job Engineers search for ways to direct forces through efficiently placed members. Reducing mass can improve a design—unless the changes introduce excessive deformation, buckling or joint failure. SOLID, MATERIAL-HEAVY SECTION OPEN-WEB TRUSS More solid material → more mass Triangulated members carry load Neither drawing proves strength, stiffness or connection quality: analysis and tests are required. A full structure Supported load per finished mass η load = supported load (N) / completed mass (g) Units: N/g . Specify whether the numerator is a qualification load or an experimentally demonstrated higher load. The same qualification load divided by bridge mass measures mass efficiency at that requirement , not ultimate failure capacity. A tested strip Bending stiffness per specimen mass η strip = k (N/mm) / specimen mass (g) Units: N/(mm·g) . The value k is the measured early linear force–deflection slope from 2.13. It describes the specimen in that test configuration. It is not ultimate strength. The 2.13 lab is non-destructive . Students did not establish ultimate failure force for the steel, carbon-fiber, wood, aluminum, polyethylene or Delrin strips, and cannot calculate a verified “breaking strength-to-weight” ratio from those data. 02 / Instructional videos Understand efficient force paths and material stiffness Understanding and Analysing Trusses — The Efficient Engineer Focus question: Why can a triangular web support load with less material? Identify two ways a member or joint might still fail. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ Understanding Young’s Modulus — The Efficient Engineer Focus question: Why do material stiffness E and shape-dependent structural bending stiffness EI give different information? Watch directly on YouTube ↗ Students can open the videos directly if embedded playback is restricted on the school network. 03 / Follow the worked examples Calculate first; interpret the result second Example A · Bridge load per gram Hypothetical bridge A supports 120 N with a mass of 100 g. Bridge B supports 150 N with a mass of 140 g. A: 120/100 = 1.20 N/g B: 150/140 ≈ 1.07 N/g A has higher N/g, while B supports a larger total load. Do not choose until you check deflection, width, span and material rules. These are instructional values, not actual classroom bridge results. Example B · Test specimen stiffness per gram In a hypothetical comparison, specimen A has k = 8 N/mm and mass 12 g; specimen B has k = 11 N/mm and mass 20 g. A: 8/12 = 0.667 N/(mm·g) B: 11/20 = 0.550 N/(mm·g) B has greater total specimen stiffness, but A has a better stiffness-per-mass ratio . Cross-section and grain/fiber orientation may differ, so this is not a pure comparison of intrinsic material properties. Example C · Predict mass from density An illustrative wood member occupies 36,000 mm³ and has assumed density 0.50 g/cm³. 36,000 mm³ ÷ 1,000 = 36 cm³ m = ρV = (0.50)(36) = 18 g This estimates the member alone ; a finished structure includes adhesives, gussets, fasteners, braces and approved fittings. Replace assumed densities with actual measurements whenever possible. 04 / Use actual 2.13 results Compare all six material specimens fairly Transfer your group's measured bending slopes and, if available, measured sample masses from the 2.13 lab. All entries begin blank ; this page does not invent test results. Unmeasurable specimens should remain blank and be explained in your report. Enter your real results Test material Measured k (N/mm) Measured mass (g) k/m [N/(mm·g)] Steel — Carbon fiber — Wood paint stick — Aluminum — Polyethylene — Delrin (acetal/POM) — Clear Material Entries Compare measured ratios Enter measurements to compare. No complete measured data entered. The paint stick has a different nominal cross-section; carbon fiber may be directional; some steel bars may not bend enough for the classroom gauge to measure safely. Do not equate k/m with intrinsic strength/density or rank missing data as zero. Bridge materials restriction: Steel, aluminum, carbon fiber, polyethylene and Delrin are teaching comparison specimens, not approved primary bridge-building materials . The eventual bridge requires approved wood or plywood primary members. Review complete construction rules ↗ 05 / Qualify before comparing The bridge must pass every required condition ≥ 400 mm Clear unsupported span ≤ 65 mm Overall width, including fittings ≤ 150 g Completed bridge mass ≥ 100 N Centered qualification load ≤ 10 mm Midspan deflection at 100 N Approved only Materials, adhesives, M3 and connector rules Passing these five numeric criteria does not automatically certify

pages.searchText: POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.15 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.15 Bridge Design Research & Concepts Engineering question: Which three bridge layouts are worth developing into detailed engineering designs under our manufacturing and performance constraints? Start Learning Compare Truss Types Watch Tutorials Concept Explorer Decision Matrix What to Submit Bridge Capstone · Phase 1 of Design Research → three concepts → choose one. Students will research three structural approaches, draw each in side and top views, show how a 100 N load transfers to the supports and select the strongest candidate for analysis —not a pre-certified winner. Materials: notebook and graph paper or Fusion, the Lesson 2.14 mass-budget analysis and credible research sources. Project launch Your challenge: generate three meaningfully different designs Until now, students have studied mechanics and materials separately. This is the first lesson in which they apply that evidence to the real 400 mm bridge capstone. 1 · Research Identify how Pratt, Howe and Warren-type webs differ, what carries the load and what connection challenges appear. 2 · Sketch Produce three structurally distinct candidate bridges, with dimensions, two side frames, lateral bracing and centered load transfer. 3 · Select Screen against required limits, compare alternatives and recommend the best concept for calculations in Lesson 2.16. What counts as a different concept? A different web triangulation, panel arrangement, truss rise or joining/load-transfer system that changes how the structure behaves. Merely changing color, adding decorative fins or renaming the same truss is not a distinct structural concept. Read criteria 5 minutes Research & videos 10–15 minutes Generate sketches 20–30 minutes Evaluate & choose 10–15 minutes Suggested pace: approximately two 45–50 minute periods if students complete all three labeled side/top concept views and evaluation in class. 01 / Nonnegotiable design rules Buildable does not mean unrestricted Your bridge design must account for both structural performance and the exact fabrication constraints. These values come from the Unit 2 challenge specification. 400 mm Clear span between supports 65 mm MAX Overall width including fittings 100 N Centered qualification load 10 mm MAX Midspan deflection at 100 N 150 g MAX Finished mass, everything included Approved materials Wood-based main members only Permitted primary structure Balsa, basswood, craft sticks or plywood may form the primary structure. A complete laser-cut open-web plywood side truss is allowed, but not a solid plywood side plate. Cross bracing and loading connection must be designed. Do not use: acrylic, steel/carbon fiber/aluminum/polyethylene/Delrin primary members from the materials lab, or fully 3D-printed bridge bodies. Connections and manufacturing Allowed: PVA or CA glue, interlocking wood joints, approved plywood gussets, approved PLA/PETG fittings and M3 nuts/bolts (washers allowed). No screws, hot glue, epoxy, wire or other bolt sizes. Plywood local gussets ≤40 × 25 mm and ≤800 mm², with overlap ≤20 mm onto each member and at most one layer per side. Printed fittings must meet separate 50 mm/15 g each, 40 g total and specified slicer restrictions. Design approval note: The concept explorer below is a geometry/mass planning aid; it does not calculate strength, buckling, deflection or real joint capacity. Final compliance requires drawings, physical inspection and teacher-controlled testing. Read the full specification here ↗ . 02 / Bridge research Three ways to organize a truss web Every example below is a schematic side elevation for comparison, not a complete build plan. Joint and diagonal orientation changes the force distribution and connection requirements. Reference pattern A Pratt-type truss 100 N centered 400 mm clear span · side elevation · h = 85 mm (example) Diagonals generally slope downward toward midspan in the typical configuration. Under common downward load cases, these diagonals often carry tension while verticals carry compression. Ask: Are short compression members and many glued joints an advantage for our wood-and-gusset build? Reference pattern B Warren-type truss 100 N centered 400 mm clear span · side elevation · h = 85 mm (example) Repeating triangles can reduce the number of vertical web members and create a simple repeated pattern. Diagonal force directions vary by location and loading. Ask: Does the central 100 N load land at a suitable joint or need a specially designed crossmember? Reference pattern C Howe-type truss 100 N centered 400 mm clear span · side elevation · h = 85 mm (example) Diagonal orientation is opposite to Pratt. Under common gravity loading, the diagonals are often in compression, while the verticals tend toward tension. Ask: How will slender diagonals resist buckling, and can the joints transfer those compressive forces? Be precise: Force directions depend on the exact geometry, restraints and loading. These are common patterns, not universal predictions for every member. In Lesson 2.16 you will test your selected load paths using free-body diagrams and analysis. 03 / Think beyond a side view How do two truss sides become a complete bridge? A single 2D truss sketch cannot explain the entire test setup. Students must plan two parallel side trusses , transverse cross-bracing, a centered load-transfer member or platform and actual joining details. Center load ≤ 65 mm overall Two connected side frames not just two separate drawings Transverse load transfer and lateral bracing Where does the 100 N go? The loading nose presses onto a designated central load-transfer point. A transverse member or joint arrangement transfers that force into both truss sides. Each side transfers force through diagonals, chords and joints to the supports. The support interface resists reaction forces without rolling, sliding or local damage. pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 2 Lightweight Rover Chassis Truss POE Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Lightweight Rover Chassis Truss Design and test a lightweight truss chassis that supports a specified payload. Intermediate 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A planetary rover chassis must protect instruments while minimizing launch mass. Your team will create a small truss structure and compare strength-to-mass performance. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify tension and compression members Use triangulation effectively Measure structural performance Calculate strength-to-mass ratio Materials What You Need Craft sticks, paper strips, or approved structural material Adhesive Mass scale Test weights Ruler Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define the required chassis span and payload location. Sketch two truss patterns and label expected tension/compression members. Estimate material quantity and mass for each concept. Select and build one chassis using consistent joints. Measure final mass and inspect alignment. Load the chassis in approved increments while observing deformation. Record maximum successful load and failure location. Calculate load-to-mass ratio and recommend one redesign. Requirements Engineering Requirements Span the required distance without intermediate support Support the assigned base payload for 30 seconds Use a clearly identifiable truss pattern Record mass before testing No repair during an official load trial Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved adhesives and cutting tools Wear eye protection during destructive testing if required Keep hands and faces away from the load path Do not exceed teacher-approved load limits Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Member-force predictions Structure mass Load-test table Failure analysis Redesign recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which members appeared to be in compression? Where did the first visible deformation occur? How did joint quality affect performance? What change would improve strength without adding much mass? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Compression members often fail by buckling before the material itself crushes. Common Mistake Adding material everywhere increases mass but may not strengthen the critical load path. Stretch Goal Rebuild one member or joint and demonstrate a 15% improvement in load-to-mass ratio. Career Connection Aerospace structures engineers design trusses, frames, and support structures to carry loads with minimal mass. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →

pages.searchText: Home Courses POE Unit 2 2.1 POE Unit 2 • Lesson 2.1 Unit Challenge Launch: Build a Better Bridge Engineering question: How can a bridge span a gap, carry a required load, and remain lightweight and stiff? Learn the Concept Apply to the Bridge What to Submit Open Bridge Mission Analysis Unit 2 Overview Phase 1 · Understand the Structure Every lesson adds evidence to your final bridge design. Read, work the examples, apply the idea to the challenge, and submit the required engineering evidence before moving on. Phase 1 · Understand the Structure Learn Apply Document Carry Forward Coming In What You Already Know Unit 1 showed that engineers use mechanisms to control force and motion. Unit 2 shifts the focus to structures: systems that must carry forces safely without moving very much. Learning Targets By the End of This Lesson Explain the difference between strength, stiffness, and structural efficiency. Identify the criteria and constraints of the bridge challenge. Generate initial ideas for how chords, verticals, diagonals, deck members, and joints could carry load. The Unit Challenge Lightweight Bridge Structural Design Challenge Design and manufacture a lightweight bridge that spans a fixed gap between two supports. The engineering problem is to carry a centered load efficiently through members and joints into the supports. 400 mm Required clear span between supports. 65 mm maximum Maximum overall bridge width. 100 N Required centered design load. ≤ 10 mm Maximum midspan deflection at 100 N. ≤ 150 g Maximum finished structural mass. Standard Supports Every team uses the same teacher-provided support locations. Manufacturing Rules Wood and plywood primary members, open-web single-piece laser-cut plywood side trusses, localized gussets, and approved PLA/PETG connectors are permitted. Only M3 nuts/bolts for mechanical fastening. No acrylic, screws, or fully printed bridges. See the complete Unit 2 specification. Left Support → Chords + Verticals + Diagonals → 400 mm Span → Right Support Learn the Concept What You Need to Know Use these ideas as your lesson notes. Focus on explaining the behavior, not memorizing vocabulary by itself. Structure vs. mechanism A mechanism is designed to move; a structure is designed primarily to carry loads while maintaining its shape. A bridge still flexes, but excessive deformation can make it unusable long before it actually breaks. Strength Strength describes how much load a material or structure can resist before yielding, fracturing, buckling, separating at a joint, or otherwise failing. Stiffness Stiffness describes resistance to deformation. A bridge may be strong enough not to break but still fail the design if its midspan deflection is too large under the required load. Structural efficiency Structural engineers cannot solve every problem by adding more material. A useful structure carries the required load with as little mass as practical. Why mass alone does not determine success Imagine Bridge A has a mass of 70 g and carries 45 N before failure. Bridge B has a mass of 45 g and carries 40 N. Bridge A is stronger in absolute load capacity, but Bridge B may be more structurally efficient because it carries nearly as much load with much less mass. Later in the unit you will quantify this tradeoff. structure strength stiffness deflection criterion constraint structural efficiency Team Project Kickoff Launch the Bridge Design Project Review the challenge parameters as a team and separate criteria from constraints. Create at least two initial internal bridge concepts. These are starting ideas, not final designs. Label likely chords/girders, verticals, diagonals, deck/cross members, and critical joints. Create a need-to-know list of at least three engineering questions the team must answer before fabrication. Student Resource Bridge Mission Analysis Use the printable mission-analysis sheet to capture criteria, constraints, initial bridge concepts, and need-to-know questions. The resource opens in a clean print-friendly layout and can be printed or saved as a PDF from the browser. Open Bridge Mission Analysis Project Kickoff Record Bridge Mission Analysis / Design Brief This is the official starting record for the Unit 2 project, not a routine worksheet. Criteria and constraints summarized in your own words. At least two labeled initial bridge-structure concepts. A need-to-know list with at least three engineering questions. Format: Use the provided Bridge Mission Analysis template or complete the same evidence in your engineering notebook when directed. Carry Forward Why This Matters Next In Lesson 2.2 you will identify the forces the bridge must resist and predict where early concepts are most likely to fail. Self-Check Can You Explain It? 1. Why is “does not break” an incomplete success criterion? Because the bridge must also meet the stiffness/deflection requirement and mass limit. A structure can remain intact yet deform too much or be too heavy. 2. Why can adding material be a poor structural-engineering solution? Added material usually increases strength or stiffness, but it also increases mass. Efficient structures must balance performance with mass. ← Unit 2 Overview 2.2 Centroids & Center of Gravity → Engineering thinking · Lesson 2.1 Start with requirements, not a shape Sketch two different open-web configurations and label how the midspan load reaches both supports. Check your understanding: How will the 65 mm width limit affect cross-bracing and connector placement? Bridge challenge connection: Apply this result to your planned 400 mm span, 65 mm maximum-width bridge; record evidence in your engineering notebook rather than assuming a design is compliant. Review approved materials and fabrication specifications

pages.description: POE Unit 2 2.19 POE • Unit 2 • Bridge Capstone • Lesson 2.19 Bridge Load Testing Engineering question: Does the finished bridge carry the required 100 N with no more than 10 mm mid
pages.searchText: POE Unit 2 2.19 POE • Unit 2 • Bridge Capstone • Lesson 2.19 Bridge Load Testing Engineering question: Does the finished bridge carry the required 100 N with no more than 10 mm midspan deflection—and what do the real measurements reveal? Start Lab Test Setup Procedure Data Recorder Graph & Qualification What to Submit Official bridge qualification Test only with an instructor. Use your approved bridge from 2.18, the school digital force gauge, a rated mounted fixture, and an independent midspan deflection reference. No repairs once official testing begins. Learning outcomes Replace predictions with evidence Measure Record real force–deflection pairs from one supervised test, including an observation at exactly 100 N if safely reached. Evaluate Check bridge mass, span, outside width and the measured ≤10 mm displacement criterion without confusing estimated or actual data. Explain Use the plotted response and observed damage to compare the test with the structural model from 2.16 and prepare for the final class presentation in 2.20. Suggested pacing: Teams rotate through the instructor-run test while others analyze evidence and prepare reports. Only the teacher selects safe test steps, gauge capacity and stopping rules; no force increments are imposed by this webpage. 01 / Qualification requirements Every requirement matters 100 N Total centered qualification load ≤10 mm Measured midpoint deflection at exactly 100 N 400 mm Clear distance between supports ≤65 mm Outside width including M3 hardware ≤150 g Completed mass including adhesive and connectors Approved only Wood/plywood structure and permitted joints The official 100 N criterion applies to the whole bridge , not independently to each side frame. Meeting a mass or load-to-mass target does not override other dimensional, deflection or manufacturing restrictions. Check complete rules ↗ . 02 / Understand the apparatus Two separate measurements: force and midpoint deflection Digital force gauge rated fixture Applied force (N) 400 mm clear supported span Fixed-datum displacement reader Deflection δ (mm) Guarded safety zone PPE and teacher control Concept only — use an approved mounted rig, never an improvised press Apparatus checklist Teacher-signed 2.18 pre-test inspection and a labeled finished bridge revision. Rigid fixed support fixture with the required clear span; no rocking or slip. Mounted calibrated digital force gauge and a teacher-approved rated loading mechanism. Independent fixed-datum midpoint displacement gauge, dial indicator or properly calibrated viewing setup. Digital scale and calipers for actual mass, clear span and maximum outside width. Guarding, eye protection and an exclusion area for failure debris. Establish an accurate zero Teacher verifies fixture capacity, alignment and support conditions. Locate the intended central loading crossmember and ensure direct vertical loading without eccentricity. Set the force gauge zero according to its operating instructions and the approved preload procedure. Measure the bridge's unloaded midpoint reference with a stationary independent datum . Record all subsequent force and midpoint movement from the same baseline; do not confuse actuator travel with actual bridge deflection. Do not improvise a press or push by hand in place of a rated mounting system. Gauge and fixture ratings must be suitable for the load being applied. 03 / Test safety Teacher controls the force; observers stay clear Before starting Verify that the finished bridge is approved, has cured, and has no unreconciled defects. Check rated capacity of force gauge, attachments, fixture and loading contact. Set teacher-defined force steps, ramp/hold time and maximum allowed force. Position the bridge securely and establish the fixed 0 mm reference. Assign one operator, a load reader, a deflection reader and a recorder. Stop immediately for Unexpected crack, joint separation or progressive splintering. Sideways twist, buckling, loss of support contact or sliding fixture. Sudden uncontrolled deformation or force drop. Force gauge or fixture operating outside its rated range. Any unsafe condition or teacher stop command. No students touch the loaded bridge. The instructor directs unloading and evaluates whether the test can safely continue. Policy: No repair is permitted after the official test begins. If the bridge cannot be tested safely, record an incomplete or stopped test. Testing beyond 100 N for a greater demonstrated load or failure study is optional, instructor-approved and requires a suitably rated guarded rig . 04 / Repeatable procedure Follow these six steps in order 1 · Record pre-test Bridge ID/revision, team, actual mass, span, overall width, gauge ID and signed inspection. 2 · Position and zero Set the supports to the real clear span, center the loading nose, zero force and record the fixed midpoint reference. 3 · Apply approved load Instructor advances to the next authorized increment and allows the reading to stabilize as required. 4 · Log a paired reading Record actual F (N), actual midspan δ (mm), reading order, visible damage and any measurement uncertainty. 5 · Document 100 N If safely achieved, enter the actual simultaneous force and deflection values at 100 N ; record whether deflection is at or below 10 mm. 6 · Stop, inspect and save Teacher stops for completion, apparatus limit or structural damage. Record why, retain photos and export data without repairing the bridge. 05 / Learning resources Watch a truss test and see how engineers use the data DiscoverE: Truss Bridge Challenge Watch the truss change under center loading. Identify the support points, the first visible bending and the differences between classroom demonstrations and our calibrated force-and-deflection test. Open on YouTube ↗ Vernier — Measuring load and deflection An engineering educator explains instrumented bridge-testing strategies and why the force and midspan displacement must be recorded together. Watch the Vernier we
