pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.12 Structural Failure Engineering question: What can failure evidence tell us about how a structure behave
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.12 Structural Failure Engineering question: What can failure evidence tell us about how a structure behaved—and how can we redesign it responsibly? Start Learning Loading Modes Watch Videos Buckling Explorer Failure Detective What to Submit Observe • Classify • Test • Redesign Failure leaves clues. Apply your knowledge of materials, forces and trusses to diagnose structural problems without confusing assumptions, observations or proven causes. Bring: engineering notebook or 2.12 case-study worksheet and a calculator for the optional column calculations. Your learning pathway What you'll learn Complete the resources in sequence. The on-page explanations, technical diagrams and practice are sufficient to complete the assigned case study independently. 01 · Classify Separate an applied loading mode from the way a component failed. 02 · Investigate Recognize buckling, fracture, excessive deformation and connection failure using observations. 03 · Justify Recommend redesign actions and explain how to verify them with evidence. Suggested 45–50 minute learning sequence Classify the forces 8 minutes Watch and take notes 10 minutes Explore column buckling 12 minutes Diagnose case studies 15–20 minutes The historical engineering investigation and extended reflection may be assigned as homework. 01 / First identify what is acting Five loading modes engineers investigate Loading mode describes the internal action or applied force effect. Failure mechanism describes how a structure stops meeting a requirement or loses its ability to carry load. 1 / Loading Axial tension Axial pull Member pulled along its axis. Look for stretching, necking in ductile material, or tensile rupture, depending on material and loading. 2 / Loading Axial compression Buckling Member pushed along its axis. A short member may crush; a slender member may become unstable and buckle first. 3 / Loading Shear Opposing shear directions Opposing parallel forces tend to slide nearby planes relative to one another; see local tearing near a connector or sheared fastener. 4 / Loading Bending Center-loaded shelf A transverse load creates curvature and bending stress. Excessive deflection can make a beam unusable even without rupture. 5 / Loading Torsion Twisting couple A turning couple twists a shaft; it creates shear stress and can cause twisting deformation or fracture. Example: “Compression” alone is not a failure mechanism. A compressed member might crush from material stress, buckle sideways through instability, or remain completely safe at the applied load. You need geometry, force and physical evidence to distinguish these possibilities. 02 / What does failure look like? Four common structural failure mechanisms Observe the difference between loss of stability, material rupture, permanent/excessive deformation and failure at a connection. BUCKLING FRACTURE EXCESS DEFORMATION JOINT SEPARATION Broken connection path Schematic mechanisms; not evidence of a particular material or failure sequence Instability Slender compression member bows sideways. A member can lose stability before its material crushes. Material failure Crack, split, rupture or permanent yielding appears in the loaded material. The failure mode depends on stress and material behavior. Connection failure Adhesive separates, a gusset tears, a fastener slips, or wood splits near a joint. The members themselves can be intact. Serviceability is different from collapse A shelf can sag too far to use, a walkway can vibrate excessively, or a beam can deform beyond its allowable limit without immediately fracturing . Structural design includes both strength and serviceability requirements. For your bridge challenge, passing the 100 N load is not enough; the deflection must also remain at or below 10 mm under that load. Observed sign ≠ proven root cause A broken gusset could result from undersized adhesive area, poor surface preparation, an off-axis load, a brittle substrate or a combination. A photo of the break does not automatically identify the single cause. Good failure analysis compares competing hypotheses to measurements and evidence. 03 / Video learning library Watch and annotate real engineering explanations Begin with column buckling and beam stresses. The short case-study video is optional for the historical investigation and should be viewed respectfully. The Efficient Engineer Understanding Buckling Pause and explain: Sketch a straight and a buckled compression member, then explain why doubling unsupported length reduces the ideal Euler load. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ The Efficient Engineer Understanding Stresses in Beams Pause and explain: Label tension and compression in a bent beam, and explain why shear may also occur. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ Optional case-study video: Hyatt Regency walkway collapse and connection design Tom Scott with Practical Engineering The Disaster That Changed Engineering: The Hyatt Regency Collapse Pause and explain: Compare the two hanger-rod arrangements and name the connection whose load path changed. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ Viewing context This video discusses a real fatal engineering disaster without requiring graphic imagery. Study the design and review decisions—not the human loss as entertainment. 04 / Interactive compression investigation What makes a slender member more likely to buckle? In this illustrative classroom model, apply Euler's elastic buckling equation to a rectangular column. Vary length, thickness, modulus and idealized support condition. The model compares the applied force to the theoretical elastic threshold—not a tested failure load. Unsupported length L 180 mm Weak-axis thickness t 3.0 mm Illustrative modulus E 9,000 N/mm² Applied axial force P 40 N Ideal end condition (effective length factor K) Pinned–pinned · K = 1.0 Fixed–pinned · K ≈ 0.7 Fixed–fixed · K = 0.5 Fixed–free · K = 2.0 18.00 mm⁴ Weak-axis I = bt³/12 49.35 N I

pages.title: Calculating Moments
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.6 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.6 Calculating Moments Engineering question: Why does the same downward load produce different support react
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.6 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.6 Calculating Moments Engineering question: Why does the same downward load produce different support reactions when it moves along a bridge? Start Learning Watch Videos Worked Examples Interactive Labs Self-Check What to Submit Learn • Watch • Calculate • Experiment Forces can cause rotation. Use moment calculations to understand levers, pivot points and why a beam shares its load unequally between two supports. Materials: ruler, pencil, calculator, notebook or Lesson 2.6 worksheet. Learning pathway What you'll learn Everything needed for the introductory calculations, diagrams and self-checks is provided below. 01 · Interpret Recognize forces, moment arms and pivots. 02 · Calculate Find positive and negative moments using perpendicular distance. 03 · Apply Find the reactions of a loaded, simply supported beam. Suggested 45–50 minute learning sequence Observe & predict 5 minutes Read & watch 10 minutes Worked example 15 minutes Experiment & check 15–20 minutes 01 / Core concept Moment = turning effect of a force When you open a door by pushing near the handle, the force acts farther from the hinge and creates more turning effect than the same force applied near the hinge. Force (F) The push or pull; measured in newtons (N). Pivot / moment center (O) The point about which we calculate rotation. Perpendicular distance (d⊥) The shortest distance from the pivot to the force's line of action; measured in meters (m). HOW A FORCE CREATES A MOMENT F = 30 N ↓ Pivot O d⊥ = 0.40 m Clockwise = negative M = −12 N·m The basic moment equation |M O | = F × d⊥ For a force perpendicular to a horizontal lever, the moment arm equals the horizontal distance. 30 N × 0.40 m = 12 N·m . To give the moment a sign, check which way the force tends to rotate the body around the selected point O. Line of action matters The lever arm is not always the distance along the object. It is the shortest perpendicular distance between the pivot and the infinite straight line of action of the force. If the force's line of action passes through O, then d⊥ = 0 and its moment about O is zero , even if the force is large. 02 / Direction and units Clockwise or counterclockwise? We will use the conventional sign system: counterclockwise (CCW) is positive , and clockwise (CW) is negative . SAME DIRECTION FORCE · OPPOSITE ROTATION Down at left Down at right Counterclockwise (+) Clockwise (−) Pivot O Choose a pivot; classify the rotational effect of each force about it. Counterclockwise Positive moment (+) Push down to the left of a pivot, or push up to its right: the tendency is counterclockwise. Clockwise Negative moment (−) Push down to the right of a pivot, or push up to its left: the tendency is clockwise. Units: Moment is N·m (newton-meters). It is dimensionally equivalent to a joule, but moments are not energy and should be labeled N·m. To convert N·mm to N·m, divide by 1,000. 03 / Angled forces Only the perpendicular part creates a moment If a force is not perpendicular to the lever, use the perpendicular force component—or the perpendicular moment arm—to calculate its moment. O 30° F F⊥ = F sin30° Distance r AN ANGLED FORCE USES THE PERPENDICULAR COMPONENT Use the angle between r and F |M| = r F |sin θ| Here r is the straight distance from the pivot to where the force acts, and θ is the angle between the position vector and the force vector. Example: 40 N at 30° below a 0.50 m horizontal lever → |M| = (0.50)(40)(sin30°) = 10 N·m , clockwise, so M = −10 N·m . Use force components instead M = rₓ Fᵧ − rᵧ Fₓ For a horizontal lever extending right from the pivot, rᵧ = 0, so M = rₓFᵧ . Horizontal force Fₓ makes no moment about the pivot in this case. This directly builds on the sine/cosine components in Lesson 2.5. 04 / Video learning library Watch, pause, and solve These two verified lessons cover both the concept of torque/moment and its application to beam support reactions. Use the direct links if YouTube embeds are blocked at school. The Organic Chemistry Tutor · Introduction Torque, Lever Arm, and Moment of Force Watch and do: Sketch one door or lever example. Label the pivot, force, perpendicular lever arm, and CW/CCW direction. Watch on YouTube ↗ Eurocoded · Applied statics Calculate Support Reactions of a Simply Supported Beam with a Point Load Watch and do: Before the example is solved, draw Aᵧ and Bᵧ. Explain why moments about the left support eliminate its reactions. Watch on YouTube ↗ 05 / Worked calculations From a lever to a bridge support reaction Always begin with a free-body diagram, choose a pivot, and write the sign convention beside your equations. Example A · Single moment 30 N downward at 0.40 m Choose the pivot at the left end of a horizontal lever. The downward force acts 0.40 m to the right. Moment magnitude: |M| = Fd = 30(0.40) = 12 N·m . Downward on the right tends clockwise → negative sign. M O = −12 N·m (CW) Interpretation: doubling the force or lever arm doubles the moment magnitude. Example B · Unequal beam reactions 80 N at 1.0 m on a 4.0 m span WORKED EXAMPLE · OFF-CENTER LOAD 80 N ↓ Aᵧ = 60 N Bᵧ = 20 N A B 1.0 m 3.0 m FBD: 80 N downward at x = 1.0 m, reaction Aᵧ at x = 0, reaction Bᵧ at x = 4.0 m. Take moments about A, CCW positive: ΣM A = +Bᵧ(4.0) −80(1.0) = 0 . Solve: Bᵧ = 80/4 = 20 N upward . Vertical equilibrium: ΣFᵧ = Aᵧ +20−80 = 0 , so Aᵧ = 60 N upward . Horizontal: Aₓ = 0 because no horizontal force acts. Aᵧ = 60 N ↑ · Bᵧ = 20 N ↑ Check the same answer about the other support Taking moments about B: ΣM B = +80(3.0) −Aᵧ(4.0) = 240 −240 = 0 N·m . Why choose a support as pivot? Any force whose line of action passes through that chosen pivot has a zero moment about it, eliminating its unknown magnitude from the equation. General rule: Bᵧ = Pa/L · Aᵧ = P(L − a)/L For one downward point load P between a pin at A and roller at B, with span L and load distance a from A. These are equilibrium reactions, not a material strength

Before destructive testing, engineers must predict the critical region and expected failure mode. Objectives What You Will Practice Draw free-body diagrams Identify bending moment trends Distinguish stress from deflection Compare prediction with test evidence Materials What You Need Uniform beam samples Clamp or support fixture Incremental masses Ruler Marker Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Measure the beam geometry and mark several observation stations. Draw the beam, support, applied load, and reactions. Predict the region of maximum bending moment and likely failure location. Predict whether the beam will bend elastically, permanently deform, buckle, or fracture. Load the beam in approved increments and record deflection at one location. Stop at your teacher limit or after failure. Compare the observed behavior with the prediction. Write one reason for any mismatch. pages.title: Introduction to Truss Systems
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.7 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.7 Introduction to Truss Systems Engineering question: How do triangles, joints and member arrangements help
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.7 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.7 Introduction to Truss Systems Engineering question: How do triangles, joints and member arrangements help a bridge support loads with less material? Start Learning Watch Videos Identify Members Explore Designs Self-Check What to Submit Learn • Watch • Explore • Sketch Discover why triangles matter. This lesson focuses on what trusses are, how they are arranged, and how they carry loads . Detailed member-force calculations begin in Lesson 2.8. Materials: pencil, ruler, engineering notebook or 2.7 guided practice materials. Learning pathway What you'll be able to do Work through the explanation, diagrams, videos, and guided practice in order. Answers are hidden until you choose to reveal them. 01 · Identify Find chords, web members, joints and supports in a truss. 02 · Explain Compare triangulated and unbraced frames; describe tension and compression. 03 · Compare Recognize Pratt, Howe and Warren arrangements and trace conceptual load paths. Suggested 45–50 minute learning sequence Predict & observe 5 minutes Read & watch 10–12 minutes Explore parts & types 15 minutes Sketch & explain 15–18 minutes 01 / Understand the engineering system What makes a structure a truss? A truss is a connected system of slender members arranged in a rigid framework, often forming triangles. Trusses appear in bridges, rooftops, towers, cranes and aerospace structures. Ideal analysis model Members meet at joints In a simple planar truss model , straight members connect through frictionless pin joints, loads and reactions act at the joints, and each member is a two-force member . For this model, members transmit axial tension or compression rather than significant bending moments. Real construction Connections are not perfectly ideal Real bridges often use bolts, gusset plates or welds, and their members also have self-weight. Loads from a deck are transferred through its floor system to the truss joints. Real joints and eccentric forces can also introduce bending. Engineering distinction: An ideal pin-jointed truss is an approximation—not a promise that every real member carries only pure axial force. Two important forces inside a member A C B Applied load P Upward reaction Upward reaction Compression (AC) Compression (BC) Tension (AB) Tension — pulled apart An axial force that stretches a member. Picture a rope being pulled from both ends. In the particular symmetric triangle above, the bottom tie AB is in tension. Compression — pushed together An axial force that shortens a member. Picture pushing both ends of a straw together. In the drawn ideal triangle under apex load, AC and BC are in compression. Important: You cannot determine whether every diagonal is in tension or compression merely from its angle or the truss's name. The answer depends on the loads, supports and member arrangement. The labels above apply only to this specific example. 02 / Why triangles? Triangles resist changes in shape With ideal pinned joints and fixed-length bars, an unbraced four-sided frame can change its angles without stretching its bars. A triangle cannot change shape without changing a bar length. Compare standard frames Push unbraced frame sideways FOUR BARS · NO DIAGONAL FOUR BARS + DIAGONAL Can deform by rotating at the pins Triangulated · in-plane geometry restrained Schematic only: not a numerical deformation or strength simulation. Unbraced vs. braced A four-bar quadrilateral can distort through joint rotation. One diagonal divides it into two triangles and eliminates this ideal in-plane mechanism. Why diagonals help A diagonal brace gives a rectangular panel two triangles and restricts sideways racking. On an ideal truss, this can maintain the geometry without requiring a joint to resist bending. Question: Would a diagonal be equally effective if it were missing its connection at one endpoint? Why? Reveal answer No. The brace must transfer force through its connections. Without a complete load path to the joints, the diagonal cannot restrain the frame as intended. Important limitation Triangulation is a geometric stability concept , not a complete structural safety check. Even a correctly triangulated truss can fail from member buckling, yielding, broken joints, poor lateral bracing or overload. Think beyond the drawing: A flat truss can be rigid in its own plane but still need out-of-plane bracing to prevent sideways buckling. 03 / Interactive truss anatomy Identify every structural component Select a member category to highlight it. This eight-joint example is a simplified pin-and-roller truss, not a full bridge design. All members Top chord Bottom chord Verticals Diagonals Joints SELECT A PART TO HIGHLIGHT Member AB, bottom Member BC, bottom Member CD, bottom Member DE, bottom Member FG, top Member GH, top Member BF, vertical Member CG, vertical Member DH, vertical Member AF, diagonal Member FC, diagonal Member CH, diagonal Member HE, diagonal A B C D E F G H 8 joints 13 members Ideal pin–roller representation Complete truss Eight joints (A–H), thirteen straight members, pin at A, roller at E. Select a category to inspect it. Top + bottom chord Main longitudinal members Web members Vertical and diagonal connections Nodes / joints Where members meet and forces are transferred How to name members and joints Joints are named with single letters such as A and F . A member joining those points is named AF . The top chord contains members FG and GH; the bottom chord contains AB, BC, CD and DE. Count check: This example has eight joints and thirteen members, with three external reaction components from the pin-and-roller support model. The ideal planar determinacy count is m + r = 2j → 13 + 3 = 2(8). This is a necessary counting check ; by itself, it does not prove every arrangement is stable. 04 / Video learning library See real trusses explained Watch the overview before the more technical video. The longer video introduces calculations from fut

pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.13 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.13 Materials Testing Lab Engineering question: Which of our actual material strips resists bending most ef
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.13 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.13 Materials Testing Lab Engineering question: Which of our actual material strips resists bending most effectively—and how confident are we in the measurements? Start Lab Build Test Station Testing Steps Enter Real Data Graph & Analyze What to Submit Hands-on experimental engineering Today we test real samples. Use pre-cut strips of different materials, a digital force gauge and measurement tools to collect paired force–deflection readings . These are actual experimental measurements—not the hypothetical material presets used in Lesson 2.11. The mission A fair comparison of materials You will load strips across two supports, measure how far the midpoint deflects, then plot force against deflection. Use the graph's early straight-line slope to compare experimental bending stiffness . 01 · Measure Record actual width, thickness, support span, orientation and force-gauge units. 02 · Test Apply increasing force carefully while measuring midspan deflection. 03 · Explain Graph your paired measurements, compare slopes and identify experimental uncertainty. Today's variables: Independent variable for comparison = material. Observed response = deflection under loading, or equivalently the force–deflection slope k = ΔF/Δδ. Controlled variables = support span, nominal specimen geometry, orientation, loading point, method and measurement technique. Always measure actual strip dimensions, even if pre-cut to identical nominal sizes. Recommended schedule Prepare & check 5–10 min Demonstration 5 min Run tests 25–35 min Graph & analyze 20–30 min, next class if needed Suggested two-session lesson: one 45–50 minute session for physical testing and another short session for analysis, reflection and final lab submission. The instructor may adjust group size and timing to match available gauges and specimens. 01 / Station inventory Equipment and responsibilities You already have the pre-cut material samples and digital force gauges. Each group also needs a stable way to support and measure the strips. Required equipment At least two materials in strips of the same nominal size; label specimen IDs. One digital force gauge with an appropriate compression range and safe contact tip. Two equally high, fixed, rounded supports with measured and adjustable center-to-center spacing. Metric ruler and calipers to measure span, width and thickness. A fixed ruler or dial indicator measuring midpoint deflection; a fixed side camera with a metric reference scale is an acceptable observation aid. Safety glasses, stable work surface and teacher-approved fixture or support arrangement. Optional: digital scale for specimen mass, camera for evidence, a gauge stand to improve axial alignment and spreadsheets for analysis. Assign a team of 3–4 Operator Applies controlled, gradual load with gauge; communicates current reading. Measurement lead Observes center movement from a safe side position without touching the specimen. Recorder / safety Records paired values and watches for damage or test-limit exceedance. Switch roles between specimens when time and equipment permit. No one holds the test strip by hand during loading. Lab kit · six different materials (one strip of each) Specimen Material Nominal dimensions Kit quantity A Steel 1/8 in × 1 in × 12 in 1 B Carbon fiber 1/8 in × 1 in × 12 in 1 C Wood paint stick Standard size; measure actual dimensions 1 D Aluminum 1/8 in × 1 in × 12 in 1 E Polyethylene (black) 1/8 in × 1 in × 12 in 1 F Delrin (white, acetal/POM) 1/8 in × 1 in × 12 in 1 Nominal metal/composite/polymer bar dimensions are 3.175 × 25.4 × 304.8 mm. These are not measured values. Caliper-measure every specimen. The wood paint stick is not necessarily the same size. Delrin is acetal (POM), not polyethylene. Instrument safety: A steel bar or carbon-fiber bar may not deflect enough to measure before reaching your gauge's allowed capacity. Do not exceed the gauge/fixture limit to get results. Record “not tested—gauge capacity” or “deflection below resolution” as appropriate. Protect against carbon-fiber splinters; do not intentionally break specimens. Record consistent timing for viscoelastic polymer strips. 02 / Set up the test Three-point bending: two supports, one center load Position the strip across two rounded supports and push straight downward at midspan using the digital force gauge. Measure the displacement of the strip itself, using a stationary reference attached to the fixture rather than the moving gauge. SIMPLE THREE-POINT BENDING FIXTURE DIGITAL FORCE GAUGE (N) MEASURED SUPPORT SPAN L (mm) δ: center deflection Fixed ruler / camera reference Sample strip width b, thickness t Teaching schematic: gauge and loading tip must be steady, aligned, and instructor-approved Before loading Secure the fixture so the supports cannot slide or tip. Both supports must have the same height and a consistent contact shape. Choose a common measured span L that safely fits the shortest strips, with enough overhang at both ends to stay seated. Mark midpoint between the supports. Align a rounded gauge tip perpendicular to the strip over the mark. Fix a ruler/indicator or camera reference so deflection is read relative to the unloaded specimen, not relative to a moving hand. Check digital gauge capacity and set compression units to N if supported; otherwise convert readings before analysis. Under instructor supervision, gently contact the specimen, tare force appropriately and set displacement to zero at the same reference state without appreciable preload. Measure each individual strip Width b t Viewed at the midpoint: record true b and t for each sample Record strip overall length , width b , and thickness t at the center (mm). Also record grain/ply/print orientation, any knots, chips or defects and measured mass if a scale is available. Cross-section I = bt³ / 12 (mm⁴) Important: t is the thickness in the direction of bending . Incorrectly swapping b an

pages.title: Truss Design & Simulation
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.10 Truss Design & Simulation Engineering question: How can we design, simulate and fairly compare trusses
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.10 Truss Design & Simulation Engineering question: How can we design, simulate and fairly compare trusses before they are fabricated? Start Learning Watch Tutorials Model Setup Interactive Comparison Practice What to Submit Model • Analyze • Verify • Improve Compare two designs using evidence. Create valid truss models, hold the test conditions constant, compare force and deflection results and justify the trade-off between stiffness and material use. Materials: computer, engineering notebook and calculator; a free on-page simulation is provided. Learning pathway Learning targets This lesson moves from the prescribed-force calculations in 2.9 to engineering decisions based on competing performance measures. 01 · Model Define connected joints, members, loads, supports, E and area. 02 · Read results Explain reactions, tension/compression and joint deflection. 03 · Compare Change one design parameter and support your recommendation with numerical evidence. Suggested 45–50 minute sequence Concepts 5 minutes Video tutorial 10 minutes Model setup 10–12 minutes Comparison 15 minutes Evidence and reflection 5–8 minutes 01 / Understand what is being calculated What can a truss simulation tell us? A truss solver models axial-only members connected at idealized joints. It combines node coordinates, member properties, restraints and external loads to calculate the forces and motion needed for equilibrium. Outputs What a simple 2D truss model estimates Support reactions: forces exerted by restraints, in N. Axial member forces: tension (+) or compression (−), in N. Nodal displacements: how far joints move in x/y, in mm, if E and member cross-section area A are provided. Total member length: useful as a material-use estimate, not finished mass. Model limitations What the solver doesn't automatically prove Axial force is not failure capacity. Even with small simulated displacement, a real member may buckle, crack or fail at a connection. A 2D side-frame model omits the deck, lateral bracing, joints, manufacturing tolerance and three-dimensional effects. Do not treat the simulated result as a safety certification or a complete check of the later Unit 2 bridge challenge. Axial stiffness = EA / L · Average axial stress = F / A E is elastic modulus (N/mm²); A is cross-sectional area (mm²); L is member length (mm). Truss force and deformation depend on geometry, loading, and stiffness under the chosen assumptions. 02 / Build a valid model Geometry, supports and loads come first Use the five-joint, seven-member truss below for your baseline. All coordinates are measured in millimeters. This is an educational side-truss model , not an approved finished bridge. Baseline geometry A B C D E 100 N ↓ 400 mm support span • 90 mm baseline rise Joint x (mm) y (mm) Function A 0 0 Pin B 200 0 100 N down C 400 0 Roller D 100 90 Upper joint E 300 90 Upper joint Members: AB, BC, AD, DB, BE, EC, DE. Design B changes only upper joint height to 140 mm. Controlled inputs for the first comparison Input Classroom value Span 400 mm Load 100 N downward at B Supports A pin (x/y); C roller (y only) Elastic modulus E 3,000 N/mm² Each member area A 25 mm² Change between designs Rise: 90 mm vs. 140 mm These material properties are hypothetical teaching values. They are not certified properties of your manufactured bridge or a guarantee of printable member strength. Before running: For a centered 100 N load, static equilibrium predicts 50 N upward at each support . Use that result as a software sanity check. Six-step simulation workflow 1. Create joints Enter coordinates from the table; avoid accidental duplicate, unconnected nodes. 2. Add members Connect the seven pairs as pin-jointed, axial truss elements. 3. Add restraints Pin A; roller C. Missing restraints can make the model unstable. 4. Apply force and EA 100 N down at B, and the same E/A for all members. 5. Solve and examine Record support reactions, member forces and vertical displacement at B. 6. Compare fairly Duplicate the model, change D/E height only and solve again. Model debugging: An unstable/singular result often means a missing restraint, unconnected joint or mechanism. Unexpectedly large displacements often indicate incorrect units or insufficient stiffness. Check N vs. kN, mm vs. m, and whether the tool uses N/mm² or another modulus unit. 03 / Video learning library Watch real modeling workflows Watch the SkyCiv lesson first to see a truss defined and solved. Use the next lesson to review how to interpret axial-force results. The third video is an optional professional-software example. SkyCiv Engineering · Software walkthrough Free Online Truss Calculator Tutorial While watching: Write the order in which the instructor specifies nodes, members, supports, applied forces and solution outputs. Watch on YouTube ↗ The Efficient Engineer · Concept review Understanding and Analysing Trusses While watching: Identify two ideal-truss assumptions and explain how tension differs from compression. Watch on YouTube ↗ Optional extension: 2D Truss Analysis with ANSYS Workbench Learn Finite Element Analysis · Advanced 2D Truss Analysis with ANSYS Workbench While watching: Observe where material settings, constraints and result plots appear. ANSYS software is not required for this lesson. Watch on YouTube ↗ What to focus on The engineering workflow is transferable. Detailed finite-element meshing and professional ANSYS interfaces are beyond today's requirements. 04 / Try a second simulator External modeling and reference resources Use the built-in model below or an approved online solver. Free tool features can differ, especially whether nodal displacements are supported. SkyCiv Free Truss Calculator Build 2D pin-jointed trusses and inspect reactions and axial forces. Check whether your chosen edition reports displacement. Open SkyCiv Truss Calculator ↗ SkyCiv's truss modeling walkthrough ↗ StructureCalcs Truss

pages.title: Calculating Truss Forces
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.8 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.8 Calculating Truss Forces Engineering question: How can we calculate the internal force in each truss memb
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.8 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.8 Calculating Truss Forces Engineering question: How can we calculate the internal force in each truss member using equilibrium at its joints? Start Learning Watch Videos Solved Example Interactive Truss Practice What to Submit Learn • Calculate • Explore • Check Find the force in every member. Build on Lessons 2.4–2.7 to solve a simple pin-jointed truss using the method of joints , including force directions and compression versus tension. Materials: pencil, ruler, calculator in degree mode and the Lesson 2.8 classwork/homework worksheet or notebook. Learning pathway What you'll be able to do Complete the modules in order. Read the worked example and sketch force arrows before revealing the practice answers. 01 · Find reactions Apply whole-truss equilibrium before calculating internal forces. 02 · Solve joints Isolate a joint and use ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣFᵧ = 0. 03 · Classify members Explain what positive and negative assumed-tension answers mean. Suggested 45–50 minute sequence Concept & conventions 5 minutes Instructional video 10–12 minutes Follow full solution 15 minutes Explorer & practice 15–18 minutes Finish the remaining practice and worksheet outside class as assigned. 01 / Fundamentals How does the method of joints work? Every joint of an ideal truss is in equilibrium. If you isolate one joint, all connected members exert forces along their own axes, and those forces must balance the applied loads and support reactions at that joint. Read the reference method ↗ Whole-truss FBD Start with supports and external forces. Reactions usually come from ΣM = 0, ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣFᵧ = 0. Joint FBD Isolate a single pin as a dot. Draw connected member forces along member directions plus any external loads at that joint. At most two unknowns A 2D joint gives two independent force equations: ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣFᵧ = 0. Start with a joint containing no more than two unknowns. Assume unknown members are in tension Initially draw an unknown member force away from the isolated joint. After solving, a positive force means tension (a pull). A negative force means compression (a push); the real force acts in the direction opposite the assumed arrow. Rule: +F = tension under the outward-arrow convention; −F = compression. Ideal-model assumptions Members are straight, weightless two-force members; ideal joints are frictionless pins; loads act at joints; and the structure is in static equilibrium. Actual manufactured bridges have connection stiffness, self-weight, imperfections and bending effects. Critical: A calculated axial force is not a load limit or proof that a bridge will withstand that force. Real designs also require member strength, buckling, connection and stability checks. Whole structure: ΣM = 0 Individual joint: ΣFₓ = 0 Individual joint: ΣFᵧ = 0 02 / Your repeatable process A five-step method students can follow 1 · Draw the truss Mark all loads, supports, geometry and joint labels. 2 · Find reactions Use whole-truss moment and force equilibrium. 3 · Choose a joint Start where at most two member forces are unknown. 4 · Resolve & solve Draw outward assumed-tension arrows; use x/y components. 5 · Transfer member forces and check When a member force is found, transfer its correct direction to the joint at the other end. For tension, the member pulls both joints toward itself along its axis (away from each isolated joint); for compression, it pushes outward on each joint. Check force equilibrium at a remaining joint to catch sign errors. Geometry shortcut: For a right triangle with rise h , horizontal run r and diagonal length d , sin θ = h/d and cos θ = r/d. Units cancel in these ratios. 03 / Video learning library Learn from fully worked examples Start with the step-by-step Jeff Hanson lesson, then use the second explanation to reinforce how negative values identify compression. Both are linked directly if embeds are blocked by the school network. Jeff Hanson · Worked statics lesson Statics Lesson 48: Trusses, Method of Joints Pause and practice: At 01:46 find support reactions; at 04:19 note how the first joint is selected; at 06:53 sketch assumed-tension member arrows. Watch on YouTube ↗ Engineer4Free · Second explanation Truss Analysis by Method of Joints Explained Pause and practice: Try drawing the joint FBD yourself. Decide whether a negative answer is a mistake or a compression force. Watch on YouTube ↗ Optional extension: a member that carries zero force Some members carry no axial force under a particular idealized load case. The on-page zero-force-member example below introduces the simplest inspection rule; identifying many zero-force members is extended in Lesson 2.9. 04 / Fully worked example Analyze an entire triangular truss A triangular truss spans 4.0 m with supports A (pin) and B (roller). Apex C is centered 1.5 m above the base. An external 120 N downward point load acts at C. Neglect the truss's self-weight. P = 120 N Aᵧ = +60 N Bᵧ = +60 N A B C AC: 100 N (C) BC: 100 N (C) AB: 80 N (T) Span: 4.0 m · rise: 1.5 m · half-run: 2.0 m Step 1 · Reactions Find Aᵧ and Bᵧ Use the whole truss , with CCW moments positive and coordinates measured from A. ΣM A = Bᵧ(4) −120(2) = 0 Bᵧ = 60 N upward . ΣFᵧ = Aᵧ +60−120 = 0 Aᵧ = 60 N upward ; Aₓ = 0 because no horizontal external load acts. Step 2 · Geometry Resolve member directions Each diagonal has a horizontal run of 2.0 m and vertical rise of 1.5 m . Diagonal length d = √(2² + 1.5²) = 2.5 m . sin θ = 1.5/2.5 = 0.6 cos θ = 2.0/2.5 = 0.8 θ = arctan(1.5/2) ≈ 36.87° above the horizontal. These two ratios will simplify both joint equations. Step 3 · Joint C Calculate AC and BC (diagonals) 100 N (AC pushes) 100 N (BC pushes) 120 N ↓ C ΣFᵧ: +60 +60 −120 = 0 N ΣFₓ: −80 +80 = 0 N Actual compression arrows PUSH on the isolated joint. Start with both unknown member forces assumed in tension: at joint C, draw arrows along CA and CB pointing down-left and down-right. Symmetry gives F AC = F B

pages.title: Free-Body Diagrams
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.4 Free-Body Diagrams Engineering question: How do we isolate a system to identify the forces that act on it
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.4 Free-Body Diagrams Engineering question: How do we isolate a system to identify the forces that act on it? Start Learning Watch Videos Worked Example Interactive FBD Builder Self-Check What to Submit Learn • Watch • Draw • Check Make invisible forces visible. Learn to isolate a body, replace constraints with reactions, and verify a diagram with equilibrium. Materials: pencil, ruler, calculator, engineering notebook or Lesson 2.4 classwork/homework packet. Your learning pathway Learning targets Follow the modules in order. Pause the videos and draw on paper before viewing the solutions. 01 · Isolate Choose a system boundary and draw only the selected body. 02 · Identify Replace supports with external forces and reactions. 03 · Check Label each force and apply simple equilibrium checks. Suggested 45–50 minute sequence Observe & predict 5 minutes Read & watch 10 minutes Worked examples 15 minutes Builder & practice 15–20 minutes 01 / Understand What is a free-body diagram? An FBD is a simplified drawing of one isolated body with all external forces and relevant external moments acting on that body . Choose the body What are we analyzing? A box, lamp, beam or an entire structure can be our body. Redraw it alone as a simplified line, rectangle or point. Remove the table, cables, ground or supports from the isolated view. We select the system boundary first: only interactions that cross this boundary create external loads on our FBD. Show the forces Replace the surroundings with arrows Every interaction with something outside the body becomes a force or moment as appropriate. Include gravity, applied loads and reactions. Draw and label arrows with correct directions. Important: Do not draw both members of a Newton's third-law pair on the same body's FBD. The table's upward force on a box belongs; the box's downward force on the table does not. Example: 12 kg box on a level table ON THE TABLE ISOLATED CRATE 12 kg N = 117.6 N W = 117.6 N Weight: W = mg = (12 kg)(9.8 m/s²) = 117.6 N downward . The stationary crate receives an upward normal reaction N = 117.6 N . The table itself does not appear in the isolated crate diagram. 02 / Force vocabulary and supports Which forces should you include? Each arrow must have a known or assumed direction, a label and a point or line where it acts. Weight W Gravity pulling the body downward; W = mg. Normal N Contact force perpendicular to a surface. Tension T Force exerted by a taut cable along its length. Applied force P or F Known push, pull or externally applied load. Friction f Force parallel to contact resisting relative sliding. Reactions Aₓ, Aᵧ, Bᵧ Unknown support forces created by constraints. Recognize the three main support symbols PIN Aᵧ Aₓ 2 force components ROLLER Bᵧ 1 normal reaction FIXED Fᵧ Fₓ M 2 forces + moment Pin and roller An ideal pin can exert horizontal and vertical forces, but no reaction moment. An ideal roller on flat ground exerts one vertical normal reaction. A roller on a sloping surface reacts perpendicular to that surface. Fixed connection and cable A fixed support can exert horizontal force, vertical force and a resisting moment. A taut cable only pulls along the cable . We will calculate reaction moments later in Unit 2. 03 / Video library Watch and sketch along Begin with the engineering mechanics introduction. Use the second video for everyday weight, tension, friction and normal-force situations. If embedded playback is blocked, use the YouTube links. Spoon Feed Me · Intro engineering mechanics Introduction to Free Body Diagrams (FBD) | Statics While watching: Pause at the simply supported beam and write down which reactions the supports can supply. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ The Organic Chemistry Tutor · Force examples Free Body Diagrams — Tension, Friction, Inclined Planes & Net Force While watching: Sketch a hanging object, then compare your chosen arrows with the explanation. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ Optional advanced video: how FBDs lead to shear and moment diagrams The Efficient Engineer · Beyond today's lesson Understanding Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams While watching: Notice that engineers draw a beam FBD before evaluating its internal shear and bending moments. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ What is optional? Internal shear/moment diagrams and their calculations are beyond Lesson 2.4. Use the video to preview why an accurate FBD matters for later engineering analysis. 04 / Worked beam example From physical setup to force diagram A simply supported beam carries a 60 N downward point load at its midpoint , with pin A and roller B 4 m apart. Neglect the beam's self-weight. 1. Physical setup PHYSICAL SETUP 60 N downward A · pin B · roller Span L = 4.0 m Beam self-weight ignored in this example Identify the beam as the body. The load, pin and roller interact with it from the outside. 2. Isolated beam FBD FREE-BODY DIAGRAM · BEAM ONLY P = 60 N Aᵧ = 30 N Bᵧ = 30 N Aₓ = 0 A B Remove the physical support symbols and add their possible reactions. Here Aₓ = 0 N because there is no horizontal load. 3. Use equilibrium and symmetry Horizontal: ΣFₓ = Aₓ = 0 . Vertical: ΣFᵧ = Aᵧ + Bᵧ − 60 = 0 . The load is at the center and the arrangement is symmetric, so Aᵧ = Bᵧ . Therefore Aᵧ = Bᵧ = 30 N upward . +30 N +30 N −60 N = 0 N Do not split off-center loads equally. For an off-center point load, support reactions differ. We'll solve those cases using moments in Lesson 2.6. 05 / Interactive FBD builder Reveal the forces step by step Before pressing each button, predict what the drawing should contain. Then adjust the centered load to test whether your reaction forces still balance. Centered load P: 60 N 1 · Isolate 2 · Add load 3 · Add reactions 4 · Check balance BEAM ISOLATED · 4.0 m SPAN A B P = 60 N Aᵧ = ? Bᵧ = ? Aₓ = ? 30 + 30 − 60 = 0 N Step 1 · Isolate The beam is alone. Which forces from the original physical setup will act on this body? Teaching

pages.title: Calculating Force Vectors
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.5 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.5 Calculating Force Vectors Engineering question: How can we describe an angled force using horizontal and
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.5 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.5 Calculating Force Vectors Engineering question: How can we describe an angled force using horizontal and vertical components—and combine several forces into one resultant? Start Learning Watch Videos Worked Examples Interactive Vectors Practice What to Submit Learn • Watch • Resolve • Combine Think in two directions. Develop the vector math you will use with force diagrams, support reactions, and diagonal members in the bridge project. Bring: calculator in degree mode, pencil, ruler, engineering notebook or 2.5 worksheet. Learning pathway What you'll learn Complete the modules in order. The diagrams and video prompts are designed for learning without a separate teacher presentation. 01 · Describe Distinguish a force's magnitude, direction and x/y components. 02 · Calculate Resolve forces using sine and cosine and assign correct signs. 03 · Combine Add component forces and find a resultant's magnitude and direction. Suggested 45–50 minute sequence Observe & predict 5 minutes Learn & watch 10–12 minutes Worked examples 12–15 minutes Explore & check 15–18 minutes For independent pacing, you can use the optional short video and additional practice after class. 01 / Start with direction A force is a vector, not just a number A scalar has magnitude only (such as 100 kg of mass). A vector has magnitude and direction (such as a 100 N pull at 30° upward and to the right). Magnitude How strong is the force? Measured in newtons (N); magnitude is never negative. Direction Which way does it act? An angle must be measured from a clearly identified reference axis. Components How much of that force acts along the x and y axes? These values can be positive, negative or zero. Think before you calculate Imagine a cable pulling a joint up and right. Do you expect both x and y components to be positive? What if the cable pulls down and right instead? Check your prediction Up/right gives +x, +y . Down/right gives +x, −y . The force magnitude stays positive; component signs tell us the direction. Our angle convention We measure θ counterclockwise from the positive x-axis , unless a problem explicitly says otherwise. A clockwise angle can be written as negative. Calculator: Set the trig mode to DEG (degrees) , not radians, for all problems on this page. 02 / Resolve one force One diagonal force = two perpendicular components To resolve means to replace one vector with horizontal and vertical vectors that add back to the original force. +x +y θ = 30° Fₓ = +86.6 N Fᵧ = +50.0 N F = 100 N O Horizontal The adjacent leg Fₓ = F cos θ Fₓ lies along the x-axis. For the drawn 30° force, cosine calculates the horizontal share. Fₓ = 100 cos 30° ≈ +86.60 N Vertical The opposite leg Fᵧ = F sin θ Fᵧ lies along the y-axis. For the drawn 30° force, sine calculates the vertical share. Fᵧ = 100 sin 30° = +50.00 N Memory trick: COS = Adjacent / Hypotenuse; SIN = Opposite / Hypotenuse. The force F is the triangle's hypotenuse. These expressions assume θ is measured from +x ; otherwise identify the adjacent and opposite legs first. 03 / Quadrants and signs Direction tells you the sign The same positive force magnitude can generate positive or negative components depending on which quadrant contains the vector. +x +y I II III IV +x, +y −x, +y −x, −y +x, −y O Standard-angle convention: 0° points right, 90° points up, 180° points left, and −90° points down. Examples using signed angles from +x Angle θ Fₓ Fᵧ +30° Positive Positive +150° Negative Positive −135° Negative Negative −60° Positive Negative Worked sign check: For 50 N at −60°, Fₓ = 50 cos(−60°) = +25.0 N ; Fᵧ = 50 sin(−60°) = −43.30 N . Angle measured from the vertical? If α is measured from the positive y-axis toward the positive x-axis in quadrant I, then Fₓ = F sin α and Fᵧ = F cos α. This is because horizontal is opposite α and vertical is adjacent α. Always sketch before choosing sine or cosine. 04 / Video lessons Watch, pause, and work along Begin with vector basics, then study analytical vector addition. The short third video is helpful if you only need a quick review of resolving one force. The Organic Chemistry Tutor Vectors — Basic Introduction — Physics Pause and practice: Write the difference between a scalar and vector, then draw one force with a positive x component and negative y component. Open on YouTube ↗ The Organic Chemistry Tutor Addition of Vectors By Means of Components — Physics Pause and practice: Pause before the resultant is calculated. Try adding x components and y components independently. Open on YouTube ↗ Short optional refresher: resolving x and y components Kim Ketelsleger · Short review Resolving a force into x & y components Pause and practice: Predict which leg is adjacent to the stated angle and label the signs. Open on YouTube ↗ Video viewing checklist Which angle is used and from which axis is it measured? Why are cosine and sine both needed? How does adding components simplify two-force problems? 05 / Complete worked examples Calculate, interpret, and verify Follow the same method every time: sketch axes → identify θ → resolve → assign signs → check the result. Example A · One force 100 N cable at +30° Draw: F points up/right. θ = +30° from +x. Calculate horizontal: Fₓ = (100)cos30° = +86.60 N . Calculate vertical: Fᵧ = (100)sin30° = +50.00 N . Check magnitude: √(86.60² + 50.00²) ≈ 100 N . Interpret: The cable's horizontal pull is larger than its upward pull. F = (86.60 i + 50.00 j) N Example B · Two forces 80 N @ +45° and 50 N @ −60° +x +y F₁ = 80 N @ +45° F₂ = 50 N @ −60° R ≈ 82.64 N @ +9.24° Force Fₓ (N) Fᵧ (N) F₁ = 80 N @ +45° +56.57 +56.57 F₂ = 50 N @ −60° +25.00 −43.30 Sum +81.57 +13.27 Magnitude: R = √(81.57² + 13.27²) = 82.64 N . Direction: θ = atan2(+13.27, +81.57) ≈ +9.24° above +x. Intermediate values are rounded for display. Calculations use unrounded component values. The complete resultant method Rₓ = ΣFₓ · Rᵧ = ΣFᵧ Add only x components together; ad

pages.title: Structural Materials & Properties
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.11 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.11 Structural Materials & Properties Engineering question: How do engineers choose a material that is stif
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.11 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.11 Structural Materials & Properties Engineering question: How do engineers choose a material that is stiff enough, strong enough and light enough for a particular job? Start Learning Watch Videos See Grain & Layers Interactive Bending Lab Selection Matrix What to Submit Observe • Calculate • Evaluate • Select Materials are engineering decisions. Connect stress–strain behavior, density, grain orientation and fabrication choices to the bridge project—then defend a selection using evidence. Bring: calculator, engineering notebook or Lesson 2.11 materials comparison worksheet. Learning pathway What you'll learn Use the reading, short videos and diagrams to learn each concept. Then compare two specimens in an interactive three-point bending model. The later materials lab will replace illustrative properties with measurements. 01 · Describe Distinguish stiffness, strength, density, ductility and toughness. 02 · Investigate Predict the effects of grain, material choice and specimen thickness on deflection. 03 · Select Use an evidence-based matrix for a beam, post and bridge connection. Suggested 45–50 minute pathway Observe 5 minutes Read and watch 10–12 minutes Run virtual tests 15 minutes Compare and explain 15–18 minutes 01 / What does “better” mean? Five important material properties Different materials may perform best for different engineering requirements. A material that is very stiff may not be the lightest or the toughest. Stiffness How strongly a material resists elastic deformation . Material stiffness is commonly measured by elastic modulus E . Structural bending stiffness depends on EI , so geometry also matters. Strength Resistance to failure or permanent deformation under a specified loading mode. Tensile, compressive and bending strengths are not interchangeable. Density Mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V . Low density can help meet a mass limit, but density alone does not establish load capacity. Ductility Ability to undergo plastic deformation before fracture. Not every material yields in the same way; brittle materials may fracture with little plastic deformation. Toughness Energy absorbed per unit volume before fracture, represented qualitatively by total area under a stress–strain curve. Directional behavior Properties may depend on orientation: wood grain, plywood plies and 3D-print layers can all make a material behave differently in different directions. Material behavior vs. structure behavior The elastic modulus E describes material stiffness. A beam's bending stiffness EI also includes its area moment of inertia I, which depends on the cross-section shape and orientation. Critical distinction: A thicker strip can bend less even if made from the same material. Lower deflection alone does not mean the material has a larger E or higher strength. Stress and strain σ = F/A · ε = ΔL/L₀ · E = σ/ε (linear elastic range) Axial stress σ is measured in N/mm², strain ε has no units, and E is the initial elastic slope of the stress–strain curve. 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa. Always state the loading mode when comparing material strengths. 02 / Learn to read evidence What does a stress–strain graph reveal? The initial slope identifies the elastic modulus. The curve's later behavior helps describe yielding, ductility and fracture—but you must not assume all materials have the same shaped curve. Strain (deformation ÷ initial length) → Stress (force ÷ area) → Ductile (qualitative) Brittle Yield region Fracture Initial slope = E Toughness relates to the area under the stress–strain curve Illustrative curves only, not data for basswood, plywood or PLA Understand the slope In a simple tensile test, stress ÷ strain in the initial linear region gives E. A steeper initial slope means greater material axial stiffness for the specific loading direction being measured. Why isn't a high E the same as high strength? Elastic modulus describes how much the material stretches under a stress in the elastic region, not the stress at which it yields, cracks or breaks. Strong and stiff are separate properties. Why toughness matters Two materials can reach similar maximum stress yet absorb very different amounts of energy before fracture. One can fail suddenly; another may deform substantially. Where is toughness on the graph? It is associated with total area under the stress–strain curve through fracture, expressed as energy per unit volume. The graphic is qualitative and contains no material-specific data. 03 / Natural and manufactured materials Wood grain, plywood plies and print orientation Structure inside a material can change its behavior. For wood, grain, moisture, knots and fiber alignment matter; plywood uses bonded cross-oriented veneer layers. SOLID WOOD · ALONG SOLID WOOD · ACROSS PLYWOOD · PLIES → long ply ⊥ cross ply → long ply ⊥ cross ply → long ply Load along fibers Load across fibers Alternating veneer directions These are schematic orientations—not guaranteed strength rankings for every species or panel. Wood strips and craft sticks Balsa and basswood strips are natural wood. A property measured along the fibers may differ greatly from a property measured across the fibers . Defects, moisture, species and sample variability complicate simple comparisons. For bridge members: record grain direction and avoid assuming each wooden strip has identical stiffness or strength. Plywood and layered fabrication Plywood bonds multiple veneer plies, usually with successive grain directions crossed. This improves directional balance and dimensional stability, but bending properties still depend on layup, thickness and panel orientation. For bridge gussets: document thickness, grain/face direction and joint layout. Cutting defects and glue quality affect real performance. Printed polymer orientation is another useful comparison A 3D-printed coupon can behave differently when loaded along deposited roads versus across layer bonds. Results depe

pages.title: Advanced Truss Analysis
pages.description: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.9 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.9 Advanced Truss Analysis Engineering question: How can we find forces in selected members of a larger trus
pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.9 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.9 Advanced Truss Analysis Engineering question: How can we find forces in selected members of a larger truss without calculating every joint first? Start Learning Watch Videos Worked Section Cut Interactive Truss Practice What to Submit Inspect • Cut • Calculate • Verify Solve smarter, not just longer. Build on the method of joints from 2.8. First spot zero-force members, then use the method of sections to find important forces efficiently. Bring: calculator in degree mode, ruler, engineering notebook or the 2.9 classwork/homework worksheet. Your learning pathway What you'll be able to do Follow the learning modules in order. This lesson adds strategy and larger structures—not a new set of physical fabrication requirements. 01 · Recognize Find zero-force members and understand when the rules apply. 02 · Choose Use joint analysis or a section cut to solve selected member forces. 03 · Verify Check force signs, support reactions and independent equilibrium equations. Suggested 45–50 minute learning sequence Zero-force inspection 5–7 min Watch & model 10–12 min Worked section cut 15 min Interact & practice 15 min The second video and additional practice may be assigned outside of class. 01 / Connect previous lessons Two tools for different jobs Both analysis methods use static equilibrium and ideal pin-jointed, joint-loaded, weightless two-force members. Method of joints · 2.8 When you need many member forces Isolate one joint at a time. Each planar joint provides ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣFᵧ = 0 , so start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces. Best for: tracing the entire truss joint by joint. Method of sections · 2.9 When you need a few selected members Imagine a cut through a small set of members. Isolate one side, replace each cut member with an unknown axial force and use ΣFₓ = 0, ΣFᵧ = 0 and ΣM = 0 . Best for: finding a key member without solving all the intermediate joints. Whole truss: 3 equilibrium equations One 2D joint: 2 equations One 2D cut: 3 equations Important nuance: A section cut crossing three unknown member forces is the standard starting point, but three equations do not guarantee a solution . If the unknown lines of action are arranged so that the equations are dependent, choose another cut or combine methods. 02 / Inspect before calculating Two zero-force-member rules These rules apply to ideal pin-jointed trusses with no applied external load or support reaction at the examined joint . The result is specific to that loading arrangement. Rule 1 Two noncollinear members at an unloaded joint J · no external force A B JA = 0 N JB = 0 N Exactly two noncollinear members at unloaded, unsupported joint J If a joint connects only two noncollinear members and has no external load or reaction, their forces must both be 0 N . Otherwise, they could not balance in two perpendicular directions. F JA = F JB = 0 N Rule 2 Three members; two lie on one line A B J C JC = 0 N AJ and JB are collinear; no external force or reaction at J At unloaded J, JA and JB lie on the same horizontal line; JC is vertical. The collinear forces cannot balance a nonzero vertical component. ΣFᵧ = F JC = 0 → JC = 0 N Do not remove real structural members: A member with zero calculated force under one ideal load case may still prevent buckling, brace the structure, or carry forces when a vehicle moves. The rules do not apply if an external force or support reaction acts at that joint. Reasoning check: does a support reaction count as an external load? Yes. An unloaded joint for these rules must have no external forces , including support reactions. A joint with a pin reaction is not automatically eligible even if no separate hanging weight is shown. 03 / Plan the solution Five steps for a section cut Use this method when the truss has more members than you want to solve individually. 1 · Inspect Determine support types, loads and zero-force members. 2 · React Solve whole-truss reactions when needed. 3 · Cut Cross selected members—usually no more than 3 unknowns. 4 · Isolate Draw one side with external loads and cut-member forces. 5 · Solve and cross-check Assume each cut member is in tension (arrows point outward from the isolated section along the member axis). Choose a moment center to eliminate unknowns, then solve horizontal and vertical equilibrium. A negative result means compression . Cutting isn't removing support: Your free-body diagram includes all external loads and support reactions acting on the chosen side. Member forces appear only along members crossed by the cut. If you analyze the opposite side, their directions reverse. 04 / Engineering videos Two worked statics tutorials These videos are from Jeff Hanson's statics course. pages.searchText: POE Unit 2 2.20 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.20 Bridge Design & Testing Presentation Engineering question: How can we convince an audience—using real design evidence and honest measurements—that we understand why our bridge performed the way it did? Assignment Brief Slide-by-Slide Guide Visual Examples 100-Point Rubric What to Submit Final Bridge Capstone Presentation Tell the engineering story of your team's bridge. Create and give a 6–8 minute presentation to the class, followed by 2–3 minutes of questions . Every team member must present a meaningful section. Product: one team slide deck and a live in-class presentation—not a newly fabricated redesign. 01 / Presentation assignment Your final deliverable is a presentation to the class Summarize the entire design–build–test process using evidence from Lessons 2.15–2.19. Your audience should understand what you designed, why you designed it, what you actually made, how it was tested, and what the results mean . 1 Challenge What mattered? 2 Design Why this shape? 3 Analyze What predicted? 4 Fabricate What was built? 5 Test What happened? 6 Conclude What next? Presentation format One team deck prepared in Google Slides, PowerPoint or equivalent. Use approximately 8–10 focused content slides (the outline below suggests ten). Embed real photos, Fusion screenshots and at least one readable test graph. Time and participation 6–8 minutes speaking plus 2–3 minutes Q&A . Every team member speaks and should be prepared to answer an engineering question. Assign slide owners, rehearse handoffs and check that the class can read your graph. Grading principle A bridge that failed can earn full presentation credit if its measurements, engineering reasoning and lessons learned are accurate and well communicated. Missing or invented results must never be presented as successes. Suggested preparation schedule: 1 period to assemble the deck and organize evidence, 1 period to refine figures and rehearse, and class presentation time as scheduled. Finished slides are submitted before speaking as directed by the teacher. 02 / What to include Five things the audience must learn Bridge design decisions Compare the three concepts, identify the final truss design, show the Fusion assembly, and name the engineering trade-offs that drove the choice. Predictions before testing Include at least one real free-body/member-force calculation or risk assessment from 2.16. Label theoretical assumptions and predicted weaknesses. Fabrication decisions Show actual photos and approved materials/joints. Report final measured mass and one fabrication issue, modification or quality check. Real experimental results Present the actual 2.19 force–deflection graph, 100 N / 10 mm target, maximum observed load, actual test condition and numerical qualification evidence. Engineering conclusion Explain what matched or differed from analysis, identify the likely failure/deflection mechanism and propose two justified design improvements —without rebuilding the bridge. Sources and credit Credit externally sourced research visuals/information and identify your own CAD, measurements and team photographs. The class should be able to distinguish actual evidence from illustrative examples. If your bridge never reached 100 N: Show the highest observed force and the actual reason the run stopped. State that the at-100-N requirement is unverified rather than inventing a value. If your bridge did not fail, do not claim an ultimate failure load. 03 / Slide planning studio Recommended ten-slide presentation Each slide below describes the required content, a visual example and a question to answer aloud. You may combine closely related slides, but all required topics must still be represented. The speaker and readiness fields help plan your group; they do not save automatically when you leave this browser page. pages.searchText: Home POE Unit 2 Lesson 2.2 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.2 Centroids & Center of Gravity Engineering question: Where is the geometric center of a shape, and how can we calculate it for irregular parts? Start Learning Watch Videos Worked Example Interactive Explorer Practice What to Submit Learn • Watch • Calculate • Check Find the balance point. Work independently or alongside the teacher. Every formula, diagram, worked solution, and practice check you need is on this page. Materials: calculator, paper or 2.2 practice packet, ruler, pencil. Your learning pathway What you'll be able to do Follow the modules in order. Pause the videos to sketch and calculate instead of only watching. 01 · Identify Recognize area centroids and explain how they relate to balance. 02 · Calculate Find the centroid of rectangles, right triangles and composite plates. 03 · Explain Predict how adding or removing material moves a centroid. Suggested 45–50 minute lesson Notice & predict 3–5 minutes Read & watch 10–12 minutes Worked example 12–15 minutes Explore & practice 15–18 minutes Additional composite-shape video and independent practice can be completed after class. 01 / Build understanding What is a centroid? Imagine balancing a uniform cardboard shape on the tip of a pencil. Where should the pencil touch? Centroid The average position of an area A centroid is the geometric center of a shape. Think of averaging the position of every tiny piece of its area. It is located using coordinates , not by guessing the middle of a bounding box. For a thin plate of uniform thickness and density in a uniform gravitational field, its area centroid also gives the horizontal location of its center of gravity. Engineering significance Why engineers care Locating centroids helps us reason about balance, mass distribution, structural cross-sections and where the weight of an object acts. In later lessons, this connects to beam bending and structural stiffness. Remember: The centroid is a location. It does not by itself tell us how strong or stiff a part is. Centroid Based on geometry : area, line or volume. Center of mass Based on how mass is distributed. Center of gravity Where the resultant gravitational force acts. Warm-up: Think before calculating You cut an L-shaped plate from plywood. Will its balance point be at half the total width and half the total height? Sketch your prediction, then revisit it after the worked example. Check your prediction Not necessarily. An L-shaped plate is uneven: there is more material near the upright and top flange. Its centroid is an area-weighted location, not necessarily the center of the surrounding rectangle. 02 / Simple geometry First learn the two building blocks Always choose an origin O and measure both centroid coordinates from the same origin. The yellow dot is the centroid. Rectangle y x 120 mm 60 mm C (60, 30) O A = bh · x̄ = b/2 · ȳ = h/2 For the 120 mm × 60 mm plate: x̄ = 60 mm, ȳ = 30 mm . A uniform rectangle has two lines of symmetry; the centroid is at their intersection. Right triangle y x 120 mm 60 mm C (40, 20) O A = bh/2 · x̄ = b/3 · ȳ = h/3 For this particular orientation, measured from the right-angle corner : x̄ = 40 mm, ȳ = 20 mm . Measure one-third from each perpendicular side, not from the sloping edge. Coordinate warning: Rectangle and triangle formulas above assume the origin shown in each drawing. Moving the origin changes the reported coordinates—even though the physical centroid stays in the same place. 03 / Watch and take notes Video learning library Use the first video as a broad introduction. The second explains the composite-area method in depth. Captions and playback speed are available through YouTube. If embedded playback is blocked, open the direct link. Start here · about 10 min Centroids and Center of Mass in 10 Minutes Less Boring Lectures. Watch especially the sections on the centroid of an area, triangles and composite bodies. While watching: Write one sentence explaining why a centroid is an area-weighted average. Open introductory video on YouTube ↗ Worked examples · about 14 min Composite Centroids — The Table Method Jeff Hanson. Shows how to organize component areas and coordinates; later demonstrates holes and the negative-area method. While watching: Copy a table header: Shape | Area | xᵢ | yᵢ | Axᵢ | Ayᵢ. Open composite-shape video on YouTube ↗ Optional extension: Jeff Hanson — How to Break Down Composite Shapes , focused on picking regions and an origin. 04 / Follow a full solution Worked example: an L-shaped plate We will solve the exact type of problem you will see in the practice packet. Study the origin, colored regions, area table and final reasonableness check. Step 1 · Divide the shape y x 20 40 mm A₂: top extension 40 × 20 mm A₁: upright web 20 × 80 mm Combined centroid (20, 50) mm All coordinates measured from the bottom-left O. O The upright is 20 × 80 mm. The separate upper extension to its right is 40 × 20 mm. They touch, but do not overlap, so their areas can be added. Step 2 · Build the area table Use the lower-left corner as origin O. Each component rectangle has its own centroid, measured from that same origin. Region A (mm²) xᵢ (mm) yᵢ (mm) Axᵢ (mm³) Ayᵢ (mm³) Web 1 1,600 10 40 16,000 64,000 Top 2 800 40 70 32,000 56,000 Total 2,400 — — 48,000 120,000 x̄ = Σ(Axᵢ)/ΣA · ȳ = Σ(Ayᵢ)/ΣA Step 3 · Solve: x̄ = 48,000 / 2,400 = 20 mm . ȳ = 120,000 / 2,400 = 50 mm . Step 4 · Check: The centroid moves toward the web because the web contributes twice as much area as the upper extension. It is not at the bounding-box center (30, 40). Why are Axᵢ and Ayᵢ measured in mm³? Area is measured in mm², and each centroid coordinate is measured in mm. Multiplying gives mm³ (a first moment of area ). Dividing by total area in mm² produces a coordinate in mm. 05 / Interactive exploration What happens when we add more material? Move the slider to change only the top extension's width. The vertical web stays 20 × 80 mm and the top

pages.searchText: POE Unit 2 2.16 Principles of Engineering • Unit 2 • Lesson 2.16 Bridge Engineering Analysis Engineering question: Do calculations support our selected bridge concept—and where must it be reinforced, braced or revised? Start Analysis Free-Body Diagram Worked Truss Interactive Explorer Risk Register What to Submit Bridge Capstone · Engineering Verification Evidence before manufacturing. Bring your preferred concept from Lesson 2.15. Calculate reactions, estimate member-force demands, document unsupported assumptions, and decide what to improve before detailed Fusion CAD. Materials: chosen concept drawings, 2.13 test results, 2.14 mass budget, notebook and calculator. Learning mission Analyze, diagnose, revise Design selection was a hypothesis. This lesson tests that hypothesis using mechanics and identifies the evidence still needed for the real, three-dimensional bridge. 1 · Free-body diagram Show the total 100 N qualification force, supports and external reactions for the entire bridge . 2 · Member-force analysis Analyze a suitable determinate side-truss model using joint equilibrium or an approved solver, marking tension and compression. 3 · Engineering risk Evaluate compression stability, load-sharing, critical joints and preliminary mass, then propose changes. Review & draw 8–10 minutes Worked mechanics 12–15 minutes Apply to your bridge 20–25 minutes Risk & revisions 15 minutes / homework Suggested pacing: two 45–50 minute periods for full individual-team analysis and documented revisions. 01 / Baseline bridge rules Numbers every design must address 400 mm Clear support-to-support span ≤ 65 mm Overall width, including hardware 100 N Centered qualification force ≤ 10 mm Measured midspan deflection at 100 N ≤ 150 g Completed structural mass Wood-based Approved primary members only Construction limits still apply: approved wood and plywood members, permitted local gussets and printed fittings, PVA/CA glue or legal joins, and M3 nut-and-bolt fasteners only. No acrylic, solid plywood plates, screws, hot glue, epoxy, or 3D-printed chords. Review the complete manufacturing rules ↗ 02 / External force equilibrium Start with the entire bridge, not individual bars A correct free-body diagram shows the bridge separated from its surroundings, with only the applied force and reactions. Assume an ideal left pin and right roller, a 400 mm span and a centered 100 N downward load. WHOLE BRIDGE FREE-BODY DIAGRAM 100 N downward Aᵧ = 50 N Cᵧ = 50 N 200 mm 200 mm 400 mm clear span (idealized pin/roller model) Step 1 · Moments about left support A ΣM A = Cᵧ(400) − 100(200) = 0 Cᵧ = 50 N upward. Step 2 · Vertical balance ΣFᵧ = Aᵧ + Cᵧ − 100 = 0 Aᵧ = 50 N upward. For no other horizontal loads, Aₓ = 0. Common errors to avoid Dividing 100 N by two before drawing the bridge-wide FBD. Placing the entire 100 N independently on each of two side trusses. Assuming every side gets exactly 50 N without checking the crossmember and load eccentricity. Using centimeters in one equation and millimeters in another. Even if the real bridge has two side frames, the whole bridge carries 100 N total . Only a symmetric and adequately connected ideal model allows an assumed 50/50 side split. How the load can reach both trusses 100 N centered load Load crossmember Nominal 50 N per side only if shared evenly Simplified perspective — loading and brace geometry require actual design Preliminary side-frame approximation: Under symmetric load sharing, each side carries 50 N downward, with 25 N upward at each end of that side. This approximation must be identified and reconsidered if the center crossmember, side stiffness, joints, or alignment are not symmetric. 03 / Learn from demonstrations Video library: solving, modeling and interpreting failures Understanding and Analysing Trusses — The Efficient Engineer While watching: Which joints could be solved with two or fewer unknown member forces? How do negative solutions indicate compression? Watch on YouTube ↗ Free Online Truss Calculator Tutorial — SkyCiv Engineering While watching: Identify nodes, members, pin/roller restraints, load locations and the force-result diagram. Watch on YouTube ↗ Understanding Buckling — The Efficient Engineer While watching: Why is compression force alone insufficient to declare a long, slender member safe? Watch on YouTube ↗ The last video extends the buckling concepts from 2.12. Watch the first two before attempting the independent analysis. Direct YouTube links are included if embedded video is blocked. 04 / From bridge to joint How to solve member forces without guessing TENSION (+) COMPRESSION (−) Member is pulled Member is pushed Axial force is a demand, not a tested failure limit 1. Label Give joints letters and members endpoints 2. Isolate Draw the complete truss FBD 3. Solve Use moments and joint ΣFₓ = ΣFᵧ = 0 4. Verify Balance a final joint, compare to solver Method of joints Choose a joint with no more than two unknown member forces. Draw unknown forces away from the joint (assume tension). Resolve horizontal and vertical components, solve equilibrium, then move to the adjacent joint. Positive: tension. Negative: compression for the chosen sign convention. ΣFₓ = 0 · ΣFᵧ = 0 Know the model assumptions Members are treated as straight two-force axial elements. Joints are ideal pins (no moment transfer) and forces act at joints. Support restraints are correctly modeled; the truss is stable. An ideal 2D truss ignores real wood joints, out-of-plane sway, eccentric load transfer, connector bending and imperfections. Important: m + r = 2j is a useful necessary count for a simple determinate planar truss, but not proof of stability or unique solvability. Check connectivity and geometry too. 05 / Fully worked example Three-member triangle: a small solvable model Consider one idealized side truss , distinct from your Pratt, Warren or Howe concept. Its joints are A = (0,0), B = (200,100) and C = (400,0) mm. It carries its assumed 50 N share of the bridg
