pages.title: Compare Absolute and Relative Motion
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion Program the same geometric production path using ab
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion Program the same geometric production path using absolute and relative motion, then recommend the better method. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Precision Robotics Inc. Department: Controls Engineering Goal: Select a reusable motion strategy for multiple workcells. Background Engineering Context Precision Robotics is creating reusable code for several similar workcells. Engineers disagree about whether the path should be programmed with absolute coordinates or relative increments. You must test both approaches using the same task. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish absolute and relative robot movement Create equivalent programs using two motion strategies Compare readability, editability, and execution Support a programming recommendation with evidence Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm with drawing tool or simulated points Python project Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Choose a rectangular or stepped path with at least eight movements. Sketch the path and label the starting coordinate and all dimensions. Program Version A using absolute move_to() coordinates. Program Version B using move_inc() for repeated or dimension-based moves. Run each version three times and record execution time and positioning success. Change the path width by 20 mm in both programs. Record how many lines or values had to change. Compare code length, readability, reuse, and risk of accumulated error. Write a recommendation for a factory that may move the fixture later. Requirements Engineering Requirements Both programs must complete the same path Use at least eight motion commands Complete three successful trials per version Include comments that identify the coordinate strategy Constraints Constraints & Safety Use identical speed settings for both versions Do not alter the physical workcell between trials Begin from the same Home position Keep the tool above the approved surface Deliverables What You Submit Absolute-motion program Relative-motion program Timing and editability comparison table Annotated path sketch Written recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which method was easier to understand? Which method was easier to resize? Where could relative error accumulate? When would a hybrid approach be best? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Absolute positions are useful for known fixtures; relative moves are useful for repeated patterns and reusable geometry. Common Mistake A relative program depends on the current position. Starting from the wrong point shifts every later move. Stretch Goal Create a hybrid program that uses absolute coordinates for setup and relative movement for the repeated pattern. Career Connection Robot programmers select coordinate strategies based on fixture stability, product variation, and maintainability. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson →

Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroParts Distribution Department: Order Fulfillment Goal: Automate three customer-specific pallet configurations. Background Engineering Context AeroParts Distribution receives small orders with different quantities and arrangements. The current program must be rewritten for every order. Your team must create a flexible program that operators can configure using variables at the beginning of the file. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate order requirements into pallet coordinates Use functions, loops, lists, or variables to create flexible code Verify several production configurations Document an operator-friendly workflow Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Cubes Three customer order cards Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the three customer order cards and draw each required pallet layout. Identify which pickup and placement actions are common to all orders. Create helper functions for pickup, safe travel, and placement. Create operator variables that select order type or quantity. Program Order A and verify every coordinate. Run Orders B and C by changing only the approved configuration values. Test each order twice and compare the physical pallet to the order card. Add clear comments and an operator instruction block at the top of the program. Requirements Engineering Requirements Correctly complete all three customer orders No code changes outside the configuration section between orders No manual product placement Begin and end at Home Include comments for operator inputs Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the provided parts and pallet area Maximum cycle time is five minutes per order The robot may carry one part at a time All motions must use safe clearance heights Deliverables What You Submit Three order-layout diagrams Configurable Python program Six-run order verification log Operator quick-start instructions Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which functions made the program easier to adapt? What input error could an operator make? How could input validation improve the system? How would a barcode scanner change the workflow? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Separate values that operators change from the motion logic that should remain protected. Common Mistake Hard-coding every order creates duplicate code and makes later maintenance difficult. Stretch Goal Use a list of coordinates so a new order can be added without changing the pickup/place functions. Career Connection Flexible manufacturing engineers design systems that switch products with minimal downtime or reprogramming. pages.title: Flexible Pick-and-Pallet Automation
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Flexible Pick-and-Pallet Automation ADM Problem 1.3.1 Flexible Pick-and-Pallet Automation Design it. Print it. Program it. Reconfigure it. Build a robotic m
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Flexible Pick-and-Pallet Automation ADM Problem 1.3.1 Flexible Pick-and-Pallet Automation Design it. Print it. Program it. Reconfigure it. Build a robotic manufacturing cell that can move student-designed parts from three pickup zones to either of two pallet locations without rewriting the core motion program. Back to Unit 1 Start the Challenge What You Submit Driving Question How can one robot program handle changing production orders? Your solution must use variables to select where a part is picked up and where it is palletized. A new order should require new variable values—not a new motion program. The Manufacturing Cell Your Challenge Create one production-part CAD design and manufacture three color-coded copies . The three physical parts will use the same CAD geometry and will be distinguished by their 3D-print color. Each colored part will begin in one of three fixed pickup zones. Your robotic arm must pick the requested part and deliver it to either Pallet A or Pallet B based on a teacher-provided pick list. Pickup Zone 1 Part / SKU Pickup Zone 2 Part / SKU Pickup Zone 3 Part / SKU Robotic Arm Variable-driven routing Pallet A / B Selected destination pickupZone = 1 # 1, 2, or 3 palletZone = 2 # 1 or 2 pick_part(pickupZone) place_part(palletZone) Core requirement: changing only the pickup and pallet variables must redirect the robot. Do not create six separate copies of the motion sequence. Learning Targets What You Will Learn Design a CAD part for reliable robotic handling and additive manufacturing. 3D print three color-coded copies of the production part and inspect them for repeatable placement and pickup. Define HOME, approach, pickup, and placement positions in a robotic workcell. Use variables and reusable functions to separate job instructions from robot motion. Commission, debug, and validate a flexible automated manufacturing process. Design Requirements Your Parts Create one CAD model that will serve as the production-part geometry. 3D print three copies of the same model in three different colors . Color is what distinguishes the three parts/SKUs. Assign each color a clear part name or SKU and document the color-to-SKU relationship. Keep the geometry and dimensions the same across all three printed parts. Use a stable bottom surface and repeatable orientation. Include an accessible pickup surface or feature for the end effector. Avoid fragile geometry or unnecessary print complexity. Get teacher approval before printing. Project Workflow Complete the Problem in Five Phases 1. Design & Manufacture Sketch and CAD one production part. Evaluate printability and robot access, export the model, and select efficient slicer settings. Print three geometrically identical copies in three different colors, then inspect the finished components for consistency. 2. Configure the Workcell Establish Pickup Zones 1–3 and Pallets A–B. Define a safe HOME position plus approach and working positions for each location. Fixtures and zone markings must remain fixed after positions are taught. 3. Build Flexible Robot Logic Create a pickup-zone variable with three valid choices and a pallet variable with two valid choices. Build reusable pickup and placement logic so the main program can execute a job using those values. 4. Commission & Debug Test motion without parts first, then validate complete transfers at reduced speed. Identify failures as mechanical, positioning, end-effector, or programming problems and make controlled revisions. 5. Run the Production Pick List Your teacher will issue a production order. Configure the variables for each requested move and execute the order. You may change job-variable values between moves, but you may not rewrite or duplicate the core motion logic. Programming Standard Required Architecture Job variables: identify pickup zone and pallet destination. Position data: HOME plus safe approach and working positions. Pickup logic: one reusable function or equivalent structure for all three zones. Placement logic: one reusable function or equivalent structure for both pallets. Main program: set/read job variables → pick → place → return to a safe state. Validation Prove All Six Routes Before the final pick list, your cell must successfully demonstrate every possible source/destination combination. 1 → A 1 → B 2 → A 2 → B 3 → A 3 → B Python Help Coding Hints — Use These When You Get Stuck These hints review Python structures that may be useful in this problem. They are intentionally general: you still need to decide how to apply them to your workcell, positions, and production logic. Hint 1 — Variables store information A variable gives a value a name so your program can use it later. The value can change without changing every line that uses it. station = 2 destination = "B" Think about which pieces of information should change from one production order to another. Hint 2 — Use if / elif / else to make decisions Conditional statements let the program choose different actions based on a value. if selection == 1: # do one action elif selection == 2: # do a different action else: # handle another case Ask yourself: where does the robot need to make a decision based on a job variable? Hint 3 — Functions prevent repeated code A function groups instructions that belong together. A parameter lets the same function receive different information each time it is called. def perform_task(location): # use location to decide what happens pass perform_task(2) If you find yourself copying and pasting nearly identical robot code, consider whether part of it belongs in a function. Hint 4 — Separate data from actions Good automation programs often separate what the current job requests from how the machine performs the task . Variables can describe the job while functions contain reusable actions. job_value = 2 def run_action(choice): # reusable action logic goes here pass run_action(job_value) A new production order should not require you to rewrite the

pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern Create and program a pallet pattern that stores aerospace compo
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Design a Stable Pallet Pattern Create and program a pallet pattern that stores aerospace components efficiently and remains stable during handling. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Falcon Launch Systems Department: Outbound Logistics Goal: Palletize eight components with high stability and repeatability. Background Engineering Context Falcon Launch Systems ships compact sensor housings in reusable pallets. The existing arrangement leaves unused space and occasionally shifts during transportation. Your team must design a new pattern and program the robot to build it repeatably. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan an efficient pallet layout Translate a layout into robot coordinates Use loops or variables to reduce repeated code Evaluate repeatability and stack stability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm 8-12 cubes Pallet area Ruler Engineering notebook Python project Procedure Instructions Measure the available pallet area and the dimensions of one cube. Sketch three possible arrangements for eight cubes. Label coordinates or spacing. Create a decision matrix using capacity, stability, robot access, and coding simplicity. Choose one pattern and plan the pickup/drop sequence. Program the first layer and test clearance between placements. Use variables or loops where repeated spacing occurs. Run the complete program five times without manually repositioning cubes. Test stability by gently moving the pallet or performing the approved classroom transport test. Revise spacing or placement order if the stack shifts. Requirements Engineering Requirements Place at least eight cubes Placement error must remain within ±5 mm No cubes may fall during the approved stability test Complete the sequence in under five minutes Return the robot to Home Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the supplied pallet footprint No manual adjustment after the cycle begins Robot must approach each placement from a safe clearance height Only approved cubes may be stacked Deliverables What You Submit Three labeled pallet concepts Decision matrix Final Python program Five-run reliability log Photo of completed pallet Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why was your selected pattern more stable? How did placement order affect robot access? Which coordinates could be generated from variables? How would fragile parts change your pattern? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A staggered or interlocking pattern can improve stability without adding packaging. Common Mistake Placing parts too close together can make the magnet or robot wrist contact previously placed parts. Stretch Goal Increase capacity to twelve cubes while keeping the same pallet footprint. Career Connection Automation engineers develop palletizing routines for aerospace, medical, food, and logistics facilities. Back to Unit 1 View Code Lesson Focus Stack, test, document Use the example as a starting point, then document how the robot picks, places, stacks, and adjusts height. Lesson Overview In this project, you will apply robotic movement, sequencing, variables, loops, and spatial planning to stack objects accurately and repeatably. The example uses a magnetic end effector to pick up cubes, move them into rows, build additional layers, and adjust placement height. Notes This project extends palletizing by stacking objects in multiple layers. The magnetic end effector must be set before pickup and placement begins. Variables such as z, yPos, and xPos control height and placement locations. Repeated pickup and drop-off patterns are handled with loops. Final submissions should include comments that clearly explain each row, layer, height change, and final placement. Code example 1.2.3: Stacking Objects Review the code, copy it when needed, and add comments before submitting your final version. VEXcode Python Example Copy Code Code examples may be incomplete or missing comments. Comments are required for code submissions. def main(): arm.set_end_effector_type(Arm.MAGNET) arm.set_speed(100) cubes = 2 yPos = 185 z = 60 arm.move_to(180, 0, 180) #place cubes in back row for x in range(cubes): #move to pick up cube arm.move_to(48, 152, 30) arm.move_to(48, 152, 25) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(True) #move to drop off cube arm.move_to(48, 152, z) arm.move_to(200, yPos, z-15) arm.move_to(200, yPos, z-19) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(False) arm.move_to(168, 160, 100) yPos = yPos - 50 xPos = 135 #front row cubes for x in range(cubes): #move to pickup cubes arm.move_to(48, 152, 30) arm.move_to(48, 152, 25) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(True) #move to drop off cubes arm.move_to(48, 152, z) arm.move_to(150, xPos, z-15) arm.move_to(150, xPos, z-19) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(False) arm.move_to(168, 160, 100) xPos = xPos + 50 stacks = 2 z = 90 yPos = 185 for x in range(stacks): #move to pick up cube arm.move_to(48, 152, 30) arm.move_to(48, 152, 25) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(True) #move to drop off cube arm.move_to(48, 152, z) arm.move_to(200, yPos, z-15) arm.move_to(200, yPos, z-19) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(False) arm.move_to(168, 160, 100) yPos = yPos - 50 xPos = 135 #front row cubes for x in range(stacks): #move to pickup cubes arm.move_to(48, 152, 30) arm.move_to(48, 152, 25) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(True) #move to drop off cubes arm.move_to(48, 152, z) arm.move_to(150, xPos, z-15) arm.move_to(150, xPos, z-19) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(False) arm.move_to(168, 160, 100) xPos = xPos + 50 #increase height z = 130 arm.move_to(48, 152, 30) arm.move_to(48, 152, 25) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(True) #move to drop off cubes arm.move_to(48, 152, 100) arm.move_to(145, 140, 90) arm.move_to(145, 140, 88) arm.set_end_effector_magnet(False) arm.move_to(168, 160, 100) ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1

pages.title: Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell Reduce robot cycle time while maintaining 100% succ
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell Reduce robot cycle time while maintaining 100% successful part transfers. Intermediate 1 class period Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Automated Assembly Goal: Increase output without purchasing a second robot. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace supplier uses a 6-axis robot to move components from an incoming fixture to a pallet. The program works, but the robot travels through several unnecessary positions and pauses longer than needed. Management wants a software-only improvement before purchasing additional equipment. Objectives What You Will Practice Analyze robot motion and identify non-value-added travel Measure and calculate average cycle time Revise movement commands while preserving safety Use test evidence to justify an improvement Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm with magnet end effector Cubes or disks Stopwatch or elapsed-time display Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Load the current pick-and-place program and verify that it completes one full cycle correctly. Run five cycles and record each cycle time. Calculate the average. Sketch the robot path and label every pickup, clearance, travel, and drop-off point. Identify at least three moves, waits, or height changes that may be reduced or combined. Create a copy of the program and make one change at a time. After each change, run five cycles and record accuracy and average time. Select the fastest version that completes ten consecutive transfers without an error. Calculate the percent improvement and summarize the changes that mattered most. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce average cycle time by at least 15% Complete ten consecutive transfers with no drops or collisions Begin and end at the approved Home position Keep all movement within the approved work envelope Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change hardware locations Robot speed may not exceed 100% The magnet must remain the end effector A safety stop must remain available Deliverables What You Submit Original and revised Python programs Robot-path sketch with identified waste Five-trial before/after timing table Percent-improvement calculation Notebook reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which change produced the greatest time savings? What tradeoff did you observe between speed and reliability? Which motion would you redesign if the workcell layout could change? How would one second saved per cycle affect a factory running 8 hours per day? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Optimize path length and unnecessary waits before increasing motor speed. Common Mistake Removing every clearance point may create a collision even when the start and end coordinates are correct. Stretch Goal Achieve a 25% improvement and verify the program for 25 consecutive parts. Career Connection Manufacturing and automation engineers optimize robot motion because small cycle-time savings compound across thousands of parts. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Manufacturing Throughput Investigation
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation Use production data to increase the number of p
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 1 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation Use production data to increase the number of parts processed per hour without reducing quality. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Manufacturing Department: Continuous Improvement Goal: Increase hourly production using verified software improvements. Background Engineering Context Orion Manufacturing expects a surge in demand. The workcell is reliable, but engineers suspect waiting, excessive clearance, and repeated setup motions are limiting output. Teams will compete for the best verified throughput improvement. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure throughput and identify bottlenecks Apply continuous-improvement methods Calculate production-rate improvement Present evidence-based recommendations Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Cubes or disks Python project Stopwatch Spreadsheet or graph paper Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define one production cycle and the required quality criteria. Run ten baseline cycles and record total time, errors, and idle periods. Create a process map showing robot motion, pickup, transport, placement, and waits. Classify at least three examples of motion, waiting, or over-processing waste. Propose three changes and predict their effect. Implement one change at a time and collect new ten-cycle data. Select the best reliable program and calculate parts per hour. Prepare a short presentation with before/after data and remaining bottlenecks. Requirements Engineering Requirements Improve verified throughput by at least 20% Maintain 100% successful transfers during the final ten-cycle run Use at least two different data displays Document each program change Constraints Constraints & Safety No hardware relocation Robot speed may not exceed approved limits A controlled stop must remain functional Only one variable should be changed between diagnostic trials Deliverables What You Submit Baseline and final Python programs Process map Ten-cycle data tables Before/after graph Parts-per-hour calculation Three-minute presentation Reflection Reflection Questions Which bottleneck limited the original system? Did the fastest trial also have the best reliability? Why should engineers change one variable at a time? What hardware investment would produce the next improvement? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Throughput depends on the slowest repeated step, not simply the maximum robot speed. Common Mistake A single successful fast run is not proof of a reliable production improvement. Stretch Goal Run fifty final cycles and calculate reliability, mean cycle time, and range. Career Connection Continuous improvement and industrial engineers use cycle studies to increase output without buying new equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Automated Circuit Assembly Cell
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell Design a virtual workcell that transports, positions, and ver
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell Design a virtual workcell that transports, positions, and verifies components for circuit assembly. Advanced 3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Satellite Electronics Systems Department: Automation Integration Goal: Simulate a complete component assembly and inspection cell. Background Engineering Context A satellite electronics supplier wants to automate a simplified circuit-board assembly process. The cell must deliver parts in order, avoid collisions, and include a quality-verification step before the product exits. Objectives What You Will Practice Integrate robot, conveyor, and sensor behavior Sequence a multi-step automated assembly Use simulation for system verification Document interfaces and production logic Equipment What You Need Digital twin environment Virtual robot and conveyors Virtual sensors/inspection point Component models Python or simulation logic Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define a three-component assembly sequence. Create a layout showing incoming parts, assembly position, inspection point, and exit. Develop a state or flow diagram for the complete cycle. Program the robot to retrieve and place components in the required order. Add conveyor logic that prevents a new board from entering while assembly is active. Add a simulated inspection decision with pass and reject routes. Run ten simulated boards and record failures and cycle times. Revise the layout or logic until ten consecutive boards pass the system test. Prepare an interface diagram showing signals between devices. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete ten consecutive simulated assemblies Place all components in the correct order Prevent simultaneous use of an occupied zone Route failed inspection results to reject Provide a documented reset procedure Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the provided virtual equipment set No overlapping robot/conveyor motion in unsafe zones All device interactions require a defined signal or condition Final program must include comments Deliverables What You Submit Workcell layout State/flow diagram Simulation program Ten-board test log Device interface diagram Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which interface was hardest to coordinate? Where was a buffer needed? What physical tolerance would matter most? How would a real camera inspect the assembly? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define device ownership of each zone so two machines never command the same space at once. Common Mistake Programming each device separately without a shared state model often creates deadlocks or collisions. Stretch Goal Add a rework loop that returns one failed board for a second assembly attempt. Career Connection Systems integrators combine robots, conveyors, sensors, and inspection equipment into complete production cells. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Digital Twin Validation Study
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Digital Twin Validation Study ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study Compare simulated and physical robot motion and quantify the mode
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Digital Twin Validation Study ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study Compare simulated and physical robot motion and quantify the model error. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroSim Manufacturing Department: Virtual Commissioning Goal: Verify that the digital twin predicts physical performance. Background Engineering Context A new robotic process was developed in a digital twin before the physical cell was available. Before production begins, engineers must verify that simulated positions, paths, and cycle times accurately represent the real workcell. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan a simulation-to-physical validation test Collect comparable position and timing data Calculate error and explain discrepancies Recommend model updates Equipment What You Need Digital twin or simulation environment Physical VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Measurement tools Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select five robot target positions distributed through the work envelope. Record each simulated coordinate and predicted travel time. Run the simulated path three times and record cycle time. Transfer the same program to the physical cell after safety review. Measure actual endpoint position or reference alignment at each target. Run three physical trials and record cycle time. Calculate position error and percent timing difference. Identify at least three causes of mismatch and update one model setting. Repeat one test to evaluate the improvement. Requirements Engineering Requirements Validate at least five positions Use three simulation and three physical timing trials Calculate error using a consistent method Document one model correction Constraints Constraints & Safety Use approved speeds during initial physical testing Verify clearance before automatic operation Do not adjust physical hardware during comparison Use the same command sequence in both systems Deliverables What You Submit Validation test plan Simulation and physical data table Error calculations and graph Updated model screenshot Validation conclusion Reflection Reflection Questions Which variable produced the largest mismatch? Why might physical acceleration differ from simulation? What tolerance is acceptable for this process? What additional sensor would improve validation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Validate the highest-risk positions first: low clearance, long reach, or near workcell boundaries. Common Mistake A simulation that looks correct is not validated until physical measurements are compared. Stretch Goal Create an acceptance limit and automatically flag positions that exceed it. Career Connection Digital manufacturing engineers validate digital twins before deploying high-cost robotic processes. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Collision-Free Path Redesign
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Collision-Free Path Redesign ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.3 Collision-Free Path Redesign Modify an unsafe robot path so it clears all obstacles while adding
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Collision-Free Path Redesign ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.3 Collision-Free Path Redesign Modify an unsafe robot path so it clears all obstacles while adding the least possible cycle time. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Precision Cell Engineering Department: Robot Safety Goal: Restore safe operation after a fixture change. Background Engineering Context A fixture was added to an existing workcell, creating a collision risk along the original direct path. Engineers need a new path that preserves production speed and maintains a documented safety margin. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify collision zones in a digital model Create safe intermediate waypoints Compare path length and cycle time Verify clearance in simulation and physical operation Equipment What You Need Digital twin Physical workcell if approved Virtual obstacle/fixture Python program Measurement tool Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Run the original path in simulation and capture the collision location. Define a required clearance margin around the obstacle. Create three alternative waypoint paths. Measure or estimate path length for each. Simulate each path and record cycle time and minimum clearance. Select the shortest path that meets the clearance requirement. Verify the selected path at reduced speed on the physical cell. Document final coordinates and the reason each waypoint exists. Requirements Engineering Requirements Zero collisions in ten simulated cycles Maintain the required clearance margin Add no more than 20% to original cycle time Verify one reduced-speed physical cycle Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not remove the obstacle Do not exceed the approved work envelope All waypoint coordinates must be documented Physical verification requires teacher approval Deliverables What You Submit Collision screenshot Three path concepts Clearance/cycle-time comparison Final code Physical verification notes Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why was the shortest geometric path not necessarily the safest? Which waypoint added the most time? How could tool orientation create a collision? What sensor could monitor unexpected obstacles? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Check the entire robot and end effector, not only the tool-center point, when evaluating clearance. Common Mistake A waypoint that clears the tool may still cause an elbow or wrist collision. Stretch Goal Create a reusable safe-travel function for several pickup locations. Career Connection Robot simulation specialists perform collision studies before expensive equipment is installed. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Offline Programming Deployment
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Offline Programming Deployment ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment Develop and debug a complete robot task in simulation before it
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Offline Programming Deployment ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment Develop and debug a complete robot task in simulation before its first physical run. Advanced 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orbital Components Group Department: Virtual Commissioning Goal: Deploy a new robot task with minimal physical downtime. Background Engineering Context A spacecraft-component line cannot pause while engineers experiment with new code. Your team must program a replacement handling task offline, verify it virtually, and deploy it with minimal physical-cell downtime. Objectives What You Will Practice Develop robot logic in an offline environment Use virtual testing to identify collisions and errors Create a controlled deployment checklist Compare predicted and actual commissioning time Equipment What You Need Simulation/digital twin environment VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Parts and fixtures Python project Deployment checklist Procedure Instructions Receive the required pickup, inspection, and placement sequence. Measure or verify all fixture coordinates in the virtual model. Write the full program without operating the physical robot. Run at least ten simulated cycles and resolve every collision or fault. Record predicted cycle time and create a risk checklist. Perform a line-by-line safety review before physical deployment. Run the physical system first at reduced speed. Correct only differences that could not be predicted virtually. Record total physical commissioning time and compare it with the predicted plan. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete ten fault-free simulated cycles before deployment Complete the first physical cycle at reduced speed Achieve five consecutive physical cycles Document every change made after deployment Constraints Constraints & Safety No physical trial-and-error before simulation approval Hardware coordinates must be verified Safety stop must be tested before deployment Use approved reduced speed for first run Deliverables What You Submit Offline Python program Simulation test log Collision/risk checklist Deployment checklist Physical commissioning record Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which issue was discovered only in the physical cell? How much physical downtime did offline programming save? Which model detail was most important? How should future fixtures be documented? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Treat the first physical run as verification, not as the first debugging session. Common Mistake Assuming fixture coordinates are identical between virtual and physical cells can cause immediate collisions. Stretch Goal Deploy a second product variation using only parameter changes. Career Connection Offline robot programmers prepare and validate production code without interrupting active factory lines. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Factory Throughput Simulation
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Factory Throughput Simulation ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation Use a digital twin to balance robot, conveyor, and buffer capacit
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 3 Factory Throughput Simulation ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation Use a digital twin to balance robot, conveyor, and buffer capacity before changing the physical line. Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Nova Factory Systems Department: Industrial Simulation Goal: Select the best production-line configuration virtually. Background Engineering Context Nova Factory Systems is considering three production-line configurations. Building each physically would be costly, so your team must simulate the alternatives and recommend the best design for throughput and reliability. Objectives What You Will Practice Build and compare production scenarios Identify bottlenecks and buffer effects Analyze throughput and utilization data Complete an evidence-based trade study Equipment What You Need Digital twin or factory simulation Three provided layout scenarios Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define the production sequence and output target. Build or load Scenario A with the baseline robot and conveyor settings. Run a simulated production period and record output, idle time, and blocked time. Create Scenario B by changing conveyor speed or buffer capacity. Create Scenario C by changing robot path or station assignment. Run each scenario for the same simulated duration. Calculate throughput, robot utilization, and average work-in-process. Create a weighted decision matrix using output, reliability, complexity, and cost. Recommend one scenario and identify one risk before physical implementation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Compare exactly three scenarios Use identical simulated production duration Report throughput and at least two additional metrics Support recommendation with a decision matrix Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved changes for each scenario Do not change multiple unrecorded variables Simulation assumptions must be listed The recommended scenario must preserve safety Deliverables What You Submit Three simulation configurations Scenario data table Graphs of key metrics Decision matrix Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which scenario had the highest throughput? Did highest throughput also produce the least work-in-process? What assumption could change the recommendation? Which result should be verified physically first? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Record every simulation assumption; a precise answer from an unrealistic assumption is still unreliable. Common Mistake Comparing scenarios with different run durations or starting inventory produces misleading results. Stretch Goal Perform a sensitivity analysis by changing demand or failure rate. Career Connection Manufacturing simulation engineers test factory layouts and schedules before companies commit capital. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval ADM Activity 4.3.4 Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval Simulate the Fusion toolpaths,
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval ADM Activity 4.3.4 Simulation, Post-Processing, and Production Approval Simulate the Fusion toolpaths, post a Mach3 .tap file, verify it in Mach3, and complete the production-readiness review. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a CAM-generated program be verified before it is allowed to control a CNC mill? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Simulate all Fusion operations and inspect tool, holder, stock, workholding, and remaining-material results. Post the approved Fusion setup using the teacher-validated Mach3Mill post processor. Verify the .tap file in Mach3 and complete the production-approval package before machine setup. Manufacturing context Why This Matters Fusion simulation checks the planned stock removal and machine motion before the setup is posted. The approved operations are then post processed with the teacher-validated Mach3Mill post to create a .tap file, which must be independently reviewed in Mach3 before it can control the DMC2 Mini. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10–15 min 1. Learn the simulation purpose Watch the Autodesk machine-simulation video and list what simulation can detect and what still requires physical verification. 10 min 2. Review post-processing Read the Autodesk post-processing overview and explain why a post must match the machine controller. 10 min 3. Compare the two classroom machine pathways DMC2 Mini: validated Mach3Mill post and .tap file. FoxAlien: exact-model controller, supported file type, and teacher-selected post. Do not assume the same post works for both. 20 min 4. Observe the approval workflow Watch the teacher complete full simulation, code review, controller preview, raised-Z dry run, and approval freeze. Detailed activity procedure Simulate, Post, Verify, and Obtain Production Approval 1 Select the complete approved setup and run simulation with tool, holder, stock, and toolpath visible. 2 Review the first operation at reduced simulation speed. Check approach, entry, cutting depth, boundary, retract, and exit. 3 Repeat the review for every operation. Do not skip directly to the end of the simulation. 4 Enable collision checking and inspect tool, holder, stock, model, workholding, and machine components when a machine model is available. 5 Review remaining stock, gouges, uncut areas, operation order, tool changes, and estimated cycle time. 6 Resolve every error and warning or document why a teacher identifies a warning as noncritical. Regenerate and rerun the complete simulation after any change. 7 Select the correct machine pathway. For the DMC2 Mini, use the teacher-validated copy of Autodesk Mach3Mill. For the FoxAlien, use only the post assigned for the exact model and controller. 8 Post only the approved operations. Confirm program name, output units, work offset, tool numbers, tool-change plan, spindle plan, and output location. 9 Open the NC file as text. Inspect the safe start, units, positioning mode, work offset, tool information, spindle behavior, feeds, depths, retracts, unsupported commands, and program end. 10 Complete a line-by-line comparison between the posted file and the Fusion operation list. 11 Transfer the file using the classroom procedure and load it into the correct controller without starting the machine. 12 Review the controller toolpath display or preview. Compare extents, origin, direction, Z range, and final position with Fusion. 13 At the assigned machine, verify stock, workholding, tool, work zero, file revision, feed override, spindle procedure, and emergency-stop readiness. 14 Complete the teacher-approved raised-Z dry run, air cut, or single-block verification. 15 Freeze the approved Fusion version and NC file. Any change to CAD, CAM, post, stock, tool, origin, or setup requires the complete approval cycle again. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Gate 1 — Simulation approved All operations, collisions, remaining stock, warnings, and workholding are reviewed. Gate 2 — NC code approved Correct machine-specific post, file, units, offsets, tools, feeds, depths, and end behavior are verified. Gate 3 — Production approval Controller preview, physical setup checks, and dry run pass before cutting. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The post processor matches the classroom CNC controller. The approved code and CAM file are the same version. No machining begins until the teacher records approval. Student deliverables What You Submit Simulation screenshots and report Posted G&M code Code-verification notes CAM verification checklist Production-readiness approval Approved post-processing standard Fusion Mach3Mill Post Use a teacher-validated copy of Autodesk’s generic Mach3Mill milling post as the baseline. Store it in the approved Fusion Post Library location and name the classroom copy so students can distinguish it from unverified generic posts. A post processor translates Fusion toolpaths into controller-specific NC code. It does not prove that the code matches the DMC2 Mini configuration; verification and dry-run approval remain required. Expected output extension: .tap Controller: Mach3 milling profile for the DMC2 Mini Required checks: units, G54/work zero, tool plan, spindle-control method, feeds, retracts, machine limits, and M30 end Never run code fr

pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems ADM Activity 4.2.1 CNC Mill Anatomy, Safety, and Coordinate Systems Identify CNC mill systems, hazards, machine coordinates, work coordinates, program zero, and safe setup practices. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How does a CNC mill translate a digital coordinate system into controlled physical movement? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Identify the DMC2 Mini milling system, Mach3 control interface, axes, spindle, tool, table, workholding, and emergency controls. Distinguish Mach3 machine coordinates from the active work coordinate system used by the Fusion setup. Complete the teacher-approved reference, jogging, zero-setting, program-loading, feed-hold, stop, reset, and dry-run sequence. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The DMC2 Mini is operated through Mach3. Students must understand the physical mill, Mach3 screen controls, machine coordinates, work coordinates, program zero, tool position, workholding, and emergency controls before any code is loaded or motion is enabled. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 5 min 1. Identify your assigned machine path Record whether the lesson uses the DMC2 Mini with Mach3 or a specific FoxAlien model. Do not mix controller procedures. 15–20 min 2. Read the correct machine documentation DMC2 teams use the official Mach3 manuals and classroom DMC2 procedure. FoxAlien teams open only the manual matching the exact assigned model. 20 min 3. Observe the teacher demonstration Watch startup, emergency stop, axis identification, jogging, workholding, work-zero setup, program preview, dry run, shutdown, and fault response. 15–20 min 4. Complete a no-cut controls check Identify controls and coordinate displays without a cutting tool contacting material. Detailed activity procedure Complete the CNC Machine Orientation and No-Cut Readiness Check 1 Record the assigned machine name, exact model, controller, spindle-control method, expected file type, and teacher-approved post-processor path. 2 Locate and identify the frame, spindle or router, collet or tool holder, cutting tool, worktable, workholding, X/Y/Z axes, limit or home devices, controller, power controls, and emergency stop. 3 Mark the machine work envelope, moving-axis hazards, pinch points, rotating-tool zone, chip zone, and operator position. 4 Identify the controller displays and controls used for position, jogging, program loading, preview, start, hold, stop, reset, feed override, spindle control, and single-block operation when available. 5 Distinguish machine coordinates from work coordinates. Explain how the Fusion setup origin must match the work zero established at the machine. 6 Complete the teacher-approved startup and machine-reference procedure. Do not use a homing command unless the assigned machine is configured and approved for it. 7 Jog one axis at a time under direct supervision. Record the positive X, Y, and Z directions and verify that the displayed movement matches the physical movement. 8 Inspect and demonstrate the approved workholding method with no cutting operation. Confirm that clamps, fasteners, and fixtures remain outside the planned toolpath. 9 Load a teacher-approved no-cut program. Verify units, coordinate mode, work offset, program extents, starting point, depth, and final position in the controller preview. 10 Complete a raised-Z, spindle-off, or other teacher-approved dry run at reduced feed. Use single block or feed hold as directed. 11 Practice the response to an unexpected motion, wrong direction, wrong coordinate display, loose stock, or program mismatch. 12 Complete the shutdown and cleanup procedure and submit the no-cut readiness record. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Machine identified Exact model, controller, spindle method, and file path are recorded. Checkpoint B — Coordinates verified Axis directions and the difference between machine and work coordinates are demonstrated. Checkpoint C — No-cut readiness Program preview, dry run, stop response, and shutdown are completed safely. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Axes and origins are labeled from the machine’s actual reference. The work envelope is clear before motion. No student reaches toward a moving spindle or unsecured workpiece. Student deliverables What You Submit CNC mill anatomy diagram Coordinate-system diagram Hazard and control table Completed preflight and safe-state check Coordinate practice results DMC2 Mini control standard Mach3 Operating Boundary Mach3 interprets the NC program and commands the DMC2 Mini axes. Students may not change ports, pins, motor tuning, soft limits, homing, spindle, or machine-profile settings. The active Mach3 profile, machine units, axis directions, work offset, tool, stock, and spindle-control method must match the approved Fusion manufacturing setup. Load only teacher-approved .tap files. Never zero an axis until the teacher-approved work-zero procedure is complete. Use Feed Hold to pause controlled motion and the emergency stop for an immediate hazard. After any reset, verify the machine state, program line, work zero, tool position, and safe restart point before continuing. pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Manufacturing Calculations ADM Activity 4.1.4 Aerospace Manufacturing Calculations Use stock, mass, tolerance, cost, spindle-speed, feed-rate, and inspection calculations to support manufacturing decisions. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How do manufacturing calculations help engineers select safe, efficient, and measurable production decisions? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Calculate material use, mass, scrap, tolerance limits, and dimensional error. Calculate preliminary spindle speed and feed rate using provided data. Explain why approved machine limits override a theoretical calculation. Manufacturing context Why This Matters Manufacturing decisions must be supported by measurements and calculations. Students will use classroom values and teacher-approved machine limits rather than guess cutting parameters. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Organize variables and units Create a known/unknown table before using any equation. Keep inch and metric quantities separate unless a conversion is explicitly required. 15 min 2. Review cutting-data relationships Watch the Haas speeds-and-feeds lesson and identify cutting speed, spindle speed, chip load, flute count, and feed rate. 15 min 3. Practice with one worked example Follow the teacher example from stock dimensions through mass, utilization, tolerance limits, spindle speed, and feed rate. 15 min 4. Verify using the calculator Use the Manufacturing Math Calculator to check—not replace—your written calculations. Correct any unit or setup error. Detailed activity procedure Complete and Defend the Manufacturing Calculations 1 Record every provided value with its variable name, unit, source, and whether it is measured, calculated, estimated, or teacher approved. 2 Calculate the initial stock area or volume using the actual stock geometry. 3 Calculate the finished-part area or volume using the approved approximation or Fusion physical properties. 4 Calculate material removed, estimated mass, material utilization, and scrap percentage. 5 Calculate the upper and lower limits for each assigned tolerance. 6 Using sample inspection data, calculate signed error, absolute error, percent error, and pass/fail status. 7 Calculate preliminary spindle speed using the teacher-provided cutting speed and tool diameter. 8 Calculate preliminary feed rate using approved chip load, flute count, and spindle speed. 9 Compare the calculated spindle and feed values with the DMC2 Mini or assigned FoxAlien limits, tool limits, material guidance, and teacher-approved classroom values. 10 Estimate machining time or production rate using the provided path length, feed rate, or cycle-time data. 11 Estimate material cost and unit cost when cost data are provided. 12 Write a recommendation that states which values are calculations, which values are machine limits, and which final values require teacher approval. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Units verified Known values, unit system, and conversions are correct. Checkpoint B — Calculations shown Work is shown for material, tolerance, speed, feed, and inspection results. Checkpoint C — Approved decision Final proposed values are compared with actual machine and tool limits. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Units remain consistent. Calculated values are not used on equipment until approved. Tolerance limits and pass/fail decisions are shown clearly. Student deliverables What You Submit Completed manufacturing calculation set Shown formulas, substitutions, units, and answers Approved cutting-parameter table Evidence-based decision summary Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Toolpath Coding Challenge ADM Project 4.2.4 Aerospace Toolpath Coding Challenge Write, simulate, revise, and validate a manual Mach3 .tap program for a simplified aerospace mounting plate. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can manually written machine code be proven safe and accurate before it reaches a CNC mill? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Develop a complete manual program from a dimensioned drawing. Use simulation and tracing to identify errors. Validate the final path through a teacher-approved non-cutting or soft-material test. Manufacturing context Why This Matters This project verifies that students can plan a simplified aerospace toolpath, write a Mach3-compatible program manually, inspect the .tap file, and prove the motion in simulation and Mach3 before any supervised validation on the DMC2 Mini. Educational prototype Aerospace Application Boundary This component is an educational manufacturing prototype. It is not approved for installation on a crewed aircraft, operational aircraft, or flight-critical system. Any real aerospace application would require additional engineering analysis, material certification, process control, inspection, documentation, and regulatory approval. Project pathway Milestones 01 Plan and manually code 02 Simulate and diagnose 03 Validate and defend Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 20 min Day 1 learning — Plan before coding Review the dimensioned aerospace mounting plate, code reference, origin, cutter reference, safe Z, and validation criteria. 15 min Day 2 learning — Code in sections Follow the teacher demonstration for writing and testing one logical section at a time while preserving each verified revision. 15 min Day 3 learning — Prove the code Review controller preview, single-block operation, dry-run evidence, and the difference between code verification and authorization to cut. Detailed activity procedure Complete the Three-Day Aerospace Toolpath Coding Challenge 1 DAY 1 — Analyze the drawing. Mark the stock, origin, axes, cutter reference, feature coordinates, safe Z, cutting depth, and final safe position. 2 DAY 1 — Create the complete cutter-center coordinate table and classify every planned move. 3 DAY 1 — Create the code plan with safe start, approach, geometry sections, retracts, return, and program end. 4 DAY 1 GATE — Obtain approval of the coordinate table and movement order before writing the full program. 5 DAY 2 — Write the first program revision using only the approved classroom command subset. 6 DAY 2 — Trace each section immediately after writing it. Correct the section before adding the next one. 7 DAY 2 — Save each verified milestone as a new revision rather than overwriting the last working version. 8 DAY 2 — Run the complete code in the path visualizer and compare the extents and direction with the drawing. 9 DAY 2 GATE — Complete a peer code review for units, modal states, depths, rapid moves, unsupported commands, and end behavior. 10 DAY 3 — Load the approved revision into Mach3 simulation or the teacher-approved controller preview. 11 DAY 3 — Compare the displayed origin, program extents, Z range, movement direction, and final position with the plan. 12 DAY 3 — Complete the assigned pen plot, raised-Z dry run, air cut, or soft-material validation under direct supervision. 13 DAY 3 — Record every discrepancy and create the final revised program. 14 DAY 3 — Present the drawing, coordinate table, code, digital verification, physical/no-cut validation, and remaining limitation. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Gate 1 — Plan approved Coordinate table, origin, cutter reference, movement order, and safe Z are correct. Gate 2 — Code approved Peer review and digital visualization identify no unresolved code error. Gate 3 — Validation complete Controller preview and assigned dry-run method match the drawing. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The final code has a safe startup, approach, retract, spindle stop, and program end. Simulation and validation use the same final version. No cutting occurs without teacher approval and machine readiness. pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Design for Aerospace Manufacturability ADM Activity 4.1.3 Design for Aerospace Manufacturability Revise a component concept so it can be machined safely with available stock, tooling, workholding, and inspection equipment. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can an aerospace component be made lighter and easier to manufacture without losing its required function? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Apply CNC design-for-manufacturability rules. Evaluate tool access, internal radii, wall thickness, edge distance, and setup count. Compare design concepts using manufacturability evidence. Manufacturing context Why This Matters A CAD model may look correct and still be difficult or impossible to machine. Design for manufacturability connects geometry to tool diameter, stock, workholding, setups, inspection, and available machine travel. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Review the available process Record the assigned stock, machine envelope, cutter diameters, maximum approved depth, workholding method, and measuring tools. 15 min 2. Connect tools to geometry Review the Fusion pocket and contour resources. Explain why cutter diameter affects internal radii, slots, and feature access. 15 min 3. Complete a guided DFM audit Use the teacher model to locate thin walls, inaccessible features, unnecessary setups, unsafe workholding, and dimensions that are difficult to inspect. 15–20 min 4. Practice with the DFM Analyzer Run a sample part through the Aerospace DFM Analyzer and justify which warnings require a design change. Detailed activity procedure Redesign the Component for the Available CNC Process 1 Create a machine-capability table containing stock limits, axis travel, approved tools, cutter diameters, flute lengths, maximum depth, and workholding restrictions. 2 Audit every internal corner, slot, hole, and pocket for tool access. Mark any feature that cannot be reached by an assigned tool. 3 Compare every internal radius with the assigned cutter radius. Increase radii where the tool cannot create the original geometry. 4 Check minimum wall thickness, hole-to-edge distance, hole-to-hole spacing, and material remaining below pockets. 5 Identify how the stock will be held. Mark clamp, vise, fixture, or tab locations and the no-cut zones around them. 6 Determine how many setups the design requires. Revise the part to use one setup when practical and safe. 7 Check whether every critical feature can be measured with available calipers, gauges, pins, or fixtures. 8 Develop Concept A and Concept B. Each concept must preserve the required interfaces while improving manufacturability or reducing mass. 9 Estimate the effect of each concept on material removed, machining time, workholding, inspection, and risk. 10 Use a weighted decision matrix to select the preferred concept. 11 Complete the final DFM checklist and identify any accepted limitation that still requires teacher approval. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Capability table Machine, stock, tool, and inspection limits are documented. Checkpoint B — Two concepts Both concepts preserve the interfaces and address DFM concerns. Checkpoint C — Design freeze Decision matrix and final DFM checklist are approved before CAD development. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Every internal corner is compatible with an available cutting tool. The proposed workholding does not block required toolpaths. Weight-reduction features preserve minimum wall and edge requirements. Student deliverables What You Submit Two annotated redesign concepts CNC manufacturability audit Concept decision matrix Selected-concept justification Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. Autodesk: Generate a 2D Pocket Toolpath Use the official procedure to create and verify a 2D pocket operation. pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component Technical Drawing ADM Activity 4.3.2 Aerospace Component Technical Drawing Create an inspection-ready technical drawing with datums, critical dimensions, tolerances, material, and revision information. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How does a technical drawing communicate what must be manufactured and inspected? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Create clear orthographic and isometric views. Dimension the component from functional datums. Identify critical tolerances and inspection methods. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The drawing is the controlled communication document for manufacturing and inspection. It must match the approved CAD revision and clearly identify the features that determine fit and function. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Review drawing purpose Explain how a drawing communicates manufacturing and inspection requirements that may not be obvious from the 3D model. 10–15 min 2. Watch the Fusion drawing overview Record the purpose of base views, projected views, center marks, hole information, revision tables, and title-block data. 20 min 3. Follow a dimensioning demonstration Observe how dimensions are organized from functional datums instead of duplicated or chained unnecessarily. 15 min 4. Practice inspection planning Choose an available measuring tool for each critical dimension before creating the final drawing. Detailed activity procedure Create an Inspection-Ready Aerospace Component Drawing 1 Open the approved CAD revision and create a new drawing from the design using the assigned standard, sheet size, units, and scale. 2 Place the base view in the orientation that best defines the primary machined face. 3 Add only the projected, section, detail, or auxiliary views required to define the geometry clearly. 4 Add an isometric view for orientation without using it as the primary dimensioning view. 5 Add center marks and centerlines for holes, arcs, and symmetric features. 6 Identify the primary and secondary datum references used to locate the interfaces. 7 Dimension overall size, thickness, hole diameters, hole locations, pocket dimensions, depths, radii, and clearances from the appropriate datums. 8 Apply the teacher-provided general tolerance and specific tolerances to critical interface dimensions. 9 Add material, finish or deburring note, units, scale, part name, author/team, date, drawing number, and revision. 10 Create an inspection-planning table matching each critical dimension with the measurement tool and method. 11 Perform a duplicate-dimension, missing-dimension, and manufacturability review. 12 Exchange drawings with another team. The reviewer must determine whether the part can be manufactured and inspected without opening the CAD model. 13 Resolve review comments, update the revision, and export the approved PDF using the required file name. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Views complete The selected views fully define the component without unnecessary duplication. Checkpoint B — Dimensions and tolerances Interfaces are dimensioned from datums and critical tolerances are identified. Checkpoint C — Drawing release Peer review, title block, inspection plan, and PDF export are complete. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The drawing does not contain missing, duplicate, or conflicting dimensions. Critical features can be measured with available tools. The drawing revision matches the CAD model. Student deliverables What You Submit Approved technical drawing PDF or file Critical-dimension and inspection table Peer-review checklist Revision record Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. pages.title: CAM Setup and Machining Strategy
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CAM Setup and Machining Strategy ADM Activity 4.3.3 CAM Setup and Machining Strategy Create the Fusion Manufacture setup, tool list, operation sequence, and
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CAM Setup and Machining Strategy ADM Activity 4.3.3 CAM Setup and Machining Strategy Create the Fusion Manufacture setup, tool list, operation sequence, and approved cutting parameters for the aerospace component. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How does CAM convert design geometry into a safe and efficient machining strategy? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Create a Fusion milling setup with approved model, stock, orientation, and work coordinate system. Select classroom tools and create safe, manufacturable Fusion toolpaths in the correct operation order. Document cutting parameters, heights, boundaries, workholding clearance, and estimated machining time. Manufacturing context Why This Matters In the Fusion Manufacture workspace, a setup defines the stock, model orientation, work coordinate system, origin, tools, and operations that will later be posted for Mach3. A correct setup is the bridge between the approved CAD component and the DMC2 Mini. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 15 min 1. Watch the design-to-CAM transition Use the Autodesk CAD/CAM Fundamentals video to identify setup, stock, WCS, tool selection, toolpath creation, and verification. 15 min 2. Learn the setup fields Review the Autodesk setup reference and identify how model, stock, orientation, origin, and work offset must match the physical setup. 15 min 3. Learn tool-library discipline Review the tool-library resource and compare cutter geometry, flute length, holder, tool number, and cutting-data preset. 20 min 4. Observe a complete teacher CAM setup Watch the teacher create a setup, drilling/pocket/contour operations, heights, boundaries, workholding model, and operation order. Detailed activity procedure Develop the Fusion CAM Setup and Machining Strategy 1 Open the approved CAD revision and save a new Fusion version for CAM development. 2 Record the assigned production machine. DMC2 Mini work uses the approved Mach3 pathway; FoxAlien work must use the exact model, controller, machine limits, and later post specified by the teacher. 3 Switch to Manufacture and create a new Milling setup. 4 Select only the approved component as the model. Define stock using the actual classroom stock dimensions and orientation. 5 Set the WCS orientation so Fusion X, Y, and Z match the assigned machine axes. Select an origin that can be located physically and inspected before cutting. 6 Document the planned work offset and work-zero method. For the DMC2 Mini this is normally the teacher-approved G54 process. 7 Select tools only from the classroom library. Verify tool number, cutter type, diameter, flute count, flute length, overall length, holder, and approved cutting-data preset. 8 Create an operation plan before generating toolpaths. Typical order may include facing, drilling, pocketing/adaptive clearing, engraving, chamfering, and exterior contouring last. 9 Create the first operation and set geometry, heights, passes, linking, spindle speed, cutting feed, plunge feed, stepdown, stepover, stock to leave, and compensation as directed. 10 Repeat the process for each required operation. Keep tool changes and operation order intentional. 11 Model or mark workholding and confirm that tools and holders cannot contact clamps, screws, vise jaws, tabs, or fixtures. 12 Check Clearance, Retract, Feed, Top, and Bottom heights for every operation. 13 Generate all toolpaths, resolve warnings, and inspect the path direction and entry motion. 14 Record estimated machining time, tool list, operation order, and all approved cutting parameters on the CAM setup sheet. 15 Save a new Fusion version and obtain CAM-strategy approval before final simulation and posting. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Setup approved Model, stock, WCS, origin, machine path, and work offset are correct. Checkpoint B — Tools and operations approved Tool definitions, operation order, and cutting parameters match the classroom process. Checkpoint C — CAM ready for simulation Heights, boundaries, workholding, warnings, and setup sheet are complete. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The setup origin matches the planned physical setup. Tools and holders clear the stock and workholding. The exterior contour does not release the part before internal operations are complete. Student deliverables What You Submit CAM setup sheet Tool and parameter table Operation sequence Toolpath screenshots Estimated machining-time record Fusion Manufacture workflow Required Setup Record Fusion file and version Setup name Milling operation type Model selected Stock dimensions and orientation WCS orientation Program origin Mach3 work offset Tool numbers and descriptions Operation order Speeds and feeds Stepdowns and stepovers Clearance and retract heights Workholding locations Estimated machining time Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction.
