pages.title: Aerospace Component Analysis
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component Analysis ADM Activity 4.1.2 Aerospace Component Analysis Analyze the function, interfaces, mass, clearances, likely loads, and manufactu
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component Analysis ADM Activity 4.1.2 Aerospace Component Analysis Analyze the function, interfaces, mass, clearances, likely loads, and manufacturing features of an aerospace mounting component. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How do function, interfaces, loading, mass, and manufacturing affect an aerospace component’s design? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Identify the component function and connected systems. Locate critical interfaces, dimensions, clearances, and possible failure areas. Recommend evidence-based design improvements. Manufacturing context Why This Matters A component can only be improved after its function and interfaces are understood. Students will analyze a teacher-provided UAV payload or sensor mounting bracket before developing a new design. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Start with function Review the mission brief and write one sentence describing what the component must do, what it connects, and what would count as failure. 10–15 min 2. Study aerospace machining context Review NASA custom CNC examples. Identify how geometry, material, accuracy, and inspection affect manufacturing decisions. 15 min 3. Learn interface analysis Follow the teacher example for identifying datums, mounting patterns, fastener access, payload location, cable clearance, and adjacent-part clearance. 20 min 4. Practice annotated analysis Annotate a sample bracket before beginning the assigned component. Your annotations must distinguish functional features from decorative or noncritical geometry. Detailed activity procedure Analyze the Function, Interfaces, Risks, and Improvement Opportunities 1 Record the component name, mission need, primary function, and the systems or parts it connects. 2 Create an interface-control sketch showing the airframe or fixture, payload or sensor, fasteners, cable path, and nearby components. 3 Identify the primary datum surface and the secondary references used to locate the mounting pattern. 4 Mark all mounting holes, slots, pockets, outer contours, clearance areas, and tool-access areas. 5 Identify critical dimensions. For each one, explain what fit, alignment, clearance, or function it controls. 6 Describe likely force or load directions qualitatively. Do not claim the classroom component is structurally certified. 7 Identify the likely material and explain how material choice could affect mass, stiffness, cutting, burr formation, and inspection. 8 Identify at least three manufacturing difficulties, such as thin walls, tight internal corners, deep pockets, excessive setups, or inaccessible measurements. 9 Identify at least three possible failure or quality risks, such as misaligned holes, insufficient edge distance, interference, or poor cable clearance. 10 Develop two improvement concepts. Each concept must preserve the required interfaces and explain one benefit and one tradeoff. 11 Complete a one-paragraph component analysis summarizing the most important functional requirement and the most important manufacturing concern. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Interface sketch All connected parts, fasteners, clearances, and datum references are visible. Checkpoint B — Critical features Critical dimensions and their functional purpose are identified. Checkpoint C — Improvement concepts Two concepts preserve the interfaces and explain tradeoffs. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Recommendations preserve the required mounting interfaces. Assumptions are clearly labeled. The analysis distinguishes functional requirements from preferences. Student deliverables What You Submit Annotated component analysis Interface diagram Critical-feature table Two design-improvement recommendations Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. pages.title: Aerospace Components as Manufactured Systems
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Components as Manufactured Systems ADM Activity 4.1.1 Aerospace Components as Manufactured Systems Trace how raw material, machining, inspection,
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Components as Manufactured Systems ADM Activity 4.1.1 Aerospace Components as Manufactured Systems Trace how raw material, machining, inspection, finishing, and documentation combine to produce an aerospace component. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How do separate manufacturing processes combine to transform raw material into an inspected aerospace component? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Identify discrete manufacturing steps and the purpose of each step. Distinguish material flow, information flow, inspection, and rework. Create a process map for an aerospace component. Manufacturing context Why This Matters Aerospace hardware is not produced by one machine or one operator. A finished bracket, mounting plate, or equipment tray moves through a controlled sequence of planning, material preparation, machining, inspection, finishing, documentation, and release. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10–15 min 1. Observe an aerospace production environment Open the NASA machine-shop resource. Record at least five different actions that happen between a design request and an accepted physical component. 10 min 2. Build the vocabulary Define process, operation, routing, inspection, nonconformance, rework, scrap, release, material flow, and information flow in your engineering notebook. 15 min 3. Follow a worked example With the teacher, map a simple mounting bracket from stock selection through cutting, machining, deburring, inspection, documentation, and release. 15–20 min 4. Practice before the graded task Use the Manufacturing Process Router to test possible sequences. Explain why inspection and rework must appear inside the system rather than only at the end. Detailed activity procedure Build a Complete Aerospace Manufacturing Process Map 1 Select the assigned aerospace component, drawing, photograph set, or case study. Record the component name, function, and final acceptance requirement. 2 Identify the starting material and its initial form, such as sheet, plate, bar, billet, or partially finished stock. 3 Create a draft operation list. For every operation, record the input condition, action, equipment, output condition, and required documentation. 4 Place the operations in a logical sequence. Separate material preparation, machining, finishing, inspection, documentation, and release. 5 Add material-flow arrows showing where the stock or part physically moves after each operation. 6 Add information-flow arrows showing where drawings, programs, setup sheets, inspection results, approvals, and revision information move. 7 Add at least two inspection points. Place each inspection where it can prevent defective work from continuing into a later operation. 8 Create a nonconformance branch. Show whether a failed part is reworked, returned to an earlier process, held for review, or scrapped. 9 Identify the operation most likely to control quality, cost, or schedule. Support the choice with evidence from the process map. 10 Exchange maps with another team. Use the peer review to identify a missing operation, missing decision, or unclear handoff. 11 Revise the map and add a short explanation of how one early error could affect at least two later operations. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Component defined Function, starting stock, and final acceptance requirement are recorded. Checkpoint B — Draft system mapped Operations, material flow, information flow, inspection, and rework are visible. Checkpoint C — Final review Risk analysis and peer-review revision are complete. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Process steps are shown in a logical order. Material flow and information flow are both visible. Inspection and rework are included rather than treated as afterthoughts. Student deliverables What You Submit Aerospace component manufacturing process map Manufacturing-step purpose table Risk and rework analysis Short individual reflection Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. pages.title: CAD Design of the Aerospace Component
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CAD Design of the Aerospace Component ADM Activity 4.3.1 CAD Design of the Aerospace Component Create a fully constrained, machinable Fusion model for the U
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 CAD Design of the Aerospace Component ADM Activity 4.3.1 CAD Design of the Aerospace Component Create a fully constrained, machinable Fusion model for the UAV payload sensor mounting bracket. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can mission requirements and machining constraints be translated into a complete CAD component? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Create a parametric model that satisfies the approved interface. Apply tool-compatible radii, edge distances, wall thicknesses, and stock limits. Use physical properties and measurements to evaluate the design. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The aerospace component is designed in Fusion so the same file can move directly from the Design workspace into the Manufacture workspace. Modeling choices must support reliable Fusion toolpaths, one approved setup, practical workholding, and inspection on the completed part. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Reopen the approved requirements Highlight every interface dimension, clearance, feature, mass target, stock limit, and DFM rule that must appear in the model. 10–15 min 2. Review parametric sketching Use the Autodesk sketch-dimension resource to review fully constrained geometry and dimension-driven design intent. 20 min 3. Follow a teacher modeling demonstration Observe the recommended feature order: base stock, mounting interfaces, payload interface, clearance, pockets, radii, and finishing features. 15 min 4. Complete a model-readiness practice check Use a sample model to locate an underconstrained sketch, unsupported feature, wrong material, or unmachinable internal corner. Detailed activity procedure Create the Parametric Aerospace Component Model 1 Create the Fusion project and descriptive file name. Record the first design revision and verify the assigned unit system. 2 Create or activate a single component for the aerospace bracket and identify the model origin and primary datum plane. 3 Create user parameters for the major interface dimensions, stock thickness, hole spacing, pocket offset, wall thickness, and cutter-compatible radius when directed. 4 Sketch the primary airframe interface from the approved datums. Add constraints before adding dimensions. 5 Add the payload or sensor mounting interface using the approved hole pattern and alignment requirements. 6 Add cable, connector, fastener, and adjacent-component clearance geometry. 7 Create the exterior contour and base thickness within the approved stock boundary. 8 Add weight-reduction pockets or openings while maintaining wall thickness, edge distance, and tool-access requirements. 9 Apply tool-compatible internal radii, fillets, or chamfers only where approved. 10 Assign the approved material and record the Fusion-estimated mass or physical properties. 11 Inspect the timeline, component structure, sketch status, feature names, and warning symbols. Correct all unresolved errors. 12 Run the DFM Analyzer and complete the manufacturability checklist. 13 Complete a peer review against the requirements and interface-control sketch. 14 Save the approved CAD revision for drawing and CAM. Later changes require a new revision and renewed downstream verification. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Interface model Airframe, payload, fastener, and clearance features match the approved requirements. Checkpoint B — Parametric model Sketches are fully constrained and key dimensions use approved parameters. Checkpoint C — CAD release DFM audit, material, mass, and peer review are complete. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit All critical interface dimensions are driven by parameters or dimensions. The model fits inside the assigned stock. No unsupported feature requires an unavailable tool or setup. Student deliverables What You Submit Final parametric CAD model Fully constrained sketch evidence Mass or physical-property evidence Completed manufacturability checklist Peer-review notes and revision record Fusion file standard Design-to-Manufacture File Organization Create the component in the Fusion Design workspace using the approved document units. Use one clearly named component and fully constrained sketches. Name important sketches and features so they can be selected reliably in Manufacture. Preserve the approved design version before creating or revising CAM operations. Keep the same Fusion file for CAD and CAM unless the teacher directs a separate manufacturing model. Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. pages.title: G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing ADM Activity 4.2.2 G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command set and co
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing ADM Activity 4.2.2 G&M Code for Aerospace Manufacturing Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command set and connect each block to DMC2 Mini machine behavior. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How do G and M codes communicate motion, units, feeds, speeds, and machine states to a CNC device? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command subset used by the DMC2 Mini. Identify modal states, coordinates, feeds, spindle commands, work offsets, and safe start/end behavior. Trace a Mach3 program and compare each block with the intended cutter motion and Fusion setup. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The DMC2 Mini uses Mach3 to interpret the posted NC program. Understanding the Mach3 milling command set allows students to predict motion, identify unsafe code, compare manual instructions with Fusion output, and verify that the machine state matches the manufacturing plan. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Read code as machine states Use the Mach3 G&M Code Reference to classify each word as motion, coordinate, feed, speed, machine function, or program-control information. 15 min 2. Learn modal behavior Follow the teacher trace showing how units, plane, absolute/incremental mode, work offset, feed mode, and motion mode remain active until changed. 15 min 3. Connect code to the controller display Load a teacher-approved file in Mach3 simulation or the classroom visualizer and compare each code block with the predicted path and machine state. 15–20 min 4. Complete a safety error hunt Find wrong units, wrong modal state, unsafe rapid motion, missing retract, incorrect depth, unsupported commands, or incomplete program ending. Detailed activity procedure Interpret and Verify a Mach3-Compatible Milling Program 1 Copy the assigned program into the code-tracing worksheet without changing it. 2 Label the program name, comments, block numbers, G words, M words, coordinates, feed values, speed values, tool information, and end command. 3 Identify the safe-start states. Record the active plane, units, positioning mode, feed mode, work offset, compensation state, and canned-cycle state. 4 Create a modal-state table. Update the table only when a block changes a modal command. 5 Trace all G00 moves using a different line style from G01 cutting moves. 6 For each G01 move, record start coordinates, end coordinates, direction, distance, feed rate, and whether the move occurs above or inside the stock. 7 When assigned, interpret G02 or G03 using the classroom-approved center-offset or radius method and identify the selected plane. 8 Explain how M03, M05, and S values apply to the DMC2 Mini only when the Mach3 profile electronically controls the spindle. Otherwise mark the teacher-approved manual spindle action. 9 Predict the machine and program state at the end of every section, including Z height, coordinate mode, spindle state, and next expected action. 10 Load the program into Mach3 simulation or the visualizer and compare the displayed extents with your trace. 11 Complete the error hunt. For every error, identify the risk, corrected block, and reason for the correction. 12 Write a final verification statement explaining whether the program is ready for manual-programming practice, not physical cutting. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Modal table Units, coordinate mode, work offset, feed mode, and motion mode are tracked correctly. Checkpoint B — Path trace Rapid, feed, depth, and arc movements match the code. Checkpoint C — Error correction Every unsafe or unsupported condition is corrected and explained. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Machine-specific commands are verified before use. Every movement is connected to a coordinate and positioning mode. Students distinguish a rapid move from a feed-controlled cutting move. Student deliverables What You Submit Annotated G&M code reference Line-by-line sample program trace Unsafe-code error analysis Short reflection on modal commands Teacher-approved code subset Mach3 Commands Used in This Unit G00 — rapid positioning G01 — linear feed motion G02/G03 — circular interpolation when assigned G17 — XY plane G20/G21 — inch or metric units G40 — cancel cutter compensation G49 — cancel tool-length compensation when the course setup does not use it G54 — approved work coordinate system when configured G80 — cancel canned cycle G90/G91 — absolute or incremental positioning G94 — feed per minute F — feed rate S — commanded spindle speed M03/M05 — spindle start/stop only when configured and teacher-approved M30 — program end and reset Outside learning resources Official References and Videos Use these resources for learning and verification. Machine operation must still follow the classroom procedure and teacher direction. pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component Requirements Review ADM Project 4.1.5 Aerospace Component Requirements Review Define the mission need, interfaces, criteria, constraints, process route, material plan, and inspection strategy for the capstone component. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a manufacturing team prove that an aerospace component concept is ready for detailed design? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Translate a mission need into measurable component requirements. Document interface, manufacturing, material, safety, and inspection constraints. Defend a preliminary component concept during a requirements review. Manufacturing context Why This Matters The capstone component is a lightweight UAV payload sensor mounting bracket or another teacher-approved non-flight-critical prototype. Teams must pass a requirements review before creating the final CAD model. Educational prototype Aerospace Application Boundary This component is an educational manufacturing prototype. It is not approved for installation on a crewed aircraft, operational aircraft, or flight-critical system. Any real aerospace application would require additional engineering analysis, material certification, process control, inspection, documentation, and regulatory approval. Project pathway Milestones 01 Mission and interface definition 02 Concept generation and process planning 03 Requirements review and approval Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 15 min 1. Review the capstone mission Read the Aerospace Component Mission Brief and highlight the mission need, required interfaces, measurable requirements, and educational-prototype limitation. 20 min 2. Convert needs into requirements Follow the teacher model for writing measurable requirements using a value, unit, tolerance or limit, verification method, and source. 20 min 3. Plan the manufacturing route Use the manufacturing process map and process-selection matrix to define the path from stock to inspected component. 20 min 4. Prepare for a formal review Organize evidence so another manufacturing team can determine whether the concept is ready for detailed CAD development. Detailed activity procedure Complete the Aerospace Component Requirements Review 1 Write the mission statement and component function in language that clearly identifies the need, user, system, and intended outcome. 2 Create a requirements table. Each requirement must be measurable and include a verification method. 3 Create the interface-control sketch showing all mounting patterns, payload or sensor location, cable path, fastener access, clearances, and datums. 4 Document criteria, constraints, assumptions, and non-flight-critical application boundaries. 5 Select the approved material or compare the teacher-provided material options using mass, machinability, cost, and availability. 6 Define the starting stock dimensions and calculate preliminary utilization, mass, and tolerance limits. 7 Develop at least two concepts and label how each concept satisfies the required interfaces. 8 Use a weighted decision matrix to select the concept that will proceed to detailed design. 9 Create the preliminary manufacturing route, tool list, workholding concept, inspection plan, and estimated operation order. 10 Complete a preliminary risk table covering design, CAM, setup, machining, inspection, and schedule risks. 11 Prepare a concise requirements-review presentation with the mission, interfaces, requirements, concept comparison, process plan, calculations, risks, and requested approval. 12 Record reviewer feedback and classify every item as accepted, revised, deferred, or rejected with a reason. 13 Submit the revised requirements package and obtain the design-gate approval before Activity 4.3.1. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Gate 1 — Requirements ready Requirements are measurable and each includes a verification method. Gate 2 — Concept selected Interfaces, calculations, decision matrix, and manufacturing route support the selected concept. Gate 3 — Review closed Feedback is resolved and the concept is approved for CAD. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit Requirements are measurable and testable. The selected concept fits the assigned interface and stock. The team identifies unresolved risks rather than hiding them. pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge ADM Problem 4.3.5 Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge Use Fusion and Mach3 to set up the DMC2 Mi
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge ADM Problem 4.3.5 Aerospace Component CNC Manufacturing Challenge Use Fusion and Mach3 to set up the DMC2 Mini, manufacture the approved component, inspect it, complete a fit test, and defend the process. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a verified digital manufacturing plan be transformed into an accurate, inspected aerospace component prototype? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Complete a supervised CNC setup and dry run. Manufacture and inspect the approved component. Use dimensional and fit evidence to recommend a process or design revision. Manufacturing context Why This Matters This challenge connects the complete classroom workflow: aerospace requirements, Fusion CAD, Fusion Manufacture toolpaths, Mach3Mill post processing, Mach3 verification, supervised DMC2 Mini machining, dimensional inspection, interface fit testing, and process revision. Educational prototype Aerospace Application Boundary This component is an educational manufacturing prototype. It is not approved for installation on a crewed aircraft, operational aircraft, or flight-critical system. Any real aerospace application would require additional engineering analysis, material certification, process control, inspection, documentation, and regulatory approval. Project pathway Milestones 01 Production readiness review 02 Machine setup and dry run 03 Supervised machining 04 Deburring and dimensional inspection 05 Interface fit testing 06 Final manufacturing design review Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. Full class period Day 1 — Production readiness Review the complete digital thread from mission requirements through CAD, drawing, CAM, simulation, posted code, setup sheet, and inspection plan. Full class period Day 2 — Setup and dry run Observe the teacher model for workholding, work zero, tool setup, program preview, raised-Z run, and stop conditions on the assigned machine. pages.title: Manual Toolpath Programming
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Manual Toolpath Programming ADM Activity 4.2.3 Manual Toolpath Programming Convert a dimensioned aerospace pattern into a manually planned Mach3-compatible
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Manual Toolpath Programming ADM Activity 4.2.3 Manual Toolpath Programming Convert a dimensioned aerospace pattern into a manually planned Mach3-compatible .tap program. Back to Unit 4 Learning Steps Student Task What You Submit Focus Question How can a dimensioned toolpath be translated into a safe sequence of CNC instructions? Design. Verify. Manufacture. Inspect. Learning targets Today You Will Learn To Establish a program origin and coordinate table. Write an instructional program using safe approach, cutting, retract, and end blocks. Trace and verify every programmed movement before simulation. Manufacturing context Why This Matters Manual programming reveals the machine logic that Fusion later creates automatically. Students will write a short Mach3-compatible milling program, plot the cutter-center path, save it as a teacher-reviewed .tap file, and validate the motion before any machine run. Learning sequence Learn Before You Build Complete these steps in order. Record the requested notes or evidence before moving to the graded activity. 10 min 1. Separate part geometry from cutter motion Review the dimensioned drawing and identify whether each coordinate represents the part edge, hole center, pocket boundary, or cutter center. 15 min 2. Practice coordinates Use the CNC Coordinate Trainer to compare absolute and incremental movement from a known starting point. 15 min 3. Watch a teacher code build Follow the conversion from drawing dimensions to coordinate table, safe-start block, approach, cut, retract, and program end. 15 min 4. Verify with the visualizer Enter a short approved G00/G01 program and compare the plotted path with a hand-drawn trace. Detailed activity procedure Write a Complete Manual Toolpath Program 1 Review the drawing, stock orientation, assigned cutter, tool diameter, origin, safe Z height, cutting depth, and active unit system. 2 Mark the program origin on the drawing and label positive X, Y, and Z directions. 3 Determine whether the coordinates describe the tool center directly or require a cutter-radius offset. Complete the assigned offset calculations. 4 Create a cutter-center coordinate table listing every point in movement order. 5 Classify every move as rapid positioning, plunge, linear cutting, arc cutting, retract, or return. 6 Write the teacher-approved safe-start block and identify the intended work offset. 7 Write the approach sequence so all XY rapid motion occurs above the safe clearance plane. 8 Write the cutting sequence using the assigned feed rate and depth. Keep comments beside major sections. 9 Add spindle instructions only when the assigned machine/controller supports the approved automatic spindle workflow; otherwise add the required operator instruction. 10 Write the final retract, return, spindle stop when applicable, and M30 program end. 11 Trace the completed code by hand. Record the coordinate and active mode after every block. 12 Save the program with the required revision and .tap or teacher-specified file extension. 13 Run the code in the classroom visualizer and Mach3 simulation when assigned. Compare origin, direction, depth, extents, and final position. 14 Correct all discrepancies and submit the final annotated code with a revision record. Required checkpoints Stop and Verify Before Moving On Checkpoint A — Coordinate plan Origin, cutter reference, safe Z, depth, and point table are correct. Checkpoint B — Code complete Safe start, approach, cut, retract, and end are present. Checkpoint C — Digital verification Hand trace, visualizer, and controller preview agree. Safety and process control Required Operating Habits Use only teacher-approved files, tools, stock, speeds, feeds, and procedures. Preserve the last verified working file or code version. Stop immediately for unexpected motion, unusual sound, vibration, loose workholding, tool damage, or an unclear condition. Do not operate the CNC mill without the required certification, permission, and supervision. Record failed trials, defects, and interventions honestly. Quality check Before You Submit The cutter path accounts for the assigned tool and reference point. The tool retracts before rapid travel. The final path matches the dimensioned drawing. pages.title: Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake
pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake Create a safe request-ready-transfer-confirm handshak
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake Create a safe request-ready-transfer-confirm handshake between two connected workstations. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Robotics Department: Systems Integration Goal: Exchange parts safely between two automated stations. Background Engineering Context Orion Robotics is connecting two manufacturing cells. Station A must never release a part until Station B is ready, and Station B must confirm receipt before Station A begins the next cycle. A failed signal could damage equipment or lose a product. Objectives What You Will Practice Design machine-to-machine communication logic Represent a process with states and flowcharts Program confirmation and timeout behavior Validate communication under normal and fault conditions Equipment What You Need Two connected VEX CTE workcells or a simulated two-station setup Object sensors Conveyors Signal tower Python projects Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Define four signals: request, ready, transfer complete, and receipt confirmed. Create a sequence diagram showing which station sends each signal. Program Station B to announce ready only when its receiving zone is clear. Program Station A to wait for ready before releasing a part. Program Station B to confirm receipt after its sensor detects the part. Add a timeout that stops both stations if confirmation does not arrive. Run five normal transfers. Simulate a blocked receiving zone and a missing confirmation; verify safe response. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete five consecutive normal transfers Never release into an occupied receiving zone Stop safely after a communication timeout Provide visible fault indication on the signal tower Constraints Constraints & Safety No assumptions based only on elapsed time Each transfer requires positive confirmation Stations must start from a documented reset state Fault testing must use approved simulations only Deliverables What You Submit Handshake state/sequence diagram Station A and B code Normal and fault test log Reset procedure Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why are both ready and receipt signals needed? What could happen if one station resets unexpectedly? How did the timeout improve safety? How would a PLC implement this handshake? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Name signals by meaning and state, such as receive_zone_clear, rather than vague names like flag1. Common Mistake A single ready signal is not enough if the sending station never verifies that the product arrived. Stretch Goal Coordinate three stations and include a line-wide stop and reset procedure. Career Connection Controls engineers design handshaking logic between robots, PLCs, conveyors, and inspection machines. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →

Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Falcon Manufacturing Department: Production Engineering Goal: Increase verified line throughput by at least 20%. Background Engineering Context Falcon Manufacturing must raise output without purchasing a second line. The conveyors, robot, and routing cylinders are not synchronized, producing idle time in some zones and part bunching in others. Teams will optimize the coordinated process. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure system throughput and spacing Analyze interactions between robot and conveyor timing Use data to optimize a multi-device process Balance speed, accuracy, and reliability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Conveyors Sensors Pneumatics 6-Axis Arm if used Thirty parts Stopwatch Spreadsheet Procedure Instructions Run a ten-part baseline trial and record total time, part spacing, and failures. pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Machine Vision Quality Inspection ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Machine Vision Quality Inspection Use an optical sensor to classify parts and reject items that do not meet the color specification. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Quality Assurance Goal: Automatically identify and route production batches. Background Engineering Context An aerospace connector supplier uses color to identify production batches. Parts from the wrong batch must not reach assembly. Your workcell must measure hue, classify each incoming disk, and route it to an accepted or rejected location. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect and interpret optical-sensor data Select threshold values from repeated measurements Use conditional logic for automated decisions Calculate inspection accuracy Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Optical sensor 6-Axis Arm Red and green disks plus one unknown/test disk Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Turn on the optical sensor light at a consistent power. Collect at least ten hue readings for each known color and record the range. Choose threshold values that separate the two groups. Create an inspection function that returns the detected class. Program the robot to inspect and route each disk. Test a randomized sequence of twenty disks without changing thresholds. Record true color, detected color, and destination. Calculate accuracy and revise thresholds only if the data supports a change. Requirements Engineering Requirements Inspect twenty randomized parts Achieve at least 95% correct classification Send uncertain readings to a reject location Return to a safe position between parts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use one optical sensor Keep lighting and inspection distance consistent Do not identify colors manually during the final run Hardware locations remain fixed Deliverables What You Submit Hue calibration table Python inspection and routing program Twenty-part confusion/accuracy table Threshold justification Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why were repeated readings necessary? Which color had the widest range? How should the system handle an uncertain value? How could ambient light affect production? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the midpoint between non-overlapping data ranges as a starting threshold, then verify it with randomized tests. Common Mistake Choosing a threshold from one reading often fails when lighting or part position changes. Stretch Goal Add a third color or a confidence band that automatically rejects borderline readings. Career Connection Machine-vision and quality engineers build inspection systems that prevent defective or incorrect parts from reaching customers. Background Engineering Context AeroPack Systems packages flight-control components. Parts occasionally arrive too close together, causing collisions at pneumatic routing gates. Objectives What You Will Practice Coordinate conveyor and pneumatic actions Use sensors instead of fixed delays where appropriate Create a state-based production sequence Test and document reliability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Entry, transport, and exit conveyors Object or distance sensor Pneumatic cylinders Twenty disks/cubes Python project Procedure Instructions Draw a flowchart from part entry through final destination. pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Anatomy of an Automated Workcell ADM Activity 2.1.1 Anatomy of an Automated Workcell Analyze how the controller, sensors, robotic arm, conveyors, pneumatic
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 2 Anatomy of an Automated Workcell ADM Activity 2.1.1 Anatomy of an Automated Workcell Analyze how the controller, sensors, robotic arm, conveyors, pneumatic actuators, safety devices, and operator work together as one automated manufacturing system. Back to Unit 2 System Model Student Workflow What You Submit Essential Question How do the individual components of an automated workcell operate together as one manufacturing system? 2 class periods · 10 points Learning Targets By the end of this lesson Identify the major mechanical, electrical, sensing, control, material-handling, and safety subsystems of the VEX CTE Workcell. Explain the role of the EXP Brain as the controller for the workcell. Classify workcell components as inputs, processing/control, or outputs. Trace both material flow and information flow through an automated production process. Explain how sensor feedback can change system behavior. Analyze how a subsystem failure can affect the overall manufacturing process. Lesson Purpose Think in systems Unit 1 focused on programming and robotic movement. Unit 2 begins by stepping back and examining how individual devices become a complete automated system. The goal is not to learn another movement program. Your goal is to understand what each subsystem does, what information it uses, and how its behavior affects the rest of the workcell. Core Model Input → Control → Output → Feedback Automated systems follow a repeatable information pattern. A sensor or operator provides an input . The controller processes that information using the program. The controller commands an output such as a motor, robotic arm, signal tower, or pneumatic actuator. Additional sensing can then provide feedback to verify what actually happened. Example: Product Detection Object Sensor → EXP Brain → Conveyor Motor → Product Moves → Sensor verifies the next condition Example: Product Sorting Optical Sensor → EXP Brain → program decision → Diverter / conveyor action → product reaches the selected route Workcell Anatomy Major Components and Their Roles Component / System Primary Role System Classification EXP Brain Receives information, runs the program, and commands connected devices. Controller / Processing 6-Axis Arm Manipulates and transfers products. Output / Actuator Entry Conveyor Introduces products into the manufacturing process. Output / Material Handling Transport Conveyor Moves products between workcell operations. Output / Material Handling Exit Conveyor Moves completed or routed products out of the process. Output / Material Handling Optical Sensor Measures product color information. Input / Sensor Object Sensor Detects whether a product is present. Input / Sensor Distance Sensor Measures position or distance to an object. Input / Sensor AI Vision Sensor Identifies and locates products using visual information. Input / Sensor Pneumatic Cylinders Create linear motion for loading and routing operations. Output / Actuator Solenoids Control airflow to pneumatic cylinders. Output / Control Device Disk Loader Feeds products into the process. Material Handling Diverters Route products to different paths. Output / Material Handling Signal Tower Communicates workcell status to an operator. Output / Human Interface Emergency Stop / Operator Controls Allow human intervention when operation must stop or change state. Safety / Human Interface Operator Loads, monitors, verifies, and safely interacts with the automated system. Human System Element Material Flow Where the product moves Material flow describes the physical path followed by the product. Your system map should show where a part enters the workcell, what equipment moves or manipulates it, and where it leaves or reaches its final destination. Information Flow Where the data moves Information flow describes how sensor readings, program decisions, controller commands, and operator feedback move through the system. A product can remain stationary while information about that product moves through the controller. Student Workflow Two-Day Activity Day 1 Understand the Workcell Complete the bellwork: What makes a group of machines a system rather than just separate machines? Participate in the workcell tour and identify the major mechanical, sensing, control, material-handling, safety, and human-interface components. Classify each major component as an input, controller/processing element, output/actuator, material-handling device, or safety/human interface. Begin your labeled Workcell System Map. Before leaving, identify one complete Input → Control → Output example from the workcell. Day 2 Analyze the System Review the Input → Control → Output → Feedback model. Complete the Workcell System Map and show both material flow and information flow. Complete the Input–Control–Output–Feedback table for at least four workcell operations. Analyze three possible component or subsystem failures. Review your work for technical accuracy and submit the completed systems analysis. Required Analysis Input–Control–Output–Feedback Table Analyze at least four operations in your workcell. Each row must explain how information causes a physical or communication response. System / Operation Input Controller Decision Output Feedback / Verification Product Detection Object Sensor Object is present Conveyor stops or changes state Sensor confirms product remains in position Color Sorting Optical Sensor Determine detected product color Routing behavior is selected Product reaches the intended route Robotic Transfer Program or sensor state Transfer is permitted 6-Axis Arm moves product Next sensor or position confirms arrival Pneumatic Routing Sensor / program condition Select product path Pneumatic cylinder extends or retracts Product exits through the correct path Failure Analysis What happens when one part of the system fails? pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Resource Center Fusion-to-Mach3 CAM Workflow ADM Unit 4 Resource Fusion-to-Mach3 CAM Workflow Follow the approved workflow for creating Fusion toolpaths, po
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Resource Center Fusion-to-Mach3 CAM Workflow ADM Unit 4 Resource Fusion-to-Mach3 CAM Workflow Follow the approved workflow for creating Fusion toolpaths, posting a Mach3 .tap file, validating it in Mach3, and operating the DMC2 Mini. Back to Unit 4 DMC2 Mini Workflow Fusion → Mach3 → CNC Use only the teacher-approved machine profile, post processor, files, tools, stock, and procedures. Required Safety Boundary A successful Fusion simulation or Mach3 toolpath display does not prove that a program is safe to run. Every new or revised setup requires teacher review, code verification, a workholding check, and an approved dry run before cutting. Digital thread Approved Production Workflow 1 Design in Fusion. Complete the approved component, technical drawing, material, tolerances, and revision. 2 Enter Manufacture. Create a Milling setup, select the model, define stock, and orient X/Y/Z to match the DMC2 Mini. 3 Define the origin. Select an accessible stock-box point or teacher-approved datum that can be established as the Mach3 work zero. 4 Select tools. Use only tools from the classroom Fusion library and verify diameter, flute length, holder, flute count, and tool number. 5 Create toolpaths. Use the assigned operations and approved speeds, feeds, stepdowns, stepovers, heights, and boundaries. 6 Simulate. Show tool, holder, stock, and toolpath. Inspect collisions, rapids, plunges, remaining stock, gouges, workholding clearance, and operation order. 7 Post process. Use the teacher-validated DMC2 Mini copy of Autodesk Mach3Mill. Post only approved operations and create the .tap file. 8 Inspect the code. Verify units, G90/G91 state, work offset, safe Z, minimum Z, feeds, speeds, spindle behavior, tool plan, and M30. 9 Load in Mach3. Use the approved DMC2 Mini Mach3 profile. Compare the toolpath display and extents with Fusion. 10 Set up the mill. Inspect tool, stock, workholding, axis condition, work zero, program, feed override, spindle method, and emergency stop. 11 Dry run. Complete the teacher-approved raised-Z, air-cut, or single-block verification. 12 Manufacture and inspect. Run under supervision, record interventions, inspect the component, and preserve traceability. Fusion setup checklist Before Simulation Correct Fusion design version Milling setup Correct model selected Approved stock dimensions X/Y/Z orientation matches mill Origin can be established physically G54/work-zero plan documented Classroom tool library used Heights and boundaries checked Clamps and fixture represented Mach3 checklist Before Cycle Start Correct DMC2 Mini Mach3 profile Correct .tap file and revision Units match Fusion Tool and stock match setup Work zero matches Fusion origin Toolpath extents reviewed Minimum Z and safe Z verified Spindle procedure confirmed Feed override set as directed Emergency stop accessible Dry run approved File traceability Record These Identifiers Fusion file and version Manufacture setup name Tool library revision Post processor name and revision NC program name .tap filename Mach3 profile Work offset Stock and tool Teacher approval date

pages.description: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Resource Center Mach3 G&M Code Reference ADM Unit 4 Resource Mach3 G&M Code Reference Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command subset used with
pages.searchText: Home Courses ADM Unit 4 Resource Center Mach3 G&M Code Reference ADM Unit 4 Resource Mach3 G&M Code Reference Interpret the teacher-approved Mach3 milling command subset used with the DMC2 Mini. Back to Unit 4 DMC2 Mini Workflow Fusion → Mach3 → CNC Use only the teacher-approved machine profile, post processor, files, tools, stock, and procedures. Classroom Code Boundary This reference is for the teacher-approved DMC2 Mini Mach3 milling profile. A command may be supported by Mach3 but still be inappropriate for the classroom machine, tooling, spindle configuration, or current setup. Use only commands assigned by the teacher. Motion and coordinates Core G Codes G00 — rapid positioning; use only with verified clearance G01 — linear feed motion using F G02 / G03 — clockwise / counterclockwise circular interpolation when assigned G17 — XY plane G20 / G21 — inch / metric units G54 — teacher-approved work coordinate system G90 / G91 — absolute / incremental positioning G94 — feed per minute Machine states Safety and M Codes G40 — cancel cutter compensation G49 — cancel tool-length compensation when not used G80 — cancel canned cycle F — feed rate S — commanded spindle speed M03 — spindle clockwise only when the DMC2 Mini profile controls the spindle M05 — spindle stop only when configured M30 — program end and reset Instructional example Teacher-Reviewed Program Pattern (ADM U4 PRACTICE - NOT FOR MACHINE USE WITHOUT APPROVAL) G17 G21 G40 G49 G80 G90 G94 G54 G00 Z10.000 G00 X0.000 Y0.000 (M03 S____ only when configured and approved) G01 Z-1.000 F____ G01 X25.000 Y0.000 F____ G01 X25.000 Y15.000 G01 X0.000 Y15.000 G01 X0.000 Y0.000 G00 Z10.000 (M05 only when configured) M30 The numeric values are placeholders. Tool diameter, stock, origin, depth, feeds, speeds, and spindle behavior must come from the approved setup. Modal-state check Ask Before Every Run What units are active? Is positioning absolute or incremental? Which work offset is active? What plane is active? Are compensation and canned cycles canceled? What feed mode is active? Where is the tool now? What is the next Z movement? Mach3 file check Inspect the .tap File Correct program and revision Expected units Expected work offset Safe initial Z Correct minimum Z No unsupported commands Spindle behavior matches machine configuration Feeds and speeds approved Safe retract before rapid travel M30 at program end

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 5 IED Unit 5 Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone Unit mission: Design, prototype, test, revise, and present an aerospace solution that responds to real user needs while considering safety, ethics, sustainability, life cycle, and impact. Lesson Map Back to IED Hub Unit Project Complete a human-centered aerospace capstone and final engineering portfolio. Research Prototype Present Every lesson builds evidence for the final portfolio, prototype review, and capstone presentation. Unit Overview What Unit 5 Builds You will connect user research, ethics, sustainability, project management, prototyping, testing, feedback, revision, portfolio evidence, and professional presentation. Human-Centered Research You will define stakeholders, user needs, criteria, constraints, and a design brief before choosing a solution. Prototype + Feedback You will generate concepts, select a final direction, plan fabrication, build, test, collect feedback, and revise. Responsible Communication You will evaluate ethics, safety, sustainability, and life cycle, then assemble a portfolio and final presentation. Open Lesson PPTX 5.3 Problem Statement, Criteria, Constraints, and Design Brief How do engineers turn user needs into a clear design problem? Open Lesson PPTX 5.10 Prototype Build Day 2: Integration and Refinement How do engineers refine a prototype so it is ready to be tested by a user or evaluated with data? Open Lesson PPTX 5.11 Testing Protocol and User Feedback Plan How can engineers test whether a prototype solves the user problem? Open Lesson PPTX 5.12 Prototype Testing and User Feedback What evidence shows whether a prototype is successful for the user? Open Lesson PPTX 5.13 Data Analysis and Stakeholder Feedback Review How can engineers combine data and user feedback to decide what should improve? Open Lesson PPTX 5.14 Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life-Cycle Analysis How do engineers make responsible design decisions beyond simply making a prototype work? Open Lesson PPTX 5.15 Final Prototype Revision and Refinement How do engineers use evidence and feedback to make final improvements before presenting a design? Open Lesson PPTX 5.16 Final Engineering Portfolio Workday How can engineers use a portfolio to communicate the complete story of a design project? pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 3 IED Unit 3 • 14 Lessons Assembly Design, Prototyping & Documentation Unit mission: Build on the rigid-joint and exploded-view skills from Unit 2 by learning revolute joints, slider joints, motion limits, and mechanical verification; then design, manufacture, revise, and test a modular compressed-air rocket. Start Lesson 3.1 Back to IED Hub Unit Progression From moving mechanisms to a flight-tested modular rocket Motion Joint Limits Verify Rocket CAD Manufacture Flight Test Unit 3 applies the drawing and manufacturing skills from the Puzzle Cube Challenge to a real multi-part rocket assembly with removable interfaces, laser-cut fins, and a final compressed-air flight test. How the Unit Fits Together Four Focus Areas Lessons 3.1–3.5 Motion-Based Assembly Skills Build revolute and slider mechanisms from teacher-provided parts, apply joint limits, combine different relationships, and diagnose fit and motion faults. Lessons 3.6–3.8 Compressed-Air Rocket Design Plan the modular rocket, design the 3D-printed components and laser-cut fins, and complete a formal digital design review. Lessons 3.9–3.11 Manufacture, Assemble & Revise Prepare STL/DXF files, assemble and fit-test the physical rocket, and complete an engineering change before flight. Lessons 3.12–3.14 Document, Inspect & Flight Test Create the assembly drawing/BOM, pass a formal flight-readiness review, and complete the teacher-controlled compressed-air flight test. Unit 3 Lesson List Lessons 3.1–3.5 develop motion-based assembly skills using provided mechanisms; Lessons 3.6–3.14 form one continuous modular rocket project. Open Lesson 3.4 Rover Assembly: As-Built Joints How do As-Built Joints constrain an already-positioned rover while allowing its wheels to rotate? Open Lesson 3.5 Interference, Clearance & Motion Verification How can engineers find and repair interference or motion faults? Open Lesson 3.6 Rocket Design Challenge & Concept Development How can a launch requirement become a modular, manufacturable rocket design? Open Lesson 3.7 Rocket Component Design & CAD Assembly How can the rocket's individual components and removable interfaces be modeled together? Open Lesson 3.8 Digital Assembly Design Review What evidence confirms that a rocket assembly is ready to manufacture? Open Lesson 3.9 Manufacturing & Fabrication Preparation How do CAD components become accurate STL and laser DXF files? Open Lesson 3.10 Physical Rocket Assembly & Fit Testing What can physical assembly reveal about fit, alignment, and manufacturing? Open Lesson 3.11 Engineering Change & Final Revision How can prototype evidence guide a controlled design revision? Open Lesson 3.12 Assembly Drawing, Exploded View & BOM How can drawings, exploded views, and a BOM document the final assembly? Open Lesson 3.13 Flight Readiness Review & Final Design Package What must pass inspection before an instructor-controlled flight test? Open Lesson 3.14 Compressed-Air Rocket Flight Test & Post-Flight Review What does flight testing reveal about the quality of the engineered assembly? Open Lesson Major Project Modular Compressed-Air Rocket Assembly & Flight Test Challenge Students design a fully 3D-printed modular rocket with laser-cut fins, create at least two removable printed interfaces, verify compatibility with a 0.840 in (21.34 mm) OD PVC launch tube, manufacture and assemble the rocket, complete a prototype-driven engineering change, document the final assembly, and finish with a teacher-controlled compressed-air flight test.

pages.title: Course Launch & Engineering Mindset
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.1 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.1 Course Launch & Engineering Mindset Focus Question: How do engineers think, document, and make evidence-based decisions?
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.1 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.1 Course Launch & Engineering Mindset Focus Question: How do engineers think, document, and make evidence-based decisions? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Think like an engineer Define the problem, test the idea, and use evidence to make and communicate decisions. Define Test Decide Mission Briefing Today’s Plan A complete opening lesson that launches the engineering mindset you will use throughout IED. Learning Targets Describe the purpose of IED through an aerospace lens. Explain how engineering problems differ from typical assignments. Identify evidence engineers use to support design decisions. Success Looks Like… You can explain a design decision using more than “I think.” Core habit: Connect each design claim to evidence another person can inspect. Opening prompt Engineer-actions vote IED + aerospace Mindset shift Evidence challenge Quick check Exit debrief Opening Prompt What do engineers do? Think about actions, habits, and decisions—not job titles. Quick class share: Give one short answer using an action word such as design, build, test, fix, invent, solve, measure, or improve. Reveal the working definition Engineers use knowledge, tools, and creativity to solve problems under real constraints. 1 Define Clarify the need, user, criteria, and constraints. 2 Generate Create multiple possible solutions before choosing one. 3 Test Collect evidence from models, prototypes, data, and feedback. 4 Communicate Document decisions so others can understand and improve the work. Interactive Vote Engineer Actions: Which One Fits? Hold up fingers 1–4 or vote silently. Then justify your choice. Which action sounds most like engineering work? 1 Copying exact instructions to make the same model as everyone else 2 Choosing the first idea because it seems easiest to build 3 Testing two versions and comparing data before deciding 4 Making a design look impressive without checking if it works Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 3 Testing two versions and comparing data before deciding uses comparison, data, and a decision based on evidence. The other choices prioritize copying, ease, or appearance rather than proof. Carry-forward idea: In IED, an answer becomes stronger when it connects to evidence. Course Launch IED Through an Aerospace Lens Build transferable engineering habits through aerospace contexts and projects. Core Engineering Skills Sketching and visual communication Engineering notebook documentation CAD modeling and technical drawings Prototyping, testing, and data analysis Design reviews and evidence-based explanations Aerospace Connections Rocket launch pad design challenge Rocket models and assemblies Aircraft, drones, satellites, and rovers FabLab tools and manufacturing routines Human-centered aerospace capstone Turn + Talk Aerospace Connection Map Choose a rocket, drone, satellite, rover, or aircraft . Identify one design choice an engineer must make, then connect it to one kind of evidence. Sketch What features or shapes matter? Model What could be represented in CAD? Measure What dimensions or data matter? Test What would prove it works? Share-out target: one system + one design decision + one kind of evidence. Mindset Shift Assignment vs. Engineering Problem The goal is not just to finish; the goal is to make a design claim you can defend. Completion Mindset Typical Assignment Often has one expected answer Can be completed and put away Usually judged as correct or incorrect Mistakes are avoided Evidence Mindset Engineering Problem Has multiple possible solutions Must satisfy criteria and constraints Uses testing to compare designs Mistakes become evidence for improvement Key Idea Evidence-Based Engineering Engineers connect what they claim to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the design → 2 Evidence What proves or challenges the claim → 3 Decision What you do next because of the evidence Evidence can include: sketches; measurements; test data; observations; photos; prototypes; user feedback. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the two pieces of evidence that best support the claim. Claim: “Our launch pad design supports the rocket safely and is ready for testing.” A A labeled sketch showing where the rocket contacts the support B A photo that makes the prototype look finished C A stability test showing the pad does not tip with the rocket placed on it D A teammate saying the design is probably strong enough E A list of the materials used to build the base and support Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows design intent and the support locations. C provides direct performance evidence against a safety and stability criterion. Photos, material lists, and teammate opinions can support the story, but they do not prove the claim by themselves. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A team builds a small rocket support. During the first test, it stands up, but the rocket leans to one side. A Keep it because the prototype did not fall over. B Add decorations so the design looks more complete. C Record the lean, identify where the support is uneven, revise, and retest. D Start over without writing down what happened. Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: C Record the lean, identify where the support is uneven, revise, and retest. Record Write down what happened during the test. Identify Find the likely cause of the lean. Revise + Retest Change the design and collect new evidence. Engineering move: Use the problem as evidence, not as a reason to hide or restart the work. Quick Check Evidence or Opinion? Vote on all three statements before revealing the answers. A. “Our design is the best because it looks strong.” B. “Version 2 traveled 12 ft farther than Version 1 in the official test.” C. “We changed the wing fold

pages.title: Emergency Communications Tower
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Emergency Communications Tower IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Emergency Communications Tower Build the tallest free-standing paper tower that supports a 200
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Emergency Communications Tower IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Emergency Communications Tower Build the tallest free-standing paper tower that supports a 200 g payload for 30 seconds. Intermediate 45 minutes Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context After a hurricane, a temporary communications antenna must be raised above nearby debris. The emergency team has limited materials and needs a structure that is tall, stable, and quick to deploy. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply structural design principles Plan within strict material limits Test and improve a prototype Use measurements to compare performance Materials What You Need 20 index cards 30 cm masking tape Scissors Ruler or tape measure 200 g test mass Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Study the materials without building for two minutes. Sketch one tower concept and label the base, vertical supports, and payload platform. Predict the tower height and identify the most likely failure point. Build for 15 minutes using only the issued materials. Measure the height before adding the payload. Place the 200 g mass on the top platform for 30 seconds. If the tower fails, document the failure location and make one repair using remaining material. Retest and calculate a performance score: successful height in centimeters divided by grams of material used. Requirements Engineering Requirements Stand without being attached to the table or floor Support 200 g for 30 seconds Use no more than 20 cards and 30 cm of tape Include a platform that prevents the payload from sliding Provide a measured final height Constraints Constraints & Safety 15-minute initial build time No glue, staples, string, or added materials Payload must be placed by hand without holding the tower Height is measured from table surface to top of payload Deliverables What You Submit Initial sketch and height prediction Photo before testing Measured height and material use Failure observation or success evidence Performance score calculation Three-sentence redesign recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions How did the base width affect stability? Where did compression or bending appear? Which material use produced the most strength? What would you change with five additional cards? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Folded card sections resist bending better than flat cards. Test triangular, tubular, and layered shapes. Common Mistake A very tall narrow tower may score well before testing but fail under the payload. Stability is part of performance. Stretch Goal Rebuild with only 12 cards and attempt to achieve at least 80% of your original height. Career Connection Structural and civil engineers design temporary towers, supports, and deployable structures for emergencies and field operations. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Engineering Failure Investigation
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Engineering Failure Investigation IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Engineering Failure Investigation Investigate a major engineering failure and identify how
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Engineering Failure Investigation IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Engineering Failure Investigation Investigate a major engineering failure and identify how design-process improvements could have reduced the risk. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering failures are rarely caused by a single bad decision. They often involve technical limits, communication problems, testing gaps, and pressure from schedules or cost. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish immediate causes from root causes Connect evidence to design-process decisions Identify ethical and communication factors Develop prevention recommendations Materials What You Need Internet research access Engineering notebook Presentation or document software At least two credible sources Procedure Instructions Choose an approved case such as Challenger, Columbia, Mars Climate Orbiter, Tacoma Narrows Bridge, Hyatt Regency walkway, or another teacher-approved failure. Create a short timeline of at least five events before the failure. Identify the system or component that failed first. Use a five-whys analysis to identify at least one technical root cause and one organizational root cause. Find evidence of a warning, test result, or concern that was missed or misunderstood. Map the failure to stages of the engineering design process. Develop three specific prevention actions involving design, testing, communication, or decision-making. Present the investigation in a one-page visual brief or three-minute presentation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use at least two credible sources Separate facts from your own conclusions Include both technical and human/organizational factors Provide three actionable prevention recommendations Cite sources in a consistent format Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not use graphic images Do not copy a prewritten case summary Keep the final product to one page or three minutes Use respectful language when discussing injuries or loss of life Deliverables What You Submit Timeline Five-whys root cause analysis Engineering design process map Three prevention actions Source list One-page brief or short presentation Reflection Reflection Questions Which warning sign was most important? Where could better testing have changed the outcome? How did communication influence the failure? What responsibility does an engineer have when a safety concern is ignored? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask “What allowed this condition to exist?” instead of stopping at “Which part broke?” Common Mistake A root cause is not simply the last event before failure. Look for deeper design, process, and communication conditions. Stretch Goal Compare two failures and identify one recurring pattern in engineering decision-making. Career Connection Safety, reliability, systems, and quality engineers study failures to prevent recurrence and improve standards. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson →

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.7 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.7 Fabrication Readiness Focus Question: How do safe tool use and careful planning prepare a design for fabrication? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Demonstrate safe hand and cutting tool practices and prepare the approved launch-pad design for fabrication. Suggested pacing: 1 × 45-minute class period Prepare Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Every task advances the same Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge. Learning Targets Complete the required Hand & Cutting Tool Certification before building. Create an efficient foam-board cutting layout. Verify the build sequence, material allocation, and tool plan before fabrication. Success Looks Like… Every student who will use hand/cutting tools is certified and the team has an approved design, cutting layout, and build sequence ready for the next lesson. Project connection: Your work today becomes evidence used in the next stage of the Engineering Design Process. Fabrication Gate Certification comes before construction Required Before Build Hand & Cutting Tool Certification No student may independently perform cutting or applicable hand-tool operations on the launch-pad prototype until the required certification has been completed. Open Certification Study Guide Practice Safety Focus Demonstrate safe fabrication habits Cutting-tool readiness Use the correct cutting surface. Keep hands out of the cutting path. Cut away from the body and other people. Use controlled passes instead of excessive force. Inspect tools before use and return them correctly. Hot-glue readiness Keep the heated tip away from skin and materials not being joined. Use only the amount of glue needed for the joint. Allow joints to cool before loading them. Keep cords and tools organized at the workstation. Clean the work area before leaving. Cutting Layout Plan the 12 in × 18 in foam-board sheet Before cutting, sketch or mark a layout showing every foam-board component your design requires. Fit all planned foam-board parts on the single 12 in × 18 in sheet. Label critical dimensions. Check the layout against the final design drawing. Leave enough room for safe, accurate cuts. Do not cut until the teacher approves the readiness check. Readiness Check Ready means design + tools + materials + sequence Final design is teacher-approved. Hand & Cutting Tool Certification is complete for students performing those operations. Foam-board cutting layout is complete. Material quantities fit within the team kit. Build sequence is clear. Rocket-fit checkpoints are identified. Next lesson: Build only after this gate is complete. Mission Debrief What You Submit Required Deliverable Hand & Cutting Tool Certification + Fabrication Readiness Check Submit the complete team evidence required by this lesson. Use clear labels, dimensions, test data, and reasoning where applicable. Project Resources Launch Pad Challenge Reference Standard Team Materials 1 × 12 in × 18 in foam-board sheet 20 craft sticks 10 straws 48 in string Hot glue as needed Core Constraints Use the provided rocket; do not modify it. 12 in × 12 in maximum footprint. 12 in maximum pad height, not including the rocket. Rocket must be installable and removable. Use only approved team-kit structural materials. ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson: Prototype Build

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.6 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.6 Develop the Design Focus Question: How can a detailed plan turn an idea into a buildable prototype? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Convert the selected concept into a dimensioned final design and a clear materials and construction plan. Learning Targets Create a final sketch with enough dimensions and labels to guide fabrication. Plan how each provided material will be used. Create a logical construction sequence before cutting materials. Success Looks Like… Another team could look at your final design and explain what to cut, where the rocket sits, how the structure is braced, and how the parts connect. Project connection: Your work today becomes evidence used in the next stage of the Engineering Design Process. Design Development Move from an idea to a buildable plan Define Imagine Select Develop Build Test Improve Communicate A prototype should be built from a plan—not from memory. Final Sketch Communicate the geometry clearly Required drawing information Overall footprint dimensions Overall launch-pad height Rocket location and support contact points Major support and brace dimensions Material labels Joint / hot-glue locations Features that allow the rocket to be installed and removed Design-envelope check Before approval, confirm that the final design stays within the 12 in × 12 in footprint and 12 in pad-height limits. Place the real provided rocket in the intended support position to verify the interface before building. Materials Plan Assign material before you cut it Part / Feature Material Approx. Size / Quantity Why this material? Identify every cut before cutting the limited foam board. Plan the order that major components will be assembled. Identify when the provided rocket will be used for fit checks. Identify the hand/cutting tools needed for each operation. Fabrication gate: The design must receive teacher approval before moving into the certification/readiness lesson.
