pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.9 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.9 Test & Improve Focus Question: How can test evidence guide a meaningful design improvement? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Conduct standardized qualification tests, identify the most important weakness, and make one evidence-based improvement before final competition. Suggested pacing: 1 × 45-minute class period Test Improve Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Every task advances the same Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge. Learning Targets Collect comparable evidence using the standard qualification procedure. Identify the strongest and weakest features of the prototype from test evidence. Make and document one targeted design improvement. Success Looks Like… Your team can point to a specific test result, explain what it revealed, and show one change made because of that evidence. Project connection: Your work today becomes evidence used in the next stage of the Engineering Design Process. Test Use the same procedure for every team Define Imagine Select Develop Build Test Improve Communicate A test is useful when it produces evidence that can change a decision. Qualification Sequence Prototype testing 1. Dimensional Check Footprint ≤ 12 in × 12 in ; pad height ≤ 12 in without the rocket. 2. Rocket Fit The provided rocket installs, remains upright, and can be removed without damage. 3. Level Stability Rocket + pad remain freestanding and unsupported for 60 seconds . 4. Required Tilt Hold at 10° for 5 seconds in forward, backward, left, and right directions. 5. Disturbance Complete the instructor-controlled disturbance test without tipping, losing the rocket, or experiencing structural failure. Analyze Find the weakness that matters most Use evidence Where did movement first appear? Did the base slide, rotate, or tip? Did the rocket move inside its support? Did a brace bend, buckle, or detach? Which direction was least stable? Choose one improvement Make one targeted change that responds to a specific observation. Do not redesign the entire project. Examples: move a support, reinforce a joint, add/reposition a brace, change a rocket-contact point, or modify the base geometry within the size limit. Engineering Change Record Evidence → Change → Expected Effect Record the test evidence that triggered the change, describe exactly what you changed, and predict what should improve during the final competition. Mission Debrief What You Submit Required Deliverable Qualification Test Record + Engineering Change Record Submit the complete team evidence required by this lesson. Use clear labels, dimensions, test data, and reasoning where applicable. Rocket must be installable and removable. Use only approved team-kit structural materials. ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson: Final Challenge & Design Review

pages.title: Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.2 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object Analyze a classroom object and create an engineering
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.2 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object Analyze a classroom object and create an engineering record that explains its parts, materials, assembly, and likely manufacturing methods. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineers often study an existing product before they redesign it. Reverse engineering begins with careful observation, component identification, and reasoned predictions about how a product works. Objectives What You Will Practice Practice technical observation Identify product components and functions Connect materials to manufacturing processes Create an exploded concept sketch Materials What You Need One approved classroom object Engineering notebook Ruler Colored pencils or fine-tip pens Optional magnifier Procedure Instructions Select an object with at least four visible parts, such as a stapler, tape dispenser, scissors, hole punch, or marker. Create a clean isometric sketch of the complete object. Number every visible component and create a matching parts list. For each component, record its function and likely material. Predict how each part was manufactured: molding, stamping, extrusion, machining, forming, or another process. Create an exploded sketch showing the likely assembly order. Identify one design feature that improves safety, comfort, durability, or ease of assembly. Propose one redesign and explain the problem it solves. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least four components Use labels and leader lines correctly Include a material and process prediction for every component Show a logical exploded assembly order Support predictions with visible evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not disassemble sealed, sharp, powered, or school-owned equipment without permission Complete all sketches by hand Do not use an internet image as the primary drawing Deliverables What You Submit Complete-object isometric sketch Numbered parts list Material and manufacturing table Exploded sketch Redesign annotation and explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which component was hardest to understand? What visible clues helped identify the manufacturing process? Which material choice appeared most important? How would your redesign affect manufacturing cost? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Look for seams, draft angles, fasteners, surface textures, and repeated shapes. These are clues about manufacturing. Common Mistake Do not confuse a component function with its material. “Spring” is a component; “spring steel” is a material choice. Stretch Goal Compare your object with a competing version and identify three design differences. Career Connection Product design and manufacturing engineers routinely analyze competitor products to understand performance, cost, and assembly decisions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Evaluate & Select
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.5 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.5 Evaluate & Select Focus Question: How can engineers use evidence to choose between competing ideas? View Lesson Plan What
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.5 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.5 Evaluate & Select Focus Question: How can engineers use evidence to choose between competing ideas? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Use a weighted decision matrix to select and refine the launch-pad concept that best satisfies the project requirements. Suggested pacing: 1 × 45-minute class period Select Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Every task advances the same Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge. Learning Targets Develop evaluation criteria that match the challenge goals. Use a weighted decision matrix to compare all three concepts. Refine the selected concept and explain the tradeoffs accepted by the team. Success Looks Like… Your selected concept is supported by the decision matrix and has enough detail to begin final development. Project connection: Your work today becomes evidence used in the next stage of the Engineering Design Process. Decision Making Do not build the idea you simply like best Engineers compare alternatives using criteria that connect directly to the problem. Define Imagine Select Develop Build Test Improve Communicate Weighted Decision Matrix Turn project goals into evaluation criteria Suggested criteria Predicted stability Ability to hold the rocket securely Compact footprint Ease of construction Efficient material use Ease of installing/removing the rocket Weighting rule More important criteria receive larger weights. Your weights should reflect the challenge—not personal preferences. Example: Stability should normally matter more than appearance because stability is directly tested. Evidence Check Scores need reasons For each concept, ask what feature supports the score. A number without a reason is only an opinion. Example: evidence-based scoring Weak: “Concept B gets a 5 for stability because we think it is stable.” Stronger: “Concept B gets a 5 for stability because it uses a wide triangular base and four support points located near the footprint corners.” Refine the Winner Develop the selected concept before the next lesson Show the selected base geometry and rocket support. Add preliminary overall dimensions. Identify where foam board, craft sticks, straws, string, and hot glue will be used. Show major braces and joints. Identify one tradeoff the team accepted. Record the decision using Decision → Evidence → Reasoning . Mission Debrief What You Submit Required Deliverable Decision Matrix + Selected Concept + Design Justification Submit the complete team evidence required by this lesson. Use clear labels, dimensions, test data, and reasoning where applicable. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.4 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.4 Launch Pad Challenge: Define & Imagine Focus Question: How do engineers define a problem and generate multiple possible solutions? View Lesson Plan What You Submit Download Presentation Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Define the launch pad problem and generate multiple feasible concepts before committing to one direction. Suggested pacing: 1 × 45-minute class period Define Imagine Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Every task advances the same Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge. Learning Targets Explain how the Engineering Design Process will guide the Launch Pad Challenge. Identify the challenge criteria and non-negotiable constraints. Create three annotated concepts that solve the same problem in meaningfully different ways. Success Looks Like… Your team has a concise design brief and three understandable concepts that another student could interpret without a verbal explanation. Project connection: Your work today becomes evidence used in the next stage of the Engineering Design Process. Challenge Reveal Design a stable launch pad for the provided rocket The project is intentionally constrained so your engineering effort can focus on structure, stability, and decision making. Mission Your engineering team will design and build a tabletop launch pad. The launch pad must securely support the instructor-provided rocket in an upright position, remain stable during qualification testing, and be built only from the standardized team material kit. The rocket is provided. Do not modify it. Real launch systems use structure, bracing, access, and carefully planned interfaces. Look for ideas you can adapt at classroom scale. Engineering Design Process The project is the process You are not memorizing a sequence before the project. You will experience the process by completing the challenge. Define Research Imagine Select Develop Build Test Improve Communicate Today: understand the problem, identify what cannot change, then create options. Challenge Requirements Know the rules before sketching Size Maximum launch-pad footprint: 12 in × 12 in . Maximum pad height: 12 in , not including the rocket. Rocket Interface Use the provided rocket . It may not be cut, drilled, glued, taped, or otherwise modified. The rocket must be removable without damaging either item. Function The launch pad must be freestanding and hold the rocket upright without being held. It must remain functional after qualification testing. Materials Use only the standardized team material kit and approved joining methods. You are not required to use every material . Standardized Material Kit Every team starts with the same resources 1 × 12 in × 18 in foam board 20 craft sticks 10 straws 48 in string Hot glue as needed Engineering habit: Material is useful only when it contributes to function. Do not add parts simply because they are available. Design Brief Define the engineering problem Criteria — goals to improve Stability Secure rocket support Compact footprint Easy rocket installation/removal Efficient use of limited materials Clear, buildable construction Constraints — rules that cannot change 12 in × 12 in maximum footprint 12 in maximum pad height Provided rocket; no rocket modification Standardized material kit only Freestanding structure Must pass required qualification tests Concept Generation Create three different structural approaches Do not draw the same idea three times with cosmetic changes. Every sketch should show: Base shape and approximate footprint Rocket location and support method Major structural members and bracing Approximate overall dimensions Which provided materials are used where Labels explaining why important features exist Quality check: Another team should be able to understand the concept without you standing beside it. Mission Debrief What You Submit Required Deliverable Launch Pad Design Brief + 3 Annotated Concept Sketches Submit the complete team evidence required by this lesson. Use clear labels, dimensions, test data, and reasoning where applicable. Document changes from the approved plan and explain why they were necessary. Success Looks Like… The prototype is complete, the rocket can be installed and removed, and the build record explains any important deviations from the final drawing. Project connection: Your work today becomes evidence used in the next stage of the Engineering Design Process. Prototype Build the approved design Fabrication is part of the engineering process. If reality forces a change, document it. Define Imagine Select Develop Build Test Improve Communicate Day 1 Fabricate the primary structure Review certification status and the approved cutting layout. Measure and cut foam-board components. Prepare craft sticks, straws, and string as required by the plan. Assemble the base and primary supports. Use the provided rocket for controlled fit checks. Add major braces and allow hot-glue joints to cool before loading. Photograph or sketch the build status before cleanup. Day 2 Complete, brace, and inspect Complete the rocket-support interface. Add planned bracing and structural connections. Confirm the rocket installs and removes without damage. Check the 12 in × 12 in footprint and 12 in pad-height limits. Check that the structure stands on its own. Complete workmanship and safety cleanup. Build Record Do not quietly change the design Original Plan What Changed? Why? Evidence / Observation Describe the planned feature. Describe the change. Explain the reason. Fit issue, material behavior, measurement, etc. Engineering rule: A change made during fabrication is still a design decision. Record it. pages.title: Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.3 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.3 Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation Focus Question: How do safe habits make engineering work possible? Downlo
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.3 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.3 Safety Acknowledgment, PPE & FabLab Orientation Focus Question: How do safe habits make engineering work possible? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Protect people and the workspace Recognize the behaviors, PPE, and permission systems required before using tools, machines, and materials. Notice Protect Report Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Connect safe behavior to engineering quality, shared responsibility, and permission to use equipment. Learning Targets Identify major safety expectations for the engineering classroom and FabLab. Explain PPE and safe behavior expectations around tools and materials. Understand the signed acknowledgment requirement before tool use. Success Looks Like… You can recognize an unsafe condition, stop, and explain the correct next action. Core habit: When something seems unsafe, stop immediately and ask before continuing. Opening prompt Why safety matters PPE + behavior FabLab orientation Scenario vote Acknowledgment Debrief Opening Prompt What can go wrong before a tool is even turned on? Safety begins with awareness, preparation, and behavior—not only with emergency response. Quick class share: Identify one unsafe condition that could affect a person, a tool, a material, or the quality of a project. Reveal the engineering connection Safety is an engineering requirement. Unsafe behavior can injure people, damage equipment, waste materials, and make test results unreliable. Professional Workspace Safety protects more than people Technical spaces use controlled procedures because quality and safety are connected. Professional technical spaces depend on controlled behavior, clear procedures, and attention to the work area. Image: NASA Glenn Research Center, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Non-Negotiables Know the baseline expectations These expectations apply before activity-specific tool rules are introduced. PPE Prepare yourself Wear safety glasses when directed or required. Wear closed-toe shoes for fabrication activities. Tie back long hair. Secure loose clothing and dangling jewelry. Use gloves only when appropriate and directed. Behavior Protect the workspace No horseplay, rushing, or distracting others. Use tools and materials only with permission. Keep work areas and walkways clear. Respect active build zones. Report damage, injuries, and unsafe conditions immediately. Scenario Vote What should happen first? Vote before opening the answer. A student notices that a cutting tool has a loose handle, but the class is already behind schedule. A Use it carefully and tell the teacher later. B Ask a teammate to test it first. C Stop, keep others from using it, and report it immediately. D Put it back without saying anything. Reveal the safest response Best answer: C Stop, prevent use, and report the condition. Schedule pressure never overrides safety. Stop Do not continue with unsafe equipment. Protect Keep others away from the hazard. Report Tell the teacher immediately. Access Requirement Signed acknowledgment comes before tool use Orientation does not replace individual equipment certifications. 1 Review Student and parent/guardian review classroom and FabLab expectations. 2 Return Submit the signed paper acknowledgment as a graded completion item. 3 Certify Complete separate tool certifications before operating specific equipment. Until the acknowledgment is returned: you may participate in class, but you may not use FabLab tools or machines. Mission Debrief What You Submit Complete the safety-readiness requirement before future fabrication work. Safety Acknowledgment The completed safety acknowledgment with required student and parent/guardian signatures. pages.title: Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad Redesign the launch pad to use less material while maintaining
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad Redesign the launch pad to use less material while maintaining stability, rocket fit, and safe classroom handling. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Your original launch pad proved that a free-standing structure can support the classroom rocket. A launch systems team now wants a lighter, easier-to-build version that still protects and supports the vehicle. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply criteria and constraints to a redesign Generate and compare multiple concepts Collect stability test evidence Justify a final design using data Materials What You Need Original launch pad or drawings Provided 3D printed rocket Approved classroom build materials Ruler or tape measure Scale if available Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the original design and list three specific weaknesses. Measure and record the original mass, footprint, and rocket contact points. Create two new annotated concept sketches. Each concept must show how the rocket is supported. Use a decision matrix with at least four criteria to select a concept. Build the selected concept using fewer materials than the original. Test the pad on a level surface and on a 5-degree inclined surface. Place the rocket on the pad and perform three gentle disturbance tests from different directions. Record results, revise one feature, and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Support the provided rocket without assistance Stand on its own for at least 60 seconds Remain upright during three disturbance tests Use at least 20% less material by mass or measured quantity Include at least one research-informed launch pad feature Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved classroom materials No adhesives or fasteners may contact the rocket body Must fit within a 30 cm by 30 cm footprint Must be completed within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Problem statement and criteria/constraints Two annotated concept sketches Decision matrix Before-and-after material comparison Test table with at least six trials Photo of final prototype One-paragraph design justification Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion had the greatest influence on your final design? What failed or moved during testing? What tradeoff did you make between mass and stability? What would you test next if the pad were used outdoors? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Move material away from low-stress areas and keep support members near the rocket contact points. Common Mistake Reducing material everywhere usually weakens the base. Remove material strategically instead of simply making every part smaller. Stretch Goal Reduce material use by 35% while keeping the same test performance. Career Connection Aerospace ground-support engineers design stands, fixtures, and launch equipment that protect vehicles before flight. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Final Launch Pad Challenge & Design Review
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.10 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.10 Final Launch Pad Challenge & Design Review Focus Question: How can engineers use performance evidence to defend a desig
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.10 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.10 Final Launch Pad Challenge & Design Review Focus Question: How can engineers use performance evidence to defend a design? View Lesson Plan Design Review Form Download PDF What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Complete final qualification and stability competition testing, analyze performance, and communicate the engineering decisions behind the final launch pad. Suggested pacing: 1 × 45-minute class period Communicate Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Every task advances the same Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge. Learning Targets Demonstrate that the final launch pad satisfies the required constraints and qualification tests. Record final measurements, stability data, and observations directly on the Engineering Design Review form. Use evidence from the full project to defend design decisions, explain iteration, and propose a future improvement. Success Looks Like… You complete final testing and a two-page Engineering Design Review that uses specific project evidence—not guesses or general statements—to explain how and why the design performed as it did. Project connection: This is the Communicate stage of the Engineering Design Process. Your final claims should be supported by evidence collected throughout the unit. Class Flow Prepare the form: Put your name, period, team members, and date on the Engineering Design Review before testing begins. Qualify: Complete Part A as your launch pad moves through each required test. Compete: Record the maximum successful tilt angle and final observations. Review: Use your earlier sketches, decision matrix, build notes, and test evidence to complete Parts A–E, then submit the two-page form. Final Qualification Pass the required tests before entering the competition Define Research Imagine Select Develop Build Test Improve Communicate Dimensions 12 in × 12 in maximum footprint and 12 in maximum pad height. Rocket Interface Provided rocket installs, remains upright, and removes without damage. Level Stability 60 seconds unsupported. Required Tilt 10° in four directions for 5 seconds each. Disturbance Pass the standardized instructor-controlled disturbance test. Use the worksheet while you test: Complete the Part A qualification table as each test happens. Record actual measurements, pass/fail results, and short observations. Do not wait until the end of class and try to reconstruct your data from memory. Competition Maximum Tilt Challenge Most Stable Launch Pad After qualification, increase the test-platform angle in consistent increments until the design can no longer maintain the required stable condition. The design with the highest successful tilt angle wins the stability challenge. Mass is not part of the competition. Record the result on Part A Write your team’s maximum successful tilt angle on the Engineering Design Review form immediately after competition testing. Use the Evidence / Observation column to capture anything that helps explain the result, such as where the structure began to shift, flex, or tip. If multiple teams achieve the same maximum angle, the smaller qualifying footprint is the tie breaker. Design Review Worksheet Complete the two-page Engineering Design Review The worksheet is your written final evidence for the Launch Pad Challenge. Complete it individually unless your instructor directs otherwise. Required PDF IED 0.10 Engineering Design Review Use this form during testing and competition, then finish the analysis and reflection sections before submitting the lesson. Download / Print PDF What counts as strong evidence? Measured footprint, height, time, or tilt angle. Pass/fail results from qualification testing. A specific observation of flexing, shifting, joint failure, tipping, or stability. Evidence from your decision matrix, sketches, build record, or engineering change. A before-and-after comparison from testing and improvement. Page 1 — Final Performance & Iteration Header: Fill in your name, period, team members, and date. Part A: Complete the qualification table during testing. Enter actual results and mark Y/N for each required check. Maximum tilt: Record your highest successful competition angle. A1–A2: Identify the strongest and weakest parts of the final design and support each answer with evidence. Part B: Explain why your team selected its concept, describe the most important change made after testing, and evaluate whether the change improved performance. Page 2 — Engineering Process & Judgment Part C: Give one specific example from your project for each EDP step: Define, Research, Imagine, Select, Develop, Build, Test, and Improve. C1: Explain how your team communicated its engineering work using sketches, the decision matrix, build documentation, test records, or the design review. Part D: Propose one Version 2 improvement, identify the strongest evidence that your design solved the original problem, and explain what the project taught you about engineering design. Part E: Complete your self-assessment. Leave the teacher scoring boxes blank. Evidence rule: Avoid answers such as “it worked well” or “we made it stronger.” Name the feature or change, describe what happened, and point to a measurement, test result, observation, or earlier design document that supports your claim. Engineering Design Process You completed the full cycle Define → Research → Imagine → Select → Develop → Build → Test → Improve → Communicate The point of Unit 0 is not only the launch pad. It is learning how engineers use a process, evidence, and documentation to move from a problem to a defensible solution. Mission Debrief What You Submit Required Deliverable Final Launch Pad + Completed 2-Page Engineering Design Review Your completed worksheet is the written competition record and design review for Lesson 0.10. Part A contains the final qualification and stability data; Parts B–E explain the engineering process, evidence, iteration, and reflection. Submit all pa

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 0 Lesson 0.2 IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.2 Engineering Notebook Setup & Course Resources Focus Question: How will you organize evidence so your engineering work can be understood later? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Build an evidence system Set up a chronological engineering notebook and verify access to the digital resources used throughout IED. Organize Access Name Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Set up the physical and digital systems that will keep engineering evidence organized all year. Learning Targets Set up the binder-based engineering notebook system. Explain chronological organization and table-of-contents routines. Locate course resources, templates, downloads, and submission locations. Success Looks Like… Your binder and digital files are organized so another person can find and understand your work. Core habit: Record work in order and use consistent names so decisions remain traceable. Opening prompt Notebook purpose Binder setup Resource access File naming Readiness check Debrief Opening Prompt What makes a notebook useful later? Think beyond neatness: what must another person be able to find or understand? Quick class share: Name one piece of engineering evidence that would be difficult to recreate if it were not recorded. Reveal the working definition An engineering notebook is a chronological evidence record. It captures what happened, when it happened, and why decisions changed so the work can be reviewed, repeated, or improved. Notebook System Build the binder in the correct order The table of contents is the map; numbered documents are the evidence trail. Binder Setup Required structure Place the printed Table of Contents first. Do not number the Table of Contents. Start page numbering with the first actual document. Add new work in the order it is completed. Update the Table of Contents as documents are added. Why It Matters Professional habits Makes design thinking visible Helps teams trace decisions Creates evidence for design reviews Supports revision and inspection Prevents lost or disconnected work Live Setup Notebook Readiness Check Complete the physical setup before moving to digital resources. 1 Binder has six dividers and a clear place for Unit 0. 2 Table of Contents is placed first and left unnumbered. 3 Lined and graph paper are available. 4 Name and course are clearly identified. 5 First numbered document location is ready. Digital Access Confirm the course systems work Do the access check now so project time is not lost later. Access sequence Log in to Google Classroom. Open and bookmark the LockwoodSTEM IED Course Hub. Locate lesson pages, downloads, templates, and certifications. Confirm that required Drive or submission locations open correctly. Ask for help now if any account or permission fails. Where information lives Projected agenda Warm-up, announcements, and today’s sequence Google Classroom Assignments, submissions, and posted resources LockwoodSTEM.org Lesson pages, downloads, references, and course tools File Naming Make digital work findable A useful name should make sense before the file is opened. Required format: LastName_FirstName_Unit_AssignmentName Which name is stronger? 1 finalfinal2.pptx 2 Lockwood_Jonathan_Unit0_PaperAirplaneEvidence.pptx Reveal the stronger file name Best answer: 2 It identifies the student, unit, and assignment without opening the file. Avoid vague names such as final , new , or thing . Check: Save files in the correct location and keep a backup when work is important. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.5 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.5 • 2 class periods Dimensioning & Technical Sketching Focus question: How do engineers choose and place enough dimensions
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.5 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.5 • 2 class periods Dimensioning & Technical Sketching Focus question: How do engineers choose and place enough dimensions to completely define a part without making the drawing confusing or redundant? Start the Assignment View Bracket Choices Download Sketch Sheet Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Choose one aerospace bracket and create a complete technical sketch package that fully communicates its shape and dimensions. Choose Sketch Dimension Success: Another student could understand the bracket geometry and reproduce the part using only your completed technical drawing. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Lesson 1.5 combines the view-selection and multiview skills from Lesson 1.4 with complete technical dimensioning. Learning Targets Distinguish size dimensions from location dimensions. Choose the views that communicate a part clearly. Use dimension lines, extension lines, arrowheads, diameter, radius, and angle notation correctly. Avoid missing, duplicate, and poorly placed dimensions. Create a fully defined multiview technical sketch from a 3D model. Success Looks Like Your chosen bracket is shown with an isometric sketch plus aligned Front, Top, and Right-Side views. Dimensions fully define the part while remaining readable and non-redundant. Inspect Choose Sketch Dimension Check Core Ideas Dimension for Manufacturing Clarity Size Communicate how large each feature is: overall length, width, height, thickness, diameter, radius, slot size, or angle. Location Communicate where features are positioned: offsets from edges, center locations, spacing, symmetry, and center-to-center distances. Clarity Place each dimension on the view where the feature is shown most clearly. Do not repeat the same dimension in multiple views. Engineering Check Could someone rebuild the bracket from your drawing? If another student would have to guess a feature size, location, radius, hole center, slot angle, or thickness, your drawing is not fully defined yet. Your Task Choose One Bracket and Fully Sketch & Dimension It Inspect all three interactive STL models below, then select one bracket for your completed technical drawing package. Rotate and inspect all three bracket choices. Choose one bracket to complete. Choose the face that should serve as your FRONT view based on which orientation communicates the geometry most clearly. Create an isometric sketch and aligned Front, Top, and Right-Side views. Apply object, hidden, and center lines correctly. Use the dimension reference below your selected model to add all necessary size and location dimensions to the orthographic views. Do not dimension the isometric view and do not duplicate dimensions. Perform a final completeness check: every important feature must be both sized and located. You choose both the bracket and the FRONT view. The model viewer is a reference, not an orthographic answer. Your Front choice must remain consistent when you construct the Top and Right-Side views. Interactive Bracket Choices Choose 1 of 3 STL Models Drag to rotate, scroll/pinch to zoom, and use the dimension list beneath each viewer. All listed dimensions are in inches and were measured directly from the STL geometry; values are rounded to the nearest 0.001 in. Bracket 1 Bracket 2 Bracket 3 What You Will Submit One Fully Dimensioned Bracket Technical Drawing One isometric sketch of your selected bracket. Aligned Front, Top, and Right-Side views. A clearly chosen and consistently used Front orientation. Correct object, hidden, and center-line conventions. Complete size and location dimensions in inches. No unnecessary duplicate dimensions. Before submitting: Use the STL model and dimension reference one final time to verify that your four views describe the same geometry and that no important feature is left undefined. Resources Lesson Resources Use the combined sketch sheet for your selected bracket. Required Template Orthographic + Isometric Sketch Sheet Use this sheet to organize the isometric, Front, Top, and Right-Side views for your selected bracket. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.12 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.12 • 2–3 class periods Engineering Change & Product Improvement Proposal Focus question: What should be improved in the rocket assembly, why should it change, and what evidence supports the recommendation? Start the Lesson Your Task What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Use evidence from the entire reverse-engineering process to propose one meaningful engineering change and defend the expected benefit and tradeoffs. Identify Improve Justify Success: Your work communicates engineering information clearly enough that another student can understand and use it. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Use this webpage, your engineering notebook, and the listed lesson resources to complete the work in order. Learning Targets Identify a meaningful improvement opportunity using evidence. Document the existing condition and proposed change in an engineering change request. Create an annotated sketch of the revised concept. Evaluate expected benefits, tradeoffs, and impacts on manufacturing or assembly. Communicate the proposal in a concise engineering design review. Success Looks Like Use evidence from the entire reverse-engineering process to propose one meaningful engineering change and defend the expected benefit and tradeoffs. Learn Practice Apply Check Submit Class Flow Work Through the Lesson Day 1 — Define the Change Review your documentation for evidence of a weakness, inefficiency, difficult interface, unnecessary complexity, or other improvement opportunity. State the existing condition and the specific problem. Select one change that addresses the problem. Begin the Engineering Change Request with evidence and affected components. Day 2 — Develop the Proposal Create an annotated sketch of the proposed revision. Explain expected benefits and possible tradeoffs. Describe impacts on manufacturing, assembly, serviceability, mass, cost, or reliability where relevant. Complete the written proposal package. Day 3 — Engineering Design Review Prepare a concise explanation of what should change and why. Use drawings, measurements, observations, or assembly evidence to support the recommendation. Respond to questions and record useful feedback. Complete a final reflection describing what evidence most strongly supports your decision. Core Ideas What to Pay Attention To Evidence before preference A design change should solve a documented problem—not simply make the product look different. Tradeoffs A change can improve one criterion while making another worse. Strong proposals acknowledge both. Configuration control Document what changes, what remains unchanged, and which components or instructions are affected. Engineering Check Stop and verify before moving on Your proposal should answer three questions clearly: What should change? Why should it change? What evidence shows that this change is worth making? Your Task Develop the Final Rocket Improvement Proposal Use the documentation you built throughout Unit 1 as engineering evidence. Your proposal should be specific enough that another engineer understands both the existing problem and your recommended revision. Identify one evidence-supported improvement opportunity. Complete the Engineering Change Request. Create an annotated revised sketch. Explain benefits, tradeoffs, and affected components/processes. Organize the final documentation for a short engineering design review. Use evidence: Keep sketches, measurements, observations, and revisions visible. Unit 1 is building one connected engineering documentation package. What You Will Submit Final Rocket Improvement Package Engineering Change Request describing the existing condition and proposed revision. Annotated sketch of the proposed improvement. Evidence supporting the change. Expected benefits and tradeoffs. Concise engineering design review/reflection using the completed documentation package. pages.title: Engineering Documentation Challenge
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Project 1.8 IED Unit 1 • Project 1.8 • Multi-day project Engineering Documentation Challenge Focus question: Can you accurately document a real manufactured
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Project 1.8 IED Unit 1 • Project 1.8 • Multi-day project Engineering Documentation Challenge Focus question: Can you accurately document a real manufactured object so another engineer can understand and inspect it without guessing? Download Templates View Deliverables Back to Unit 1 Final Unit Challenge Select and document your own manufactured object using sketching, measurement, multiview drawing, dimensioning, tolerances, and engineering review. Document Verify Improve Success: Your approved object is documented clearly enough that another student can understand its geometry, important dimensions, features, and manufacturing details without a verbal explanation. Project Overview Document an Object You Select You will provide a real manufactured object, qualify it for the project, measure it, and create a complete engineering documentation package. The project is divided into checkpoints so each part is reviewed before you move forward. Learning Targets Select appropriate views to communicate a physical object. Create accurate isometric and aligned multiview sketches. Use object, hidden, and center lines correctly. Measure features with appropriate tools and precision. Apply clear, non-redundant dimensions. Identify dimensions where tolerance or fit matters. Produce technical documentation that another person can interpret without verbal explanation. Final Goal Your completed package should communicate the shape, size, location, and important features of your object using the engineering documentation skills developed throughout Unit 1. Before the Project Choose Your Object You are responsible for bringing an object that meets the requirements below. Do not begin detailed drawings until your object has been approved. Size Easy to Handle The object must fit completely inside a 6 × 6 × 6 inch envelope and be rigid enough to measure repeatedly. Geometry Enough Complexity It must contain at least three distinct geometric features such as holes, slots, steps, curves, fillets, chamfers, bosses, recesses, or cylindrical features. Views Meaningful Multiviews The front, top, and right-side views must communicate useful and meaningfully different information. Features Technical Drawing Evidence Include straight or planar geometry plus at least one curved or circular feature and at least one feature that benefits from a centerline, hidden line, or symmetry indication. Measurement Measurable The object must allow meaningful measurements with classroom rulers and/or calipers and should require roughly 8–15 dimensions to describe its important geometry. Appropriate Safe and Practical The object must be clean, school-appropriate, nonvaluable, and safe to handle. Avoid soft/flexible objects, highly irregular freeform shapes, transparent objects, or extremely simple objects such as a plain block, ball, washer, bottle, or pencil. Assemblies are allowed but not required. If your object contains multiple parts, you may also document an important interface or joining method. Project Checkpoints Turn In the Project in Stages Each deliverable is submitted separately. Feedback from one checkpoint should be used before beginning or finalizing the next. Deliverable 1 Object Qualification & Approval Turn in: object identification, approximate overall dimensions, feature inventory, proposed front view, and teacher approval. Bring the physical object to class. Verify the 6 × 6 × 6 in. limit. Identify at least three geometric features. Explain why the object will produce useful front, top, and right-side views. Checkpoint: Your object must be approved before continuing. Deliverable 2 Object Analysis & Isometric Sketch Turn in: labeled object analysis and a clean isometric sketch. Identify major features, symmetry, curves, holes, slots, or other geometry. Establish the intended orientation. Create an isometric overview showing the complete object. Label important features that will need measurement. Deliverable 3 Measurement & Inspection Record Turn in: completed measurement table. Record the dimensions needed to describe the object. Identify the measuring tool used for each measurement. Record values using appropriate precision. Identify several dimensions that are especially important to fit, alignment, or function. Deliverable 4 Multiview Technical Drawing Turn in: front, top, and right-side views with technical line conventions. Keep views aligned. Use object, hidden, and center lines correctly. Show circular, symmetric, and hidden features appropriately. Add the dimensions needed to size and locate important features without unnecessary duplication. Deliverable 5 Tolerance & Documentation Review Turn in: critical-dimension analysis plus peer review. Select important dimensions and propose reasonable tolerances. Explain why tighter or looser control matters. Have another student review the documentation without using the physical object as an explanation. Record unclear or missing information and make revisions. Deliverable 6 Final Engineering Documentation Package Turn in: the revised complete package. Approved object qualification. Final isometric sketch. Measurement record. Dimensioned multiview drawing. Tolerance analysis. Peer-review revisions. Short final reflection on the hardest information to communicate and how you solved it. Submission Rule Do Not Wait Until the End This project is graded through multiple submissions. A later deliverable does not replace a missed earlier checkpoint. Keep every returned checkpoint because the corrected work becomes part of your final documentation package. Final Package What the Completed Project Must Show An approved student-selected manufactured object. Accurate isometric and aligned front, top, and right-side views. Correct technical line conventions. Actual measurements recorded with appropriate tools and precision. Clear, non-redundant size and location dimensions. Critical-dimension and tolerance reasoning. Evidence of peer review and revi

pages.title: Multiview Sketching from Interactive 3D Models
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.4 Multiview Sketching from Interactive 3D Models Focus question: How can you translate a three-dimensional object into accu
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.4 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.4 Multiview Sketching from Interactive 3D Models Focus question: How can you translate a three-dimensional object into accurate, aligned technical views without being given the orthographic solution? Start the Assignment Open 3D Models Download Drawing Paper Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Inspect each model, then communicate the same geometry through four hand-drawn views. Inspect Project Dimension Success: Front, Top, Right-Side, and Isometric views all describe the same object and use clear engineering drawing conventions. Your Assignment Eight Models • Four Views Each The interactive model on this page is your only 3D reference. No printed isometric reference is provided. For Every Model Rotate and zoom to inspect the entire model. Choose the face you believe should be the FRONT view. Select the view that communicates the shape and important features most clearly. Sketch your chosen FRONT view first using light construction lines. Project and align the TOP and RIGHT-SIDE views. Add visible/object, hidden, and center lines where appropriate. Sketch the ISOMETRIC view in the isometric-grid quadrant. Add the necessary dimensions to the orthographic views. Check that all four views describe the same object. Drawing & Dimensioning Rules Dimension the orthographic views, not the isometric sketch. Place each dimension on the view where the feature is shown most clearly. Avoid duplicating the same dimension in multiple views. Use the Ø symbol and centerlines for circular features. Keep dimensions outside the object when practical. Use straight, dark final object lines after geometry is aligned. You choose the FRONT: There is not one assigned camera face. Choose the face that best communicates the part, then keep that FRONT choice consistent when constructing the Top and Right-Side views. Be prepared to briefly justify your choice. □ FRONT complete □ TOP complete □ RIGHT SIDE complete □ ISOMETRIC complete □ Dimensions complete Interactive Reference Set Models 1–8 Drag to rotate and scroll/pinch to zoom. Reset View returns the model to its starting camera angle, but that angle does not define the required FRONT view. What You Submit Completed 8-Model Multiview Drawing Set One completed drawing sheet for each of the eight models. Front, Top, Right-Side, and Isometric views for every model. Correct view alignment and consistent feature locations. Appropriate object, hidden, and center lines. Complete, non-duplicated dimensions on the orthographic views. Before submitting: Label each model sheet clearly and perform a four-view consistency check. Resource Multiview Drawing Paper Required Template Multiview Sketch Paper — Landscape Use the square-grid quadrants for Front, Top, and Right-Side views and the isometric-grid quadrant for the isometric sketch. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.3 • 2 class periods Isometric Sketching & Curved Features Focus question: How can engineers represent three-dimensional geo
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.3 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.3 • 2 class periods Isometric Sketching & Curved Features Focus question: How can engineers represent three-dimensional geometry—including circles and curves—on a flat page? Start the Lesson Download Worksheet Your Task What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Construct readable isometric sketches using the three isometric axes, then extend the method to holes, cylinders, arcs, and rounded features. Construct Visualize Refine Success: Your work communicates engineering information clearly enough that another student can understand and use it. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Use this webpage, your engineering notebook, and the listed lesson resources to complete the work in order. Learning Targets Use vertical and 30° isometric axes to build three-dimensional forms. Maintain proportion while adding steps, cutouts, and changes in depth. Represent circles as isometric ellipses. Sketch holes, cylinders, arcs, and rounded features without flattening the object. Success Looks Like Construct readable isometric sketches using the three isometric axes, then extend the method to holes, cylinders, arcs, and rounded features. Learn Practice Apply Check Submit Class Flow Work Through the Lesson Day 1 — Build Isometric Forms Set up the three isometric axes. Use a bounding box to control width, height, and depth. Add steps, notches, and cutouts while keeping edges parallel to the correct axis. Practice several block-based objects. Day 2 — Add Curved Geometry Review why a circle appears as an ellipse in an isometric view. Use a box or four-center approach to place isometric ellipses. Add holes, cylinders, arcs, and rounded corners. Create one complete isometric sketch that combines straight and curved features. Core Ideas What to Pay Attention To Isometric axes Vertical, 30° left, and 30° right directions establish the three principal dimensions. Bounding geometry Light boxes and construction lines help keep proportion accurate before details are added. Isometric circles Circles on isometric planes appear as ellipses and must follow the orientation of that plane. Engineering Check Stop and verify before moving on Do not “eyeball” a curved feature in empty space. First establish the plane and the bounding geometry that controls its size and location. Your Task Complete the Isometric Sketching & Curved Features Worksheet Read each drawing description carefully and construct the object from scratch on the provided isometric grid. Use light construction lines first, then darken the final visible geometry. Curved features should appear as ellipses in isometric view. Establish the overall width, height, and depth using a light isometric box. Add the major straight-edged features while preserving axis direction. Construct any circular or curved features inside their bounding geometry. Darken only the final visible edges. Check proportion and clean up unnecessary construction lines without erasing all evidence of your process. Use evidence: Keep sketches, measurements, observations, and revisions visible. Unit 1 is building one connected engineering documentation package. What You Will Submit Isometric Sketching Practice Completed four-page IED 1.3 Isometric Sketching & Curved Features Worksheet. At least one sketch containing a correctly oriented circle, hole, cylinder, or arc. Consistent line quality and proportional geometry. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.2 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.2 • 1 class period Centerlines & Symmetry Focus question: How do engineers show the center of a circular or symmetric featu
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.2 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.2 • 1 class period Centerlines & Symmetry Focus question: How do engineers show the center of a circular or symmetric feature without drawing a physical edge? Start the Lesson Download Worksheet Your Task What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Use centerlines to communicate axes, centers, and symmetry without confusing them with visible or hidden edges. Locate Align Clarify Success: Your work communicates engineering information clearly enough that another student can understand and use it. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Use this webpage, your engineering notebook, and the listed lesson resources to complete the work in order. Learning Targets Recognize the long-short-long centerline pattern. Place centerlines through circular and cylindrical features. Use centerlines to communicate symmetry and axes. Distinguish centerlines from object and hidden lines. Success Looks Like Use centerlines to communicate axes, centers, and symmetry without confusing them with visible or hidden edges. Learn Practice Apply Check Submit Class Flow Work Through the Lesson Today — Centerlines in Technical Drawings Identify the centerline pattern in sample drawings. Add centerlines to holes, circles, cylinders, and symmetric shapes. Compare correct and incorrect centerline placement. Complete a short practice set and self-check your line types. Core Ideas What to Pay Attention To Axis of a feature A centerline shows the axis of a hole, cylinder, or other rotational feature. Center of a circle Two perpendicular centerlines can locate the exact center of a circular feature. Symmetry A centerline can show that geometry is intended to be symmetric about an axis. Engineering Check Stop and verify before moving on A centerline represents an axis or center—it is not a physical edge. Do not replace visible or hidden edges with centerlines. Your Task Complete the Centerlines & Symmetry Worksheet Work through the worksheet problems by identifying circular, cylindrical, and symmetric features. Add centerlines only where they communicate a useful center, axis, or line of symmetry. Identify every circular, cylindrical, or clearly symmetric feature. Decide whether a centerline is needed in each view. Draw centerlines using a consistent long-short-long pattern. Extend centerlines slightly beyond the feature when appropriate. Review the drawing to make sure line types are visually distinct. Use evidence: Keep sketches, measurements, observations, and revisions visible. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Peer Design Review of the Rocket IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.4 Peer Design Review of the Rocket Conduct a professional, evidence-based review of another te
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Peer Design Review of the Rocket IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.4 Peer Design Review of the Rocket Conduct a professional, evidence-based review of another team’s rocket design and recommend prioritized improvements. Intermediate 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering teams use formal reviews to identify risk before spending time and money on fabrication. Objectives What You Will Practice Use criteria to evaluate a design Separate observations from opinions Identify design risk Give actionable technical feedback Materials What You Need Another team’s rocket sketches or model Design review form Engineering notebook Ruler or calipers if permitted Procedure Instructions Review the project criteria and constraints before seeing the design. Inspect the design silently for three minutes and record only observations. Ask the design team three clarifying questions. Evaluate fit, stability, manufacturability, assembly, documentation, and safety. Identify two strengths supported by evidence. Identify three risks and rate each as low, medium, or high. Write one specific recommendation for each risk. Meet with the team for five minutes and explain the highest-priority recommendation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use respectful, technical language Support every rating with observed evidence Identify at least two strengths and three risks Make recommendations specific enough to act on Prioritize the recommendations Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not redesign the project for the team Do not change or handle a model without permission Keep feedback focused on criteria and constraints Deliverables What You Submit Completed design review form Risk-priority table Three recommendations Brief feedback summary signed by both teams Reflection Reflection Questions Which risk was most likely to affect performance? How did the team’s explanation change your evaluation? Which recommendation could be completed fastest? What feedback would help your own design? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the pattern “I observed..., which may cause..., so I recommend...” for clear feedback. Common Mistake “I do not like it” is not engineering feedback. Tie comments to requirements, evidence, or risk. Stretch Goal Review the revised design later and document whether each high-priority risk was reduced. Career Connection Design review engineers and project teams use preliminary and critical design reviews to find issues before production or flight. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Measurement Accuracy Competition IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Measurement Accuracy Competition Measure a set of mystery parts as accurately and consistent
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Measurement Accuracy Competition IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Measurement Accuracy Competition Measure a set of mystery parts as accurately and consistently as possible. Beginner 45 minutes Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Quality inspectors must make fast, repeatable measurements and report them with the correct precision. Objectives What You Will Practice Select appropriate measuring tools Read scales and calipers correctly Record units and precision Analyze measurement variation Materials What You Need 10-15 mystery objects Ruler Dial or digital calipers Measurement data sheet Calculator Procedure Instructions Create a data table with object ID, feature, tool, measurement, and units. Measure each assigned feature once without seeing the reference value. Repeat three selected measurements after a five-minute delay. Calculate the difference between repeated measurements. Compare your results with teacher reference values after all data are submitted. Calculate absolute error for each reference measurement. Identify the tool and feature associated with your largest error. Write a two-step plan for improving measurement reliability. Requirements Engineering Requirements Measure at least ten features Use the most appropriate available tool Record all values with units and realistic precision Repeat at least three measurements Calculate error or variation correctly Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not alter or mark the objects Do not share measurements before the class reveal Use safe caliper pressure on fragile parts Deliverables What You Submit Completed measurement table Repeated-measurement comparison Absolute error calculations Accuracy ranking or score Improvement plan Reflection Reflection Questions When was a ruler sufficient? When were calipers necessary? Did your repeated measurements agree? What caused your largest error? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Close calipers gently. Excess force can compress a part or tilt the jaws. Common Mistake Extra decimal places do not make a measurement accurate. Report only the precision supported by the tool. Stretch Goal Calculate the class mean and range for three measurements and identify possible outliers. Career Connection Quality technicians, machinists, and manufacturing engineers rely on repeatable inspection data to approve parts. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.1 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.1 • 2 class periods Engineering Sketching & Line Conventions Focus question: How do engineers use sketches and standardized
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.1 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.1 • 2 class periods Engineering Sketching & Line Conventions Focus question: How do engineers use sketches and standardized line types to communicate design ideas clearly? Start the Lesson Download Worksheet Your Task What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Build a strong sketching foundation by using purposeful line quality and the correct line convention for visible and hidden geometry. Sketch Interpret Communicate Success: Your work communicates engineering information clearly enough that another student can understand and use it. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Use this webpage, your engineering notebook, and the listed lesson resources to complete the work in order. Learning Targets Explain why engineers sketch before CAD or fabrication. Use light construction lines and darker final object lines. Identify and correctly apply object lines and hidden lines. Recognize center, dimension, and extension lines when they appear in technical drawings. Use an isometric reference to decide which edges are visible or hidden in front, top, and right-side views. Success Looks Like Build a strong sketching foundation by using purposeful line quality and the correct line convention for visible and hidden geometry. Learn Practice Apply Check Submit Class Flow Work Through the Lesson Day 1 — Sketching as Engineering Communication Compare an engineering sketch with an artistic drawing and identify what makes the engineering sketch useful. Practice straight-line quality, proportion, light construction lines, and darker final lines. Learn the purpose and appearance of object, hidden, center, dimension, and extension lines. Work through visible-versus-hidden examples as a class. Day 2 — Object & Hidden Line Practice Review how viewing direction changes which features can be seen. Use the isometric reference in each problem to inspect the front, top, and right-side views. Complete the Object & Hidden Line Practice Worksheet by adding only the missing lines. Check line type, location, alignment, and neatness before submitting. Core Ideas What to Pay Attention To Object lines Thick, continuous lines show edges and boundaries that are directly visible in the selected view. Hidden lines Short, evenly spaced dashes show important edges that exist behind visible surfaces. Construction lines Very light lines help establish proportion and alignment before final linework is darkened. Engineering Check Stop and verify before moving on Before you darken a line, ask: “Can I actually see this edge from this viewing direction?” If yes, use an object line. If the edge is blocked but still needs to be communicated, use a hidden line. Your Task Complete the Engineering Sketching & Line Conventions Worksheet Use the isometric reference in each problem to complete the incomplete orthographic views. Add only the missing geometry, choosing object lines for visible edges and hidden lines for obscured edges. Begin with the Front view and identify features that face you directly. Move to the Top and Right views while keeping corresponding features aligned. Add missing visible edges with object lines. Add missing obscured edges with hidden lines using consistent dash spacing. Compare all three views to the isometric reference before submitting. Use evidence: Keep sketches, measurements, observations, and revisions visible. Unit 1 is building one connected engineering documentation package. What You Will Submit Engineering Sketching & Line Conventions Practice Completed IED 1.1 Engineering Sketching & Line Conventions Worksheet. Correct use of object and hidden lines in all assigned views. Neat line quality that clearly distinguishes visible and hidden geometry. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Reverse Engineer a Hand Tool IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Reverse Engineer a Hand Tool Produce accurate multiview and isometric documentation for an approved hand tool. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A maintenance team needs replacement documentation for a hand tool whose original drawings are unavailable. Your team must create a clear measured sketch package. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure real objects accurately Create multiview and isometric sketches Apply dimensioning conventions Estimate functional tolerances Materials What You Need Approved hand tool Ruler and calipers Graph and isometric paper Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Select an approved tool such as an Allen wrench, screwdriver, small wrench, or pliers. Identify the primary functional features and measurement datums. Measure overall dimensions, thicknesses, diameters, and feature locations. Create front, top, and right-side orthographic views aligned correctly. Add dimensions without duplication. Create an isometric sketch using the same measurements. Identify two dimensions that require tighter tolerance and explain why. Have a peer use only your drawings to identify the tool and verify three dimensions. Requirements Engineering Requirements Include three aligned orthographic views Include one isometric view Show at least eight dimensions with units Avoid duplicate or missing critical dimensions Identify two tolerance recommendations Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not measure moving or sharp surfaces unsafely All drawings must be created by hand Use only the approved measuring tools Deliverables What You Submit Measurement table Three-view drawing Isometric drawing Tolerance notes Peer verification results Reflection Reflection Questions Which view communicated the most information? Which dimension was hardest to measure? Where could measurement error affect function? What would be needed to manufacture the tool? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Choose datums before measuring so feature locations are referenced consistently. Common Mistake Dimensioning every visible line creates clutter. Dimension the features needed to define the part. Stretch Goal Create a sectional or detail view of the most complex feature. pages.title: Joining Methods & Assembly Systems
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.7 • 1 class period Joining Methods & Assembly Systems Focus question: How do engineers choose the best way to connect parts
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.7 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.7 • 1 class period Joining Methods & Assembly Systems Focus question: How do engineers choose the best way to connect parts in an assembly? Download Student Packet Download Presentation Start the Lab Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Inspect purpose-made connection samples, identify how the parts are joined, and justify when each method is appropriate. Identify Compare Justify Success: You can explain not only what joins two parts, but why that joining method makes sense for the interface. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Joining methods are engineering decisions. The best connection depends on what the joint must do, how it will be assembled, and whether it needs to come apart later. Learning Targets Identify common mechanical fasteners, bonded joints, fit-based joints, and integrated features. Distinguish removable, semi-permanent, and permanent connections. Explain how load, serviceability, alignment, manufacturing, cost, and permanence affect joint selection. Identify the components on each side of an interface and the purpose of the connection. Recommend an appropriate joining method and support the choice with engineering reasoning. Success Looks Like Your analysis connects the physical joint to its engineering purpose. You can compare alternatives and explain what would improve or worsen if the joining method changed. Inspect Classify Compare Select Justify Materials What You Need Your Work Connection Decision Lab Packet Use the packet for the joining-method reference, station records, design scenarios, and final comparison. Lab Samples Stations A-F Handle each purpose-made sample carefully and return it assembled for the next group. Engineering Mindset Evidence-Based Decisions Use physical evidence and decision factors instead of relying on guesses or preference. Core Ideas A Joint Is More Than the Fastener You Can See Mechanical Fasteners Designed for assembly and service Bolts, screws, nuts, washers, rivets, and pins can provide clamping, alignment, retention, or load transfer. Some are removable; others are not. Bonded & Fit-Based Joints Process and dimensions matter Adhesives and press fits can reduce hardware, but performance depends on surface preparation, contact area, material behavior, and dimensional control. Integrated Features The part geometry can become the joint Tabs, slots, and snap features can locate and retain parts with little or no separate hardware, but they may be harder to repair or more sensitive to wear. Engineering Selection Decision Factors A strong justification uses more than one factor. Load What force, torque, vibration, impact, or repeated use must the joint survive? Serviceability Does the product need to be opened, repaired, adjusted, or have components replaced? Alignment Does the connection need to hold parts in a precise location or orientation? Manufacturing Can the joint be assembled consistently with the available tools, materials, access, and production process? Cost & Complexity Does the chosen method add unnecessary hardware, labor, steps, or specialized processes? Permanence Should the joint come apart easily, only with work, or not at all during normal use? Your Task • Connection Decision Lab Inspect Six Purpose-Made Joining Samples At each station, identify the joining method from the physical evidence. Then evaluate what the connection does well and what tradeoff comes with that choice. Identify the joining method used at the station. Classify the connection as removable, semi-permanent, or permanent. Describe what the connection must accomplish. Record the main advantage and main limitation of the method. Choose the most important decision factor for that interface. Use the design scenarios to recommend appropriate joining methods for new situations. Compare one station with a reasonable alternative and justify your final recommendation. Engineering rule: "It is strong" is not enough. A good justification connects the joining method to the actual requirements of the interface. Station Set Purpose-Made Samples Station A Bolt + Nut + Washer Two coupons clamped together with a threaded fastener, nut, and washer. Station B Screw Into Threads A screw joins two parts by engaging threads in one part, an insert, or a captured nut. Station C Riveted Overlap Joint Two overlapping coupons joined by a one-piece fastener that is not unscrewed for removal. Station D Adhesive Lap Joint Two overlapping coupons bonded together with no separate mechanical hardware. Station E Press / Friction Fit A printed pin and three receiving holes show loose, snug, and tight fit behavior. Station F Tab/Slot + Snap Feature Integrated geometry locates the parts and a flexible feature retains the assembly. Connection to the Unit 1 Challenge Document the Interface, Not Just the Hardware In the final Unit 1 challenge, you will need to communicate how parts relate to one another. Record the joint type, the components it connects, and the reason the connection works so that another engineer can understand the assembly without relying on verbal explanation. What You Will Submit Connection Decision Lab Packet Joining-method reference notes. Station records for Samples A-F. Classification of each connection as removable, semi-permanent, or permanent. Main advantage, limitation, and decision factor for each sample. Design-scenario recommendations using at least three decision factors. Deep comparison of one existing joining method with a reasonable alternative. Before submitting: Check that your answers explain why the joining method fits the interface requirements. Resources Lesson Resources Open the files you need for the Connection Decision Lab. Student Packet Connection Decision Lab Use this packet to record station observations, design-scenario choices, and your final joining-method comparison. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.10 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.10 • 2 class periods Exploded Views & Bills of Materials Focus question: How do engineers connect a visual assembly drawing with a structured list of every part required? Start the Lesson Your Task What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Create an exploded view and BOM that use the same item numbers so another person can understand what the assembly contains and how the parts relate. Explode Identify Account Success: Your work communicates engineering information clearly enough that another student can understand and use it. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Use this webpage, your engineering notebook, and the listed lesson resources to complete the work in order. Learning Targets Create an exploded representation that preserves assembly order and relationships. Use item balloons/callouts consistently. Build a bill of materials with item number, part name, quantity, material, and notes. Cross-check the exploded view and BOM so every item matches. Success Looks Like Create an exploded view and BOM that use the same item numbers so another person can understand what the assembly contains and how the parts relate. Learn Practice Apply Check Submit Class Flow Work Through the Lesson Day 1 — Exploded View Choose a clear viewing direction for the assembly. Separate components along logical assembly directions without losing relationships. Add item numbers/callouts to significant components. Show important fasteners and subassembly order. Day 2 — Bill of Materials Create the BOM using the same item numbers as the exploded view. Enter part name, quantity, material, and useful description/notes. Check that every BOM item appears in the exploded view and every callout appears in the BOM. Complete a team cross-check for missing or duplicated parts. Core Ideas What to Pay Attention To Exploded view Shows components separated in space while preserving how they relate and assemble. Item number A unique identifier that links a drawing callout to a BOM row. BOM A structured accounting of the parts and quantities required for an assembly. Engineering Check Stop and verify before moving on Trace five random item numbers from the exploded view to the BOM and back. If any item is missing, duplicated, or named differently, fix the documentation. Your Task Create a Matched Exploded View + BOM These two documents must function as one system. The exploded view shows where the parts belong; the BOM identifies exactly what those parts are. Create the exploded assembly drawing. Assign sequential item numbers. Build the BOM with matching item numbers. Verify quantities and material descriptions. Cross-check the drawing and table before submitting. Use evidence: Keep sketches, measurements, observations, and revisions visible. Unit 1 is building one connected engineering documentation package. What You Will Submit Exploded View & Bill of Materials Rocket exploded view with clear component relationships. Item-number callouts. Completed BOM with matching item numbers. No missing, duplicated, or mismatched items between the two documents. Before submitting: Check that your work is labeled, readable, complete, and consistent with the technical conventions used in this lesson.
