Start the Lesson Your Task What You Submit Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Convert your component documentation, exploded view, and BOM into a clear reassembly sequence that can be tested by another student. Sequence Explain Verify Success: Your work communicates engineering information clearly enough that another student can understand and use it. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Use this webpage, your engineering notebook, and the listed lesson resources to complete the work in order. Learning Targets Write assembly steps in a logical sequence. Reference parts consistently using established names or item numbers. Include orientation, joining, and verification information where needed. Test technical instructions with a peer and revise unclear steps. Success Looks Like Convert your component documentation, exploded view, and BOM into a clear reassembly sequence that can be tested by another student. Learn Practice Apply Check Submit Class Flow Work Through the Lesson Today — Write, Test, Revise Identify the major stages of reassembly before writing individual steps. Write concise action-based instructions using consistent part names/item numbers. Add diagrams or callouts where words alone may be unclear. Have another student review or test a portion of the instructions. Revise steps that caused hesitation, questions, or mistakes. Core Ideas What to Pay Attention To Action first Start steps with a clear action such as insert, align, attach, tighten, position, or verify. Orientation Use specific references—front/back, left/right, tab/slot, item number—instead of “like this.” Verification Include checkpoints that tell the assembler how to know a step was completed correctly. Engineering Check Stop and verify before moving on If the instructions only make sense while you are standing next to the reader explaining them, they are not finished. Your Task Write Reassembly Instructions Another Student Can Use Use your existing technical documentation as the source of truth. Your instructions should make the reassembly process repeatable. Outline the major assembly stages. Write numbered action steps. Reference item numbers or exact component names. Add orientation and verification details. Peer-test the instructions and revise unclear language. Use evidence: Keep sketches, measurements, observations, and revisions visible. Unit 1 is building one connected engineering documentation package. What You Will Submit Rocket Assembly Instructions Numbered assembly sequence. Consistent component names/item numbers. Necessary orientation, fastener, and verification notes. Evidence of at least one revision after peer review. Before submitting: Check that your work is labeled, readable, complete, and consistent with the technical conventions used in this lesson. pages.title: Measurement, Precision & Tolerances
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.6 • 2 class periods Measurement, Precision & Tolerances Focus question: How do engineers decide how accurately a part must
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 1 Lesson 1.6 IED Unit 1 • Lesson 1.6 • 2 class periods Measurement, Precision & Tolerances Focus question: How do engineers decide how accurately a part must be measured and manufactured? Download Student Packet Download Inspection Drawings Download Presentation Back to Unit 1 Mission Focus Measure like an engineer, then inspect manufactured parts against engineering drawings to determine whether they meet tolerance requirements. Measure Inspect Decide Success: You can defend the tool you selected, report a realistic measurement, calculate allowable limits, and make a pass/fail decision from evidence. Mission Briefing What You Are Learning Lesson 1.6 connects the dimensions you learned to communicate in Lesson 1.5 with the measurements and tolerances used to inspect real manufactured parts. Learning Targets Select an appropriate measuring tool for a feature and engineering need. Record measurements with units and realistic precision. Use repeated measurements to evaluate consistency. Calculate upper and lower limits from a nominal dimension and tolerance. Inspect a manufactured feature and determine whether it conforms to a drawing. Explain why some dimensions require tighter control than others. Success Looks Like Your measurements match the capability of the tool, your calculations establish the allowable range, and your accept/reject decisions are supported by the drawing and the value you actually measured. Measure Repeat Calculate Inspect Decide Materials What You Need Your Work Student Packet Use the Measurement & Inspection Record for both class periods. Keep all measurements, calculations, and decisions in the same packet. Measurement Ruler & Caliper Use the measuring tool that fits the feature and the precision required by the engineering drawing. Inspection Models A, B & C Use the printed Through Hole Block, Two Level Stair Block, and Slotted Bracket with their matching engineering drawings during the inspection lab. Core Ideas Measurement Creates Evidence Measurement Choose the right tool A ruler and a caliper do not provide the same level of detail. Use a tool that can resolve the feature accurately enough for the engineering decision. Tolerance Define acceptable variation A nominal dimension gives the target size. The tolerance defines the acceptable range around that target and creates upper and lower limits for inspection. Inspection Compare evidence to the drawing A part passes only when its measured features satisfy the requirements on the engineering drawing. Looking correct is not enough. Engineering Check More decimal places do not automatically make a measurement better. Recorded precision should match the measuring instrument. A tolerance should be tight enough to protect function without being unnecessarily difficult to manufacture. Day 1 Measurement & Precision Practice Complete Page 1 of your student packet and build the measurement habits you will use during inspection. Tool Selection Match the tool to the feature Compare the useful precision of a ruler and caliper. Select an appropriate tool for overall dimensions, thicknesses, outside dimensions, and hole diameters. Record the tool resolution before recording measurements. Use consistent contact and alignment each time you measure. Repeatability Can you get the same result again? Measure the assigned features three times. Choose one feature and identify the smallest and largest values. Calculate the range of the repeated measurements. Use the reflection questions to identify sources of measurement variation. Day 2 Preparation • Student Packet Page 2 Calculate the Allowable Limits First Before you measure a production part, determine what the drawing allows. Read the nominal dimension and its tolerance. Calculate the lower limit: nominal - tolerance . Calculate the upper limit: nominal + tolerance . Treat the limit values as inclusive unless the drawing states otherwise. Only after the limits are established should you compare an actual measurement to the requirement. Example: 0.500 ± 0.005 in produces an acceptable range from 0.495 in through 0.505 in. Day 2 • Manufacturing Inspection Lab • Student Packet Pages 3–4 Do the Printed Parts Meet the Drawings? Your team will inspect three manufactured parts. The engineering drawing defines the requirement; your measurements provide the evidence. Match each printed model to its engineering drawing. Identify every feature listed in your inspection table. Calculate the lower and upper limits for each toleranced dimension. Select the appropriate measuring tool and record the actual dimension. Mark each inspected feature PASS or FAIL . If every required feature passes, mark the part ACCEPT . If any required feature fails, mark the part REJECT . For a rejected part, identify the feature that caused the rejection. Inspection rule: Do not decide from appearance. Always compare an actual measurement to the limits established by the drawing. Inspection Set Three Parts, Three Levels of Inspection Model A Through Hole Block Inspect overall dimensions, hole diameter, and hole-center location. This part emphasizes basic size and location requirements. Model B Two Level Stair Block Inspect overall dimensions, step runs, and step heights. This part emphasizes several related linear features. Model C Slotted Bracket Inspect overall size, hole size and location, slot geometry, and thin wall/web features. This part combines multiple feature types and tighter tolerances. Connection to the Unit 1 Challenge Critical Dimensions Control Function As you inspect the parts, notice which dimensions would matter most if a component had to fit, align, move, or connect to another component. In the final Unit 1 challenge, you will use measurements and tolerance information as part of a complete engineering documentation package. What You Will Submit Measurement & Inspection Record Day 1 measurement table with tool choices, tool resolution, and three measurements for each assi

pages.title: Rover Assembly: As-Built Joints
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.4 IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.4 Rover Assembly: As-Built Joints Focus question: How can we make an already-positioned rover function using rigid and revo
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.4 IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.4 Rover Assembly: As-Built Joints Focus question: How can we make an already-positioned rover function using rigid and revolute As-Built Joints? Go to Assignment What to Submit Back to Unit 3 Assembly Motion • Autodesk Fusion Your six-wheel rover is already positioned correctly—including its frame, motors, suspension links, payload box, and gripper—but has no functioning assembly joints. Engineering challenge: Define what is fixed and what can rotate without repositioning or remodeling the supplied parts. Unit 3 Learning Studio • Lesson 3.4 Understand, visualize, and apply the concept Visual Explanation Video Tutorial Fusion / Lab Guide Practice Assignment What to Submit Concept As-Built Joint Applies a mechanical relationship to components that are already in their correct locations. It defines motion without moving the parts into alignment. Decision Rigid or revolute? Use Rigid when two parts must move as one. Use Revolute when one part must rotate around a specified axle or pivot axis. Proof A functional rover Stationary chassis or frame grounded. Fixed brackets and supports attached correctly. All intended wheels rotate around the correct axis; nothing else drifts or detaches. Joint limits stop suspension and arm mechanisms before they move through parts or beyond their mechanical range. 01 / Real rover reference Identify the components in your actual Fusion rover These names were recovered from Rover Assembly Practice.f3d , the instructor's supplied model. Fusion may append occurrence numbers (for example, Wheel:1 ) to repeated components. Do not rename parts until you understand the assembly structure. Preview extracted from the exact teacher-supplied .f3d model, not a generic example. Component names from file Likely role in joint plan Base Body Primary frame reference; ground the stationary base component. Wheel (six visible) Revolute at each wheel hub; six independent wheel-rotation checks. Motor Motor housing is rigid to its mounting leg or bracket; wheel rotates relative to the support. Rear Legs , Rear Legs 2 , Leg Shaft Suspension support and shaft parts. Determine which connections are rigid and which form real pivots before adding a joint. Payload Box Rigid to its intended frame mount. Arm Base , Arm , Gripper Wrist Articulated arm subsystem; identify pivot axes for the optional extension. GripperMechanism , Servo MG966R_Predeterminado , holder and small hardware Additional gripper and servo parts; keep fixed housings rigid and identify only genuinely articulated mechanisms as pivots. Important distinction: Component names and six wheels are confirmed from the provided archive and preview. The design names identify the parts, while pivot origins and clearance-limited angles must be established in Fusion using the procedures in this lesson. 02 / Fusion command reference As-Built Joint — when parts are already in position Official Autodesk walkthrough Use Design → Solid → Assemble → As-Built Joint . Select two existing components . For wheels, choose Revolute , identify the hub center and orient the rotation axis down the axle. For fixed mounts, choose Rigid . Autodesk: Create an As-Built Joint ↗ Use Preview Motion before accepting and Animate Joint from the Joints folder for verification. For joints with physical stops, also use Edit Motion Limits to define allowable minimum and maximum positions. Joint types and motion Rigid: zero movement between parts. Revolute: rotation about one chosen axis. A rigid motor housing can support a revolute wheel without becoming a moving body itself. Autodesk: Joint Relationships Tutorial ↗ Do not substitute Move, Align, standard Joint or a rigid group for the required As-Built Joint demonstrations. 03 / Exact assembly work order Build the rover one subsystem at a time Starting condition: every component is already positioned. Each student opens Rover Assembly Practice.f3d , saves their own copy and creates As-Built Joints —not standard Joints, Move commands or new geometry. Expand the relevant component in the Browser and use Select in Canvas to distinguish repeated occurrences. Stage A — Frame and payload Ground Base Body . This is the stationary reference. Right-click its top-level occurrence and choose Ground . Never ground a wheel, leg or arm. Payload Box → Base Body : Create a Rigid As-Built Joint at the frame where the gray electronics box is mounted. Test: selecting and dragging the box must not move it separately from the chassis. ELECTRIC BOX DHAKNA → Payload Box : Create a Rigid As-Built Joint for the gray box cover. Test: the lid cannot move relative to the box. Stage B — Suspension and leg shafts Leg Shaft → Base Body : Use a Revolute As-Built Joint at the blue upright suspension pivot. Put the origin at the center of the cylindrical shaft; align the revolute axis along the shaft, not across the leg. Rear Legs → their matching Leg Shaft : Create a Rigid As-Built Joint at the shaft-to-leg attachment. The leg and shaft form one rotating support; the shaft pivots relative to the chassis. Rear Legs 2 → their matching Leg Shaft : Repeat the Rigid As-Built Joint for the second rear-leg structure. Use the occurrence that occupies the same side and pivot as the leg being constrained. Motion limit on each leg-to-chassis Revolute: Set a minimum and maximum that keep the blue leg links from passing through the chassis or adjacent rods. Follow the limit-measurement procedure below; record the two resulting angles. Selection rule: for repeated leg and shaft occurrences, first hide and show the specific part in the Browser. Join the components at the same physical pivot, never arbitrary identically named occurrences. Stage C — All six drive wheels and motors Label the wheels by their positions: left-front (LF), left-middle (LM), left-rear (LR), right-front (RF), right-middle (RM), right-rear (RR) . Treat the gripper end as the rover's front. Wheel position Required As-Built Joints LF

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 3 Lesson 3.8 IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.8 Digital Assembly Design Review Focus question: What evidence is needed before a multi-part rocket assembly is ready to manufacture? Go to Assignment Project Requirements What to Submit Back to Unit 3 Digital Design Review Prove that the rocket is manufacturable, serviceable, lightweight, and compatible with the launch interface before files are exported. Expected result: A reviewed assembly with no unexplained interference and a documented pass/fix decision for every critical interface. IED Unit 3 • Lesson 3.8 • Learning Studio Learn the concepts before completing the assignment Diagram Video & Resources Guided Steps Practice Assignment What to Submit Understand Engineering concept Before manufacturing, check launcher clearance, actual assembly geometry, fin symmetry, removable interfaces, support-free orientation and predicted filament mass. Apply Today's engineering work Measure the launch interface; inspect both couplers; confirm fin spacing at 120° or 90°; check walls, collisions and support-free print orientations; record PASS/FIX/UNVERIFIED. Calculate & verify Worked example Example: 33 + 39 + 20 = 92 g predicted printed mass, within the 100 g printed-material planning threshold. This does not prove finished rocket weight. 01 / Illustrated concept Digital Rocket Design Review Nose / removable upper module Lightweight printed body Lower fin / launch module Launcher tube: 21.34 mm OD reference Instructional schematic • not a dimensioned manufacturing drawing What the diagram means: Before manufacturing, check launcher clearance, actual assembly geometry, fin symmetry, removable interfaces, support-free orientation and predicted filament mass. The example values illustrate the principle and do not replace actual teacher-assigned dimensions. 02 / Watch and research Instructional video and technical resources Fusion assembly inspection Use the relevant modeling or assembly technique; the demonstration project may differ from the rocket assignment. Watch directly on YouTube ↗ Expert references Use these official Autodesk or NASA guides when the video alone does not explain the underlying workflow. Primary technical reference ↗ Additional learning resource ↗ Self-study: identify a key technique, pause the tutorial, apply the operation and verify the result before continuing. 03 / Step-by-step guide From theory to your own project Guided task sequence Measure the launch interface inspect both couplers confirm fin spacing at 120° or 90° check walls, collisions and support-free print orientations record PASS/FIX/UNVERIFIED. Continue to the full detailed assignment and checklist → Worked example and verification Example: 33 + 39 + 20 = 92 g predicted printed mass, within the 100 g printed-material planning threshold. This does not prove finished rocket weight. Important: Do not substitute illustrative numbers for actual CAD dimensions, real measurements or instructor approvals. 04 / Independent practice Explore one key parameter Interactive concept explorer Estimated printed mass (g): 92 Illustrative values only; not a completed engineering inspection or teacher authorization. Check your reasoning Does predicted filament mass equal finished rocket mass? No. Fin material, hardware and real production affect final assembled mass. What if a criterion has not been checked? Mark NOT VERIFIED, not PASS. Use the lesson's original assignment and “What to Submit” sections below for exact deliverable requirements. Print learning notes Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Use Measure, Interference, and Section Analysis on critical rocket interfaces. Verify fin symmetry and assembly alignment. Review printed mass and wall thickness for material efficiency. Confirm disassembly and launcher compatibility before fabrication. Unit 3 Progression This is the formal gate between digital design and manufacturing. Components Assemble Verify Fabricate Revise Flight Test Compressed-Air Rocket Challenge Project Requirements These requirements apply throughout Lessons 3.6–3.14. Launcher Interface 1/2 in PVC Reference Tube The launcher tube outside diameter is 0.840 in (21.34 mm) . Model the launch tube as a separate grounded Fusion reference component. You choose the rocket's internal launch clearance, but the finished rocket must slide freely over the actual PVC tube without binding. Before choosing the rocket's internal bore dimension, measure the actual unpressurized classroom launch tube. The 0.840 in (21.34 mm) diameter is the nominal outside-diameter reference, not the target bore size. The launcher itself is teacher equipment and is not modified as part of this project. Printed Structure Modular 3D-Printed Rocket The structural rocket body is 3D printed in classroom-approved filament. Use at least 3 major printed modules : a lower launch/fin module, a main body module, and a nose/upper module. The rocket must have at least 2 removable printed-to-printed interfaces . Major printed modules must be disassembled without damaging the parts; permanent adhesive is not allowed between major modules. Student Choice Connection Method You choose how major modules connect. Examples include keyed/slip couplers with retention, twist-lock/bayonet features, screws/inserts, snap-fit features, or another approved method. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 3 Simplify the Rocket Assembly IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Simplify the Rocket Assembly Redesign the assembly to reduce part count or assembly time while preserving required function and overall envelope. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context The current rocket assembly works, but technicians report too many parts, repeated fasteners, and slow assembly. Objectives What You Will Practice Analyze assembly complexity Apply design for assembly principles Preserve interfaces and motion Compare original and revised assemblies Materials What You Need Existing rocket assembly CAD Fusion 360 Bill of materials Stopwatch or assembly-time estimate sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Create a baseline BOM and count unique parts, total parts, fasteners, and assembly steps. Identify three assembly pain points. Generate two redesign concepts that combine parts, replace fasteners, improve alignment, or reduce orientation errors. Use a decision matrix to select a redesign. Modify the CAD assembly and update joints or constraints. Create an updated BOM and assembly sequence. Compare predicted assembly time and part count. Check for new manufacturing, repair, or tolerance problems. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce total part count or assembly steps by at least 20% Preserve rocket exterior envelope and required interfaces Maintain access to parts that may require replacement Use realistic manufacturing methods Update the assembly and BOM completely Constraints Constraints & Safety No change may interfere with the provided rocket requirements Use only available manufacturing processes Do not hide separate components by merely grouping them in CAD Deliverables What You Submit Baseline BOM and sequence Three identified pain points Two concept sketches Decision matrix Revised assembly file Updated BOM Before/after comparison Reflection Reflection Questions Which assembly step created the greatest difficulty? How did your redesign affect repairability? What tolerance issue could appear in the combined part? What physical test should verify the change? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every time a technician must pick up, orient, or fasten a part is an opportunity for simplification. Common Mistake Combining parts can make manufacturing harder or prevent repair. Evaluate the full life cycle. Stretch Goal Create a mistake-proof feature that prevents one part from being installed backward. Career Connection Design-for-assembly engineers reduce part count, handling, fastening, and orientation errors to improve production. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson →

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Friction Surface Investigation IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Friction Surface Investigation Compare friction for three surface materials and recommend the best tray liner. Beginner 60-90 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A payload tray slides during rover motion. The team needs evidence about which surface pairing provides the most resistance to sliding. Objectives What You Will Practice Design a controlled friction test Measure force or critical angle Collect repeated data Use averages to make a recommendation Materials What You Need Small test block Wood, plastic, foam, or other approved surfaces Spring scale or adjustable ramp Protractor Ruler Data sheet Procedure Instructions Choose either a pull-force method or incline-angle method. Define the independent, dependent, and controlled variables. Prepare three surfaces with equal test area. Run at least five trials per surface using the same block and load. Record force or critical angle for every trial. Calculate mean and range for each surface. Create a graph and identify any outlier. Recommend a liner and explain one limitation of the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Test at least three surfaces Complete five trials per surface Keep block mass and contact area constant Calculate mean and range Create one labeled graph Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved surfaces Do not exceed spring-scale capacity Keep hands clear of a moving block Recommendation is based on dry classroom conditions Deliverables What You Submit Test plan and variables Raw data table Mean/range calculations Graph Material recommendation Test limitation Reflection Reflection Questions Which surface had the most consistent data? What variable was hardest to control? How could dust or moisture affect the result? Would the best high-friction material always be best for a moving mechanism? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark a consistent starting position and pull direction for every trial. Common Mistake Do not base a conclusion on the single highest measurement; use repeated data. Stretch Goal Repeat the chosen surface with two different loads and compare the effect. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace support task needs a device that senses or receives an input and produces a mechanical or visual output. Objectives What You Will Practice Create a system block diagram Build a basic electrical circuit Integrate electrical and mechanical components Test and revise a device Materials What You Need Low-voltage power source Switch or approved sensor Motor, buzzer, LED, or actuator Wires and breadboard as appropriate Approved mechanical materials Multimeter Procedure Instructions Choose an approved task and write a one-sentence function statement. Create an input-process-output block diagram. Draw a circuit diagram and label voltage, components, and polarity. Create a mechanical sketch showing how the output does useful work. Build and inspect the electrical circuit before connecting the mechanical load. Test one subsystem at a time. Run at least five full-system trials and record success, current, speed, or another performance measure. Revise one feature and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use only teacher-approved low-voltage components Include a user-controlled stop or power-disconnect method Show both circuit and mechanical diagrams Complete five repeated trials Document one revision Constraints Constraints & Safety No connection to wall power No projectiles, exposed blades, or unsafe pinch points Keep current within component ratings Power must be disconnected before rewiring Deliverables What You Submit Function statement System block diagram Circuit diagram Mechanical sketch Working device or demonstration Five-trial test table Revision reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which subsystem caused the most problems? How did electrical limits affect mechanical performance? What safety feature was most important? How would you make the device more reliable? Your Task Model and Check Prototype Components Develop the required CAD components and evaluate fit, motion space, and manufacturability before construction. Model the assigned components from the approved layout. Use parameters or dimensions to control critical geometry. Assemble or position the parts for a fit check. Pin clearance Clearance: 0.10 mm Motion limit Travel: 90° Model status: Revise model How should moving parts be organized? Choose Separate components One merged body Sketches only Target: 0.30 mm clearance and 70° travel. Check CAD Model A usable motion model needs separate components, realistic fit clearance, and a defined motion limit. What You Will Submit Prototype CAD Check The saved component or assembly CAD files. One annotated fit or motion-clearance screenshot. Your Task Evaluate Variation and Measurement Error Use the material-test data to summarize typical performance, variation, and possible sources of error. Measured Diameter Data: 9.9, 10.1, 10.2, 10.0, 10.3 mm Accepted value: 10.0 mm 10.0 mm target Mean (mm) Range (mm) Percent error (%) Check Statistics Mean describes the center, range describes spread, and percent error compares the mean with the accepted value. pages.title: Design a 5:1 Gear Reduction
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Design a 5:1 Gear Reduction IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Design a 5:1 Gear Reduction Design a gear system with an overall reduction close to 5:1 and demon
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Design a 5:1 Gear Reduction IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Design a 5:1 Gear Reduction Design a gear system with an overall reduction close to 5:1 and demonstrate the expected speed and torque tradeoff. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover motor spins too quickly and does not provide enough output torque for a wheel or lifting mechanism. Objectives What You Will Practice Calculate gear ratios Design single- or multi-stage systems Connect ratio to speed and torque Build or model a mechanism Materials What You Need Gear sets or CAD gear models Axles and supports Calculator Tachometer or rotation-count method Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the required input and desired approximate 5:1 reduction. Create three possible gear-train layouts and calculate each overall ratio. Select a design based on ratio accuracy, part count, size, and direction of rotation. Build or model the selected train. Mark input and output gears. Rotate the input a known number of turns and count output turns. Compare measured and calculated ratio. Explain the expected effect on output speed and ideal torque. Requirements Engineering Requirements Target an overall reduction between 4.8:1 and 5.2:1 Show calculations for three concepts Support and align every axle Demonstrate rotation without gear skipping Compare calculated and measured ratio Constraints Constraints & Safety Use available gears only Do not force mismatched gears Ignore friction only when labeling the result as ideal Mechanism must fit within the assigned footprint Deliverables What You Submit Three gear-train sketches Ratio calculations Selection justification Built or CAD mechanism Measured ratio data Speed/torque explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Why might measured rotation differ from the calculation? What changed when an idler gear was added? How would you reverse output direction? Where is energy lost in the real system? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip For a compound train, multiply the ratio of each stage. Common Mistake Counting gear teeth only within one stage will not give the total ratio of a compound system. Stretch Goal Add a selectable second ratio for high speed and high torque. Career Connection Mechanical and drivetrain engineers design transmissions and gearboxes for aircraft systems, vehicles, robotics, and manufacturing equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Select a Material for a Drone Arm
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Select a Material for a Drone Arm IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.1 Select a Material for a Drone Arm Compare candidate materials and recommend the best choice
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Select a Material for a Drone Arm IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.1 Select a Material for a Drone Arm Compare candidate materials and recommend the best choice for a defined drone-arm scenario. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small inspection drone needs a replacement arm. The material must be light, stiff enough, manufacturable, and affordable. Objectives What You Will Practice Use material properties in a trade study Distinguish strength, stiffness, density, and toughness Apply weighted decision criteria Defend an engineering recommendation Materials What You Need Candidate material data sheets Decision matrix template Calculator or spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Review the mission profile, arm dimensions, expected load, and available manufacturing processes. Compare aluminum, PLA, ABS, nylon, and carbon-fiber composite using density, stiffness, strength, toughness, cost, and manufacturability. Choose weighting factors that total 100%. Normalize or score each material consistently. Complete the weighted decision matrix. Perform one simple mass comparison using equal part volume. Identify one property not captured well by the numerical matrix. Write a recommendation with one risk and one verification test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Compare at least five candidate materials Use at least six criteria Explain all weighting choices Include one quantitative mass comparison Identify a verification test before flight use Constraints Constraints & Safety Use provided or credible property data Do not treat all composites as identical Recommendation applies only to the stated mission and geometry No physical load testing beyond approved classroom limits Deliverables What You Submit Material-property comparison table Weighted decision matrix Mass calculation Recommendation memo Risk and test plan Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion controlled the result? How would a crash-resistance requirement change the choice? Why might the lightest material not be best? What data would you verify with a supplier? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Strength and stiffness are different. A material may resist breaking but still bend too much. Common Mistake A decision matrix does not replace judgment. Poor data or arbitrary weights can produce a misleading winner. Stretch Goal Recalculate the matrix for a cold-weather mission or a low-cost training drone. Career Connection Materials and aerospace engineers select materials by balancing performance, environment, manufacturing, cost, and risk. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson →

Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can identify basic circuit components and explain safe circuit-building expectations. Identify Build Check Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The circuit operates as intended with no exposed short circuit, reversed polarized component, or unsafe connection. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Build and Verify a Safe Simple Circuit. Learning Targets Identify power source, load, conductor, switch, and circuit path. Explain why safe circuit setup protects people, components, and prototypes. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can simple circuits safely support an engineering prototype? Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The circuit operates as intended with no exposed short circuit, reversed polarized component, or unsafe connection. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A circuit must have a complete path for current to flow. Key Idea 2 Electrical safety includes low-voltage habits, correct polarity, secure connections, and inspection before power. Key Idea 3 A prototype circuit should be tested before it is integrated into a larger system. Your Task Build and Verify a Safe Simple Circuit Construct the assigned low-voltage circuit and verify current path, polarity, and safe component use before connecting it to a prototype. Identify the source, load, conductors, and control component. Sketch or follow the approved circuit diagram. Build the circuit with power disconnected. Perform the safety check, power it briefly, and record the result. Quality check: The circuit operates as intended with no exposed short circuit, reversed polarized component, or unsafe connection. Lesson Interactive Complete a Safe LED Circuit Close the electrical path and include the component that protects the LED. Status: Open or incomplete Close the switch Include the series resistor Why is the resistor needed? Choose Limit current through the LED Increase source voltage Store charge indefinitely Check Circuit A working circuit needs a complete path. A safe LED circuit also needs current limiting. What You Will Submit Simple Circuit Verification One approved circuit diagram or clear build photo. A recorded functionality and safety check. Submission standard: The circuit operates as intended with no exposed short circuit, reversed polarized component, or unsafe connection. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision Analyze a class data set, create ap
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 4 Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Turn Class Data into an Engineering Decision Analyze a class data set, create appropriate visualizations, and make an evidence-based engineering recommendation. Intermediate 60 minutes Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineers must convert raw measurements into a clear conclusion that supports a design decision. Objectives What You Will Practice Organize and clean data Select appropriate graph types Use descriptive statistics Connect evidence to a decision Materials What You Need Class data set Spreadsheet software Calculator Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Import or enter the data and check units, labels, blanks, and obvious entry errors. State the engineering question the data should answer. Calculate mean, median, range, and one additional useful statistic. Create at least two graph types and choose the one that communicates the result best. Identify any outlier and decide whether to keep, correct, or investigate it. Compare at least two groups or conditions. Write a claim supported by two specific pieces of evidence. Make one recommendation and state one limitation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use a data set with at least 15 values Label all axes and units Calculate at least four statistics Create at least two candidate graphs Support the recommendation with numerical evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not delete outliers without explanation Use graph scales that do not exaggerate differences Protect student names or private information Conclusions must stay within the available data Deliverables What You Submit Clean data table Statistic calculations Two candidate graphs Final selected graph Claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph Recommendation and limitation Reflection Reflection Questions Which graph communicated the data best? How did the mean and median differ? What did the outlier change? What additional data would strengthen the recommendation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Start with the decision question, not the graph type. Common Mistake A visually dramatic graph can still be misleading if the scale or labels are inappropriate. Stretch Goal Create a dashboard with a filter or comparison control. Career Connection Test, quality, and systems engineers use data visualization to monitor performance and support decisions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson →

Lesson Interactive Turn Stakeholder Quotes into Design Evidence Classify each interview statement so the team can separate user pain points, context, goals, and preferences. Choose Would a larger handle solve the problem? Do you like the current latch? Walk me through the last time the latch was difficult to use. Check Research Notes Use open questions to learn about real experiences rather than confirm a solution idea. What You Will Submit Stakeholder Research Summary One stakeholder map or research summary. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 5 Client Design Brief Sprint IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.3 Client Design Brief Sprint Interview a client, convert their needs into a design brief, and recommend a concept. Intermediate 2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering projects often begin with incomplete client statements such as “make this easier” or “we need a better holder.” Objectives What You Will Practice Ask effective stakeholder questions Separate needs from proposed solutions Write measurable requirements Present and justify a concept Materials What You Need Client interview form Engineering notebook Sketching tools Decision matrix template Presentation materials Procedure Instructions Pair with a classmate and assign client and designer roles. The client chooses an approved small problem but does not prescribe the final solution. Conduct a five-minute interview using open and follow-up questions. Summarize the problem and ask the client to confirm your interpretation. Create at least five criteria and three constraints, including measurable targets. Generate three concepts independently before discussing them. Use a decision matrix to select a recommendation. Present the recommendation in two minutes and record client feedback. Requirements Engineering Requirements Ask at least eight interview questions Include measurable criteria and clear constraints Generate three distinct concepts Use a decision matrix Show how the final recommendation responds to client needs Constraints Constraints & Safety Problem must be safe and classroom appropriate No personal or sensitive information Designer may not simply build the client’s first suggested solution Complete within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Interview notes Confirmed problem statement Criteria and constraints Three concept sketches Decision matrix Two-minute recommendation Client feedback Reflection Reflection Questions Which question produced the most useful information? What did the client want that was not stated initially? How did feedback affect the recommendation? What would you prototype first? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask “What are you trying to accomplish?” before asking “What should it look like?” Common Mistake Clients often describe a preferred solution instead of the underlying need. Your job is to uncover the need. Stretch Goal Switch roles and complete a second brief in half the time. Career Connection Design consultants, systems engineers, and project managers translate stakeholder needs into requirements and concepts. Recommend a responsible improvement or limitation statement. Success Looks Like You can evaluate a design using ethical, safety, sustainability, and life-cycle considerations. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How do engineers make responsible design decisions beyond simply making a prototype work? Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A working design is not automatically a responsible design. Key Idea 2 Engineers consider who benefits, who may be affected, and what happens over the product life cycle. Key Idea 3 Responsible design decisions should be stated clearly in the final documentation. Your Task Evaluate Responsible Design Impacts Examine the current design for ethical, safety, sustainability, life-cycle, accessibility, and broader stakeholder effects. Identify hazards and who could be affected. Review materials, energy, waste, repair, and end-of-life considerations. Consider accessibility, fairness, privacy, or unintended consequences relevant to the project. Record one required responsibility-driven change or justified decision. Quality check: The analysis addresses project-specific impacts and goes beyond a generic statement that the design is safe or sustainable. Lesson Interactive Review Ethics, Safety, Sustainability, and Life Cycle Select the actions that make the design more responsible across use, maintenance, communication, and end of life. Select every responsible action Add a guard around the pinch point Disclose that the prototype was not tested in rain Use replaceable wear components instead of sealing the assembly Label separable materials for end-of-life recovery Hide failed test data to strengthen the presentation Which issue has the highest immediate priority? Background Engineering Context A user can understand a classroom product but has difficulty gripping, twisting, or pressing it because of limited hand strength. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify user needs through empathy and evidence Translate needs into measurable requirements Generate accessible concepts Evaluate a human-centered prototype Materials What You Need Approved classroom product User-needs interview sheet Sketching materials Cardboard, foam, clay, or other prototype materials Force gauge if available Procedure Instructions Select a product with a grip, cap, button, lever, or control. Create a respectful user profile based on limited hand strength; do not simulate a disability in an unsafe way. Observe the product and identify at least three barriers. Convert barriers into measurable requirements such as diameter, force, reach, or texture. Sketch three concepts and collect feedback from a peer acting as a reviewer. Build a low-fidelity prototype of the selected concept. Run a usability test using the same task for the original and redesign. Document feedback and make one revision. What feedback changed your design? Did improving accessibility help other users too? What would require additional real-user testing? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask what task is difficult and why. Avoid assuming the solution before understanding the user. Common Mistake Making a handle larger is not automatically accessible; reach, force, texture, feedback, and context all matter. Stretch Goal Redesign the product for one additional user need without reducing the first improvement. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 5 Aerospace Product Life-Cycle Analysis IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Aerospace Product Life-Cycle Analysis Map the life cycle of an aerospace-related produc
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 5 Aerospace Product Life-Cycle Analysis IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Aerospace Product Life-Cycle Analysis Map the life cycle of an aerospace-related product and recommend two realistic improvements. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A product can meet its immediate performance goal while creating hidden environmental or social impacts during material extraction, manufacturing, use, maintenance, or disposal. Objectives What You Will Practice Use life-cycle thinking Identify impacts across product stages Distinguish evidence from assumptions Recommend feasible design changes Materials What You Need Research access Life-cycle map template Engineering notebook At least three credible sources Procedure Instructions Choose an approved product such as a drone battery, aircraft seat component, composite panel, satellite enclosure, or rocket packaging. Define the product function and expected service life. Map raw materials, processing, manufacturing, transportation, use, maintenance, and end-of-life. For each stage, identify energy, material, waste, emissions, safety, or labor considerations. Mark the three stages with the greatest likely impact and support the choice with evidence. Generate four improvement ideas. Evaluate ideas for impact reduction, technical feasibility, cost, and possible unintended consequences. Recommend two improvements and identify how success would be measured. Requirements Engineering Requirements Include every major life-cycle stage Use at least three credible sources Identify at least three impact categories Recommend two feasible improvements Include one unintended consequence or tradeoff Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not claim precise environmental numbers without a valid source Keep the scope clear and manageable Use respectful language when discussing labor or community impacts Deliverables What You Submit Life-cycle map Source list Impact hotspot analysis Four improvement ideas Two recommendations with metrics Tradeoff statement Reflection Reflection Questions Which life-cycle stage was easiest to overlook? Which recommendation had the best impact-to-feasibility balance? What assumption most affected your analysis? How could product life be extended? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define the system boundary. State what is included and excluded from the analysis. Common Mistake “Recyclable” does not guarantee recycling will occur. Consider collection, separation, contamination, and market demand. Stretch Goal Compare a reusable and single-use version of the same product. Career Connection Sustainability, materials, supply-chain, and systems engineers evaluate product impacts beyond initial manufacture. Advanced 2-3 class periods Creative Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An engineering portfolio should show how you think, not only display a final object. Objectives What You Will Practice Curate technical evidence Explain a design process clearly Improve visual and written communication Reflect on growth and tradeoffs Materials What You Need One completed IED project Original notebook and files CAD/screenshots/photos Presentation or page-layout software Portfolio checklist Procedure Instructions Select a project with enough evidence to show at least one meaningful revision. Write a 40-60 word project overview including the problem, user or client, and final outcome. Choose 6-10 artifacts that show problem definition, concepts, CAD, build, test, and revision. Improve one weak artifact, such as a sketch, drawing, photograph, graph, or CAD view. Create a before/after or problem/revision comparison. Write three short captions that explain decisions rather than merely name images. Create a one-page case study or 3-5 slide presentation. Deliver a two-minute presentation and use feedback to make one final revision. Requirements Engineering Requirements Show the problem, process, evidence, revision, and result Use only your own work or clearly identify team contributions Include at least one quantitative result Include one honest limitation or unresolved issue Use consistent visual hierarchy and readable text Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not include private student information Do not claim sole credit for team work Keep the final case study to one page or five slides Use high-quality, appropriately cropped images Deliverables What You Submit Project overview 6-10 curated artifacts One improved artifact Before/after comparison Final case study or slides Two-minute presentation Final reflection Reflection Reflection Questions What does the portfolio reveal about your engineering process? Which artifact provides the strongest evidence? What did you remove and why? How would you describe your growth this year? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every image needs a job. Include it only if it supports a decision, test, revision, or result. Common Mistake A portfolio made only of polished final images hides the engineering process that employers and programs want to see. Stretch Goal Create a second version tailored to an internship, college program, or competition audience. Career Connection Engineers use portfolios and technical presentations to communicate capability, design thinking, and project impact. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 5 Sustainable Packaging for a Rocket Component IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.2 Sustainable Packaging for a Rocket Component Design, build, and test sustainable packaging for a provided component. Intermediate 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A precision rocket component must be shipped to a test site. The package must protect the part while minimizing material and waste. Objectives What You Will Practice Balance protection and material use Apply life-cycle thinking Design packaging around a product Use test evidence to revise a solution Materials What You Need Provided rocket component or surrogate Corrugated cardboard, paperboard, paper, or approved recycled material Scale Ruler Drop-test area Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Measure the component and identify surfaces that must be protected. Define shipping hazards such as drop, vibration, abrasion, and moisture. Set criteria for protection, package size, mass, material type, and recyclability. Sketch three packaging concepts using minimal material. Select and build one concept. Record package mass and external dimensions. Perform three approved drop tests from increasing heights. Inspect the part and package, revise one feature, and retest. Requirements Engineering Requirements Prevent visible damage in three approved drop tests Use at least 70% recyclable or reusable material by mass Use no loose plastic foam Keep package volume below the teacher-set limit Allow the component to be removed without damage Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved drop heights and test area No hazardous or messy filler Component must be returned in original condition Adhesive use must be measured or documented Deliverables What You Submit Hazard and criteria list Three concept sketches Material and mass record Final package Drop-test results Sustainability justification Revision notes Reflection Reflection Questions Which hazard controlled the design? Where was material unnecessary? How did protection compete with sustainability? What would change for repeated shipping? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Protect the component by controlling movement and distributing impact, not just by adding more material. Common Mistake A package made from recyclable material is not sustainable if it uses far more material than necessary. Stretch Goal Design a reusable package that completes ten shipping cycles. Your Task Collect Prototype and User Evidence Run the approved tests and feedback activities while recording results, observations, comments, and limitations accurately. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 5 Lesson 5.1 IED Unit 5 • Lesson 5.1 Human-Centered Aerospace Design Capstone Launch Focus question: How can engineers design aerospace solutions that meet real user needs while considering safety, ethics, sustainability, and impact? Download Presentation Flight Plan Interactive What You Submit Back to Unit 5 Mission Focus You can explain the capstone mission and describe how user needs, safety, ethics, sustainability, and impact will shape the final design. Frame Connect Plan Use the required lesson evidence to demonstrate this standard: The launch note centers a user need and does not begin with a predetermined product. Mission Briefing Today’s Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, and the tools or evidence assigned for Launch a Human-Centered Aerospace Capstone. Learning Targets Describe the Unit 5 human-centered aerospace capstone challenge. Identify why user needs, safety, ethics, sustainability, and impact matter in aerospace design. List the major evidence teams will build during the capstone. Success Looks Like You can explain the capstone mission and describe how user needs, safety, ethics, sustainability, and impact will shape the final design. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers design aerospace solutions that meet real user needs while considering safety, ethics, sustainability, and impact? Connect your response to the decision, evidence, or quality standard required for Launch a Human-Centered Aerospace Capstone. Reveal: useful engineering move This lesson is ready to move forward when the evidence meets this standard: The launch note centers a user need and does not begin with a predetermined product. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Human-centered design begins with people, not just products. Key Idea 2 A strong aerospace solution must consider users, safety, context, ethics, sustainability, and real constraints. Key Idea 3 The final capstone is defended through evidence, reflection, and professional communication. Your Task Launch a Human-Centered Aerospace Capstone Frame the capstone around a real user or stakeholder need and identify the responsible-design questions the project must address. Review the capstone scope and required final evidence. Identify a possible user, stakeholder, or context. List initial needs, risks, and unanswered questions. Define what successful project evidence would look like. Quality check: The launch note centers a user need and does not begin with a predetermined product. Lesson Interactive Frame the Capstone Around a Human Need Choose the launch brief that begins with a user and context rather than a predetermined product. Then identify the responsible-design lenses that must guide the project. Which brief is human-centered? Brief A: Design a 3D-printed handle with a blue grip and two screws. Brief B: A ground-crew technician wearing gloves needs to open and secure an access panel quickly without losing small parts. Brief C: Improve the panel by adding a spring, a larger button, and a warning light. Which lenses belong in a responsible capstone launch? Safety and foreseeable misuse Ethics and stakeholder impact Sustainability and life-cycle impact Evidence needed to evaluate success Check Capstone Frame Start with a person, a context, and an unmet need. Do not choose the final product yet. What You Will Submit Capstone Launch Brief One launch brief naming the user or stakeholder, possible need, and key research questions. Submission standard: The launch note centers a user need and does not begin with a predetermined product. pages.title: Design for 3D Printing
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Design for 3D Printing IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Design for 3D Printing Redesign the part to improve printability while preserving its function. Interm
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Design for 3D Printing IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Design for 3D Printing Redesign the part to improve printability while preserving its function. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A part was designed in CAD without considering how it would be printed. It requires excessive supports, wastes material, and takes too long. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common additive manufacturing limitations Modify geometry for reduced supports Compare slicer estimates Justify design-for-manufacturing decisions Materials What You Need Teacher-provided CAD part Fusion 360 Slicer software Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Import or open the baseline part. Write the part’s intended function and identify features that must not change. Slice the baseline in the most reasonable orientation and record print time, material, and support amount. Identify at least three printability problems. Create two redesign sketches and select one. Modify overhangs, holes, wall thickness, orientation surfaces, or part segmentation. Slice the redesign using the same printer and comparable settings. Compare estimates and check that all functional dimensions remain correct. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce support material by at least 50% or eliminate supports Reduce print time or material use by at least 15% Preserve specified functional dimensions Maintain minimum printable wall thickness Document all slicer settings used for comparison Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the same printer profile and layer height for baseline and redesign Do not remove functional features No print is required unless approved Use classroom-safe geometry and scale Deliverables What You Submit Baseline slicer screenshot and estimates Three identified printability problems Two redesign sketches Revised CAD file Final slicer screenshot Before/after comparison table Design explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which geometry caused the most support? What change produced the largest improvement? Did reducing print time create a new tradeoff? How would injection molding change the design rules? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Before changing the part, rotate it in the slicer. Sometimes orientation solves more than redesign. Common Mistake Comparisons are invalid if the baseline and redesign use different layer heights or infill settings without explanation. Stretch Goal Create a two-part version that prints even faster and compare assembly complexity. Career Connection Additive manufacturing engineers adjust geometry, orientation, supports, and process settings to improve quality and cost. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →

pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.1 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.1 Getting Started with Fusion Focus question: How do engineers organize and navigate a CAD workspace before creating a model? Go to Assignment Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Learn the Fusion interface, file organization, and navigation controls before creating geometry. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Navigate the major Fusion workspace areas. Create, name, save, close, and reopen a design. Use orbit, pan, zoom, the ViewCube, Home View, Browser, and Timeline. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Assignment Getting Started with Fusion This lesson is about learning how to work efficiently inside Fusion before you begin modeling. Do not create a part yet. Your goal is to become comfortable finding files, changing views, and locating the major interface areas you will use throughout Unit 2. Step-by-Step Instructions Create and name your design: Open Fusion and create a new design. Rename it using the class naming convention before doing anything else. Make sure the correct project/folder is selected in the Data Panel so you will be able to find the file again later. Identify the major interface areas: Locate the Data Panel, Browser, Origin folder, main Toolbar, ViewCube, Canvas, and Timeline. Be prepared to explain what each area is used for. Expand and collapse the Browser so you understand where sketches, bodies, components, and origin planes will appear. Practice camera controls: Use orbit, pan, and zoom until you can intentionally move to front, top, right, and isometric views. Use the ViewCube and Home command to return to a known orientation. Do not rely only on the mouse wheel; practice each navigation method shown by the instructor. Work with the provided model: Open the teacher-provided practice model and reproduce the assigned views. Move between standard and isometric orientations without changing the model geometry. Practice file management: Save the design, close it, locate it again in the Data Panel, and reopen it. Confirm that the filename and project location are correct before the end of class. Before You Submit You can find the file again after closing it. You can return to a standard view without guessing. You can identify the Browser and Timeline and explain the difference between them. Submission What You Will Submit Interface screenshot: Fusion window showing the correctly named file with the Browser and Timeline visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_1_Interface.png . Navigation screenshot: teacher-provided model shown in the assigned orientation. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_1_View.png . Written response: Answer: “Where does Fusion display the sequence of features used to create a model?” File requirements: Use the Windows Snipping Tool or screenshot tool to save each image as PNG. No Fusion archive is required for this lesson. pages.title: Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint Model a randomly assigned object accurately within 30 minutes, then evaluat
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint Model a randomly assigned object accurately within 30 minutes, then evaluate which modeling choices improved speed and quality. Intermediate 30 minutes plus review Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Rapid CAD work is useful when engineers need a concept model for a meeting or prototype decision. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan an efficient feature sequence Use constraints and parameters quickly Prioritize critical geometry Review CAD quality under time pressure Materials What You Need Fusion 360 One approved object or dimension card Calipers or ruler Timer Engineering notebook Procedure Instructions Draw or receive an object such as a LEGO-style brick, die, battery spacer, USB shell, or simple bracket. Spend three minutes identifying the base feature, repeated features, symmetry, and likely parameters. Record a short modeling plan before opening a sketch. Model for 25 minutes. Use the final two minutes to rename features, check constraints, and inspect dimensions. Export one screenshot showing the browser and completed model. Compare the model with the object or dimension card. Record one shortcut that helped and one rushed decision that caused rework. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use at least one named parameter Keep all major sketches fully constrained Include every critical feature Use patterns or symmetry where appropriate Finish within 30 minutes Constraints Constraints & Safety No imported models No help from another student during the timed period Accuracy is more important than decorative details Object must be teacher-approved Deliverables What You Submit Modeling plan Fusion file Final screenshot Accuracy checklist Short time-management reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which feature should have been created first? Where did you lose the most time? Did a pattern or parameter improve speed? What would you change in a second attempt? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Spend a few minutes planning. A strong feature order saves more time than sketching immediately. Common Mistake Fast modeling is not the same as careless modeling. Unconstrained sketches create hidden problems later. Stretch Goal Remodel the same object in 20 minutes using lessons from the first attempt. Career Connection CAD designers frequently create rapid concept models before detailed engineering work begins. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Puzzle Cube Technical Drawing & Exploded View
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.12 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Day 4 Puzzle Cube Technical Drawing & Exploded View Focus question: How can engineers use drawi
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.12 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.12 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Day 4 Puzzle Cube Technical Drawing & Exploded View Focus question: How can engineers use drawings and exploded views to communicate a multi-part design clearly? Go to Assignment Video Help What to Submit Back to Unit 2 20 Points • 1 Class Period Document the completed puzzle using Fusion drawing views, dimensions, and an exploded view. Expected result: Professional documentation that communicates the assembled cube and the geometry of all five individual pieces. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Create drawing views from a multi-body Fusion design. Select orthographic and isometric views that communicate geometry efficiently. Dimension the 20 mm unit structure without unnecessary duplicate dimensions. Create an exploded view that clearly shows the relationship of the five pieces. Documentation Workflow Your drawing should communicate the design to someone who did not create it. Include the complete cube, all five pieces, and enough dimensional information to understand the unit-cube geometry. Drawing Views Dimension Explode Export Puzzle Cube Challenge Project Requirements These requirements apply throughout Lessons 2.10–2.13. Finished Cube 3 × 3 × 3 Unit Cube 27 total unit cubes. Each unit cube is exactly 20 mm × 20 mm × 20 mm . The assembled puzzle must be 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm . The final puzzle contains exactly 5 pieces . Piece Geometry Five Connected Pieces Each piece contains at least 3 unit cubes . Every piece must be one continuous solid with cubes connected face-to-face. At least 1 of the 5 pieces must span at least 2 unit cubes in X, Y, and Z. Pieces may repeat the same shape. Color & Printing Plan for Manufacturing Use five different colors consistently in the sketch, Fusion model, and final printed puzzle. Each piece must have a practical flat-face orientation that can print without support material. No additional clearance is required; use the exact 20 mm unit geometry. Assignment Create the Technical Drawing and Exploded View Use the five-body Puzzle Cube model from Lesson 2.11. You will create a Fusion drawing from the design and a separate exploded-view image. Step-by-Step Instructions Open the final assembled model: Confirm all five bodies are visible and positioned to form the 60 mm cube before starting the drawing. Create a drawing from the design: Start a new Fusion drawing using the class sheet size and drawing standard specified by the instructor. Add an assembled isometric view: Place a clear isometric view of the complete puzzle cube. Choose a scale that makes the model easy to read. Add assembled orthographic views: Include front, top, and right-side views of the completed cube. Add all five individual pieces: Place separate views for Piece A, Piece B, Piece C, Piece D, and Piece E. Use orientations that make the geometry of each piece understandable. Add dimensions: Show the overall 60 mm cube dimensions and enough 20 mm-based dimensions to communicate the unit-cube structure and important steps/extents of the individual pieces. Avoid repeating dimensions that are already obvious from another view. Check drawing quality: Make sure views do not overlap, dimensions are readable, and every piece can be identified. Export the technical drawing: Save/export the completed drawing as a PDF using the required filename. Create the exploded view: Return to the 3D model. Save a copy or make sure you can restore the assembled positions. Use Move/Copy to separate the five bodies outward while keeping their relative orientation understandable. Capture the exploded view: Create a clean isometric screenshot showing all five separated colored bodies and how they relate to the assembled cube. Restore the design: Undo the temporary body moves or reopen the original assembled model so your main design remains in its correct assembled position. Before You Submit The drawing includes an assembled isometric view. Front, top, and right orthographic views are included. All five individual pieces have their own clear views. Overall and unit-geometry dimensions are readable and useful. The exploded view clearly separates all five colored pieces. Your original Fusion model remains assembled after the exploded-view image is created. Assignment Video Resources Videos for Lesson 2.12 Use these three reference videos while working through your Fusion technical drawing and exploded-view assignment. Pause and replay sections as needed. The lesson instructions and submission checklist still apply. Reference Video 1 Watch Reference Video 1 on YouTube ↗ Reference Video 2 Watch Reference Video 2 on YouTube ↗ Reference Video 3 Watch Reference Video 3 on YouTube ↗ If a video cannot play on the school network, use its Watch on YouTube link to open it directly. Submission What You Will Submit Technical drawing PDF: assembled isometric, front/top/right orthographic views, all five individual piece views, and required dimensions. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_12_PuzzleCube_Drawing.pdf . Exploded-view image: clear color-coded exploded isometric showing all five pieces. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_12_Exploded.png . Drawing standard: The drawing should be readable without opening the original Fusion model. Use clean view placement and only the dimensions needed to communicate the geometry clearly. Grading 20-Point Lesson Rubric Criteria Points Assembled isometric view is clear and appropriately scaled 3 Front, top, and right orthographic views are complete and readable 4 Separate views clearly communicate all five individual pieces 4 Dimensions communicate the 60 mm overall cube and 20 mm unit geometry 4 Exploded view clearly shows the relationship among all five colored pieces 3 Drawing/export is organized, readable, and correctly submitted 2 Total 20 Resources Lesson Resources Unit Hub IED Unit 2 Return to the Unit 2 lesson list and course sequence. pages.title: Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook Measure and model a tape measure hook as a fully co
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook Measure and model a tape measure hook as a fully constrained, parametric CAD part. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A maintenance department needs a replacement tape hook, but the supplier no longer provides the part file. Objectives What You Will Practice Use calipers to collect part dimensions Create fully constrained sketches Build a parametric model Compare CAD geometry to a physical part Materials What You Need Tape measure hook or similar flat metal part Calipers Fusion 360 Engineering notebook Optional flatbed photo with scale Procedure Instructions Identify the part’s datums and create a measurement plan. Measure overall length, width, thickness, holes, slots, bends, and feature spacing. Create a parameter table before sketching. Build the base profile with geometric and dimensional constraints. Add holes, slots, fillets, and bends or approximations in a logical feature order. Verify that every sketch is fully constrained. Create a technical drawing with the dimensions needed for inspection. Compare at least five CAD measurements with the physical part and calculate error. Requirements Engineering Requirements Fully constrained sketches All critical dimensions driven by parameters Five comparison measurements within +/-0.5 mm Realistic fillets and feature order Complete drawing and STL export Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not disassemble a tape measure spring mechanism Model only the approved hook component Use metric units Complete within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Measurement plan and table Fusion 360 file Parameter list Technical drawing PDF STL file CAD-to-part error table Reflection Reflection Questions Which measurement controlled the most geometry? Where was the largest error? How did constraints make revision easier? What manufacturing process likely created the original part? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Photographing the part next to a ruler can help verify overall proportions, but use calipers for final dimensions. Common Mistake Do not trace a photo and assume it is accurate; camera perspective can distort geometry. Stretch Goal Redesign the hook for easier grip while preserving all connection dimensions. Career Connection Reverse-engineering and sustaining engineers recreate legacy parts when drawings or suppliers are unavailable. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →
