Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Create sketches on existing planar faces. Use Extrude Cut for custom removed geometry. Use the Hole tool for engineered circular holes. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Reference Resources Bracket 3 Reference Model and Sketch Use the 3D model to understand the geometry and the three drawing PDFs as your main references while building the part. Download Front View Download Side View Download Bottom View Loading model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom Overall dimensions: 3.000 × 2.000 × 1.250 in Display Shaded model Show hidden edges Standard Views Isometric Front Top Right Viewer Controls Auto rotate Reset View Full Screen Important: Use the interactive viewer to interpret shape, orientation, and feature location. Use the downloaded Bracket 3 drawing views as the main drawing references for your CAD model. Recommended workflow: Keep the Bracket 3 drawing PDFs open while modeling. Use the 3D viewer when you need help interpreting the part geometry, and use the drawing views as your primary 2D references. Assignment Cut Features and Holes — Bracket 3 Continue the same Bracket 3 file from Lesson 2.5. This lesson focuses on removing material accurately using Extrude Cut and the Hole tool. Step-by-Step Instructions Open the existing Bracket 3 design: Do not start a new model. Use the same cloud design so the Timeline shows the progression from the original base feature. Plan each removed feature: Use the technical drawing to identify which features are custom cutouts and which are true circular holes. Create custom cut geometry: Sketch the required non-circular openings on the correct face. Fully constrain their position and size, then use Extrude with the Cut operation. Create engineered holes: Use the Hole tool for circular holes where appropriate. Set the location, diameter, and extent from the drawing rather than approximating the hole with an arbitrary sketch circle. Check cut extent: Verify whether each cut is Through All, To Object, or a specified depth. Make sure the result matches the documentation. Measure the finished features: Use Inspect/Measure to confirm hole diameters, center locations, spacing, and cut geometry. Before You Submit Custom openings use appropriate cut features. Circular engineered holes use the Hole tool where directed. Feature locations and diameters match the drawing. The original base feature remains editable in the Timeline. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive snapshot: updated Bracket 3 model exported as LastName_FirstName_2_6_Bracket3.f3d . Isometric screenshot: completed cuts and holes with the Timeline visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_6_Bracket3.png . File requirements: Continue editing the same Bracket 3 cloud design. Create the submission snapshot with File → Export → Fusion 360 Archive Files (*.f3d) . pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.7 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.7 Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent — Bracket 3 Focus question: How do edge features improve the function, manufacturability, and appearance of an engineered part? Go to Assignment Download Front View Download Side View Download Bottom View Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Finish Bracket 3 with the required edge treatments and perform a complete model verification. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Apply fillets and chamfers appropriately. Explain why an edge treatment is used. Verify the complete part against the original documentation. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Reference Resources Bracket 3 Reference Model and Sketch Use the 3D model to understand the geometry and the three drawing PDFs as your main references while building the part. Download Front View Download Side View Download Bottom View Loading model… Drag to rotate • Scroll or pinch to zoom Overall dimensions: 3.000 × 2.000 × 1.250 in Display Shaded model Show hidden edges Standard Views Isometric Front Top Right Viewer Controls Auto rotate Reset View Full Screen Important: Use the interactive viewer to interpret shape, orientation, and feature location. Use the downloaded Bracket 3 drawing views as the main drawing references for your CAD model. Recommended workflow: Keep the Bracket 3 drawing PDFs open while modeling. Use the 3D viewer when you need help interpreting the part geometry, and use the drawing views as your primary 2D references. Assignment Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent — Bracket 3 You will complete Bracket 3 by adding edge treatments and then perform a final model verification. The goal is not just to make the part look finished; each feature should exist for a reason. Step-by-Step Instructions Compare the current model with the technical drawing: Identify every remaining fillet, chamfer, radius, or finishing feature that is still missing. Add fillets: Select only the edges that should receive the specified radius. Confirm the correct radius value before accepting the feature. Add chamfers: Apply the required chamfer type and distance/angle. Verify that the chamfer removes material from the intended edge. Review feature order: Look at the Timeline and confirm the feature order is logical. If a feature fails when an earlier dimension changes, investigate whether the model references are robust. Perform a complete dimensional check: Measure the overall part and at least the critical holes, cutouts, and edge features. Compare the final model directly with your Unit 1 documentation. Clean the file: Remove unused sketches or accidental geometry only if they are truly unnecessary. Leave the model organized so another person can understand how it was built. Before You Submit All required edge treatments are present. Final dimensions match the technical drawing. Timeline is readable and does not contain obvious accidental features. Bracket 3 is complete at the end of this lesson. Submission What You Will Submit Final Fusion archive: completed Bracket 3 exported as LastName_FirstName_2_7_Bracket3_Final.f3d . Final model screenshot: isometric view with Browser and Timeline visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_7_Bracket3_Final.png . pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.13 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.13 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Day 5 Puzzle Cube Manufacturing & Final Verification Focus question: How can engineers prepare
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.13 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.13 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Day 5 Puzzle Cube Manufacturing & Final Verification Focus question: How can engineers prepare a multi-part CAD design for manufacturing and verify that the physical result matches the design intent? Go to Assignment Video Help What to Submit Back to Unit 2 20 Points • Day 5 + Post-Print Check Prepare the final Fusion and STL files for teacher batch printing, then demonstrate the printed puzzle after manufacturing. Expected result: Five print-ready pieces that can be manufactured without supports and assembled into the final 60 mm cube. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Verify a CAD design before manufacturing. Export individual bodies as correctly named STL files. Evaluate whether each piece has a support-free print orientation. Compare a finished physical product with the original digital design. Two-Stage Grade The digital manufacturing package is graded first. After the instructor batch-prints the pieces in five colors, the final points are earned by checking the physical pieces and assembling the completed puzzle. Verify Export Submit Print Demonstrate Puzzle Cube Challenge Project Requirements These requirements apply throughout Lessons 2.10–2.13. Finished Cube 3 × 3 × 3 Unit Cube 27 total unit cubes. Each unit cube is exactly 20 mm × 20 mm × 20 mm . The assembled puzzle must be 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm . The final puzzle contains exactly 5 pieces . Piece Geometry Five Connected Pieces Each piece contains at least 3 unit cubes . Every piece must be one continuous solid with cubes connected face-to-face. At least 1 of the 5 pieces must span at least 2 unit cubes in X, Y, and Z. Pieces may repeat the same shape. Color & Printing Plan for Manufacturing Use five different colors consistently in the sketch, Fusion model, and final printed puzzle. Each piece must have a practical flat-face orientation that can print without support material. No additional clearance is required; use the exact 20 mm unit geometry. Assignment Prepare the Puzzle Cube for 3D Printing Complete a final quality check, export each body as its own STL file, and submit the manufacturing package. The instructor will handle batch slicing and printing. Step-by-Step Instructions Open the assembled Fusion model: Verify the design still contains exactly five separate bodies and that none were accidentally joined during Lesson 2.12. Perform the final size check: Use Inspect/Measure to confirm the complete puzzle is exactly 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm and the design is based on exact 20 mm units. Recheck the project rules: Confirm each piece contains at least three unit cubes, each piece is face-connected, and at least one piece satisfies the X/Y/Z span requirement. Check printability: Inspect each body and identify a flat-face orientation that will allow the piece to print without support material. If a piece cannot be printed support-free, revise the design while preserving the required puzzle geometry. Save the final Fusion design: Make sure the five pieces are assembled and the bodies are clearly named Piece A through Piece E. Export Piece A: Select only Piece A and use Save as Mesh/Export Mesh to create an STL file. Export Pieces B–E: Repeat the process so there are exactly five separate STL files. Do not export the entire assembled cube as one STL. Name the files clearly: Include the piece letter and intended print color in each STL filename so the instructor can batch-print the correct colors. Submit the digital manufacturing package: Upload the final Fusion archive plus all five STL files. The instructor will handle slicing and printing. After printing: Inspect your five colored physical pieces and confirm they match the intended Piece A–E geometry. Demonstrate the final puzzle: Assemble all five printed pieces into one 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm cube for the instructor. Before You Submit Exactly five separate STL files are included. Each STL contains only one puzzle piece. Every piece has a support-free print orientation. The final .f3d file contains all five assembled bodies. STL filenames clearly identify the piece and intended color. Submission What You Will Submit Final Fusion archive: LastName_FirstName_2_13_PuzzleCube_Final.f3d . Five STL files: one file each for Pieces A–E, named in the format LastName_FirstName_PieceA_Color.stl . Physical verification after printing: show the instructor the five printed pieces and successfully assemble them into the completed 60 mm cube. Teacher printing: Students are responsible for correct print-ready geometry and STL exports; the instructor will handle batch slicing and printing. Printer failures or manufacturing defects outside the student's control do not reduce the grade. pages.title: Lightweight Bracket Redesign
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lightweight Bracket Redesign IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Lightweight Bracket Redesign Redesign an Teacher-provided bracket to reduce modeled mass by at l
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lightweight Bracket Redesign IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Lightweight Bracket Redesign Redesign an Teacher-provided bracket to reduce modeled mass by at least 20% while preserving interfaces and basic load capability. Advanced 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An aerospace bracket meets the required shape but is heavier than necessary. Every gram matters in flight hardware. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply design-for-lightweighting strategies Use CAD mass properties Preserve functional interfaces Document design tradeoffs Materials What You Need Starter bracket file or drawing Fusion 360 Material property assignment Engineering notebook Optional 3D printer Procedure Instructions Open the baseline bracket and record material, mass, envelope dimensions, and interface locations. Highlight no-change zones such as mounting holes and contact surfaces. Sketch two lightweighting concepts using ribs, pockets, tapered walls, or pattern changes. Select one concept and predict the mass reduction. Create the redesigned model using parameters. Assign the same material and measure final mass. Inspect minimum wall thickness, sharp internal corners, and print orientation. Create a before/after comparison and explain how load could travel through the redesigned part. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce modeled mass by at least 20% Preserve all mounting hole locations and interface dimensions Maintain minimum 2 mm wall thickness unless approved Avoid unsupported features that make printing impractical Use at least one rib or load-path feature Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the same assigned material for both mass calculations Do not simply scale the entire part Part must remain printable on classroom equipment No formal claim of structural safety without testing or analysis Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Baseline and final mass-property screenshots Fusion file Before/after visual comparison Manufacturability check Design justification Reflection Reflection Questions Where did you remove the most material? How did you preserve the load path? What new failure risk did the redesign create? What physical test would you perform next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep material along likely load paths and remove it from large low-stress areas. Common Mistake Cutting random holes may reduce mass but can create stress concentrations and weak connections. Stretch Goal Print both versions and compare mass, print time, and a simple non-destructive stiffness test. Career Connection Aerospace mechanical engineers use topology, ribs, pockets, and material selection to reduce mass while maintaining function. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →

pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.10 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Day 1 Puzzle Cube Concept Design & Sketching Focus question: How can an engineer communicate a
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.10 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.10 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Day 1 Puzzle Cube Concept Design & Sketching Focus question: How can an engineer communicate a three-dimensional puzzle design clearly enough to build it accurately in CAD? Go to Assignment What to Submit Back to Unit 2 20 Points • 1 Class Period Design a five-piece puzzle cube on paper before opening Fusion. Expected result: A complete color-coded plan showing how all 27 unit cubes are divided among five connected puzzle pieces. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Translate a 3D idea into a clear color-coded isometric sketch. Represent each puzzle piece separately while preserving its 3D geometry. Check a concept against measurable design constraints before CAD modeling. Project Workflow This is the first milestone of a four-lesson project. Your sketches become the design plan you will reproduce in Fusion during Lesson 2.11. Plan Color-Code Check Sketch Pieces Submit Puzzle Cube Challenge Project Requirements These requirements apply throughout Lessons 2.10–2.13. Finished Cube 3 × 3 × 3 Unit Cube 27 total unit cubes. Each unit cube is exactly 20 mm × 20 mm × 20 mm . The assembled puzzle must be 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm . The final puzzle contains exactly 5 pieces . Piece Geometry Five Connected Pieces Each piece contains at least 3 unit cubes . Every piece must be one continuous solid with cubes connected face-to-face. At least 1 of the 5 pieces must span at least 2 unit cubes in X, Y, and Z. Pieces may repeat the same shape. Color & Printing Plan for Manufacturing Use five different colors consistently in the sketch, Fusion model, and final printed puzzle. Each piece must have a practical flat-face orientation that can print without support material. No additional clearance is required; use the exact 20 mm unit geometry. Example Example Color-Coded Puzzle Cube This example shows how five different puzzle pieces can be represented with color in an assembled isometric view. Use it as a visual reference for communicating piece boundaries—not as a design to copy. Notice: The colors make the five pieces easy to distinguish while the completed form still reads as one 3 × 3 × 3 cube. Your design should use the same idea with your own five-piece arrangement. Assignment Design Your Five-Piece Puzzle Cube Create a paper design for a 3 × 3 × 3 puzzle cube made from five separate interlocking-style pieces. You will use this drawing as the blueprint for the Fusion model in Lesson 2.11. Step-by-Step Instructions Draw the full cube: Create a 3 × 3 × 3 isometric cube grid. The grid represents all 27 unit cubes in the finished puzzle. Divide the cube into five pieces: Decide which unit cubes belong to Piece A, B, C, D, and E. Every one of the 27 unit cubes must belong to exactly one piece. Choose five colors: Assign one distinct color to each piece. Use those same five colors throughout the entire Puzzle Cube Challenge. Color the assembled isometric: Clearly color each visible unit cube so the boundaries between the five pieces can be interpreted. Check the piece sizes: Count the unit cubes in each piece. Every piece must contain at least 3 unit cubes. Check connectivity: Confirm each piece is one continuous shape. Every unit cube in a piece must connect face-to-face to another cube in that same piece. Check the 3D-piece rule: At least one piece must extend at least 2 unit cubes in the X, Y, and Z directions. These pieces should occupy at least a 2 × 2 × 2 bounding region, even though they do not need to fill it. Sketch each piece separately: Draw a separate isometric sketch for Pieces A–E. Use the same color as the assembled drawing and make the location of every unit cube clear. Perform a final count: Add the cube counts from all five pieces. The total must equal exactly 27. Before You Submit Your assembled drawing represents a 3 × 3 × 3 cube. Exactly five colors and five pieces are shown. All five individual piece sketches match the assembled design. Every piece has at least 3 unit cubes and is face-connected. At least one piece satisfies the X/Y/Z span requirement. The piece cube counts total exactly 27. Submission What You Will Submit Color-coded assembled isometric: one complete drawing of the 3 × 3 × 3 cube showing all five pieces. Five individual piece sketches: one separate isometric sketch for Piece A, B, C, D, and E. Piece cube counts: clearly label how many unit cubes are used in each of the five pieces. File requirement: Combine your sketches into one clear PDF or scan named LastName_FirstName_2_10_PuzzleSketches.pdf . Keep the original sketches available because you will use them while modeling in Lesson 2.11. Grading 20-Point Lesson Rubric Criteria Points Color-coded isometric view clearly communicates the assembled five-piece cube 5 Five separate individual-piece sketches are complete and match the assembled design 5 Design satisfies the 27-cube, minimum-piece-size, connectivity, and 3D-span requirements 6 Sketches are neat, readable, consistently color-coded, and ready to use as a CAD plan 4 Total 20 Resources Lesson Resources Unit Hub IED Unit 2 Return to the Unit 2 lesson list and course sequence. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.8 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.8 Creating Rotational Parts with Revolve Focus question: How can engineers create rotationally symmetric 3D parts from a 2D profile? Go to Assignment Download Revolve Part Drawing Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Create a standalone rotational component from a dimensioned half-profile and center axis. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Identify when Revolve is appropriate. Create and constrain a half-profile with an axis. Use Revolve and edit source dimensions parametrically. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Reference Drawing Revolve Part Drawing Use this drawing as the dimensional reference for the rotational part you will create with the Revolve tool. Download Revolve Part Drawing Modeling focus: Create a single half-profile from the drawing, use a construction centerline as the axis of revolution, and build the finished part with the Revolve command. Use the drawing PDF as the dimensional authority for this lesson. Assignment Creating Rotational Parts with Revolve Revolve is used when a part is primarily defined by a profile rotated around an axis. You will build a rotational component from a dimensioned half-profile. Step-by-Step Instructions Interpret the drawing: Identify the center axis and determine which half of the part should be represented in the sketch. Create the half-profile: Sketch only one side of the cross-section. Use a construction centerline for the axis of rotation. Constrain and dimension the profile: Apply the required geometric relationships and dimensions until the profile is fully defined. Create the Revolve feature: Select the profile, choose the construction centerline as the axis, and revolve the profile 360 degrees. Test parametric behavior: Edit one assigned source dimension and confirm that the 3D model updates correctly. Then return the value to the specified final dimension. Verify the solid: Use Inspect/Measure to confirm the major diameters, lengths, and any stepped geometry. Before You Submit Only a half-profile was needed to create the full part. The revolve axis is a construction line. The model updates when a source dimension changes. Final values match the assigned drawing. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive: completed rotational component exported as LastName_FirstName_2_8_Revolve.f3d . Profile screenshot: fully constrained half-profile with dimensions visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_8_Profile.png . Final model screenshot: completed revolved solid in isometric view. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_8_Final.png . File requirements: Export the editable design using File → Export → Fusion 360 Archive Files (*.f3d) . Save both evidence images as PNG. pages.title: 3D Print Failure Detective
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 3D Print Failure Detective IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.5 3D Print Failure Detective Inspect failed prints, identify likely causes, and recommend a controll
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 3D Print Failure Detective IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.5 3D Print Failure Detective Inspect failed prints, identify likely causes, and recommend a controlled correction for each failure. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A print farm has produced several failed parts. Before changing settings, the team needs evidence-based diagnoses. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common print defects Use physical evidence to diagnose causes Separate printer, material, model, and setup issues Plan controlled troubleshooting tests Materials What You Need Set of failed prints or failure photographs Magnifier Ruler or calipers Failure inspection sheet Slicer access Procedure Instructions Number each failed sample and photograph it from two angles. Describe only visible evidence before naming a cause. Classify the failure as adhesion, extrusion, temperature, support, geometry, layer shift, stringing, or another category. Identify the most likely cause and one alternative cause. Locate the slicer or printer setting connected to the likely cause. Recommend one controlled change; do not change multiple variables at once. Rank the samples from easiest to hardest to correct. Choose one sample and outline a three-print troubleshooting sequence. Requirements Engineering Requirements Analyze at least four samples Include visible evidence for every diagnosis Provide one likely and one alternative cause Recommend only one primary change per test Use correct printing vocabulary Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not operate or service a printer unless authorized Do not touch hot components Do not claim certainty when evidence is incomplete Deliverables What You Submit Failure inspection sheets Annotated photographs or sketches Cause/evidence/correction table Ranked correction list Three-print troubleshooting plan Reflection Reflection Questions Which failure had the clearest evidence? Which diagnosis was most uncertain? Why should only one variable change at a time? What information from the original print job would improve your diagnosis? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Describe the defect before diagnosing it. “The first layer detached at one corner” is stronger evidence than “bad adhesion.” Common Mistake Changing temperature, speed, bed level, and material at once may fix the print but prevents you from learning the cause. Stretch Goal Slice a small test coupon that isolates the suspected problem and predict the result. Career Connection Additive manufacturing technicians and quality engineers diagnose defects using visual evidence, process data, and controlled testing. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson →

pages.title: Dimensioned CAD Sketches
pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.4 Dimensioned CAD Sketches Focus question: How do dimensions and constraints work together to create a precise CAD sketch?
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.4 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.4 Dimensioned CAD Sketches Focus question: How do dimensions and constraints work together to create a precise CAD sketch? Go to Assignment Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Create precise, fully defined CAD sketches from engineering documentation. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Apply linear, angular, radius, and diameter dimensions. Avoid redundant dimensions and over-constraint. Create a fully constrained sketch that matches a technical drawing. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Reference Image Dimensioned CAD Sketches Reference Sheet Use this sheet to study how dimensions and constraints define sketch geometry. Assignment Dimensioned CAD Sketches You will combine geometric constraints with dimensions to create a precise sketch from engineering documentation. The final sketch must be both fully constrained and dimensionally correct. Step-by-Step Instructions Read the technical drawing before sketching: Identify the overall size, feature locations, hole sizes, radii/diameters, and any angular information before opening Sketch Dimension. Create the geometry: Draw the required lines, arcs, circles, and other profiles. Focus first on the correct topology and approximate arrangement. Apply geometric relationships: Add constraints such as horizontal, vertical, tangent, concentric, symmetry, and equal before entering dimensions. Add dimensions strategically: Use linear, angular, radius, and diameter dimensions to control size and location. Dimension from stable references such as the origin or centerlines when appropriate. Resolve over-constraint warnings: If Fusion reports that a dimension is redundant or over-constraining the sketch, stop and identify which existing relationship already controls that geometry. Do not simply delete random constraints. Verify the final sketch: Compare every critical dimension against the drawing. A black sketch is not automatically correct; it must also match the required geometry and dimensions. Before You Submit All required dimensions match the drawing. No over-constraint warnings remain. The sketch is fully constrained without unnecessary Fix constraints. Dimensions are readable and not duplicated. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive: completed precision sketch exported as LastName_FirstName_2_4_PrecisionSketch.f3d . Sketch screenshot: all required dimensions visible and the sketch fully constrained. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_4_PrecisionSketch.png . Written response: identify one geometric constraint and one dimension you used and explain why both were necessary. File requirements: Export the editable Fusion file using File → Export → Fusion 360 Archive Files (*.f3d) . Save the evidence screenshot as PNG. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Plan a base feature from technical documentation. Create a fully constrained base sketch. Use Extrude and Inspect/Measure to build and verify the primary solid. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Reference Resources Bracket 3 Reference Model and Sketch Use the 3D model to understand the geometry and the three drawing PDFs as your main references while building the part. Use the downloaded Bracket 3 drawing views as the main drawing references for your CAD model. Recommended workflow: Keep the Bracket 3 drawing PDFs open while modeling. Use the 3D viewer when you need help interpreting the part geometry, and use the drawing views as your primary 2D references. Assignment Creating 3D Parts with Extrude — Bracket 3 You will begin modeling Bracket 3 using the technical drawing you created in Unit 1. This is the first part of one continuous model that will continue through Lessons 2.6 and 2.7. Step-by-Step Instructions Open the correct source information: Have your Bracket 3 technical documentation visible before modeling. Identify the best base face and the overall thickness of the part. Create the base sketch: Choose the origin plane that most directly matches the primary view of Bracket 3. Sketch the outside profile of the base geometry and fully constrain it using the dimensions from the drawing. Check the sketch before extruding: Confirm that the profile is closed and that every critical base dimension matches the technical drawing. Create the first solid feature: Use Extrude to give the base sketch the specified thickness. Make sure the operation creates a new solid body and that the direction and distance are correct. Verify the model: Use Inspect/Measure to check the overall width, height, and thickness. If a dimension is wrong, edit the original sketch or Extrude feature instead of adding corrective geometry. Keep the Timeline organized: Rename the base sketch or Extrude feature if directed by the instructor. Do not create holes, cuts, fillets, or chamfers yet. Before You Submit Base sketch matches the Unit 1 drawing. Extrude thickness is correct. Overall dimensions verify correctly. Only the base solid exists at the end of the lesson. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.11 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.11 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Days 2–3 Puzzle Cube CAD Modeling Focus question: How can a hand-sketched design be translated
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.11 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.11 • Puzzle Cube Challenge Days 2–3 Puzzle Cube CAD Modeling Focus question: How can a hand-sketched design be translated into an accurate multi-body parametric CAD model? Go to Assignment Video Help What to Submit Back to Unit 2 20 Points • 2 Class Periods Build all five puzzle pieces as separate bodies in one Fusion design. Expected result: A color-coded five-body model that assembles into an exact 60 mm cube and matches the Lesson 2.10 sketches. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Translate an isometric sketch into accurate CAD geometry. Create and manage multiple bodies inside one Fusion design. Use any appropriate modeling method while maintaining exact 20 mm unit geometry. Verify an assembled multi-body model using Fusion measurement tools. Modeling Freedom You may use any Fusion modeling method you already know. The grade is based on the accuracy and organization of the final model, not on using one required feature sequence. Build Separate Bodies Color Assemble Verify Puzzle Cube Challenge Project Requirements These requirements apply throughout Lessons 2.10–2.13. Finished Cube 3 × 3 × 3 Unit Cube 27 total unit cubes. Each unit cube is exactly 20 mm × 20 mm × 20 mm . The assembled puzzle must be 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm . The final puzzle contains exactly 5 pieces . Piece Geometry Five Connected Pieces Each piece contains at least 3 unit cubes . Every piece must be one continuous solid with cubes connected face-to-face. At least 1 of the 5 pieces must span at least 2 unit cubes in X, Y, and Z. Pieces may repeat the same shape. Color & Printing Plan for Manufacturing Use five different colors consistently in the sketch, Fusion model, and final printed puzzle. Each piece must have a practical flat-face orientation that can print without support material. No additional clearance is required; use the exact 20 mm unit geometry. Assignment Model the Puzzle Cube in Fusion Use your approved Lesson 2.10 sketches to build the five puzzle pieces. All five pieces must remain as separate bodies inside one Fusion design file. Step-by-Step Instructions Create and name the design: Start one new Fusion design and save it immediately using the required filename. Use a 20 mm unit: Every small cube in the design must measure exactly 20 mm × 20 mm × 20 mm. Build from sketches, extrusions, patterns, combined cube features, or another method you understand. Model Piece A: Reproduce the first piece from your sketch. Keep it as its own body and rename the body Piece A . Model Pieces B–E: Repeat the process until the Browser contains exactly five puzzle-piece bodies. Do not Join the five final pieces into one body. Match the sketch colors: Apply a different appearance color to each body. Use the same color assignment from Lesson 2.10. Check each piece: Confirm every piece contains at least three unit cubes and remains one continuous face-connected solid. Check the 3D-piece rule: Verify that at least one piece spans at least 40 mm in X, Y, and Z, corresponding to at least two unit cubes in every dimension. Assemble the cube: Position the five bodies so they form one complete 3 × 3 × 3 cube with no missing unit spaces and no overlapping bodies. Verify the finished size: Use Inspect/Measure to confirm the assembled cube is exactly 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm. Verify all 27 units: Compare the finished CAD model with your sketches and confirm the five pieces collectively represent exactly 27 unit cubes. Prepare for Lesson 2.12: Save the model with all five bodies assembled in the final cube position. Do not combine the bodies. Before You Submit The Browser shows exactly five named puzzle-piece bodies. Each unit cube is exactly 20 mm. The five bodies assemble into a 60 mm × 60 mm × 60 mm cube. No gaps or overlapping bodies are present. Each body matches its Lesson 2.10 sketch and color. All geometry requirements are satisfied. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive: one design containing five separate bodies, exported as LastName_FirstName_2_11_PuzzleCube.f3d . Assembled model screenshot: color-coded isometric view of the completed 60 mm cube with the Browser visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_11_Assembled.png . Important: Keep all five bodies separate. You will use this same design in Lesson 2.12 to create the technical drawing and exploded view. Grading 20-Point Lesson Rubric Criteria Points Five separate, named bodies accurately match the approved Lesson 2.10 sketches 5 20 mm unit geometry, 27 total units, and 60 mm assembled cube are accurate 5 All piece rules are satisfied: minimum 3 cubes, face-connected geometry, and 3D-span requirement 4 Five bodies are assembled correctly and use consistent color coding 3 Fusion file is organized, editable, and free of unnecessary or conflicting geometry 3 Total 20 LockwoodSTEM Tutorial Lesson Video IED 2.11 — Puzzle Cube CAD Modeling Tutorial Use this video to review the Fusion modeling workflow for building, organizing, and verifying your five-piece puzzle cube. pages.description: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.9 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.9 Mirror and Pattern Tools Focus question: How can symmetry and repetition be used to create CAD models more efficiently? G
pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.9 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.9 Mirror and Pattern Tools Focus question: How can symmetry and repetition be used to create CAD models more efficiently? Go to Assignment Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Use Mirror and Pattern features to create repeated geometry efficiently and maintain design intent. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Use Mirror to reproduce symmetric features. Use Rectangular Pattern to repeat a source feature. Edit a source feature and observe dependent geometry update. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Assignment Mirror and Pattern Tools You will build an equipment mounting plate while learning to reuse geometry efficiently. Repeated features should be controlled from a source feature rather than manually recreated. Step-by-Step Instructions Create the base plate: Sketch and extrude the plate using the assigned dimensions. Create one mounting hole: Position and create a single source mounting hole accurately. Mirror symmetric geometry: Use Mirror to reproduce the mounting hole across the appropriate centerline/plane rather than drawing a second independent hole. Create one ventilation opening: Model a single opening that will become the source for the repeated ventilation pattern. Build the rectangular pattern: Use Rectangular Pattern to control the number of instances and spacing. Make sure the pattern remains inside the usable plate area. Complete the engineering change request: Edit the source ventilation feature quantity/spacing and the mounting-hole diameter as directed. Confirm that the mirrored and patterned features update automatically. Inspect the Timeline: Verify that the repeated geometry is represented by Mirror/Pattern features instead of a long sequence of individually modeled duplicates. Before You Submit Repeated geometry comes from source features. The ECR can be completed by editing source features. Pattern quantity and spacing are intentional. No manually duplicated holes are used to imitate a pattern. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive: completed equipment mounting plate exported as LastName_FirstName_2_9_PatternPlate.f3d . Final model screenshot: isometric view with Timeline visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_9_Final.png . ECR evidence screenshot: model after editing the source feature and allowing dependent patterned/mirrored features to update. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_9_ECR.png . Written response: state which source feature you edited and which dependent features updated automatically. File requirements: Export the Fusion model using File → Export → Fusion 360 Archive Files (*.f3d) . Save both evidence images as PNG. Go to Assignment Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Create clean 2D sketch geometry on an intentional origin plane using Fusion sketch tools. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Identify the XY, XZ, and YZ origin planes. Use Line, Rectangle, Circle, Arc, and Trim. Use the sketch origin intentionally and create clean profiles. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Sketch Reference Lesson 2.2 Sketch Practice Sheet Use this image as a geometry reference while you recreate the required sketch shapes in Fusion. Open the image in a new browser tab if you need a larger view while you work in Fusion. Important for Lesson 2.2: Use this sheet to recreate the shapes only. Do not worry about fully constraining or dimensioning the sketches yet unless your instructor specifically tells you to. Constraints are the focus of Lesson 2.3, and fully dimensioned sketches are the focus of Lesson 2.4. Assignment Sketch Planes and 2D Sketching You will create your first Fusion sketches. The focus is choosing the correct sketch plane and producing clean 2D geometry. Do not add dimensions or formal constraints yet unless the instructor specifically directs you to. Step-by-Step Instructions Start on the correct origin plane: Turn on the Origin folder and identify the XY, XZ, and YZ planes. Before each sketch, decide which plane gives the clearest view of the shape you are about to create. Practice basic sketch tools: Create the assigned Line, Rectangle, Circle, and Arc examples. Use Trim to remove unwanted portions. Keep profiles closed when they are intended to become future solid features. Use the origin intentionally: Place geometry relative to the sketch origin instead of drawing randomly in empty space. The origin should help you control the location of the sketch later. Create the mounting-plate profile: Start a new sketch for the independent mounting plate. Reproduce the required overall shape using only the sketch tools introduced in this lesson. Do not dimension or formally constrain the plate yet. Inspect the sketch: Zoom in and check for doubled lines, tiny gaps, stray geometry, or accidental open profiles. Delete construction mistakes rather than leaving extra geometry in the file. Before You Submit The intended profile is closed. No unnecessary duplicate lines are present. The mounting plate is on an intentional origin plane. No dimensions or formal constraints have been added unless directed. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive: design containing all required sketches. Export as LastName_FirstName_2_2_Sketching.f3d . Mounting-plate screenshot: completed mounting-plate sketch with the Fusion Browser visible. Save as LastName_FirstName_2_2_MountingPlate.png . File requirements: In Fusion, open the design and choose File → Export . Select Fusion 360 Archive Files (*.f3d) , save it with the required filename, and submit that exported file. Save the screenshot separately as PNG. pages.searchText: Home Courses IED Unit 2 Lesson 2.3 IED Unit 2 • Lesson 2.3 Sketch Constraints Focus question: How can constraints make a CAD sketch behave the way an engineer intends? Go to Assignment Video Help Back to Unit 2 Lesson Goal Control geometric relationships so sketches behave predictably when edited. Expected result: Complete the required work and verify the CAD or manufacturing evidence before submitting. Lesson Overview What You Are Learning Learning Targets Apply common geometric constraints. Diagnose under-constrained geometry by dragging. Use constraints to preserve design intent without relying on Fix/UnFix. How to Approach the Work Use the instructor demonstration to understand the tool or design decision, then complete the assigned work independently and verify the result before submission. Learn Model Verify Revise Submit Reference Image Sketch Constraints Practice Sheet Use this reference while repairing and discussing common sketch-constraint relationships. This image is a visual guide. If your instructor provides a Fusion practice file, complete the repairs in that editable file. Assignment Sketch Constraints Constraints control how sketch geometry is allowed to move. Your job is to repair sketches using geometric relationships rather than locking geometry in place with Fix/UnFix. Step-by-Step Instructions Test each broken sketch first: Before adding any constraint, click and drag geometry to see how the sketch currently moves. Use the motion to identify what relationship is missing. Apply geometric constraints: Use Horizontal/Vertical, Coincident, Parallel, Perpendicular, Tangent, Equal, Concentric, Midpoint, and Symmetry as appropriate. Use the smallest number of constraints needed to communicate the design intent. Re-test the sketch: Drag the geometry again after each repair. A correct constraint should stop the unwanted motion while still allowing any intended freedom. Avoid unnecessary Fix/UnFix: Do not use Fix/UnFix as a shortcut to make geometry turn black. A sketch is only well constrained when its relationships and dimensions control it for a reason. Revise the Lesson 2.2 mounting plate: Open your mounting-plate sketch and add the appropriate geometric relationships. Leave dimensions for Lesson 2.4, so some controlled dimensional freedom should remain. Identify remaining degrees of freedom: Determine what can still move or change in the mounting plate and be ready to explain what dimension would eventually control it. Before You Submit Constraints match the intended geometry. The sketch does not rely on Fix/UnFix as the primary control method. The mounting plate still has intentional dimensional freedom. Submission What You Will Submit Fusion archive: one design containing the five repaired sketches and revised mounting plate. Export as LastName_FirstName_2_3_Constraints.f3d . Written response: identify one remaining degree of freedom in the mounting plate and explain what information would be needed to remove it. File requirements: Export the editable design using File → Export → Fusion 360 Archive Files (*.f3d) . Submit the exported .f3d file rather than a link to your Fusion project.
